_note: The simplest layer of each finding: a short answer and its main catch, in everyday words (target: a reader of about 8 to 11). Written by the AI co-editor from the claim's own plain and precise text on 2026-10-17, for the senior author's review (the 'In short' decision: the senior author asked for answers simple enough for an 8-year-old, without losing rigour). Never says more than the claim; the catch carries its most important limit. 'freq': numbers shown as pictures of 100 (icon arrays), taken from the claim's anchors. 'quiz': 'Test yourself' questions built only from these lines. 'v': the version of the claim each entry was written from; when the claim has moved on, the site shows the claim's own plain text instead until the entry is rewritten. 'how': two to four short points shown under 'How we know', written from the claim's plain text and never saying more. 'tf': the home page's True or false? statements, each built only from its claim's simple line, with the version it was written from ('v'); a statement whose claim has moved on is left out until it is rewritten. 'how_src' (31 October): for each 'how' point, the reference ids of the sources it rests on (from that answer's own evidence; an empty list for a point about the evidence as a whole), shown as labels that open each source's findings. True-or-false statements and quick questions (tf, quiz): written 31 October 2026 by two AI quiz writers from the checked short, But and How-we-know lines only (scratchpad brief quiz/BRIEF.md), each carrying the version of the claim it was written from; reviewed by the editor, who removed items on routes, on what a second dose does to the effects, and study-design details too minor to teach anything.

cl_meth_pk_halflife.short: After the blood level peaks, it takes about 10 to 12 hours to fall by half.
cl_meth_pk_halflife.but: It differs from person to person, and it is not the same as how long the effects last.
how: It takes about 10 to 12 hours for the blood level to fall by half.
This is about the same whether meth is snorted, smoked, injected or swallowed.
People differ: from about 8 to 18 hours in one study.
How long it stays in the blood is not how long the effects last.
cl_meth_pk_halflife.rate: Four lab studies in three separate labs measured the drug in blood directly, and they agree within about two hours. But they were small, and in most, people knew what they were given.

cl_meth_pk_intranasal_timecourse.short: Snorted, its effects on the heart and on mood peak within about 15 minutes.
cl_meth_pk_intranasal_timecourse.but: The amount in the blood keeps rising for hours. The timing of the effects comes from one lab.
how: People who use meth regularly were given single snorted doses in a lab.
Heart rate and blood pressure peaked within about 15 minutes. So did the high, in the one study that timed it.
The amount in the blood was still rising 3 to 4 hours later.
Both studies came from one lab.
cl_meth_pk_intranasal_timecourse.rate: Two studies from one lab, with 11 and 13 people who use meth regularly, each also given a dummy. Few took part, some results come from graphs, and lab conditions differ from everyday use.

cl_meth_mechanism_release.short: It makes nerve cells let out three brain chemicals: dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
cl_meth_mechanism_release.but: How it does this is not fully known. So far we have only read a review about it.
how: Meth makes nerve endings let out dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
It seems to push them out of their storage sacs and run their pumps in reverse.
The details are not fully known. This comes from a review; we have not read the lab studies yet.
cl_meth_mechanism_release.rate: Lab and animal studies, known only through one review; the original studies haven't been read yet, so how good they are is unknown.

cl_meth_pk_bioavailability_route.short: Most of a snorted dose reaches the blood. For smoking, the figures vary a lot.
cl_meth_pk_bioavailability_route.but: The snorting figure comes from one study of 8 men. For smoking, studies measure it in different ways.
how: About four fifths of a snorted dose reaches the blood (one study of 8 men).
For smoking, figures run from about a third to nine tenths; there is no single number.
The blood level peaks a couple of hours after snorting or smoking.
The felt effects peak within about a quarter of an hour.
cl_meth_pk_bioavailability_route.rate: Two small lab studies, of 8 and 6 men, who knew what they were given and had no dummy comparison. Some figures rest on measurements that varied a lot between people.

cl_meth_pk_stereoisomers.short: Yes: in one study, the 'l' form felt weaker and its effects ended sooner.
cl_meth_pk_stereoisomers.but: One small lab study of injected doses in 12 men.
how: Meth comes in two mirror-image forms; which one depends on how it was made.
In 12 men, the 'l' form stayed in the blood longer but felt weaker and shorter.
It also raised blood pressure less.
One small study of injected doses, in men only.
cl_meth_pk_stereoisomers.rate: One careful trial, but only 12 men took part, and their ratings varied widely. Nobody checked whether they could tell which form they got.

cl_meth_acute_lab.short: One snorted dose raises heart rate and blood pressure and makes people feel high.
cl_meth_acute_lab.but: These were single lab doses in people used to meth, not binges. One lab only.
how: In lab studies, one snorted dose raised heart rate and blood pressure.
People felt good, high and stimulated, more with bigger doses.
They also felt more jittery and sweaty, mostly at the largest dose.
These were single doses in people used to meth, all from one lab.
cl_meth_acute_lab.rate: Careful lab studies, both from one lab, where the same people got meth and a dummy, with large, machine-measured effects. But people may have recognised the drug, and some results went unreported.

cl_meth_acute_cognition.short: In lab tests, single doses did not measurably worsen attention or memory.
cl_meth_acute_cognition.but: The studies were small, so small or moderate harm can't be ruled out. Binges were not tested.
how: Lab studies gave people mostly single doses.
Attention, memory and reaction time did not get measurably worse. On some tasks people did better.
The studies were small. The two main ones, and the review of the others, came from one research group.
Binges and long-term use were not tested.
cl_meth_acute_cognition.rate: Two small lab studies, of 11 and 13 people, from one lab that did not report all its results. The 'no worse' finding is the shakiest, since so few people took part.

cl_meth_acute_tolerance.short: The good feelings fade within one dose and within three days; hunger stays gone.
cl_meth_acute_tolerance.but: All of this used small oral doses in six to nine people in a laboratory.
how: Within one dose, the effects peak in about a quarter of an hour, then fade.
Over three days of twice-daily doses, the good feelings were gone by day three.
Eating stayed down over the three days, while dizziness, sickness and a pounding heart grew.
The body did not clear the drug faster; that was measured and had not changed.
cl_meth_acute_tolerance.rate: Four small lab studies, 6 to 9 people each, the key ones from one lab. One had no dummy comparison at all, and none printed how much the effects faded.

cl_meth_food_intake.short: One dose cut how much people ate that day by about two fifths.
cl_meth_food_intake.but: One small study of eight people living in a lab.
how: Eight people lived in a lab, where everything they ate was recorded.
One dose of meth cut what they ate that day by about two fifths.
They also said they felt less hungry.
One small study; the calorie figures are only shown in a graph.
cl_meth_food_intake.rate: One lab study of just 8 people. Food was measured, not guessed, but the reporting was patchy, and that eating fell is much surer than by how much.

cl_meth_acute_toxicity.short: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive. The heart races, breathing speeds up, and people get very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality.
cl_meth_acute_toxicity.but: That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
One review found psychosis (losing touch with reality) in 12 to 80 in 100 people seen in hospital. Suicidal thoughts or acts showed up in 6 to 50, depending on the study.
Neither review says how many patients die.
cl_meth_acute_toxicity.rate: Two reviews of hospital records and case reports; the original studies could not be checked through them. Some of those studies were about amphetamine or other stimulants, not meth.

cl_meth_dependence_baserate.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
cl_meth_dependence_baserate.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.

freq.what: of people who had used stimulants other than cocaine had been dependent at some point
freq.note: US survey, 1990 to 1992: stimulants other than cocaine, not meth alone. Tobacco was measured differently.
freq.compare_k: For comparison, in the same survey:

how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.
cl_meth_dependence_baserate.rate: Two household surveys, in the US in 1990 to 1992 and Australia in 2007. The US one lumped meth with other stimulants, prescription pills included, and the Australian one never said which stimulants.

cl_meth_choice_alternatives.short: In lab choice tests, people often chose small amounts of cash over a stimulant dose.
cl_meth_choice_alternatives.but: Only 13 men, in one lab. Different men got different cash amounts, so it can't show what more cash does.
how: In a lab study, 13 men who used meth chose between small portions of a dose and small amounts of cash.
When the cash was a tenth of $5, they chose the drug about 4 times in 10.
When it was a tenth of $20, fewer than 2 times in 10.
The groups were tiny and got different amounts, so this does not prove money made the difference.
cl_meth_choice_alternatives.rate: Two small lab studies. The cash comparison set 7 men against 6 different men, not shown to be alike, and no test of the difference was reported.

cl_meth_withdrawal.short: After stopping, most symptoms people reported eased within one to two weeks. Low mood and craving lasted longer.
cl_meth_withdrawal.but: It was one small study on a hospital ward. The people in it were not seeking treatment.
how: People dependent on meth stopped using on a hospital research ward.
Most symptoms they reported eased within one to two weeks.
Low mood lasted about three weeks; craving lasted to week five, at a lower level.
They were not looking for treatment. None had another mental-health diagnosis at the time.
cl_meth_withdrawal.rate: One ward study with no comparison group, so being in hospital, or people arriving at their worst, could explain some changes. Only 25 to 32 of 56 people were counted.

cl_meth_dopamine_damage.short: Nobody has shown either way whether meth, as people use it, damages dopamine nerve cells.
cl_meth_dopamine_damage.but: Scans show changes, but those can happen without nerve cells dying. Experts disagree.
how: People who used meth heavily have less of one dopamine protein, but it can drop without nerve cells dying.
Other markers of dopamine nerve endings are not always lower.
In two small studies the protein rose again after people stopped. Other studies found no link with time off meth.
On the other side, two health-record studies found Parkinson's more often in people with meth or amphetamine diagnoses (in one, about 3 vs 1 in 1,000 over 7 years). Some may be other conditions.
cl_meth_dopamine_damage.rate: Small brain-scan studies, animal tests, and brains of people who died soon after using, which mixes short-term and lasting changes. Animal tests don't match human use. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_meth_dat_lower.short: People who used meth heavily have less of one dopamine protein on scans than people who don't, on average.
cl_meth_dat_lower.but: Scans cannot tell if this is damage, the brain making less of the protein, or a difference from before use.
how: After heavy use, scans show about 13 to 28% less of one dopamine protein (the transporter).
Many research groups found this, but how big it is is very uncertain.
Some people's values are in the normal range.
Scans can't tell if this means damage, the brain making less of the protein, or a difference that was there before.
cl_meth_dat_lower.rate: Scans and brain tissue after death, from independent teams, all point the same way. But they compare different groups, unmatched on smoking and other drugs, so the size of the gap is unclear.

cl_meth_dat_recovery.short: In five people, that protein rose after a year without meth.
cl_meth_dat_recovery.but: Only five people, with nobody who doesn't use scanned twice. Four other small studies found no link with time off meth.
how: Five people were scanned twice. After a year without meth, the protein rose by about a sixth to a fifth.
Nobody who doesn't use meth was scanned twice to compare.
Four small studies found no link between time off meth and the protein level.
Five people is too few to know how typical this is.
cl_meth_dat_recovery.rate: Scans of just five people in a court-supervised programme, who already had more of the protein at the start. Four studies comparing different people found no link with time off meth.

cl_meth_vmat2.short: A few days after use, another dopamine marker looks higher. After about 10 days off meth, it is not clearly different.
cl_meth_vmat2.but: Researchers think this shows low stored dopamine, which the study could not test. One lab only, and the studies are small.
how: Another dopamine marker (VMAT2) gave a higher scan signal a few days after use.
In people who stayed off meth for about 10 days, it no longer differed clearly.
Researchers think this shows low stored dopamine; the study could not test it.
In the one scan study of people who had stopped for more than 3 years on average, it was about 10% lower.
cl_meth_vmat2.rate: Brain scans from one lab: only 17 people who stayed off meth and 9 who don't use it were scanned again. Leftover drug may have affected the early scan.

cl_meth_grey_matter.short: Some brain areas looked smaller soon after stopping. Other studies found some larger.
cl_meth_grey_matter.but: Smoking, schooling and low mood also differ, and some differences may not last.
how: Soon after stopping, some brain areas had less grey matter (up to about 11% in one study).
Other studies, after 3 to 4 months off meth or during use, found some areas larger.
Smoking, less schooling and low mood also differed between the groups.
In one study, grey matter grew in several areas over the first month without meth, but only by a lenient test.
cl_meth_grey_matter.rate: Brain-scan studies comparing people dependent on meth with people who don't use it. The groups differ in smoking and schooling too, and the studies point to different brain areas.

cl_meth_glucose_metabolism.short: The results are mixed: the differences found were small, uncertain or not repeated.
cl_meth_glucose_metabolism.but: The groups also differed in smoking and in other ways. That could explain the results.
how: One study found a bit more brain energy use overall in people who had stopped meth. By the study's own test, it was not a clear difference.
Some deep brain areas looked clearly lower only compared with that overall level.
Another research group did not find the overall difference.
Smoking and the share of women also differed, so scans can't show what meth did.
cl_meth_glucose_metabolism.rate: One brain-scan study of 15 people against 21 who did not use. The groups differed in smoking and sex, and another team did not find the same overall result.

cl_meth_metabolism_recovery.short: In five people, one deep brain area got more active after a year off meth, compared with the rest of the brain.
cl_meth_metabolism_recovery.but: Only five people, with no group to compare. The paper's numbers also have errors.
how: Five people were scanned again after a year without meth.
One deep brain area (the thalamus) became more active, compared with the rest of the brain.
No comparison group was scanned twice, and the paper's statistics have errors.
cl_meth_metabolism_recovery.rate: Brain scans of just five people picked from those who finished treatment, probably the same five as in another study, with no comparison group scanned again.

cl_meth_siblings.short: Brothers and sisters who never had drug or alcohol problems shared some brain differences with their sibling dependent on stimulants.
cl_meth_siblings.but: One study, and 94 in 100 of the dependent people were dependent on cocaine.
how: The study scanned 50 pairs of brothers and sisters and 50 unrelated volunteers. In each pair, one was dependent on stimulants. The other had never been dependent, apart from tobacco.
Both siblings shared some of the same differences, so some may run in families and come before drug use. But nobody was scanned before they started.
More of the brothers and sisters smoked than the volunteers, and smoking was checked for only part of the scans.
94 in 100 of the dependent people were dependent on cocaine, the rest on amphetamines. The study does not mention meth.
cl_meth_siblings.rate: One UK brain-scan study of 50 sibling pairs, but for 94 in 100 pairs the drug was cocaine, and no one is said to have used meth. Smoking and sex also differed between groups.

cl_meth_parkinson.short: Parkinson's was diagnosed more often in people with a meth or amphetamine diagnosis and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis.
cl_meth_parkinson.but: It stays rare: about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years. Some diagnoses are probably other conditions, and medicine side effects were not ruled out.
how: In Utah health records, Parkinson's was diagnosed about 3 times as often in people with meth or amphetamine diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnoses.
That is about 3 in 1,000 against 1 in 1,000, over about 7 years.
A California study found a smaller increase.
The records probably include other movement conditions.

freq.title: Out of every 1,000 people, how many got a Parkinson's diagnosis in about 7 years?
pairs: people with a meth or amphetamine diagnosis and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis
people of the same age and sex with no drug, alcohol or HIV diagnosis
freq.note: Utah health records (15 of 4,935 against 27 of 24,675). The records probably include other movement conditions too.

cl_meth_parkinson.rate: Health records from Utah and California, where Parkinson's codes may be wrong and people who see doctors more may simply get more diagnoses. Cases were few: 15 and 51.

cl_meth_cognition.short: On average, people dependent on meth score somewhat lower on memory and thinking tests than healthy volunteers.
cl_meth_cognition.but: This does not show that meth caused it. Group averages are mostly still in the normal range.
how: On average, people dependent on meth score somewhat lower on thinking and memory tests.
Learning and remembering words was lower in every review.
Results vary a lot, and small studies with big gaps may be over-represented.
This does not show that meth caused it. Group averages are still mostly in the normal range.
cl_meth_cognition.rate: Many one-time comparisons of people dependent on meth with healthy volunteers, who often had more schooling. And studies that found nothing may never have been published.

cl_meth_cognition_normal_range.short: On average, their scores were in the normal range, not the impaired range.
cl_meth_cognition_normal_range.but: Some people did score low. And nobody was tested before they started using.
how: Compared with the usual scores on these tests, group averages were low-normal to normal.
In two studies, about a quarter to a third of people who used meth scored as impaired. In people who don't, it was about 1 in 9 to 1 in 6.
In one of those studies, more than half of the people who used meth had HIV. That could explain part of the gap.
Nobody was tested before they started. In one study, school grades from before were already lower, and adult scores were lower than those grades predicted.
cl_meth_cognition_normal_range.rate: Small studies: one compared just 27 people with 18. Scores were often compared with public averages without matching for background, and in one study HIV appeared only in people who used meth.

cl_meth_cognition_causal.short: It has not been shown that meth causes lasting problems with thinking and memory in people.
cl_meth_cognition_causal.but: Nobody was tested before use, and the groups differ in other ways. Experts disagree.
how: People dependent on meth score somewhat lower on average.
But nobody was tested before they started using.
The groups differ in other ways, and scores mostly don't track how much people used.
After stopping, scores have not been shown to rise more than in people who don't use.
cl_meth_cognition_causal.rate: Mostly snapshots of people who already used meth, never tested before they started. Animal studies and one twin study of stimulants in general can't settle it for people. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_meth_cognition_abstinence.short: We don't know yet. In retests, people who stopped did not clearly improve more than people who don't use.
cl_meth_cognition_abstinence.but: Only two small studies also retested people who don't use, so a moderate gain can't be ruled out. Very few looked beyond a year.
how: Two studies retested people who had stopped and people who don't use.
Those who stopped did not improve clearly more. People who don't use also improved from taking the tests again.
Across many studies, people tested after longer abstinence did not score closer to people who don't use.
Very few studies looked beyond a year.
cl_meth_cognition_abstinence.rate: Small studies that retested people after they stopped meth. People who manage to stay off may differ in other ways, staying off was only what they said, and dropouts went unreported.

cl_meth_psychosis_association.short: Psychotic symptoms are more common in people who use meth, most of all in those who use it often.
cl_meth_psychosis_association.but: No study has settled which comes first.
how: In studies mostly in treatment, hospitals or prisons, a meth or amphetamine use disorder went with about 2.5 times the odds of psychosis.
In New Zealand, about 1,000 people followed from birth: use went with slightly more psychotic experiences.
In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs got a psychosis diagnosis within 10 years. Among people with no drug record, it was under 1 in 100.
None of these studies shows which came first.
cl_meth_psychosis_association.rate: Mostly one-time studies of people in treatment, hospitals or the justice system. Things they didn't measure, like family history of psychosis or childhood trauma, could explain part of the link.

cl_meth_psychosis_dose.short: In people dependent on meth, psychotic symptoms were much more common in months of heavy use.
cl_meth_psychosis_dose.but: One study. It cannot prove that the drug caused the symptoms.

freq.title: Out of every 100 months, how many had psychotic symptoms?
pairs: months with no meth
months with meth on 16 or more days
freq.note: The study's estimate, in about 280 people dependent on meth, for months without heavy cannabis or alcohol use.

how: About 280 people dependent on meth were each compared with themselves over three years.
Psychotic symptoms were predicted in about 7 in 100 months without meth.
And in about half of the months with meth on 16 or more days.
Use and symptoms were measured over the same month, so this cannot show which came first.
cl_meth_psychosis_dose.rate: One Australian study compared each person's months with and without meth use. The more people used, the stronger the link, but only 278 of 501 were analysed, and people reported their own use.

cl_meth_psychosis_course.short: In a typical study of people with meth psychosis, about 1 in 4 still had symptoms over a month after stopping.
cl_meth_psychosis_course.but: Studies ranged from none to almost all, and most were of hospital patients.

freq.title: In the typical study, out of every 100 people with meth psychosis:
freq.what: still had symptoms over a month after stopping
freq.note: From a review of 27 studies. Single studies ranged from none to almost all.

how: A review of 27 studies, mostly of hospital patients, looked at how long symptoms lasted.
In the typical study, 1 in 4 still had symptoms over a month after stopping.
How many were later told they had schizophrenia varied a lot between studies, from about 1 in 20 to 2 in 5. One review's average was about 1 in 5. This does not show that meth caused it.
Psychosis often comes back when people use again.
cl_meth_psychosis_course.rate: Two weak reviews of mostly hospital studies, passing on figures they didn't check. Nobody verified that people stayed off meth, and medicines and other drugs weren't accounted for.

cl_meth_psychosis_vs_schizophrenia.short: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look alike.
cl_meth_psychosis_vs_schizophrenia.but: Flatness and withdrawal were milder in meth psychosis. No symptom has been shown to reliably tell them apart.
how: In 12 small studies, hallucinations and delusions were not clearly different.
That pooled result is less certain than the review reported.
'Negative' symptoms, like flatness and withdrawal, were somewhat milder in meth psychosis.
No symptom has been shown to reliably tell the two apart.
cl_meth_psychosis_vs_schizophrenia.rate: One-off comparisons of patients, lumping together brief and lasting psychosis, from a review whose numbers do not all match its own table. Studies disagree on symptoms like hallucinations, though most agree on flatness and withdrawal.

cl_meth_depression.short: People who use meth report low mood somewhat more often than people who don't.
cl_meth_depression.but: Other differences, such as using other drugs or a hard life, may explain part of it: against people who use other drugs, there was no clear difference.
how: Across 6 studies, after allowing for some other differences, the odds of low mood were about 1.3 times higher.
Most studies measured symptoms, not diagnosed depression.
Two studies that followed people over time, allowing for how they felt before, found about 1.5 to 1.6 times the odds.
Among people who use other drugs, those who used meth did not report clearly more low mood.
cl_meth_depression.rate: Mostly one-off surveys, plus two studies that followed people over time. The main figures allow for some other differences, but not all: people who use meth may differ in other ways too.

cl_meth_suicidality.short: People with a meth use disorder report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often.
cl_meth_suicidality.but: Most studies were of people in emergency rooms, the justice system or treatment. Drug use in general and earlier problems may explain much of it.
how: People with a meth use disorder reported suicidal thoughts or attempts with about 1.5 times the odds.
These studies measured both at once, so they cannot show which came first.
The authors think much of it may be shared with drug use in general and people's earlier problems.
In people with regular or problematic use, suicide deaths were about 12 times as common as in others of the same age and sex. This figure is less certain.
cl_meth_suicidality.rate: One weak review pooling 4 studies of 21,753 people, each measured only once. They agree, but depression and other mental illness, strongly tied to suicidal thoughts, could explain the link.

cl_meth_violence.short: Two long-term studies linked meth use to more violence. This held after other things were counted.
cl_meth_violence.but: Both studies share authors, and neither could show which came first.
how: A review of mostly weak studies found the link shrank and became unclear once other things were counted.
In New Zealand, about 1,000 people followed from birth reported somewhat more violence in times they used meth or speed. This held after other things were counted.
In Australia, 469 people dependent on meth reported violent crime in 12 of 100 months with meth use and 3 of 100 without.
That study compared each person with themselves. But people reported use and crime for the same months.
cl_meth_violence.rate: A review of mostly one-time studies plus two long-term studies. Everyone reported their own use and violence, one study did not take other drugs into account, and some results barely differ from no link.

cl_meth_naltrexone_bupropion.short: In one big trial, for every 9 people given two medicines, about 1 more had mostly meth-free urine tests.
cl_meth_naltrexone_bupropion.but: Most people were not helped. What happened after treatment ended was not reported.
how: In one large US trial, about 1 in 7 people on two medicines had mostly meth-free urine tests at the end.
On dummy medicines, about 1 in 40.
That is about 1 extra person for every 9 treated.
Most people did not reach this, and what happened after treatment was not reported.
cl_meth_naltrexone_bupropion.rate: One big trial against dummy medicines, judged by urine tests rather than people's own reports. But it is only one trial, and just 31 people on the medicines responded.

cl_meth_mirtazapine.short: In three trials, people on a depression medicine, mirtazapine, used somewhat less meth than on a dummy pill.
cl_meth_mirtazapine.but: Most people kept using, and in the largest trial drug tests showed no difference.
how: Two small San Francisco trials, in men who have sex with men who also had counselling, found fewer meth-positive urine tests on mirtazapine.
A larger Australian trial: people said they cut down by about 2 more days in 4 weeks.
Its saliva drug tests showed no difference, and most people kept using.
Drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine.
cl_meth_mirtazapine.rate: Three trials with 519 people. Many urine tests were missing, drowsiness may have shown who got the medicine, and the largest trial's drug tests disagreed with the two smaller ones.

cl_meth_bupropion_modafinil.short: Bupropion and modafinil did not help more people stop than a dummy pill.
cl_meth_bupropion_modafinil.but: The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out.
how: Putting five trials together: about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, on medicine or on a dummy pill.
The trials were small and uneven, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.
A later review of bupropion found about a tenth fewer positive urine tests. This result is uncertain.
cl_meth_bupropion_modafinil.rate: Five small trials from two research groups, poorly reported, with many people missing at the end. Only 132 people stopped using in all, too few to rule out a useful benefit or a harm.

cl_meth_withdrawal_medication.short: No medicine on sale has clearly been shown to ease meth withdrawal.
cl_meth_withdrawal_medication.but: The trials were few and small, so a benefit cannot be ruled out either.
how: Nine small trials tested six medicines for withdrawal.
None clearly helped more than a dummy pill, except one drug that is no longer sold.
The trials were few, small and flawed, so a benefit can't be ruled out either.
cl_meth_withdrawal_medication.rate: Nine trials against dummy pills, six with serious flaws. Each medicine had only one or two trials of 19 to 74 people, too few to tell help from harm.

cl_meth_psychosis_treatment.short: Few trials have tested medicines for meth psychosis: eight small, short ones and one longer one.
cl_meth_psychosis_treatment.but: None of the short trials had a dummy-pill group, so they can't show if medicines help more than stopping meth. Some have serious flaws.
how: Three reviews found eight small, short trials, with about 500 people in all.
Six compared one medicine with another. None was a clear winner.
Two small trials against a dummy pill, in people already getting better, and one two-year trial favoured the medicine on some measures. These trials have serious flaws.
Nobody has studied what happens when people stop the medicine.
cl_meth_psychosis_treatment.rate: Small trials of 37 to 120 people; in some everyone knew who got what, and none clearly separated one medicine from another. The one long trial changed its main measure after collecting the data.

cl_meth_mortality.short: Among people with regular or problematic use, about 1 in 90 died each year.
cl_meth_mortality.but: These were people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Not all of it is the drug.
how: In studies of people with regular or problematic use, about 1 in 90 died each year.
That is nearly 7 times the rate of people of the same age and sex.
Overdose deaths were about 25 times as common; suicide and homicide about 12 times. These figures are less certain.
Many also used opioids or injected, so this does not show how much is due to the drug itself.
cl_meth_mortality.rate: A review of groups followed over time: people in treatment, hospital or justice records, or who inject. Every region shows several times more deaths, but only age and sex were taken into account.

cl_meth_us_trends.short: In the US, meth use rose from 2015 to 2019, and deaths involving meth kept rising through 2023, the latest year counted.
cl_meth_us_trends.but: Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids. The rise slowed after 2021.
how: In US surveys, past-year meth use rose by about a fifth from 2015 to 2019.
Deaths involving meth rose from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023. The rise slowed after 2021.
Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024: about 7 in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids. This is a different kind of record from the death counts.
The surveys miss people who are homeless or living in places like prisons and hospitals.
cl_meth_us_trends.rate: Yearly US surveys and death records. The surveys miss people on the streets or in institutions, and death records undercount, but these limits blur exact numbers more than the rise itself.

cl_mdma_csf_5hiaa.short: In one study, a serotonin by-product in spinal fluid was lower in people who used MDMA.
cl_mdma_csf_5hiaa.but: It was clear only in the women, and that group had used many other drugs too.
how: Thirty people who had used MDMA at least 25 times were compared with 28 who had not.
Their spinal fluid held about a third less of a serotonin by-product.
The gap was clear in the women and not in the men, and it did not grow with more use.
A lower level of a by-product cannot show that nerve cells were harmed.
cl_mdma_csf_5hiaa.rate: One study of 58 volunteers who signed up themselves. The spinal-fluid by-product is only a rough clue to what happens in nerve cells, and nobody was measured before using MDMA.

cl_mdma_memory.short: On average, people who use ecstasy score lower on some memory and thinking tests.
cl_mdma_memory.but: The studies disagree a lot, and none can show that ecstasy caused it.
how: Two reviews looked at small studies that compared people who use ecstasy with people who do not.
Scores were lower on average, but results differed so much between studies that the size is uncertain.
Almost everyone in these studies also used other drugs, most often cannabis.
Everyone was tested after they had started, so the difference may have been there first.
cl_mdma_memory.rate: Mostly one-time comparisons of people who use ecstasy with people who don't, seen only through reviews. The groups differ in other drug use too, and each figure rests on four or five small studies.

cl_mdma_minimal_polydrug.short: In people who used ecstasy but hardly any other drug, memory scores were no different.
cl_mdma_minimal_polydrug.but: It was one study, and medium-sized differences could not be ruled out.
how: 52 people who used ecstasy were compared with 59 people from the same all-night dance scene.
Breath, urine and hair tests checked that they had used little else.
Memory scores did not differ, and most of the 40 measures were similar.
People who had used it more than 50 times did worse on one planning test.
cl_mdma_minimal_polydrug.rate: One study comparing 52 people who used ecstasy with 59 who didn't, tested once. The groups differed in background and cannabis use, and so few people could miss medium-sized differences.

cl_mdma_prospective.short: In one Dutch study, people who started using ecstasy improved less on a word-memory test.
cl_mdma_prospective.but: They also used more cannabis and cocaine, and were tested again sooner.
how: Young people were tested before they had ever used ecstasy, then again 1 to 2 years later.
Those who started had used very little by the second test.
They improved less at learning a word list; nine other scores did not differ.
Everyone's scores stayed in the normal range.
cl_mdma_prospective.rate: One Dutch study tested 118 people before and after some started using ecstasy. Those who started also differed in cannabis and cocaine use, and the true gap could be close to zero.

cl_mdma_abstinence.short: Nobody knows yet whether scores recover after people stop using ecstasy.
cl_mdma_abstinence.but: The studies compared different people, not the same people over time.
how: A review pooled a few small studies of people who had stopped for at least 6 months.
They scored about the same as people still using, and both scored lower than people who had never used.
Breaks longer than 6 months were not tested, although the review's summary says otherwise.
Most of the studies were rated poor quality.
cl_mdma_abstinence.rate: Mostly one-off comparisons of different people, with 9 of 14 studies judged poor, known only through one review. The results disagree, and the main comparison rests on five small studies.

cl_mdma_sert_binding.short: Scans show less of a serotonin marker in people who use ecstasy.
cl_mdma_sert_binding.but: Nobody in these studies was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.
how: The marker sits on the endings of serotonin nerve cells in the brain.
Four teams used the same scan and all found less of it in the outer brain.
Deeper parts of the brain mostly looked the same as in other people.
Less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone.
cl_mdma_sert_binding.rate: Brain scans from four independent labs agree, with drug use checked in hair in the largest. But they compare small groups at one time, so how big the difference is remains unclear.

cl_mdma_retraction_2002.short: A 2002 study said ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains. It was withdrawn a year later.
cl_mdma_retraction_2002.but: Fewer newspapers told readers about the mistake than told the first story.
how: The animals had been given a different drug, from a wrongly labelled bottle.
Two of the ten animals given the drug died during the study.
Of 50 big US newspapers, 26 wrote about the study and 20 about the withdrawal.
The notice does not say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.
cl_mdma_retraction_2002.rate: The retraction itself is on record. The one bar is for the count of 50 newspapers, made by authors with a stake in the topic, whose archive searches were not checked.

cl_mdma_dopamine_human.short: It has not been shown that ecstasy harms dopamine nerve cells in people.
cl_mdma_dopamine_human.but: Very little has been measured in people, so this does not show it is safe.
how: The study that claimed this harm was withdrawn: the animals got a different drug.
A review found five human scan studies, and none showed a clear dopamine change.
In one, the dopamine marker was lower only in people who had also used amphetamine recently.
A by-product in spinal fluid cannot show whether nerve cells were harmed.
cl_mdma_dopamine_human.rate: Only letters and one article by people on opposite sides of the dispute. The human studies they argue about were not read here. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_mdma_neurotoxicity_contested.short: Experts disagree about whether ecstasy leaves lasting harm to the serotonin system.
cl_mdma_neurotoxicity_contested.but: Almost nobody was scanned before they started, so a difference may have come first.
how: Four teams scanned people who use ecstasy and found less of a serotonin marker.
The one study that scanned people before their first use found no change.
Less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone.
Nobody has been scanned while using and again years after stopping.
cl_mdma_neurotoxicity_contested.rate: Mostly one-time scans and tests comparing people who use ecstasy with people who don't, and they differ in other drug use too. The scan signal can drop without damage. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_meth_crime.short: People dependent on meth reported more crime in months when they used it.
cl_meth_crime.but: One study, and it could not show which came first.
how: In Australia, 469 people dependent on meth were followed for up to three years. Each person's months with meth were compared with their own months without.
Some crime was reported in 56 of 100 months with meth use and about 18 of 100 without.
The link was strongest for selling drugs and property crime. It stayed after other drug use and money and housing problems were counted.
People reported use and crime for the same months, and treatment or time in prison was not counted.
cl_meth_crime.rate: One Australian study comparing the same people's months with and without meth. People reported use and crime for the same month, so crime could have led to use, and a third dropped out.

cl_mdma_ptsd_efficacy.short: Yes, in two trials. With the same therapy, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill.
cl_mdma_ptsd_efficacy.but: In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.
how: In two trials run for one sponsor, 194 adults with PTSD had up to three long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
Both groups improved a lot. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped about 9 to 12 points more with MDMA, on a scale of 0 to 80.
Counting everyone who started, 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA no longer had PTSD at about 4 months, against 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The trials report nothing after 4 months, and none we read compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused talking therapy.
cl_mdma_ptsd_efficacy.rate: Two trials of 193 people in all, where chance decided who got MDMA. But most people probably knew which pill they had, and hope or disappointment could explain an unknown part of the difference.

cl_mdma_ptsd_blinding.short: In the trial that asked, most people could tell MDMA from the dummy pill.
cl_mdma_ptsd_blinding.but: Only one of the two trials asked, and only at the very end.
how: At the end of the second trial, 94 in 100 people on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right.
About 8 in 10 people on MDMA were sure they had it. One person stopped because they thought they had the dummy pill.
The first trial did not ask. Critics say up to 9 in 10 people there may have guessed right.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected, so we cannot tell how much of the gain came from MDMA itself.
cl_mdma_ptsd_blinding.rate: One end-of-trial survey of 96 people, taken after they knew whether they had improved, so noticing the drug and feeling better get tangled. Still, so many guessed right that this hardly changes the picture.

cl_mdma_ptsd_adverse_events.short: MDMA often gave brief side effects, like tight muscles, feeling sick and sweating.
cl_mdma_ptsd_adverse_events.but: The trials were too small and short to show rare or later harms.
how: In two trials, 99 people took MDMA and 95 took a dummy pill, with therapy. No serious side effects were seen on MDMA.
Tight muscles affected about 59 to 63 in 100 people on MDMA, against 11 to 26 in 100 on the dummy pill.
In each session on MDMA, the top blood pressure number reached 160 or more in up to 22 in 100 people, against 4 in 100 on the dummy pill.
Feeling very happy was written down only if people mentioned it, and there were no heart tracings or blood tests after the doses.
cl_mdma_ptsd_adverse_events.rate: Two trials of 90 and 104 adults with PTSD, where chance decided who got MDMA. Both show the same common side effects, but the therapists recording them probably knew who had MDMA.

cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.short: No. The US regulator turned it down in August 2024, after its expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data didn't show it works.
cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.but: We read the panel's notes, but we only know the decision second-hand.
how: In June 2024, the regulator's expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data didn't show the treatment works, and 10 to 1 that the benefits didn't outweigh the risks.
Panel members worried that people could tell which pill they'd had. In one trial, 94 in 100 on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right.
They also doubted the later check of whether benefits lasted, and noted that no study separated the drug's effect from the therapy's.
The regulator's own staff said the main trials had no lab tests on treatment days, and the company didn't log euphoria as a side effect, so misuse risk was harder to judge.
cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.rate: The panel's votes come from the regulator's own documents, but the final decision letter was not read, so the decision and its reasons are known mainly from news reports.

cl_mdma_retractions_2024.short: In 2024 a journal withdrew three earlier studies from the MDMA therapy research.
cl_mdma_retractions_2024.but: The journal did not say how much of the data came from that site.
how: The three studies came from the earlier, smaller trials of the same research programme.
The journal said the authors knew of serious rule-breaking at one study site, did not tell it, and had not fully declared their ties to the sponsor.
The company's own papers, written two months before, say one person in that study was seriously harmed by sexual misconduct.
Most of the authors who answered the journal disagreed with the withdrawals.
cl_mdma_retractions_2024.rate: Based on the journal's own three notices, read in full. Descriptions of events get at most two bars here, and what went wrong rests on a second-hand account.

cl_mdma_ptsd_cost.short: Two critics say price and comparison decide if MDMA therapy is good value.
cl_mdma_ptsd_cost.but: The cost studies come from the company or from people with money ties to it.
how: The company's study compared MDMA therapy with the same talking therapy plus a dummy pill.
The critics, who also have money ties to the company, say it should be compared with the treatments people would otherwise get.
At the company's price, the critics' model needs about 8 years before savings cover the cost; at a much lower price it could save money.
The company's papers for the regulator give no results on health-care use, and no independent study was among the papers read.
cl_mdma_ptsd_cost.rate: Calculations of future costs, not real results, all by the company or people with money ties to it, mostly known second-hand. None allowed for people guessing their treatment, which can inflate trial results.

cl_mdma_therapy_contested.short: It's not settled. Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill, but can't show how much was the drug itself, or for how long.
cl_mdma_therapy_contested.but: One sponsor ran both trials, and in the one that asked, most people knew their pill.
how: Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA and therapy than with a dummy pill and the same therapy. Neither tested MDMA against usual talking therapy.
But in the second trial most people could tell which pill they had, and neither trial reports measuring what they expected.
The company says a later visit showed the benefit lasted. The regulator said it wasn't built to show that: about 3 in 10 didn't come, some knew their pill, and some had other treatment in between.
In 2024 the US regulator said no, after its advisers voted 9 to 2 that it wasn't shown to work. Three papers on earlier trials were withdrawn for not disclosing rule-breaking at one site.
cl_mdma_therapy_contested.rate: Two trials, where people often knew their pill and rated their own symptoms, and neither compared MDMA with existing therapy or looked beyond 18 weeks. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_mdma_ptsd_durability.short: Months to years later, people who had MDMA still scored lower on PTSD.
cl_mdma_ptsd_durability.but: Only about 7 in 10 came back for one check, and many had other treatments in between.
how: One check-up visit scored PTSD again, 6 months to over 2 years after the trials.
137 of 195 people came back, and those who came back had done better at the end of the trials.
Of those checked, about 7 in 10 who had MDMA and 3 in 10 who had the dummy pill still had no PTSD, the company says.
People from the first trial knew which pill they had, and the US regulator said this visit was not set up to show if the benefit lasts.
cl_mdma_ptsd_durability.rate: A single check, months to years later, on people from two trials who chose to return. Those who came had done better, and nearly all could tell whether they had MDMA.

cl_mdma_aud.short: In one small study, 9 of 14 people drank much less after MDMA therapy.
cl_mdma_aud.but: There was no group without MDMA. And all had just been through detox.
how: 14 adults with alcohol use disorder, all just out of detox, had ten therapy sessions. Two of them included MDMA.
Three months later, 9 of the 14 said they were drinking much less than at the start.
The start seems to have been before detox, so a big drop was likely anyway.
People reported their own drinking. No study we read compared people who had MDMA with people who did not.
cl_mdma_aud.rate: One study of 14 people, all given MDMA therapy. Their drinking was apparently compared with before detox, so a drop was expected anyway, and they reported it themselves, knowing what they took.

cl_mdma_lti_anxiety.short: In one small trial, anxiety fell more with MDMA than with a dummy pill.
cl_mdma_lti_anxiety.but: The difference could be chance: only 18 people took part, and most could tell which pill they had.
how: 18 adults with anxiety about cancer or another serious illness took part. They had two long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
A month later, anxiety scores had dropped about 24 points with MDMA. They dropped 9 points with the dummy pill. The scale runs from 20 to 80.
With so few people, the true difference could be anywhere from none to very large.
Later everyone got MDMA. Scores stayed lower a year later, but there was no group left to compare.
cl_mdma_lti_anxiety.rate: One trial of 18 people, just 5 on the dummy pill. People named their pill correctly in 86% of sessions and rated their own anxiety, and the MDMA group started more anxious.

cl_mdma_autism_social_anxiety.short: In one small trial, social anxiety eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill.
cl_mdma_autism_social_anxiety.but: Only 12 autistic adults took part, and almost all could tell which pill they got.
how: 12 autistic adults with strong social anxiety took part. They had two long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
A month later, social anxiety scores had dropped about 44 points with MDMA and 19 with the dummy pill.
People guessed their pill right in 22 of 23 sessions, so what they expected may have shaped what they reported.
With so few people, the true benefit could be small or large.
cl_mdma_autism_social_anxiety.rate: One trial with only 11 autistic adults counted. People knew which pill they got in 22 of 23 sessions, and the result rests on their own reports.

cl_mdma_couples.short: After couples therapy with MDMA, PTSD eased and couples were happier.
cl_mdma_couples.but: Neither study had a group without MDMA. And this couples therapy helps PTSD even without it.
how: Two small studies, 14 couples in all, added two MDMA sessions to couples therapy for PTSD.
PTSD scores dropped a lot after treatment. Both partners felt happier together.
In the second study, part of the gain faded by 6 months, and one partner felt worse.
No one had a serious side effect. Without a comparison group, we cannot tell what MDMA added.
cl_mdma_couples.rate: Two small studies, 14 couples in all, with no comparison group, and everyone knew they got MDMA. The therapy itself helps PTSD, so MDMA's part is unclear.

cl_mdma_depression.short: In one small study, depression dropped a lot after two MDMA sessions.
cl_mdma_depression.but: There was no group without MDMA. And the people who scored depression knew everyone had taken it.
how: 12 adults in Norway with depression had two MDMA sessions. They also had talking therapy before and after.
About two months later, depression scores had fallen from about 30 to about 10, and 9 of the 12 were much better.
No one had a serious side effect. But 4 to 6 of the 12 had worse thoughts of suicide at some point. 2 needed medicine for anxiety and sleep.
Most people signed up on their own. So many probably expected to get better.
cl_mdma_depression.rate: One study of 12 people, all given MDMA, with no comparison group. The therapy alone can ease depression, and people picked when their depression scores are high often improve anyway.

cl_mdma_ptsd_alcohol_drug_use.short: MDMA therapy for PTSD did not clearly change drinking or drug use.
cl_mdma_ptsd_alcohol_drug_use.but: Almost no one had a drinking or drug problem to start with. And people reported their own use.
how: In one PTSD trial, 82 people filled in forms about alcohol and drugs. They did this before and after treatment with MDMA or a dummy pill.
Drinking scores fell by 1 point with MDMA and rose slightly with the dummy pill, on a scale of 0 to 40.
The MDMA group started with higher scores. Allowing for that, the difference could be chance.
Drug-use scores went down a little in both groups.
cl_mdma_ptsd_alcohol_drug_use.rate: One trial in people with PTSD, where drinking and drug use were extra questions people answered themselves. The period asked about changed between visits, and people could probably tell if they got MDMA.

cl_mdma_trial_side_effects.short: In small trials, MDMA's side effects were common and brief, and none were serious.
cl_mdma_trial_side_effects.but: These trials were too small to show rare or later harms.
how: Five small studies gave MDMA to 58 people. They had anxiety, depression, social anxiety with autism, or PTSD in couples.
A tight jaw, thirst, sweating and headache were common during sessions. Tiredness was common in the week after.
Blood pressure, pulse and body heat went up during sessions. None of this needed treatment.
Thoughts of suicide were recorded as side effects in a few people; in one trial this was as common with the dummy pill.
cl_mdma_trial_side_effects.rate: Five small studies in the US and Norway, 58 people given MDMA in all. Side effects were only recorded when people mentioned them, or by their own therapists, so some may have been missed.

cl_mdma_ptsd_durability_phase2.short: In two sets of early PTSD trials, average PTSD scores stayed about as low as at the end of MDMA therapy a year or more later.
cl_mdma_ptsd_durability_phase2.but: There was no comparison group, many people also had other therapy or medicines, and the same sponsor ran both studies.
how: In one small trial, 16 of 19 people were checked again about 4 years later, and their average score had hardly changed.
Some people got much better and some much worse; 2 had moderate-to-severe PTSD again.
In four other trials, scores a year later were a little lower than at the end of treatment, after everyone had had full doses.
Those results had to be corrected after an ethics breach by two therapists at one site.
cl_mdma_ptsd_durability_phase2.rate: Follow-ups of one sponsor's early trials, with no comparison group and raters who knew the treatment, one paid by the sponsor. Only 16 people were followed long-term, too few to be sure.

cl_mdma_ptsd_sleep.short: In early PTSD trials, people who had full doses of MDMA said they slept better than people who had a very small dose.
cl_mdma_ptsd_sleep.but: The trials were small, no one checked whether people could tell which dose they had, and the results had to be corrected after an ethics breach at one site.
how: On a 0 to 21 sleep scale, scores improved by about 4 points more with full doses, a month or two after treatment.
About half of the full-dose group improved by 3 points or more, against 2 of 14 in the small-dose group.
A year later sleep was a little better still, but by then everyone had had full doses, so there was nothing to compare with.
cl_mdma_ptsd_sleep.rate: One analysis that put four small trials together: 58 people, only 14 in the comparison group. Its groups were partly chosen after seeing the results, and people rated their own sleep.

cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.short: Common ones were a tight jaw, anxiety, less appetite, feeling sick and sweating. They happened during sessions and in the week after. Most were mild to moderate and soon passed.
cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.but: The record is patchy. Most studies only noted problems people raised themselves. Some never reached the papers, and later risks are barely known.
how: These effects were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose.
In one small trial in people with a serious illness, 11 of 13 on MDMA had a tight jaw, against 1 of 5 on a dummy pill.
One review found one serious problem linked to MDMA. Extra heartbeats the person already had got more frequent. They were watched overnight in hospital.
Trial records listed problems the papers left out. That was more than half of the less serious ones, and 4 of 13 serious ones. All 4 were in people on MDMA.
cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.rate: Reviews pooling 8 trials with 298 people, mostly PTSD trials from one sponsor. Staff noting side effects probably knew who got MDMA, and few trials looked beyond PTSD.

cl_mdma_indications_overview.short: Nobody can say yet. Outside PTSD, it's been tried for a few things. They include tinnitus, drinking problems, and anxiety in autistic adults or in people who are very ill.
cl_mdma_indications_overview.but: Each had one tiny trial at most, the biggest with 18 people.
how: Reviews up to 2024 found one trial each. There were 18 people anxious about a serious illness, 12 autistic adults with social anxiety, and 13 people with tinnitus.
A study of 14 people with alcohol problems, and one of 6 couples, had no comparison group.
In the serious-illness trial, anxiety fell more with MDMA than with a dummy pill, but the trial was too small to be sure.
A critical review found only the two later PTSD trials were randomized with over 15 people per group. It called even those results a signal needing repeating.
cl_mdma_indications_overview.rate: Each condition rests on one tiny trial at most, the largest with 18 people, so results are very unsure. People could usually tell whether they'd had MDMA, and rated their own symptoms.

cl_mdma_history.short: Before MDMA was banned in 1985, a few dozen US therapists used it in talking therapy.
cl_mdma_history.but: This comes second-hand from one history review, and the reports of the time were not designed well enough to show whether MDMA helped.
how: Therapists reported good results, and a follow-up of 29 patients found no serious side effects.
Two therapists had sexual contact with patients during sessions and lost their licences.
A US judge said the strictest ban was not needed, but the drug agency imposed it anyway.
Research applications were then blocked for years; the first approved study, in healthy people, began in 1992.
cl_mdma_history.rate: One history review by a single author, retelling memoirs, interviews and supporters' documents without checking them, so every figure is second-hand.

cl_meth_alcohol_interaction.short: With alcohol, meth raises the heart rate more and makes people feel less drunk.
cl_meth_alcohol_interaction.but: One study of nine men, with small oral doses in a laboratory.
how: Together they raised heart rate and good feelings more than either drug alone.
People felt less drunk and did better on attention tests, at the same breath alcohol.
By the third dose, a day and a half later, those extra effects were smaller.
Whether feeling less drunk leads people to drink more was not tested.
cl_meth_alcohol_interaction.rate: One lab study in which nine men were each their own comparison, with heart rate and breath tests measured directly. But so few took part, and they could tell which drinks held alcohol.

cl_mdma_tolerance_acute.short: A second dose raises the drug in your blood, but not the strongest feeling.
cl_mdma_tolerance_acute.but: Three small laboratory studies, 9 to 23 people, and none gave more than two doses.
how: Blood levels rose more than the extra dose alone explains: MDMA slows its own breakdown.
The strongest feeling was no stronger after the second dose, but it lasted about an hour longer.
Heart rate hardly rose further, while blood pressure and body temperature did.
No study worked out how much effect a given blood level should give.
cl_mdma_tolerance_acute.rate: Three small lab studies, of 9, 10 and 23 people, from two separate teams. In the one that checked, people could tell when they had MDMA, and two printed only results that stood out.

cl_mdma_tolerance_chronic.short: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well.
cl_mdma_tolerance_chronic.but: This comes from questionnaires, retold in one review; no laboratory study has tested it.
how: In surveys, most people say the first time was the strongest.
People who have used more say they take more tablets in a night.
Nobody checked what the tablets held, and different people were compared, not followed over time.
In one study, longer use did not go with more tablets.
cl_mdma_tolerance_chronic.rate: Surveys where people described their own use, with no check of what their pills held. We know them through one review with no stated search, about half its studies from the author's own team.

cl_mdma_redose_cardiovascular.short: Taking more adds strain on the heart and blood pressure without stronger good feelings.
cl_mdma_redose_cardiovascular.but: Small laboratory studies of healthy, screened people sitting in a quiet room.
how: After a second dose, 8 of 9 men went above a raised blood-pressure line, against 6 of 9.
Both cases of a racing heart in that study came after the second dose.
In another study, all ten men went above that line.
Nobody has tested hot, crowded places or the larger amounts people describe.
cl_mdma_redose_cardiovascular.rate: Three lab studies of 9, 10 and 23 healthy people. Counts of high blood pressure were an afterthought, and a gap of two people in nine can't put a number on the risk.

cl_mix_opioids_benzodiazepines.short: People on prescribed opioids and benzos had more overdoses than people on opioids alone.
cl_mix_opioids_benzodiazepines.but: The studies could not separate the benzos from the reasons people were given them.
how: Among US veterans on opioid painkillers, about 3 in 1,000 died of overdose each year while also prescribed benzos.
Without a benzo prescription, under 1 in 1,000 died each year. Higher prescribed benzo doses went with more deaths.
In insured US adults, hospital visits for opioid overdose were about twice as common with both prescriptions.
Risk was also higher after the benzo prescription stopped, so something about the people may explain part of it.
cl_mix_opioids_benzodiazepines.rate: Two large US record studies that can't separate the medicine from why people got it: risk stayed raised even after the prescriptions ended. Filled prescriptions don't show what people took.

cl_mix_opioid_deaths_benzodiazepines.short: About 1 in 5 US opioid overdose deaths in 2017 also involved benzos.
cl_mix_opioid_deaths_benzodiazepines.but: Death records miss some drugs, and a share of deaths does not measure risk.
how: US death certificates listed benzos in 21 of 100 opioid overdose deaths in 2017, up from 9 in 1999.
Benzos were listed more often with prescription opioids or methadone (about 1 in 3) than with heroin or fentanyl.
In North Carolina in 2010, medical examiners, who investigate deaths, judged benzos involved in about 6 in 10 deaths involving an opioid painkiller.
Of people on prescribed opioids who died of overdose, half (US veterans) to three in four (Ontario) had benzo prescriptions.
cl_mix_opioid_deaths_benzodiazepines.rate: Death certificates and prescription records from the US and Ontario. Certificates miss some drugs, and prescriptions do not show what was taken, so the exact shares are unsure.

cl_mix_opioids_alcohol.short: Alcohol was listed in about 1 in 7 US opioid overdose deaths.
cl_mix_opioids_alcohol.but: Alcohol is often left off death records, and these counts do not measure risk.
how: US death certificates listed alcohol in about 15 of 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share steady since 2008.
Alcohol was listed more often in men's deaths (17 in 100) than in women's (about 10 in 100).
In North Carolina in 2010, medical examiners, who investigate deaths, judged alcohol involved in about 12 in 100 deaths involving an opioid painkiller.
Without knowing how many people drink with opioids, these counts cannot say how much alcohol adds to risk. Two reviews describe no study in people that measured it.
cl_mix_opioids_alcohol.rate: Death certificates for all 399,230 US opioid overdose deaths from 1999–2017. Alcohol may be left off, and testing and reporting varied by state and year, so the real share may be higher.

cl_mix_opioid_treatment_sedatives.short: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, benzo prescriptions were linked to more poisoning deaths.
cl_mix_opioid_treatment_sedatives.but: The study did not take mental health, alcohol or street drug use into account.
how: Poisoning deaths were about 1 in 100 people per year with a benzo prescription, and 1 in 200 without.
The link was stronger when benzo doses were above the highest dose the UK drug guide advises.
Sleeping tablets called z-drugs were also linked to poisoning deaths, though deaths were few.
People prescribed benzos stayed in treatment longer, but the link with poisoning deaths was still there.
cl_mix_opioid_treatment_sedatives.rate: One UK study of health records for 12,118 people on methadone or buprenorphine. People prescribed these sedatives may differ in ways the records do not show, and the study's own tables disagree in places.

cl_mdma_sert_dose.short: People who had taken more ecstasy showed less of the serotonin marker.
cl_mdma_sert_dose.but: The amounts come from memory, and people who take more ecstasy take more of everything else.
how: Four studies found this link; two smaller ones did not.
In one, each doubling of pills went with a small further drop.
In another, years of use and the biggest dose went with the lowest levels.
Nobody measured how much people really took, or what was in the pills.
cl_mdma_sert_dose.rate: Six brain-scan studies of people who use ecstasy, comparing heavier with lighter use. Use was recalled, not checked, other drugs were not taken into account, and two studies found no link.

cl_mdma_sert_recovery.short: We do not know if the marker goes back to normal after people stop.
cl_mdma_sert_recovery.but: Nobody has been scanned while using and then again years later.
how: Three studies compared different people and found more marker in those who stopped longer ago.
Two other studies found no link with time since the last pill.
People who stop may be different from people who keep going.
The parts that looked normal again are not where the drop is biggest.
cl_mdma_sert_recovery.rate: Brain scans of people who had stopped for shorter or longer times. Those groups may differ in other ways too, and three studies found a link while two did not.

cl_mdma_sert_prospective.short: In one study, a few pills did not change the serotonin marker.
cl_mdma_sert_prospective.but: Most of these people had taken only one or two pills in all.
how: Young people were scanned before they had ever used ecstasy, then about 17 months later.
Before anyone started, the two groups' scans looked the same.
After starting, the serotonin marker and the brain chemicals had not changed.
A few other brain measures differed, each by less than five in a hundred.
cl_mdma_sert_prospective.rate: One Dutch study scanning young adults before and after they started using ecstasy. Those who started also used more of other drugs, and the authors call their scan too blunt for small changes.

cl_mix_opioids_gabapentinoids.short: Gabapentin or pregabalin with opioid painkillers was linked to more opioid overdose deaths in Ontario.
cl_mix_opioids_gabapentinoids.but: Both Ontario studies are from one team and do not say why people were given the medicines.
how: In Ontario, 12 in 100 people who died had a recent gabapentin prescription, against 7 in 100 similar living people.
For pregabalin it was about 5 in 100 people who died, against 3 in 100 similar living people.
After allowing for opioid dose and other medicines, the odds of an opioid death were about 1.5 times higher with gabapentin and 1.7 times with pregabalin.
In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, gabapentin-type medicines were not clearly linked to poisoning deaths; deaths were few.
cl_mix_opioids_gabapentinoids.rate: Two record-based studies in Ontario, comparing people who died with similar living people. They were careful, but records miss drug use that wasn't prescribed, and no other team has confirmed it.

cl_mdma_acute_body.short: One dose pushes all three up. In lab tests, 24 in 100 people went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill.
cl_mdma_acute_body.but: Healthy volunteers rested in a room at about 23 degrees. Heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses weren't tested.
how: 136 healthy adults got one lab dose. The top blood-pressure number went above 160 in 38 in 100 after MDMA, against 6 in 100 after a dummy pill.
A heart rate above 100 happened in 33 in 100 after MDMA, against 2 in 100 after the dummy pill.
Ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 after MDMA, against 9 in 100; the highest was 39.1 degrees.
Four people felt no effect and the study does not say what their bodies did. Everyone got a set dose, so taking more was not tested here.
cl_mdma_acute_body.rate: Nine trials in one Basel lab compared MDMA with dummy pills in the same people, 166 healthy volunteers in all, and machines recorded large changes. But most people could probably tell when they had MDMA.

cl_mdma_overheating.short: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others with MDMA.
cl_mdma_overheating.but: This is second-hand, from one review of small studies. They couldn't tell heat, dancing and crowds apart.
how: In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose about 0.4 degrees on average at medium doses and 0.7 at higher ones; one person in a group of 8 went up 1.9.
At clubs and parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees. But the review reports no comparison of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowds, so which matters is unknown.

Severe overheating (40 degrees and up, sometimes fatal) is known from hospital cases. In one UK report, blood levels didn't suggest high doses. In another case, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat.
People also feel it differently: in one survey, 16 in 100 people who take ecstasy did not feel hot.
cl_mdma_overheating.rate: One overview of small lab and party studies (4 to 41 people) and hospital cases. Each party study used a different comparison, or none, and their results differ widely without explanation.

cl_mdma_hyponatremia.q: Can drinking lots of water on MDMA lead to low blood salt?
cl_mdma_hyponatremia.short: Possibly. Low blood salt (sodium) after MDMA has been reported, mostly in young people; of 17 UK cases, at least 10 had drunk a lot of liquid.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia.but: These only count people who got ill. So they can't show how often it happens, or whether drinking more changes the risk.
how: Over 28 months, 17 people aged 15 to 26 were reported to a UK poisons service. Of the 15 who survived, 10 had seizures, 12 had a normal temperature at hospital, and 13 recovered fully.
The 2 who died, aged 15 and 18, had brain swelling. Both had drunk a lot of water, and drank or were given more after they began to feel ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level. 4 of those 73 died.

The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water. In one study, 8 healthy men given one MDMA capsule had a rise in the water-holding hormone, and their blood salt fell a little, not to a low level. It had no proper comparison, and a study of 32 people found no clear rise in a related marker.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia.rate: Records from two poison services, in the UK and California, which agree. But MDMA was confirmed by tests in only some cases, and in California only about a third had blood salt measured.

cl_mdma_hyponatremia_risk.short: Yes, among people who got ill: 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men, in one poison-centre study.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia_risk.but: It counts only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.
how: Only 188 of 545 people in California poison-centre records had a blood salt test. Of 105 women tested, 55 had a low level; of 83 men, 18 did.
Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma than women without one; in men the numbers were too small to tell.
A UK group (10 of 17 were women) and a review of published cases (more than 85 in 100 were female) point the same way, but the review's cases overlap with the California ones.
A review describes 8 women and 8 men given the same MDMA amount: a marker of a water-holding hormone rose only in women, with no clear difference reported in the hormone or blood salt.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia_risk.rate: Records of 188 people at one California poison centre who had blood salt measured. Body size and other differences between women and men were not recorded or allowed for.

cl_mdma_kidney.short: Kidney injury after MDMA has been reported in single cases; nobody knows how often.
cl_mdma_kidney.but: This is second-hand, from reviews of case reports, which cannot show how often it happens.
how: Most reported cases followed muscle breakdown after fits, very hard physical exertion or overheating.
A few single cases had other routes, such as inflamed blood vessels, a blocked bladder outlet or very high blood pressure.
In 164 healthy volunteers who took MDMA once or twice in a laboratory, kidney blood tests about a month later were about the same as before; nobody tested them in the hours and days after.
No study compared amounts, so the reports cannot show whether taking more makes it more likely.
cl_mdma_kidney.rate: Single case reports, seen only second-hand through two overviews. With nothing to compare them with, it is hard to tell what caused each injury.

cl_mdma_pill_content.q: Is ecstasy really MDMA, and how strong are the pills?
cl_mdma_pill_content.short: Often, but not always. In European pill tests in 2009, 19 to 64 in 100 pills held MDMA, depending on the country. By 2013 most did, and held more of it.
cl_mdma_pill_content.but: These were pills people chose to bring in, and the newest tests are from 2013. Pills today may be different.
how: A 2004 review of pill tests found MDMA in 90 to 98 in 100 ecstasy pills from the 1980s to the early 1990s, 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid-1990s, and nearly all by the early 2000s. Others held related drugs, other things such as ketamine or caffeine, or nothing active.

Drug-checking services in five European countries tested pills people brought in, from 2008 to 2013. Pills holding MDMA dropped in 2009, to about 19 in 100 in Austria and 64 in 100 in the Netherlands, then mostly recovered. Newer drugs such as mCPP or PMMA turned up in some ecstasy.

The MDMA in a pill ranged from none to about 150 mg in older tests. Where measured, the average rose from about 61 to 74 mg in 2009 to about 103 to 114 mg in 2013: nearly double in the Netherlands, less elsewhere. These are lab measurements, not amounts to take.

Some people feel little from a pill, and some then take more. A weaker pill, or one with no MDMA, is one possible reason; in an Australian survey, people thought about 1 pill in 4 or 5 was a dud. Neither source looked at other reasons, such as tolerance, or at what happens when people then take more.
cl_mdma_pill_content.rate: Lab tests of pills people chose to hand in, dropped in bins or police seized, so not a fair picture of all pills sold. Labs used different methods, and the newest data are from 2013.

cl_mdma_dependence.short: Yes, some do. How many depends on who's asked: about 4 in 100 people who'd used it recently in US surveys, but up to 73 in 100 in small groups.
cl_mdma_dependence.but: Every checklist was made for other drugs, and most studies used volunteers, so the numbers can't be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy.
how: In two US surveys of the general public, about 4 in 100 people who had used ecstasy recently met the criteria for dependence. Among clubgoers, young people in detention and volunteers, it was 16 to 22 in 100.
Three small samples gave much higher numbers: 43 to 73 in 100 met the criteria at some point in their lives. They included people in drug treatment and people who had taken at least 250 pills.
The one study that followed people found that 93 in 100 of those dependent at the start no longer were after about three years. That group was small: about 12 to 14 people, by our count.

The symptoms reported most included carrying on despite problems, lots of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal. Pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some of this may be dependence on another drug.
cl_mdma_dependence.rate: Studies of 26 to 1,662 people, seen only through one 2010 overview. Who was asked shaped the answer, from 3.6 to 73 in 100, and pills sold as ecstasy may not be MDMA.

cl_mdma_heart_valves.short: Heart valve changes were more common in people who had taken MDMA, in one small study.
cl_mdma_heart_valves.but: Nobody was scanned before taking MDMA, so this cannot show that MDMA caused it.
how: 8 of 29 people who had taken MDMA for at least six months had valve findings that met a US definition of drug-related valve disease. None of 29 students who reported no drug use did.
