The biggest gap was in the tricuspid valve, which that definition does not cover: 13 of 29 had a leak of grade 2 of 4 or more, against none. Most leaks were mild or moderate.

By their own account, the people had taken about 4 pills a week for about 6 years, on average. Those with higher leak grades said they had taken more in total, but the paper does not give the group sizes.
Other drug use is not reported, and the amounts came from what people said. The study says nothing about symptoms or illness.
cl_mdma_heart_valves.rate: One study in Brussels and Flanders scanned 29 people who used MDMA, found through psychiatry and drug services, and 29 students. The groups may differ in other ways too, such as other drug use.

cl_mdma_deaths_medicines.short: Among 19 Australian deaths with MDMA and a risky mix, antidepressants, opioids and benzos were common.
cl_mdma_deaths_medicines.but: The 19 were picked for risky mixes, so the counts do not show how common any mix is.
how: In 14,682 coroners' cases (2002 to 2008), 106 had MDMA in the blood. Six in 10 of them died of injuries such as hanging or a crash, so MDMA in the blood does not show that it caused the death.
The authors rated 19 of the 106 as having a risky drug combination. Of those 19, 15 also had methamphetamine or amphetamine, 13 an antidepressant, 12 an opioid and 8 a benzodiazepine (benzo).
Four of them had moclobemide, an antidepressant of the MAO-inhibitor type. Three of those four showed signs of serotonin toxicity before they died.

A blood test after death cannot show who took what, when or why, and where the medicines came from was mostly unknown. A second-hand report of 75 UK deaths found other drugs, mostly opiates and sedatives, in 93 in 100.
cl_mdma_deaths_medicines.rate: Reports on 19 deaths in one Australian state, hand-picked by the authors from 106. Tests after death can't show who took what, and there was no comparison group.

cl_mix_serotonin_toxicity.short: Doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking, sweating and restlessness when serotonin may be too high.
cl_mix_serotonin_toxicity.but: The checklist was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses, against that unit's own diagnosis.
how: Serotonin toxicity (also called serotonin syndrome) is too much serotonin activity, caused by drugs that raise serotonin. It ranges from mild to severe.
Doctors examine the person for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, and, when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever.
In one Australian hospital unit, a checklist of these signs matched the unit's diagnosis in about 84 of 100 people diagnosed. An older checklist matched about 75 of 100.
Everyone had taken an overdose, and mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects. No independent test of the checklist was found.
cl_mix_serotonin_toxicity.rate: Records from one Australian poisons unit, 1987 to 2002. The checklist was built and tested on overlapping patients and judged against the unit's own diagnosis, made from much the same signs.

cl_mix_mdma_maoi.short: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide, an antidepressant, in their blood.
cl_mix_mdma_maoi.but: Four deaths cannot give a rate, and all four also had other drugs in their blood or urine.
how: None of the four had been prescribed moclobemide. Pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs.
The authors thought it was serotonin syndrome, but its defining signs were not recorded. MDMA levels were about 5 to 6 times the top of the range the paper quotes.
Reviews rank MDMA with this kind of antidepressant as the highest-risk mix they list. Nobody has counted people who took both and had no such outcome.
Some people feel little from an amount of MDMA and take more. No study measured what happens then with this antidepressant.
cl_mix_mdma_maoi.rate: Four deaths in Finland, chosen by the authors, with no comparison group. MDMA by itself cannot be ruled out as the cause, and the signs of the suspected reaction were not recorded.

cl_mix_mdma_serotonergic.short: One 2007 review ranked drugs by serotonin risk with ecstasy: MAOIs highest, SSRIs lower.
cl_mix_mdma_serotonergic.but: This is the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work, not from counts of people.
how: Lower risk, the review says: SSRI-type antidepressants and a few painkillers and cough medicines, which it says weaken ecstasy's effects.
Middle: stimulants such as amphetamine and cocaine, and supplements such as tryptophan. Highest: MAOI antidepressants.
Deaths from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy alone are rare, the review says, but harm is more likely with other drugs that act on serotonin.
No study counted how often each mix causes harm. Some people feel little from an amount of ecstasy and take more; no study measured what that does to the risk.
cl_mix_mdma_serotonergic.rate: One 2007 review, resting on how the drugs work, animal studies and a few case reports. It did not check how good the studies were, and no study counted how often problems happened.

cl_mix_opioids_maoi.short: Reports link pethidine and tramadol to bad reactions with MAOI antidepressants; none for morphine.
cl_mix_opioids_maoi.but: It rests on old case reports in reviews; nobody has counted how often it happens.
how: A 2005 review says pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan (in some cough medicines) were involved in reactions with MAOIs, an older kind of antidepressant. Some cases ended in death.
It found no reports for morphine, codeine, oxycodone or buprenorphine. That is a lack of reports, not a test in people. Fentanyl and methadone are unclear.
9 of the 11 papers it cites for deaths are from 1955 to 1971. The doctor thinks the risk is probably low but hard to predict.
Some people feel little pain relief from an amount and take more. No study looked at what happens then with an MAOI.
cl_mix_opioids_maoi.rate: Mostly old case reports, seen only through reviews that did not check them. One paper cited for deaths is a rabbit study, and the full case list sits unseen on a website.

cl_mix_cocaine_alcohol.q: What happens when cocaine and alcohol are used together?
cl_mix_cocaine_alcohol.short: Together they make a new substance, cocaethylene, and hearts beat faster than with cocaine alone.
cl_mix_cocaine_alcohol.but: Small hospital studies of 8 and 6 people. None measured heart attacks or rhythm problems.
how: Eight adults who already used both drugs took cocaine by the nose on a hospital ward. With alcohol, their heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute, against 74 with cocaine alone.
There was also about 13 to 15 percent more cocaine in their blood, and cocaethylene, which the body makes only when both drugs are there and which leaves the blood more slowly than cocaine.

In a second study, cocaine went into a vein with alcohol. Cocaethylene formed again, but stayed at a small fraction of the cocaine level, and none of it appeared when cocaine was given without alcohol.

Cocaethylene has been found in people's blood after both drugs, including after deaths, but such tests cannot show what caused a death. In over 1,000 emergency-room tests, people positive for both drugs had no more heart problems than people positive for one.
cl_mix_cocaine_alcohol.rate: Two small hospital lab studies, with 8 and 6 people, plus selected blood samples. People could probably tell what they got, and apart from heart rate, the results are shaky.

cl_mix_cocaine_alcohol_drunkenness.q: Can cocaine make someone feel less drunk?
cl_mix_cocaine_alcohol_drunkenness.short: People given cocaine with alcohol did not feel more drunk, and sometimes slightly less.
cl_mix_cocaine_alcohol_drunkenness.but: This is second-hand from one review of small studies, and no one tested driving.
how: A review gathered 14 small laboratory studies. The four that asked how drunk people felt had 8 to 11 people each. Those studies have not been read here, so the figures are second-hand.
In three of the four, people said they felt a little less drunk with cocaine; in one, nothing changed. Two of the three falls were too small to be clear.
Cocaine also made some alcohol-affected test scores less poor, and blood alcohol stayed the same or was about 10 percent lower.

Nobody asked other people how drunk someone looked, and no study tested driving. Of drivers who died in crashes, about 4 in 100 had both drugs in their blood, so the mix did not protect them from alcohol's effects.
cl_mix_cocaine_alcohol_drunkenness.rate: Four small lab studies of 8 to 11 people, known only through one review that did not check them. People rated their own drunkenness in a lab, not how drunk they seemed to others.

cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.q: Why can the usual amount be dangerous after a break?
cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.short: Because tolerance may drop during a break, reviews say. In one study, 3 people died of an overdose after a hospital detox. All 3 had stayed for the whole programme.
cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.but: Nobody measured anyone's tolerance. And it's 3 deaths in one small study.
how: 137 people were followed for a year after a 28-day hospital detox in London. All 3 overdose deaths came within 4 months, among the 37 who finished both the detox and the programme. None of the 100 who left earlier died that way.

The researchers read this as lost tolerance but never measured it. The people who died also differed in other ways: 4 of the 5 who died from any cause had lived alone, against 16 in 100 of the others.
Two reviews offer the same idea but give no numbers: not how long a break must be, how fast tolerance falls, or how much the risk rises. The main study behind them looked at hair samples.
One review describes two studies of people on methadone. Their tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.
cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.rate: One small study after a hospital detox: 3 overdose deaths, and nobody measured tolerance. Plus two reviews, one citing the other, with no numbers.

cl_mdma_antidepressants.short: An SSRI muted MDMA's effects in lab tests; with paroxetine, MDMA blood levels rose.
cl_mdma_antidepressants.but: Only 28 healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most, and no one was given more MDMA.
how: 16 volunteers rated MDMA's effects about 60 percent lower after citalopram; their blood levels were not measured.
In 12 men, paroxetine lessened the rises in the upper blood pressure number, heart rate and pupil size. Yet the MDMA peak in the blood was about 1 in 6 higher.
Feeling little can have many reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, or a medicine that mutes the effect, as here.
No one was given more MDMA once its effects were muted, so what happens then is not known; the paroxetine authors suggest it could add risk.
cl_mdma_antidepressants.rate: Two careful lab studies in two countries agree. But only 16 and 12 healthy volunteers took part, and people may have noticed which session was which.

cl_mdma_antidepressants_other.short: Other antidepressants did not act alike: some muted MDMA's effects, and bupropion did not.
cl_mdma_antidepressants_other.but: These numbers are second-hand, from a 2022 review of single trials with 16 healthy people each.
how: Duloxetine and reboxetine lowered MDMA's rated effects. The MDMA peak in the blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher.
Bupropion did not lower the ratings. The MDMA level was higher too (about 14 percent at the peak, 33 percent over the day), while heart rate rose less.

Some people feel little from an amount and take more. A slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ or a muting medicine can each be the reason. No trial tested what happened then.
The review's authors guess, without data, that bupropion with MDMA might raise the chance of seizures.
cl_mdma_antidepressants_other.rate: Three trials of 16 healthy volunteers each, known only through a review that did not check them, with some numbers read off graphs. Each medicine was tested only once.

cl_mdma_medicine_reports.short: In safety reports, ecstasy cases that also named an antidepressant ended in death more often.
cl_mdma_medicine_reports.but: Voluntary reports cannot show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.
how: In 946 US reports about ecstasy, those that also named an antidepressant had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome.
Reports naming other kinds of medicine had higher odds still: about 8 times for muscle relaxants and about 7 times for anesthetics.
In a survey of 216 adults, 76 in 100 who mixed ecstasy with an antidepressant still felt euphoria. They also reported more sweating, headache, dizziness and muscle stiffness.
The review's authors suggest, without data, that people whose effects were muted may have taken more.
cl_mdma_medicine_reports.rate: Voluntary reports to a US database of side effects, plus one survey, both known only through a review that gives no counts or margins of error. Such reports cannot show how often anything happens.

cl_mdma_psychiatric_medicines.short: Few other psychiatric medicines were tested with MDMA, and the results differ by medicine.
cl_mdma_psychiatric_medicines.but: Each was tested once in 14 to 16 healthy people, and the results come second-hand from a 2022 review.
how: Haloperidol, an antipsychotic, did not change heart rate or blood pressure. It lowered well-being by about 31 percent and raised anxiety by about 47 percent.
Methylphenidate, a stimulant, delayed MDMA's peak by about 46 percent. Carvedilol, a heart medicine, cut the rise in heart rate by about 79 percent.
The review found no controlled study of MAOIs, lithium or benzodiazepines with MDMA.
A slow start, as with methylphenidate, can leave a person feeling little, and some people then take more. No trial tested what happens then.
cl_mdma_psychiatric_medicines.rate: Small trials in healthy volunteers, one per medicine, known only through a review that did not check how well they were done. Some numbers were read off graphs.

cl_mdma_cyp2d6.short: MDMA seems to switch off the enzyme that clears it, so body differences matter less.
cl_mdma_cyp2d6.but: Only 7 people had no working enzyme, and no study gave a second dose of MDMA.
how: Among 139 volunteers in eight lab studies, the 7 with no working CYP2D6 had a peak MDMA level about 15 percent higher, in the first 3 hours only.
In 15 men, tests after one MDMA dose looked like those of people with no working enzyme in 10 of them. The enzyme had not fully recovered after 10 days.
Medicines that block the enzyme raised the MDMA peak by about 15 to 20 percent. Paroxetine raised it by 16 percent in 12 men.
Bodies that differ are one reason a person can feel little from an amount and take more. None of these studies gave a second dose, so what happens then is not known.
cl_mdma_cyp2d6.rate: Lab studies of healthy volunteers: only 7 people had no working enzyme, and the other studies had 15 and 12 men. One key study had no dummy-pill comparison.

cl_mdma_nonlinear.short: Yes, it seems so: a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher, and about twice the total over the day.
cl_mdma_nonlinear.but: Only 8 men were compared, in a lab, and the study was not planned to look at this.
how: In 8 men, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher and about twice the total over the day.
The kidneys cleared MDMA at the same pace at both doses; the rest of the body cleared it about half as fast at the larger one.
The authors suggest the breakdown gets saturated or that MDMA blocks the enzyme that clears it. They also say people may be more prone to acute toxicity; toxicity was not measured.

People can feel little from an amount for several reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, or bodies that differ. Some take more. These studies didn't test that.
cl_mdma_nonlinear.rate: One lab trial in which each of 8 men was his own comparison. Blood was tested directly, but this analysis was added afterwards, and with so few men the extra rise could be chance.

cl_mdma_pregnancy.short: One study counted birth defects after ecstasy in pregnancy, but it cannot show cause.
cl_mdma_pregnancy.but: There was no comparison group, and almost half of the enquiries were lost to follow-up.
how: A UK information service followed 136 pregnancies in which ecstasy was used, nearly all in the first 3 months. 62 of them also involved other drugs.
Of 78 babies born alive, 12 (about 15 in 100) had a birth defect, a mix of minor and major ones. The authors expected 2 to 3 in 100.
Two babies had heart defects and three had a twisted foot. The authors say the study is too small to confirm a link with any one defect.

A later study followed babies of 28 women who used ecstasy but did not report a count of birth defects. One baby had a rare genetic condition, which the authors say cannot be tied to the mother's drug use.
cl_mdma_pregnancy.rate: One UK service's records of 136 pregnancies from the 1990s, with no comparison group, and 45% were never followed up. Birth defects were reported second-hand, without the babies being examined.

cl_mdma_pregnancy_infants.short: At 1 and 4 months, babies of women who used ecstasy mostly scored the same.
cl_mdma_pregnancy_infants.but: The mothers also used more cocaine, cannabis, tobacco and alcohol, and only 22 exposed babies were seen.
how: 28 women used ecstasy in or just before pregnancy. Their babies were compared with babies of 68 women who used other drugs but not ecstasy in pregnancy.
At 1 month, average scores did not differ. Two patterns leaned toward more low-energy behavior (91 in 100 against 73 in 100) and less stiffness (9 against 27).

At 4 months, one movement-quality rating was lower in exposed babies (average 59 against 74), and more of them were boys (71 in 100 against 46 in 100). Mental and other movement scores were about the same.
The authors say heavier use went with lower scores. That compares only 13 heavier-use mothers with 15 lighter-use mothers, and the lighter-use babies scored above unexposed babies on two scales.
cl_mdma_pregnancy_infants.rate: One UK study of 96 women who used drugs in pregnancy; only 22 babies exposed to MDMA were seen. Their mothers also used other drugs much more, and use was self-reported.

cl_mix_cannabis_alcohol_driving.short: Cannabis with alcohol was linked to worse driving, about the sum of each.
cl_mix_cannabis_alcohol_driving.but: Neither study measures crash risk or impairment on a road.
how: In a driving simulator, 18 healthy adults had a usual lane weave of about 31 cm. A model of their driving gave a rise of 1.3 cm with cannabis (THC 5 µg/L in blood), 2.1 cm with alcohol (breath 0.05) and 3.4 cm with both.

In US records of drivers in fatal crashes who had a blood test, a model for a man aged 45 gave 64 in 100 with a recorded unsafe driving action at a blood alcohol of 0.05, and 66 in 100 if cannabis was also found. At 0.08 it was 70 and 71 in 100.
Both studies fit the two effects adding up, not clearly more. Other studies disagree on this.
A simulator is not a road, and a positive cannabis test shows it was in the blood, not that someone was impaired. Neither study asked how impaired drivers felt.
cl_mix_cannabis_alcohol_driving.rate: A driving-simulator study of 18 healthy adults and US records of fatal crashes, where only about one in five drivers was blood-tested and police notes stood in for who was at fault.

cl_mix_cannabis_driving_alone.short: Drivers with cannabis in a test were linked to more crashes.
cl_mix_cannabis_driving_alone.but: These studies compare crashed drivers with others, so they cannot show one driver's chance of crashing.
how: Across 28 results from 21 studies in 13 countries, drivers with cannabis found in a test had about 1.2 to 1.4 times the odds of a crash, or of being at fault in one.
An older review found 1.9 times. Re-checking its counts and allowing for other factors brought the same studies to between 1.2 and 1.4.
Studies that allowed for alcohol found 1.1 to 1.2 times. Studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8 times.
A positive test shows cannabis was in the body, not that a driver was impaired.
cl_mix_cannabis_driving_alone.rate: A review of 21 studies from 13 countries comparing drivers in crashes with others. Most barely took other differences into account, and the link shrank a lot once alcohol was considered.

cl_mix_ghb_alcohol.short: People who took GHB with alcohol were less awake more often at hospital.
cl_mix_ghb_alcohol.but: Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts were not known.
how: In 609 emergency patients who took GHB or GBL, 59 in 100 of those who also had alcohol were less awake, against 49 in 100 of those who did not. People who took other drugs were left out. Less awake means a Glasgow Coma Score under 13.
Of those kept in hospital, 55 in 100 with alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Across all patients, that is about 20 and 8 in 100.

Slow breathing (8 in 100 with alcohol, 12 without), breathing tubes (6 in 100 with alcohol, 4 without) and discharge did not clearly differ, but the study could not rule out a difference. Two people died, both with alcohol.
In 16 healthy volunteers, blood oxygen fell 2.1 points with both drugs, more than with either alone. That is a different measure from the patient study.
cl_mix_ghb_alcohol.rate: Hospital records of 609 emergency patients in Europe; the two groups differed in age and other ways not accounted for, and with about 33 comparisons, some results could be chance.

cl_mdma_feelings.short: Mostly good: in lab studies, 67 in 100 called it positive afterwards. It lasted about four hours. Many also got a dry mouth or a clenched jaw.
cl_mdma_feelings.but: These were healthy volunteers in a lab, given a known pill and nothing else.
how: In Basel labs, 136 healthy adults rated the good feeling about 80 out of 100, against 3 or 4 on a dummy pill. In a study of 32, people felt more open and closer to others.
Unwanted effects came too: 55 in 100 had a dry mouth and 40 in 100 of those asked clenched their jaw. Looking back, 67 in 100 called it positive, 15 in 100 disappointing or bad.
It began in about half an hour on average and lasted about four hours. For some the start was slow; an antidepressant given first cut the effect. Nobody took more, so that wasn't tested.
At a London club, people who took ecstasy weren't clearly happier than other clubbers. Two days later they felt sadder, but not a week later. Pills were untested, so MDMA's part is unclear.
cl_mdma_feelings.rate: Lab studies gave each volunteer both MDMA and a dummy pill, and the gap was huge. One step below strong, as most could tell which they'd had and rated their own feelings; the club study alone would rate very low.

cl_nic_nrt.short: Nicotine patches, gum and similar help people who want to stop smoking.
cl_nic_nrt.but: The gain is modest, and many trials were paid for by drug companies.
how: After 6 months or more, about 16 in 100 had stopped with nicotine replacement, against about 10 or 11 in 100 without.
The gain was bigger with a lot of support (about 8 more in 100) than with little (about 2 more).
Each form, from patches to sprays, did better than its own comparison.
These were people trying to stop, so the trials say nothing about anyone else.
cl_nic_nrt.rate: In 131 trials with 64,640 people, chance decided who got nicotine replacement. The best-run trials show the same effect, though some less favourable trials may never have been published.

cl_can_smoked_lungs.short: Smoking cannabis is linked to cough, phlegm and wheeze; light smoking didn't lower lung function.
cl_can_smoked_lungs.but: Many people also smoked tobacco, so the studies can't say how much comes from cannabis.
how: In two long-running studies, breathing symptoms eased in people who stopped.
In a 20-year study of about 5,000 adults, light cannabis smoking did not lower lung function; tobacco did.
Too few people smoked cannabis heavily for years to know what that does.
In one study, symptoms eased after a month of using a vaporizer instead of smoking, but it had no comparison group.
cl_can_smoked_lungs.rate: Surveys and long-term studies where people reported their own smoking and symptoms, and many also smoked tobacco. Lung-test results disagree between studies, and much is known only second-hand.

cl_can_edibles_children.short: Calls to US poison centres about young children eating edibles rose about 15 times over, 2017 to 2021.
cl_can_edibles_children.but: These are only the calls that were made, and the study can't say why the number rose.
how: Most of the children were 1 to 4 years old and ate the edible at home.
More than 1 in 5 were admitted to hospital, and 35 needed a breathing tube. No deaths were reported.
The authors suggest changes in the law, the pandemic or more calling, but the data can't separate these.
cl_can_edibles_children.rate: A national count of 7,043 calls to US poison centres. The numbers are large, but it counts only calls that were made, and records like these cannot show why numbers rise.

cl_alc_hangover_cognition.short: The morning after heavy drinking, people remembered less and reacted slower than on alcohol-free days.
cl_alc_hangover_cognition.but: The studies were small, and a short night's sleep may explain part of it.
how: Researchers gave people memory, attention and speed tests the morning after a night of heavy drinking.
They compared the results with a day without alcohol, mostly in the same people.
One review gathered 19 of these studies and combined the numbers from 11.
cl_alc_hangover_cognition.rate: Mostly small real-life studies, where people chose their drinking nights and knew they were hungover. Lab trials mostly found smaller or no effects, and several studies that found nothing were left out.

cl_alc_hangover_driving.short: Young drivers in a lab driving test drove worse after drinking nights than after alcohol-free nights.
cl_alc_hangover_driving.but: It was a driving machine in a lab, not real roads, and nobody checked how much they slept.
how: 52 young drivers did a short pretend drive to work, twice.
Once the morning after a night out drinking, and once after a night without alcohol.
Half had no alcohol left in their breath, and they still drove worse.
cl_alc_hangover_driving.rate: One lab driving study of 52 young drivers. They chose their own drinking nights, nobody recorded their drinking or sleep, and drivers and testers knew which morning was which.

cl_alc_water_hangover.short: In one small test, men felt no better next morning when they had water between drinks than when they drank the same sake without it.
cl_alc_water_hangover.but: Only 13 men took part, so a small benefit cannot be ruled out.
how: Each man drank the same sake twice: once with water in between, once without.
They rated headache, feeling sick and tiredness the next morning.
The company that made the sake paid for the study.
cl_alc_water_hangover.rate: One trial of just 13 Japanese men in a clinic, who knew when they had water and rated their own symptoms. Real nights out, where people drink as they choose, were not tested.

cl_alc_caffeinated_drinks_hangover.short: People who drank beer with added caffeine had about the same hangover as those without caffeine.
cl_alc_caffeinated_drinks_hangover.but: The study was small and did not test energy drinks.
how: 64 young adults drank beer in a lab, and chance decided who got caffeine added.
Everyone slept in the lab and rated their hangover and sleep in the morning.
cl_alc_caffeinated_drinks_hangover.rate: One lab study of 64 young adults: too few to be sure either way. It tested a single product, not energy drinks, and people slept a full night, unlike real nights out.

cl_alc_beer_wine_order_hangover.short: Drinking beer before wine or wine before beer gave about the same hangover.
cl_alc_beer_wine_order_hangover.but: Only one kind of beer and one white wine were tested.
how: Young adults drank beer and wine on two days, in a different order each time.
Doctors watched them, and they slept at the university.
Each person's hangover after one order was compared with their hangover after the other order.
cl_alc_beer_wine_order_hangover.rate: One trial of 90 healthy adults at a German university. They knew what they were drinking and scored their own hangovers, and too few took part to rule out a small difference.

cl_alc_hangover_remedy_use.short: Young adults who had used hangover pills reported more drinking problems than those who never had.
cl_alc_hangover_remedy_use.but: A one-time survey cannot show whether the pills cause heavier drinking.
how: 1312 young adults in Los Angeles who drink answered a survey.
Only 42 of them had ever used hangover pills.
Researchers compared their drinking with the people who had never used them.
cl_alc_hangover_remedy_use.rate: One survey of 1312 young adults in Los Angeles. Only 42 had used the pills, and the survey did not account for other differences, such as how often people got hangovers.

cl_alc_paracetamol_liver.short: In short trials, paracetamol at usual doses did not raise a liver test more than dummy pills; some trials saw small, short-lived rises later.
cl_alc_paracetamol_liver.but: Most people in the trials had just stopped heavy drinking, and no trial tested paracetamol for a hangover.
how: Five trials gave people who drink either paracetamol or a dummy pill.
Doctors checked a liver blood test, and nobody had liver failure.
The researchers had links to a paracetamol maker.
cl_alc_paracetamol_liver.rate: Five trials against dummy pills, largely from one team that shares authors with the review. Most people had just stopped heavy drinking, and the main measure was one early liver blood test.

cl_amph_withdrawal_medicines.short: In the four trials reviewed, no medicine clearly eased withdrawal or craving more than a dummy pill.
cl_amph_withdrawal_medicines.but: The review found only four small trials, so a small benefit could have been missed.
how: Four trials gave people starting treatment one of two medicines or a dummy pill (placebo).
One medicine helped people stay in treatment more than a dummy pill did, but it is no longer sold.
The other medicine did not help in the better trial; a smaller trial disagreed.
The review gave no side-effect results for any of the trials.
cl_amph_withdrawal_medicines.rate: Four small trials, 125 people in all: too few to be sure. The two trials of mirtazapine disagree, and the two medicines tested behaved differently.

cl_meth_next_night_sleep.short: After one of the larger doses, people slept less and worse that night than after a dummy dose.
cl_meth_next_night_sleep.but: This was one small hospital study with single doses, not binges.
how: Each person had a dummy dose (placebo) and three real doses, on different days.
A wrist monitor measured sleep in 6 people; all 11 said how they had slept.
With the biggest dose, the monitor showed about two hours less sleep than with the dummy dose, and more waking than with any other dose.
People felt their sleep was even shorter and worse than the monitor showed.
cl_meth_next_night_sleep.rate: One hospital study of 11 people, with wrist sleep trackers working for only 6. People may have recognised the drug, which matters when they rate their own sleep.

cl_meth_next_day.short: Next morning, the biggest dose left people less alert and friendly than a dummy dose.
cl_meth_next_day.but: Memory tests showed no change, but the study was small and printed no test results.
how: Eleven people took a dummy dose and real doses on different days in a hospital unit.
Next morning they rated their mood and did memory and attention tests.
After the biggest dose, their heart beat faster and blood pressure was higher than after the dummy dose.
They did not feel sadder or more worried, or want meth more.
cl_meth_next_day.rate: One lab study of 11 people, who also had a dummy for comparison. Too few to be sure, and people rating their own mood may have recognised the drug.

cl_meth_exercise_mood.short: In one trial, exercise went with slightly less sadness and worry than health classes.
cl_meth_exercise_mood.but: Both groups got much better, and people knew their group, so hope may explain part.
how: People in a live-in treatment centre were put by chance into exercise or health classes.
Every week they filled in questionnaires about sadness and worry.
Both groups improved a lot; the exercise group improved a little more.
The exercise group started out more worried, which can make a bigger drop look like an effect.
cl_meth_exercise_mood.rate: One trial of 135 people in residential treatment, who knew their group and rated their own mood. One group started more anxious, and the trial led with results it had planned as side questions.

cl_meth_exercise_craving.short: Studies report less craving with exercise than without, but the review that lists them does not say how much less.
cl_meth_exercise_craving.but: We know these studies only through one weak review that gives no numbers.
how: One review listed studies, mostly from compulsory drug rehabilitation centres in China.
The review says craving went down during and after exercise, compared with control groups.
The review says it checked study quality but reports no results.
It counted one trial three times.
cl_meth_exercise_craving.rate: Mostly trials, known only through one review that gives no numbers and gets some studies wrong. People rated their own craving and knew whether they exercised, mostly in compulsory rehab in China.

cl_coc_abstinence_sleep.short: Over three weeks off cocaine, measured sleep got worse while people felt they slept better.
cl_coc_abstinence_sleep.but: One small study of 20 people in a hospital unit; daytime light and withdrawal from other drugs were not controlled.
how: Twenty people with cocaine dependence slept in a sleep lab during their first weeks off cocaine.
Machines showed they took longer to fall asleep and slept less by the third week.
Dreaming (REM) sleep went down, while deep sleep went up a little.
Their own ratings of sleep got better, and were no worse than healthy men's.
cl_coc_abstinence_sleep.rate: One study of 20 people in a hospital research unit, with no comparison group followed over the same weeks. The unit's routine, like fixed bedtimes, could explain part of the change.

cl_coc_modafinil_sleep.short: In one small trial, modafinil helped people fall asleep faster than a dummy pill did.
cl_coc_modafinil_sleep.but: Only 20 people in hospital, and side effects like headache were more common on modafinil.
how: Half of 20 people took modafinil and half a dummy pill, without knowing which.
Machines in a sleep lab measured their sleep on several nights over three weeks.
People on modafinil had more deep sleep than those on the dummy pill and, in the third week, more sleep overall.
They did not feel they slept better, and the study did not check whether it helped them stay off cocaine.
cl_coc_modafinil_sleep.rate: One trial with only 10 people in each group. Side effects may have let people guess what they got, and with 13 things measured, some results could be flukes.

cl_opi_withdrawal_alpha2.short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, fewer people had bad withdrawal and more finished treatment.
cl_opi_withdrawal_alpha2.but: Only three small, old trials, mostly in hospital, and none with people coming off fentanyl.
how: Three trials gave people coming off heroin either the medicine or a dummy pill, picked by chance.
Bad withdrawal happened to about 19 in 100 on the medicine and about 59 in 100 on the dummy pill.
About 56 in 100 finished treatment on the medicine, against 29 in 100 on the dummy pill.
The medicine made some people sleepy or dizzy and lowered their blood pressure.
cl_opi_withdrawal_alpha2.rate: Three trials against dummy pills in three countries, all pointing the same way, even without the weakest one. But only 148 people took part, too few to pin down the size.

cl_opi_withdrawal_alpha2_vs_methadone.short: No clear difference in how many people finished, but clonidine-type medicines caused more low blood pressure and other side effects.
cl_opi_withdrawal_alpha2_vs_methadone.but: The trials were small and some were badly run, so the answer could change.
how: Twelve trials compared clonidine-type medicines with methadone given in slowly shrinking amounts.
Withdrawal felt about as bad overall, but it started and ended sooner with clonidine-type medicines.
Low blood pressure and other side effects were about twice as common as with methadone.
Neither way seemed to take away all the aches, bad sleep and worry.
cl_opi_withdrawal_alpha2_vs_methadone.rate: In 12 small trials from several countries, chance decided which medicine people got. Without the worst-run trials, the extra side effects are no longer clear, and few people had them.

cl_opi_withdrawal_buprenorphine.short: Yes: more people finished withdrawal treatment with buprenorphine than with clonidine or lofexidine.
cl_opi_withdrawal_buprenorphine.but: No trial reported people coming off fentanyl, and two stopped early, which may have skewed the results.
how: Fourteen trials put people coming off opioids, mostly heroin, on buprenorphine or on clonidine or lofexidine, by chance.
About 72 in 100 finished treatment on buprenorphine, against about 45 in 100 on the other medicines.
On buprenorphine, withdrawal was milder on average and people stayed in treatment longer than on the other medicines.
There was no clear difference in how many had side effects, but they differed: headache with buprenorphine, dizziness and dry mouth with clonidine.
cl_opi_withdrawal_buprenorphine.rate: In 11 trials with 1264 people, chance decided which medicine people got, and all point the same way. But how big the difference is varies a lot from trial to trial.

cl_opi_withdrawal_buprenorphine_vs_metha.short: They worked about the same: similar numbers of people finished withdrawal treatment with each.
cl_opi_withdrawal_buprenorphine_vs_metha.but: Only six small trials, mostly in hospitals or a prison.
how: Six trials compared buprenorphine with methadone given in slowly shrinking amounts.
About 55 in 100 finished on buprenorphine and about 53 in 100 on methadone.
The trials could not show whether withdrawal felt different with one or the other.
cl_opi_withdrawal_buprenorphine_vs_metha.rate: Five trials of 457 people counted who finished treatment, a plain fact rather than someone's judgment, and agree. But they can't rule out about 11 more, or 5 fewer, finishing out of every 100.

cl_fent_withdrawal_severity.short: In one study, people coming off fentanyl had worse withdrawal than people coming off other opioids, such as heroin.
cl_fent_withdrawal_severity.but: The two groups were studied ten years apart, so something other than fentanyl may explain it.
how: 30 people who had used fentanyl were compared with 103 people who had used heroin or similar drugs ten years earlier.
Both groups got the same medicine on the same research ward, but only the fentanyl group could also get extra medicines for symptoms.
The fentanyl group's withdrawal got worse over the first days before easing, while the other group's eased from the start.
A fast heartbeat happened to 43 in 100 in the fentanyl group, against 19 in 100 in the other group.
cl_fent_withdrawal_severity.rate: One study at one Baltimore unit, with only 30 people in the fentanyl group, compared with people treated about a decade earlier. Everyone was getting treatment for withdrawal.

cl_mph_sleep_problems.short: Children on methylphenidate had sleep problems recorded more often than children on a dummy pill.
cl_mph_sleep_problems.but: The review says how many times more often, not how many children out of 100.
how: A review combined 35 trials in children and teenagers with ADHD.
Trouble falling asleep was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine as with the dummy pill.
Who recorded sleep problems, and whether a questionnaire was used, changed how big the difference looked.
A drug company paid for the review, and two of the authors work for its parent company.
cl_mph_sleep_problems.rate: A review of 35 trials against dummy pills, about 5700 young people, funded by a manufacturer. It did not check the trials, and single trials' results varied widely.

cl_mdma_night_sleep.short: After MDMA, people slept about two hours less than with a dummy pill, and had very little dreaming (REM) sleep.
cl_mdma_night_sleep.but: Only 7 people, one dose, in a quiet sleep lab, not a night out.
how: Seven people slept in a sleep lab after MDMA one night and after a dummy pill another night.
After MDMA they took much longer to fall asleep than after the dummy pill.
Dreaming (REM) sleep almost disappeared that night, then came back the next night.
A short night without MDMA did not remove dreaming sleep in the same way.
cl_mdma_night_sleep.rate: One sleep-lab study of just 7 people, after two of nine dropped out, with no check on whether they could tell MDMA from the dummy pill.

cl_mdma_next_day_sleepiness.short: We don't know: next-day sleepiness after MDMA was not clearly different from a dummy pill.
cl_mdma_next_day_sleepiness.but: Only 7 people were tested, too few to rule out a difference.
how: The next day, people lay down for short naps to see how fast they fell asleep.
After a short night in bed, they fell asleep faster than after a full night with the dummy pill.
After MDMA, they took about as long to fall asleep as after the dummy pill.
They were not asked how tired they felt, and mood and thinking were not tested the next day.
cl_mdma_next_day_sleepiness.rate: One sleep-lab study of only 7 people, each tested after MDMA and after a dummy pill. The MDMA results appear only in a graph, with no exact numbers.

cl_dxm_impairment_duration.short: After the highest doses, balance and coordination were still affected at the day's last test, while other effects were wearing off.
cl_dxm_impairment_duration.but: Testing stopped there, so nobody knows when it ended, and nobody was tested next day.
how: Twelve experienced volunteers took DXM, a sleeping pill or a dummy pill on different days.
They did balance and button-pressing tests several times each day.
DXM affected these tests for longer than the sleeping pill did.
More than half vomited at least once at the higher doses.
cl_dxm_impairment_duration.rate: One lab study of just 12 volunteers. The sessions came in a set order rather than by chance, people could often tell what they had, and some results are missing.

cl_dxm_month_after.short: A month later, no one reported lasting upset or lasting changes in what they saw or heard.
cl_dxm_month_after.but: Only 12 carefully chosen volunteers, in a calm lab; people with psychosis or bipolar illness, themselves or in close family, could not take part.
how: Twelve prepared volunteers had DXM, a sleeping pill or a dummy pill on different days.
They came back about a month after their last session and filled in a questionnaire.
They also reported good changes, but the questionnaire could not separate DXM days from the other days.
One person asked not to have that dose again; they had a headache after the session that they put down to DXM.
cl_dxm_month_after.rate: One study of 12 volunteers who filled in a questionnaire about a month later. It covered all their sessions at once, and their expectations and the calm setting may have shaped answers.

cl_opi_sleep.short: Studies in one review found shorter, lighter sleep in the first weeks after stopping heroin than in good sleepers.
cl_opi_sleep.but: This comes second-hand from a review that did not check how good the studies were.
how: Sleep labs recorded people in their first weeks off heroin and compared them with good sleepers.
They slept less, slept more lightly, and took longer to fall asleep.
Many people on methadone also sleep badly, and long-term opioid use is linked with pauses in breathing during sleep.
cl_opi_sleep.rate: At least two sleep-lab studies agree, but we know them only through one review that did not check their quality, so every figure is second-hand.

cl_alc_sleep_stopping.short: Alcohol can help people fall asleep at first, but studies in one review found long heavy drinking leaves sleep poor for months.
cl_alc_sleep_stopping.but: This comes second-hand from a review that did not check how good the studies were.
how: Sleep labs compared people who had drunk heavily for a long time with good sleepers.
Many slept badly while drinking and for weeks or months after stopping, with less deep sleep.
In several studies, people who said they slept badly soon after stopping were more likely to drink again than those who did not.
cl_alc_sleep_stopping.rate: Several studies of people who drank heavily for a long time, seen only through one overview article. So the figures are second-hand, and we could not check how well the studies were done.

cl_can_sleep_stopping.short: Studies in one review found that many people who used cannabis regularly sleep badly after stopping, often with strange dreams.
cl_can_sleep_stopping.but: This comes second-hand from a review that did not check how good the studies were.
how: Studies asked people how they slept after stopping regular cannabis, and some recorded their sleep in a lab.
Between about a third and three quarters of those with withdrawal symptoms had sleep problems, often with strange dreams for days or weeks.
In the lab they took longer to fall asleep and woke up more than before they stopped.
Poor sleep was linked with going back to cannabis.
cl_can_sleep_stopping.rate: Many studies of people who stopped agree, but we know them only through one review that did not check their quality, so every figure is second-hand.

cl_xc_sleep_medicines.short: Some helped sleep, but better sleep did not reliably help people stay off drugs.
cl_xc_sleep_medicines.but: This comes second-hand from a review that did not check how good the studies were.
how: Studies gave sleep medicines to people stopping a drug, some comparing them with a dummy pill.
For alcohol, gabapentin mostly helped, but in one big trial trazodone was linked with more drinking than a dummy pill.
For cannabis, several sleep medicines helped sleep, but none clearly helped people stay off it.
For opioids, trazodone did not help people on methadone sleep better.
cl_xc_sleep_medicines.rate: Mostly trials, but known only through one review that did not check them or give sizes, and results differ between medicines and measures.

cl_ghb_driving.short: Soon after GHB, people crashed far more in a driving test than after a dummy drink.
cl_ghb_driving.but: Only 16 people who had rarely or never used GHB, one dose, no alcohol, in a lab driving machine.
how: 16 healthy adults used a lab driving machine after GHB on one day and after a dummy drink on another.
On the first drive after GHB, every one of them crashed more than after the dummy drink.
Later drives that day were not clearly worse than after the dummy drink, but this small study cannot show when driving is safe again.
Four people threw up after GHB and could not finish the first drive after it, so they were left out.
cl_ghb_driving.rate: One trial of 16 people in a driving machine. They could probably tell GHB from the dummy drink, and four who felt sick after GHB were replaced by others.

cl_ghb_thinking_after.short: GHB affects memory while it works; in one study, people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than other people who used GHB or other drugs.
cl_ghb_thinking_after.but: That one Dutch study cannot show GHB caused the memory problems, and nobody checked if they improve.
how: Lab studies found that GHB affects memory and coordination while it is working.
The review says it is not yet known whether these short-term memory effects fully wear off.
One study found that people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs but never GHB.
cl_ghb_thinking_after.rate: One Dutch study of 81 people, tested once, with no stated allowance for other differences between them. We know it only through a review that gives no numbers for the gap.

cl_xc_afterglow.short: Often better than before: less low mood and stress, more wellbeing, in most studies that checked. Some people got headaches, usually for a day or two, or slept badly.
cl_xc_afterglow.but: Most studies had no blind dummy-pill group, so nobody knows the cause, and most were supported sessions, not recreational use.
how: A review gathered 48 studies of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, with 1,774 people in all. People answered the same questionnaires before, and again a day to a month after.
Most studies that checked (70 to 90 in 100) found less depression and stress, and more wellbeing, mindfulness and closeness to others. None found mental health worse on average.
Of 25 studies that said they looked for problems, 14 found some: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then poor sleep, tension and exhaustion.
One person had severe anxiety, and one went back to using methamphetamine. Half the studies didn't say whether they looked for problems at all.
cl_xc_afterglow.rate: 48 studies, most without a dummy-pill comparison, in supportive settings. The review only counted which studies found a change, not how big, and side effects were reported unevenly.

cl_xc_flashbacks.short: About 1 in 11 lab volunteers reported a short flashback, mostly in the days after.
cl_xc_flashbacks.but: These were healthy, screened volunteers in labs, with no drug-free group to compare.
how: 142 healthy adults took LSD, psilocybin or both in lab studies in Switzerland.
At the end, 13 said they had had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.
Most did not mind it; 2 people were upset by it.
Nobody was found to have the long-lasting vision condition doctors call HPPD.
cl_xc_flashbacks.rate: One look across six trials from one Basel group, 142 screened volunteers. Flashbacks were asked about with one open question, not a standard checklist, so the true figure could be higher or lower.

cl_opi_loperamide_heart.short: It can be: some people who took very large amounts got serious heart-rhythm problems.
cl_opi_loperamide_heart.but: These were only people seen by poisons doctors, who tend to see the sicker cases, and there was no group to compare with, so the study cannot show how often this happens.
how: Doctors who treat poisonings in the USA described 26 people seen after taking loperamide; 20 of them had symptoms.
Some took it to stop withdrawal, some to feel good, and a few were young children who swallowed it by accident.
About 4 in 10 had a change on their heart tracing that can lead to a dangerous heartbeat; some needed a breathing tube or a pacemaker, and no deaths were reported.
Where the amount was recorded, the people with these heart problems had taken far more than the packet says.
cl_opi_loperamide_heart.rate: Records of 26 people seen by poisons doctors, who see the sickest cases. No test confirmed loperamide, heart tracings were not rechecked, and one or two cases change the percentages.

cl_opi_constipation_medicines.short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, more people's constipation got better.
cl_opi_constipation_medicines.but: Nearly all the trials were in people taking opioids for pain; only one also included people dependent on opioids, so they say little about people using heroin or on methadone or buprenorphine treatment.
how: 27 trials gave people either a medicine or a dummy pill, chosen by chance.
About 52 in 100 got better on a medicine, against 33 in 100 on the dummy pill.
In separate trials against a dummy pill, medicines that block opioids in the gut did better than the prescription laxative lubiprostone; no trial compared them directly.
Diarrhoea and tummy pain were more common on the medicines than on the dummy pill, and slightly more people stopped them because of side effects (about 7 in 100 against 5 in 100).
cl_opi_constipation_medicines.rate: A review of 27 trials with 8881 people, from many teams, points the same way, even in the most careful trials. But small trials showed bigger benefits, so the real benefit may be smaller.

cl_opi_methadone_withdrawal_between_dose.short: In one small study, their methadone level tended to drop faster after its daily high point.
cl_opi_methadone_withdrawal_between_dose.but: Only 18 people were tested for one day, and by our check the difference fell just short of statistical significance, even after the authors left two people out.
how: Nine people who felt withdrawal before their next dose were compared with nine who did not.
Just before the dose, both groups had about the same level of methadone in their blood.
On average, in both groups, withdrawal was lowest in the hours after the dose and grew as the level fell.
The study did not test any change to treatment.
cl_opi_methadone_withdrawal_between_dose.rate: One study of 18 people on methadone, grouped by what they said they felt. Too few to be sure, and the key difference appeared only after two people were left out.

cl_pop_eye_damage.short: It seems so, in some people: reports describe blurry central vision and damage at the back of the eye.
cl_pop_eye_damage.but: These are uncontrolled reports of people who saw an eye doctor, so they cannot prove poppers were the cause, or show how often it happens or which poppers do it.
how: Doctors in at least 12 countries have written about 113 people with eye problems after poppers, some after using them once.
Most had both eyes affected: blurry or dim vision in the middle, flashes of light, or a blank spot.
In most people scanned, the scans showed damage to the light-sensing cells at the centre of the retina, at the back of the eye.
Of the people who had a second scan, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing.
cl_pop_eye_damage.rate: A review of 32 reports describing 113 patients in at least 12 countries. Only published cases are included, use was self-reported, and the product was mostly unknown.

cl_benzo_hypnotic_next_day_driving.short: Some benzodiazepine sleeping pills made people drive worse the next day than after dummy pills.
cl_benzo_hypnotic_next_day_driving.but: Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers, not people who take these pills for months.
how: Volunteers drove a real car or a driving machine the day after a pill or a dummy pill.
Researchers measured how much the car weaved inside its lane.
With some pills the weaving was worse than with alcohol at the driving limit used in several countries.
With other pills or lower doses, weaving was not clearly different from dummy pills, but each result came from one small study.
cl_benzo_hypnotic_next_day_driving.rate: Driving tests, mostly in healthy volunteers after one night, rather than real crashes or people who take these pills every night. Some trials had flaws or were paid for by drug makers.

cl_benzo_hypnotic_residual_tolerance.short: For most pills the morning effect seemed smaller after several nights than after the first, but for some it lasted or grew over a week.
cl_benzo_hypnotic_residual_tolerance.but: The studies were small and short, and none followed people for more than about two weeks.
how: Volunteers took a pill or a dummy pill every night for a few nights.
With flurazepam, driving got slightly worse over the week, not better.
Other pills behaved differently, so there is no single answer.
cl_benzo_hypnotic_residual_tolerance.rate: A few small trials, some seen only through one researcher's overview of mostly their own team's work. The pills behaved differently, and each was tested in one trial.

cl_benzo_hypnotic_accident_risk.short: Some studies found more crashes and falls soon after people started sleeping pills than without them; others did not.
cl_benzo_hypnotic_accident_risk.but: These studies watched what happened and cannot prove the pills caused the accidents.
how: Researchers compared people taking these pills with people not taking them.
The risk looked highest in the first weeks after starting.
Older people taking these pills had more falls than those not taking them.
cl_benzo_hypnotic_accident_risk.rate: Second-hand figures from one review, from studies of the 1970s to about 2002. The studies disagree, and the reasons people were given the pills could explain part of the link.

cl_benzo_hypnotic_morning_caffeine.short: After a sleeping pill, morning caffeine left young men less sleepy than a dummy capsule did.
cl_benzo_hypnotic_morning_caffeine.but: Their test scores were not clearly better, and this study did not test driving.
how: 80 young men slept in a lab after a sleeping pill or a dummy pill.
In the morning they got either caffeine or a dummy capsule.

On four sleepiness measures taken together, the caffeine groups were less sleepy than matching groups given a dummy capsule; on the nap test alone, the difference was clear only after the higher flurazepam dose.
cl_benzo_hypnotic_morning_caffeine.rate: One trial of 80 healthy young men, only ten per group. They were good sleepers who usually had little caffeine, not people who take sleeping pills for sleep problems.

cl_alc_hangover_mood.short: People felt more anxious and low when hungover than when sober, and also described guilt.
cl_alc_hangover_mood.but: The review does not say how big the changes were, and poor sleep or regret may explain part of them.
how: One review gathered 22 studies with over 6,000 people, mostly young adults.
In most studies, people rated their mood when hungover and when sober or before drinking.
Most studies found worse mood when hungover, but two found no clear change in anxiety, at least for some people.
cl_alc_hangover_mood.rate: In 22 studies, mostly from real life, people rated their own mood while knowing they were hungover. The review gives no sizes, only how many studies found a change.

cl_alc_hangover_mood_coping.short: No study in the review tested a way to ease hangover worry; people said sharing the hangover with friends helped.
cl_alc_hangover_mood_coping.but: These are people's own stories, not tests, so we cannot say what really helps.
how: Researchers interviewed about a hundred young adults about their hangovers.
Many felt bad about things they did while drunk or could not remember.
No study compared people who tried something with people who did not.
cl_alc_hangover_mood_coping.rate: Interviews with three small groups of mostly students (66, 23 and 20 people) and one survey. No one compared groups or tested whether anything actually helps.

cl_alc_sleep_rem.short: After drinking, dream sleep started later and was shorter than on nights without alcohol.
cl_alc_sleep_rem.but: These were small sleep-lab studies, and the results were not the same in every study.
how: Researchers measured sleep in a sleep lab with sensors on people's heads.
In most studies, the same people slept one night after alcohol and one night without it.
The more people drank, the more dream sleep they lost.
cl_alc_sleep_rem.rate: 27 sleep-lab studies compared nights with and without alcohol in the same people. Many had flaws, like everyone having the nights in the same order, and results varied between studies.

cl_alc_sleep_onset.short: On average, alcohol before bed did not help people fall asleep faster than on nights without alcohol.
cl_alc_sleep_onset.but: Whether it changes how long people sleep is unclear, because the studies disagreed.
how: 27 small sleep-lab studies were put together in one review.
On average, falling asleep took about the same time with or without alcohol.
Only after larger amounts was falling asleep a little quicker.
In three of five studies, people felt they fell asleep faster after alcohol.
cl_alc_sleep_onset.rate: In 27 sleep-lab studies, the same people slept on nights with and without alcohol. But 11 studies had flaws, such as not fixing time in bed, and results for total sleep vary widely.

cl_caf_sleep_that_night.short: After caffeine, people slept about 45 minutes less than on nights without caffeine.
cl_caf_sleep_that_night.but: The people studied were healthy adults with low to moderate usual caffeine intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.
how: 24 studies compared nights after caffeine with nights without it, in the same people.
Caffeine made falling asleep slower, time awake in the night longer, and sleep lighter.
The more caffeine, and the closer to bedtime, the more sleep people lost.
In five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.
cl_caf_sleep_that_night.rate: 24 sleep-lab studies, mostly of young men who usually had little caffeine, so people used to it may differ. Studies that found nothing may never have been published, and the review did not check.

cl_caf_withdrawal_headache.short: Without their usual caffeine, half got a headache by evening; people given caffeine pills did not.
cl_caf_withdrawal_headache.but: Only 40 hospital patients took part, and surgery itself can also cause headaches.
how: 40 people who drank lots of caffeine had to stop it before a small operation.
Half got caffeine pills and half got identical dummy pills, and neither the patients nor the doctor checking symptoms knew which.
By evening, 10 of the 20 with dummy pills had a headache, and none with caffeine.
cl_caf_withdrawal_headache.rate: One trial where chance decided who got caffeine or dummy pills, and no one knew which. But only 40 surgery patients took part, and the report leaves out details and has errors.

cl_caf_periop_tablets.short: In one small trial, fewer patients given caffeine pills had headaches after surgery than patients given dummy pills.
cl_caf_periop_tablets.but: The trial was small, so it cannot show whether the pills are safe for everyone.
how: The patients were people who usually had a lot of caffeine every day.
Nurses gave either caffeine pills or identical dummy pills around the operation.
The amount and acidity of stomach fluid, which caffeine can raise, did not differ significantly between the groups.
cl_caf_periop_tablets.rate: One trial of 40 surgery patients: too few to be sure, especially about side effects. The report also leaves out how people were put into groups and who dropped out.

cl_nic_abstinence_symptoms.short: After stopping smoking, people can feel grumpy, anxious and restless, and wake more at night, for weeks.
cl_nic_abstinence_symptoms.but: This comes from one expert's summary of older studies; it does not say how many people get each feeling.
how: The studies asked the same people how they felt before and after they stopped smoking.
Most of these feelings were strongest in the first week and gone within 2 to 4 weeks.
Feeling tired, headaches and sweating did not go up after stopping.
For some people the feelings lasted longer or came back after about three weeks.
cl_nic_abstinence_symptoms.rate: Studies by several teams that followed people after they quit, seen through one expert's review. Almost none had a comparison group, and people rated their own feelings.

cl_coc_crash.short: After a binge, people described a crash: very low mood, then long, heavy sleep and hunger.
cl_coc_crash.but: This is what some people in treatment told their doctors; it cannot show how often it happens.
how: Doctors talked with 30 people who came for help with heavy cocaine use; there was no comparison group.
The crash began soon after the last use and usually ended within a few days.
Some people had passing thoughts of suicide, which were limited to the crash.
Many had used alcohol or other drugs to get to sleep.
cl_coc_crash.rate: One clinic's description of 14 people in treatment in the early 1980s. Therapists rated the crash without a standard scale, and some details come from people's memories.

cl_coc_first_weeks.short: In a closed research unit, men's low mood and craving were worst on the first day and eased over the next weeks.
cl_coc_first_weeks.but: Only 12 men were studied, in a place with no cocaine and nothing to remind them of it.
how: The men were compared with 10 men with no history of drug problems, living in the same unit.
Most of the improvement came in the first two weeks.
Their reported sleep was much like the other men's, except that falling asleep was harder and feeling clear-headed on waking improved more.
An older study of people stopping at home described craving coming back after a few calm days.
cl_coc_first_weeks.rate: One study of 12 men in a locked research unit, compared with ten men without dependence. An earlier report on outpatients described craving coming back, so the two disagree.

cl_mph_sleep_objective.short: On stimulant medicine, children took longer to fall asleep and slept less than on nights without it, sleep monitors showed.
cl_mph_sleep_objective.but: The review did not say by how many minutes, and mostly compared with nights before treatment began.
how: Nine studies used wrist monitors or sleep-lab tests in children and teenagers with ADHD.
Nights on medicine were compared with nights without medicine.
The medicines were methylphenidate and amphetamine-type medicines.
In studies where children had taken the medicine for longer, the effect on the share of time in bed spent asleep looked smaller, but this does not prove sleep gets better.
cl_mph_sleep_objective.rate: 9 small studies measured children's sleep with monitors, but mostly compared medicine nights with nights before treatment began, not with dummy pills. Studies that found smaller effects may never have been published.

cl_mph_insomnia_melatonin.short: Children on ADHD medicine fell asleep about 16 minutes sooner with melatonin than with a dummy pill.
cl_mph_insomnia_melatonin.but: This was one small study of 19 children, paid for by the company that made the melatonin.
how: Each child took melatonin on some nights and a dummy pill on others, without knowing which.
Doctors did not see a bigger overall improvement with melatonin than with the dummy pill.
Reported health problems were mild or moderate, apart from one severe migraine, and about as common with the dummy pill.
All the children had first tried a bedtime routine that had not fixed their sleep.
cl_mph_insomnia_melatonin.rate: A small trial where each child had melatonin and a dummy pill, with chance deciding the order. But its figures don't match the 19 children it reports, and its plan wasn't made public beforehand.

cl_mdma_next_day_field.short: People felt very tired and had slept less, but were not sadder than others.
cl_mdma_next_day_field.but: Two small studies; nobody tested the pills or measured sleep with a machine.
how: In London, 12 people who took ecstasy at a club were compared with 12 people who only drank alcohol.
The next day the ecstasy group felt much more tired and low on energy, and did worse at a sums test.
In Melbourne, people who took ecstasy slept about two hours less than people who use ecstasy but skipped it that week.
In both studies, mood the next day was about the same as in the other group.
cl_mdma_next_day_field.rate: Two small real-life studies where people chose whether to use and rated their own mood; one had no measure from before. A small dip in mood could be missed.

cl_mdma_midweek_low.short: Two small studies disagree, so they cannot say how often a mid-week low happens.
cl_mdma_midweek_low.but: Both studies were small, and only one measured people before they took ecstasy.
how: A London study found people who took ecstasy felt sadder mid-week than people who only drank alcohol.
That study did not measure anyone before the night out, and did not count how many felt low.
A Melbourne study measured people a week before and found no difference from people who use ecstasy but skipped it.
In that study, people who slept badly felt worse, looking at both groups together.
cl_mdma_midweek_low.rate: Two small studies of 24 and 56 people. People chose whether to take ecstasy, the groups differed in age and other drug use, and nobody checked what was taken.

cl_lsd_next_day_thinking.short: A few small changes, some better and some worse, which may just be chance.
cl_lsd_next_day_thinking.but: One study of 24 people after one small lab dose; this report gives no mood or sleep data.
how: People took LSD on one day and a dummy drink (placebo) on another, in random order.
The next morning, a few memory and word tests went a little better after LSD.
One card-sorting puzzle about switching rules went a little worse after LSD.
The researchers checked many scores without allowing for that, so some differences may be luck.
cl_lsd_next_day_thinking.rate: One trial of 24 volunteers, each tested after LSD and after a dummy. It checked about 66 measures and picked its analysis after a first look, so a few differences could be chance.

cl_pcp_prolonged_psychosis.short: In three reported cases, a severe breakdown lasted two to four weeks, then passed.
cl_pcp_prolonged_psychosis.but: Only three cases from 1975, and nobody tested the drugs they had taken.
how: Three young men were treated in one hospital after street drugs thought to contain PCP.
They were confused, angry and unsteady, two heard voices, and one jumped from a high window.
All three got better, and afterwards remembered little of their illness.
Earlier studies the doctors cited said the mind effects of PCP usually last about a day.
cl_pcp_prolonged_psychosis.rate: Reports of three young men at one hospital, with no drug tests and no mental-health history given, so neither what they took nor the cause is known.

cl_pcp_psychosis_treatment.short: Nobody knows: in three cases, the medicines did not seem to shorten it.
cl_pcp_psychosis_treatment.but: Three cases, with no comparison between treatments or with no treatment.
how: Two men were given medicines for psychosis, which did not visibly help.
The third man's medicine was stopped after he had fits.
One man calmed down when he was put in a dim, quiet room.
All three got better within a few weeks, one after he left hospital.
cl_pcp_psychosis_treatment.rate: Three case reports of young men in one US hospital, with no comparison. They might have recovered on their own anyway.

cl_can_thc_impairment_duration.short: For several hours; probably longer after eating it than smoking it, and longer after bigger doses.
cl_can_thc_impairment_duration.but: These are averages from lab studies, not a safe time to drive for you.
how: Researchers pooled 80 studies in which people took THC or a dummy (placebo), then did driving and attention tests.
Soon after THC, people weaved more in their lane and reacted more slowly than after the dummy.
The effects faded over several hours, probably more slowly when THC was eaten than when it was smoked or vaped.
People who use cannabis weekly or more were less affected than people who use it less often, but the study could not work out for how long.
cl_can_thc_impairment_duration.rate: Many lab trials, but how long effects last is a calculated estimate. It differs a lot between driving skills, gives no range, and rests on little data beyond about 4 hours.

cl_can_sleep_lab.short: In sleep labs, cannabis taken by mouth did not reliably change sleep, compared with a dummy pill or with sleep before treatment.
cl_can_sleep_lab.but: Most were CBD or mild THC medicines for people with sleep problems; smoking was not tested.
how: Six studies compared cannabis medicines swallowed by mouth with a dummy pill (placebo) or with sleep before treatment.
Sleep length, time to fall asleep, waking in the night and deep sleep did not change.
Results for dream (REM) sleep did not agree with each other.
Small early studies (1972 to 1982), mostly with high doses of THC, often found less dream sleep.
cl_can_sleep_lab.rate: Sleep-lab studies with 178 people in all, mostly trials. The review lumped CBD and THC products and different patient groups together, and too few people took part to rule out small effects.

cl_can_stopping_sleep_lab.short: Sleep got shorter and slower to start, with more dream sleep, in the first nights.
cl_can_stopping_sleep_lab.but: Three small studies, two of them from the 1970s with very strong lab doses.
how: Sleep was measured in a lab while people were still using cannabis and after they stopped.
After stopping, they slept less, took longer to fall asleep and had more dream (REM) sleep.
The pooled data came from the first week after stopping, so this review cannot say how long the changes last.
cl_can_stopping_sleep_lab.rate: Three small sleep-lab studies, about 38 people, with no separate comparison group. Two had people stop THC given in a lab rather than their usual cannabis, and only the first week was studied.

cl_can_chs_capsaicin.short: Nobody knows yet: in small studies it sometimes helped and sometimes did not.
cl_can_chs_capsaicin.but: One small fair test and four weaker studies, mostly at moderate to high risk of bias.
how: Cannabis hyperemesis means being sick again and again in some people who use a lot of cannabis.
In one small fair test, the cream did not ease sickness more than a dummy cream at the first check.
A few more people felt fully better with the cream, and sickness was lower at a later check.
Other studies disagreed; in one, more people given the cream than not given it were admitted to hospital, a difference that could be chance.
cl_can_chs_capsaicin.rate: One small trial of about 30 patients, which lost people and changed its rules midway, and four studies that looked back at hospital records. Their results disagree.

cl_can_chs_dopamine_antagonists.short: In two small studies, haloperidol eased sickness more than a usual anti-sickness medicine, and people given haloperidol or droperidol went home sooner than people given other care.
cl_can_chs_dopamine_antagonists.but: Only two small studies, and both medicines can cause sudden muscle spasms.
how: In a small fair test, haloperidol was compared with a usual anti-sickness medicine (ondansetron).
With haloperidol, pain and sickness eased more and people left hospital sooner.
In hospital records, people given droperidol left sooner than people not given it.
A few people had sudden muscle spasms (dystonia) after these medicines.
cl_can_chs_dopamine_antagonists.rate: One small trial of 30 patients, some lost along the way, and a look back at 76 patients' hospital records, where chance did not decide who got the medicine.

cl_scb_hangover_vs_cannabis.short: People who had used both said synthetic cannabis gave a slightly worse hangover.
cl_scb_hangover_vs_cannabis.but: These are memories from a 2011 online survey; nobody tested the products.
how: About a thousand people who had used both compared them in an online survey.
They said synthetic cannabis made it harder to get on with things afterwards.
They said it gave more bad feelings and fear of others while high, and much less enjoyment.
Most preferred ordinary cannabis, and said synthetic cannabis wore off sooner.
cl_scb_hangover_vs_cannabis.rate: One 2011 online survey of people who chose to answer, rating both from memory; ratings may follow which they preferred. These are impressions, not measured after-effects.

cl_dc_fts_detects_fentanyl.short: Almost always, in lab tests: 98 in 100 seized drug samples with fentanyl showed it on the strip.
cl_dc_fts_detects_fentanyl.but: Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand. Testing at home was not studied.
how: Two labs tested strips on 106 police-seized drug samples that had fentanyl. The strips showed it in 104.
A lab machine had already found fentanyl in all of these samples. Samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way.
Strips can find very small amounts of fentanyl. But the smallest amount found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches.
It also depended on how a faint line was read. Trained staff did all of these tests.

freq.what: seized samples with fentanyl showed it on the strip
freq.note: 104 of 106 police-seized samples in which a lab machine had already found fentanyl. One brand, read by trained staff in two labs, 2017.

cl_dc_fts_detects_fentanyl.rate: Teams in five labs agree. But the main check sorted 210 drug samples with a lab test that spots traces less well than the strip, so samples with only traces were left out.

cl_dc_fts_false_positives.short: Sometimes. Large amounts of meth, MDMA or two medicines made strips positive with no fentanyl there.
cl_dc_fts_false_positives.but: These were lab tests, mostly of one drug at a time. How often it happens when people test their own drugs is not known.
how: Of 104 seized samples in which a lab machine found no fentanyl, 6 still read positive on the strip.
In the lab, strong solutions of meth or MDMA turned strips positive. So did two medicines, diphenhydramine and lidocaine. Cocaine and several other drugs did not.
It took thousands of times more of these drugs than the smallest amount of fentanyl the same strips could find.

With take-home strips, 28 in 100 crystal meth samples showed fentanyl, against 5 in 100 other samples tested on site by staff. The authors think most were false positives. No lab checked these results.

freq.what: seized samples in which a lab machine found no fentanyl still read positive
freq.note: 6 of 104 samples, one brand, two labs. Some may have held fentanyl, or a related drug, in amounts too small for the lab machine to find.

cl_dc_fts_false_positives.rate: Four lab studies, mostly of single substances in water rather than messier street samples, with one or two strips per strength. Only one checked real drugs: 104 samples seized by police.

cl_dc_fts_analogues.short: In lab tests, strips found most related drugs, but not all. Carfentanil needed large amounts.
cl_dc_fts_analogues.but: These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by lab staff. The largest study reported no repeat tests.
how: One lab tested 28 related drugs on four brands. At high amounts, 21 to 24 of them showed up.
At lower amounts, only 5 to 12 of the 23 tested showed up.
Three never showed up on any brand. Carfentanil showed only at high amounts, and never on one brand.
A second lab found 11 of 13 related drugs on all five batches of one brand. On two of the three newer batches, carfentanil showed only in very large amounts.
cl_dc_fts_analogues.rate: Two labs tested pure related drugs in water, not street drugs. Readers may have known what each sample held, and one lab set its scoring after seeing the results.

cl_dc_fts_brands_lots.short: No. In lab tests, brands and batches differed. Some batches needed ten times more fentanyl.
cl_dc_fts_brands_lots.but: Each difference comes from one or two lab studies, and why batches differed is not known.
how: Batches of one brand bought in 2021 needed ten times more fentanyl to show it than batches bought in 2017.
With no fentanyl there, the 2021 batches read positive with 10 to 40 times less lidocaine or MDMA than the 2017 batches.
Four brands picked up different numbers of related drugs. The one that found the most at a low amount never showed carfentanil. It also read positive with large amounts of vitamin C alone.

Two weeks of heat did not change one kind of strip. Strips more than four years out of date still worked, but needed more fentanyl than their label said. No new strips of that kind were tested to compare.
cl_dc_fts_brands_lots.rate: A few lab studies, using samples in water or urine read by trained staff, not street drugs. Each strength was tested only a few times, so small differences may be chance.
