cl_dc_nitazene_strips.short: Mostly, in the lab. They picked up 24 of 33 kinds of nitazene but missed most desnitazenes, so a negative doesn't rule nitazenes out.
cl_dc_nitazene_strips.but: Only pure or nearly pure drugs were tested, not mixed street drugs.
how: One lab tried 33 kinds of nitazene. The strips picked up 24. They missed 6 of the 7 desnitazenes, even at high strength.
Six nearly pure powders from the drug market all showed up.
A second lab found the strips did not react to 76 other drugs and cutting agents.
No study we read tested street drugs where a nitazene is a small part of a mix. So how often strips get it wrong on real samples is unknown.
cl_dc_nitazene_strips.rate: Two labs tested one brand of strip on pure or nearly pure samples in water, not messy street drugs. Most kinds of nitazene were tested with just one strip per strength.

cl_dc_xylazine_strips.short: Yes, if there's at least as much xylazine as they're made to find: 37 of 38 such samples read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did.
cl_dc_xylazine_strips.but: It's one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment, not powders or pills.
how: A lab tested 100 residue samples wiped from used syringes, bags and pill bottles, and checked them with a lab machine.
With enough xylazine, 37 of 38 read positive; with less, 6 of 28. That's 43 of all 66 with xylazine. None of 34 without it read positive.
In pure water, every strip read positive only from 2.5 times the amount the strip is made to find.
Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, also made strips read positive. At the one level tested, they didn't react to medetomidine. That's a similar drug used on animals.

freq.title: Out of every 100 samples with xylazine, how many read positive?
pairs: samples with at least the amount the strip is made to find
samples with less than that
freq.note: 37 of 38 and 6 of 28 residue samples, one batch of strips, read in a lab.

cl_dc_xylazine_strips.rate: Two lab studies by one team. Their main figure leaves out samples with only a little xylazine, and neither tested the strips on powders or pills as people use them, or outside a lab.

cl_dc_benzo_strips.short: Not reliably. At drug-checking sites in Canada, strips caught newer benzos in 15 of 24 samples that had them, and just 8 of 16 with etizolam alone.
cl_dc_benzo_strips.but: A lab checked only some samples, not chosen at random: some were picked because of a suspected benzo overdose.
how: At eight health sites, samples were tested with strips, and a lab checked some of them.
Strips caught 7 of 8 samples with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam. With etizolam alone, they caught only 8 of 16.
They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which the lab found none; what set those off wasn't reported.
The same maker's strip never reacted to pure etizolam, even at 40 or more times the level at which it caught other benzos. An earlier report said similar strips seemed to pick it up.

freq.what: samples with a newer benzodiazepine showed it on the strip
freq.note: 15 of 24 samples at one drug-checking service, 2018 to 2020. With etizolam alone, 8 of 16.

cl_dc_benzo_strips.rate: One brand of urine strip, tried at one Canadian drug-checking programme and on pure samples in a lab. Only 159 of 1368 samples were lab-checked, and those were not picked at random.

cl_dc_colour_mdma.short: In a lab, experts got MDMA right. Two first-time testers made many mistakes.
cl_dc_colour_mdma.but: One small lab study from 2003, with a kit and pills of that time.
how: Three lab experts read all 35 samples with MDMA as positive, and nearly all of the 4 without MDMA as negative.
Seven MDMA samples also had another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine. The colour looked the same.
Two people new to the kit tested 8 known drugs. One missed both MDMA samples. The other called four other drugs MDMA.
A review says MDA and MDEA, drugs close to MDMA, give a similar colour. It adds that, read by eye, the tests do not show how much MDMA a pill holds.
cl_dc_colour_mdma.rate: One lab study of a 2003 kit, where experts knew the samples were sold as MDMA. Only four samples lacked MDMA, two first-time testers took part, and newer drugs were untested.

cl_dc_home_vs_service.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often: 28 in 100 meth samples, against 5 in 100 tested by staff.
cl_dc_home_vs_service.but: The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.
how: In British Columbia in 2019, people took strips from ten harm-reduction sites and used them at home a little over half the time. Staff tested other samples at the sites.
Opioids: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site.
Crystal meth: 28 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, against 5 in 100 on site; cocaine, 17 against 1. The authors think most extra positives were false, but didn't test it.
People told the study their own results, often from memory.

freq.title: Out of every 100 crystal meth samples, how many showed fentanyl?
pairs: tested by the person with a take-home strip
tested on site by trained staff
freq.note: 73 of 265 and 5 of 97 samples, British Columbia, 2019. Different samples; no lab checked which results were right.

cl_dc_home_vs_service.rate: One study in British Columbia in 2019 compared results people noted themselves with staff results on different samples. Nobody knows how many kits never came back, and many results were recalled later.

cl_dc_home_what_tests_miss.short: A test for one drug did not show other drugs in the mix, or how much.
cl_dc_home_what_tests_miss.but: Only two small studies tested this directly. The rest is how the tests are made.
how: In one lab study, MDMA samples with caffeine or amphetamine mixed in looked the same on a colour test.
At one drug-checking service, 24 of 159 samples checked by a lab had a newer benzodiazepine. None of the people who brought them expected it. Most also had fentanyl.
Fentanyl strips only show if fentanyl is there. They do not show how much.
No study tested whether a negative result makes a drug less risky.
cl_dc_home_what_tests_miss.rate: Two small studies: a 2003 colour kit read in a lab, and one Canadian checking service's selected samples. Few samples held a second drug, and neither tested use at home.

cl_dc_uptake_offered.short: It varies a lot. In different places, from 1 in 100 to 77 in 100.
cl_dc_uptake_offered.but: This is what people said or what services wrote down. Nobody checked.
how: In a paid study in Rhode Island in 2017, 62 of the 81 young adults who came back and were counted said they used at least one of their ten strips.
At a supervised injection site in Vancouver, staff offered a check on every visit. About 1 visit in 100 included one.
A review gives figures of 1 to 80 in 100. But these mostly count people who had used strips before a study began, not people the study gave strips to.
One programme did not report how many kits it gave out, so how many were used is unknown.
cl_dc_uptake_offered.rate: A paid research pilot, service records and a review, all in North America and each counting differently. The results differ more than the counting explains, and places outside North America may differ again.

cl_dc_after_positive.q: What do people do when a strip shows fentanyl?
cl_dc_after_positive.short: Some say they use less or go slower; many keep the same amount.
cl_dc_after_positive.but: This is what people said or planned. Nobody watched what they actually did.
how: In a 2023 US study of 541 people, most strip results were followed by using the same amount.
In that study, 23 in 100 results with no fentanyl were followed by using more. For results with fentanyl, it was 6 in 100.
In Rhode Island and Baltimore, 45 in 100 and 31 in 100 of people whose strip showed fentanyl said they used a smaller amount.
No study compared people given strips with people who were not given them.

freq.title: Out of every 100 checks before use at one supervised injection site, how many ended with the person saying they would use less?
pairs: when the strip showed fentanyl
when the strip did not show fentanyl
freq.note: Vancouver, 2016 to 2017 (142 of 391 against 7 of 122 checks). What people then did was not recorded.

cl_dc_after_positive.rate: Surveys and staff records from people who chose to test, in North American places where fentanyl was common. People may tell staff what they think staff want to hear.

cl_dc_disposal_unexpected.short: Sometimes. At one festival, 67 in 100 people handed over drugs that were not as sold.
cl_dc_disposal_unexpected.but: That was one festival, where chemists tested the drugs. After a strip showed fentanyl, few did.
how: At an English festival in 2016, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not as sold handed drugs over to be destroyed.
When the drug matched, 15 of 164 did. Staff saw these handovers, but people may have kept other drugs.
At a supervised injection site, people said they would throw the drug away after 11 in 100 checks that showed fentanyl, and after 7 in 100 that did not.
A review of drug checking services printed rates of 0 to 10 in 100 from four studies.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people at one festival whose drug was tested by chemists, how many handed over drugs to be destroyed?
pairs: drug was not what it was sold as
drug matched what it was sold as
freq.note: England, 2016 (30 of 45 against 15 of 164). Staff saw the handovers; people may have kept other drugs elsewhere.

cl_dc_disposal_unexpected.rate: Mainly one festival in 2016, where chemists tested drugs, not home kits. People chose to come, many already worried about their drug, and nobody checked what they did afterwards.

cl_dc_overdose_strip_users.q: Do people who use test strips have fewer overdoses?
cl_dc_overdose_strip_users.short: No one knows yet. One study found no clear difference over four weeks.
cl_dc_overdose_strip_users.but: The result was too uncertain to rule out fewer or more overdoses.
how: One US study followed 732 people at harm-reduction sites for four weeks in 2023. Once other differences were allowed for, overdoses that people survived were about as common in people who used strips as in those who did not.
That comparison also allowed for safety steps people took during the study, which could hide a difference. Before anything was allowed for, overdoses looked twice as common in people who used strips.

In Baltimore, 103 women were given strips, and 68 were asked again about 8 weeks later. 6 said they had an overdose in the month before the start, and 1 in the month before the last visit. There was no comparison group, and women who used no strips also reported fewer.
A review of 91 research papers found only two that looked at overdoses, and neither compared people who tested with people who did not.
cl_dc_overdose_strip_users.rate: One study of 732 people at US harm-reduction services, who chose for themselves whether to use strips. People reported their own overdoses, which were rare over four weeks, and deaths were not counted.

cl_dc_continued_use.short: In the one study that lasted a year, fewer people had used a strip in the past month by the end than at the start.
cl_dc_continued_use.but: Many people left the study, and it did not find out why use fell.
how: 541 people who inject drugs, met at two services that give out clean needles in rural North Carolina and West Virginia, answered surveys at the start, after 6 months and after 12 months.
After a year, people were less likely than at the first survey to have used a strip in the past month. At 6 months there was no clear change.
Even so, more people had tried strips at some point: 65 in 100 at the first survey and 80 in 100 a year later, among those who answered all three surveys.
In two shorter studies, about 95 in 100 said they would use strips again. That is a plan, not a measure of use.
cl_dc_continued_use.rate: One study followed people at two rural US services for a year. Those who dropped out, 39 in 100, had used strips less, and people reported their own use.

cl_dc_festival_hospital.short: We can't tell. Fewer people were taken to hospital for drugs, but other things changed too.
cl_dc_festival_hospital.but: One festival, one year before and one after, with no festival to compare.
how: At an English festival in 2016, chemists tested drugs on site for the first time.
People taken into hospital because of drugs: 19 in 2015 and 1 in 2016.
Other hospital admissions rose from 40 to 49, and paramedics were said to treat more people on site.
The author says the study cannot show what part the testing played.
cl_dc_festival_hospital.rate: One festival's unpublished counts, a year before and after. The way hospital cases were counted changed, paramedics treated more people on site in 2016, and the numbers are tiny.

cl_dc_uptake_who_tests.short: Yes. In the largest US study, they more often injected and used fentanyl.
cl_dc_uptake_who_tests.but: This is what people said, and most were already using drug services.
how: At US sites that hand out strips, 75 in 100 people who had used strips had injected in the past month, against 57 in 100 who had not.

In the same study, people who used strips already said they did more to lower their risk before it began. For example, 64 in 100 said they always had naloxone nearby when they used drugs, against 39 in 100 people who did not use strips.
Their overdose rate looked twice as high before anything was allowed for, and not clearly different after.
In a rural US study, people who had seen an overdose were more likely to use strips. In a small study, the two groups differed little.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people at US harm-reduction sites that hand out strips, how many had injected drugs in the past month?
pairs: people who had used strips in the past month
people who had not used strips
freq.note: Kentucky, New York and Ohio, 2023 (414 and 318 people). Self-reported.

cl_dc_uptake_who_tests.rate: Two US studies of 732 and 541 people mostly agree. But strip use and everything else were asked in the same interviews, where people may give the answers they think are wanted.

cl_dc_caution_harms.short: No study has measured this. Riskier use after a positive strip was rare when asked.
cl_dc_caution_harms.but: The studies said little about what people did after a strip showed no fentanyl.
how: In one programme, 6 of 336 answers described riskier use after a strip showed fentanyl.
Some people misread strips, and strips do not show other drugs, such as xylazine.
With take-home strips, people found fentanyl in 28 in 100 meth samples, against 5 in 100 tested by staff.
Critics worry that a negative result could make people feel safe when they are not. This has not been measured.
cl_dc_caution_harms.rate: Surveys of people who chose to test; no study compared people given kits with people without them, and riskier responses rest on just 6 answers. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_dc_law_deaths.short: After the law, drug deaths ran about 3 a year per 100,000 people below other states' trend.
cl_dc_law_deaths.but: It looked at laws, not at people using strips. Other changes at the same time could explain it.
how: Researchers used death records from every US state from 2018 to 2022. They counted 15 states and Washington, DC as making the strips legal in that time.

After the law, there were about 3 fewer drug deaths a year for every 100,000 people, about 7 in 100 fewer than expected. Once age, rural living and income were allowed for, this was about the same for White and Black people, though less certain for Black people.
The study did not check whether more people got or used strips. It counted deaths from any drug, and the drop came in the very first month of each law.

The researchers chose the law dates themselves. They kept Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico among the states without a law, though laws started there in 2021 and 2022, and moved two other dates later. They showed no results with their source's dates.
cl_dc_law_deaths.rate: One study comparing US states before and after their laws. It did not take into account other changes, such as in each state's drug supply, and the drop could be tiny or sizeable.

cl_alc_low_volume_mortality.short: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths. Compared with people who never drank, there was no clear difference.
cl_alc_low_volume_mortality.but: Few studies made that comparison. So a small gain or a small loss is still possible.
how: Researchers put together dozens of studies. These followed millions of people for years and counted who died.
In most studies, the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill. People who had stopped died more often.
Six studies started with younger people and compared them with people who had never drunk. There, people who drank a little died about as often.
Allowing for how the studies differed also shrank the gap. Researchers still disagree, and studies like these cannot show whether alcohol itself helps or harms.
cl_alc_low_volume_mortality.rate: Huge studies followed people over time, but most counted people who had quit, or drank rarely, as non-drinkers. The fairer comparisons are too few to be sure. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_alc_lowest_risk_amount.short: Under 40, overall risk was lowest with almost no alcohol. Over 40, one model said half to two thirds of a drink a day.
cl_alc_lowest_risk_amount.but: These are averages for whole populations, not one person's risk, and the over-40 dip rests on heart findings that gene studies mostly did not find.
how: Researchers built world models that added up the risks of 22 or 23 diseases and injuries linked to alcohol. A drink here means 10 grams of alcohol.
For young people, much of this illness is injuries, and injury risk rose with any drinking. Older people have more heart disease, where some studies saw lower risk with small amounts.
The lowest point is where gains for some illnesses balance losses for others. In the older model, the risk of every cancer it looked at still rose with drinking.
The models describe whole populations, not one person. They left out drinking a lot on some days.
cl_alc_lowest_risk_amount.rate: Computer models built on studies where people reported their own drinking. The slight drop below non-drinkers' risk is the most disputed part. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_alc_drinking_mortality_threshold.short: Deaths rose above about 100 grams of alcohol a week. The comparison was with very light drinking.
cl_alc_drinking_mortality_threshold.but: People who drank more also smoked more. The studies could only partly allow for that.

freq.what: of the people who drank in these studies said they drank more than 100 grams of alcohol a week
freq.note: 83 studies in high-income countries; people with no known heart disease; amounts as people reported them.

how: Researchers pooled 83 studies of about 600,000 people who drank and had no known heart disease. They followed them for about 7 years.
They compared people with those who drank least (up to 25 grams a week), not with people who did not drink. 100 grams a week is about 14 grams a day.
The researchers used a model for 40-year-olds. Those drinking more than 350 grams a week could expect 4 to 5 fewer years of life than those drinking up to 100 grams.
Other studies compared with people who did not drink. They found more deaths in their groups drinking 45 grams a day or more, but their groups were too broad to show where the rise begins.
cl_alc_drinking_mortality_threshold.rate: 83 studies followed people who drink for years. Drinking was asked about once and smoking only partly allowed for, but deaths rose step by step with heavier drinking.

cl_alc_heart_cohorts.short: In many studies, people who drank a little had less heart disease than people who didn't.
cl_alc_heart_cohorts.but: The group who didn't drink included people who had stopped, perhaps because they were ill, so alcohol may not be the reason.
how: Researchers pooled dozens of long studies. They asked adults how much they drank, then counted heart disease over the years.
People who drank had about a quarter lower risk than people who didn't. No study said how many people out of 100 that is.
Compared with people who had never drunk, men's heart deaths at one or two drinks a day were not clearly lower.
In a large UK study, the gap at moderate drinking was no longer clear once smoking, weight, exercise, diet and health were counted. The gene studies we read did not find the gap.
cl_alc_heart_cohorts.rate: Studies following people over time, but the non-drinkers included people who quit, some because of illness, and in one study the link disappeared once lifestyle was taken into account. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_alc_heart_genes.short: The gene studies we read did not find that drinking a little protects the heart.
cl_alc_heart_genes.but: Gene studies have possible biases of their own, and they cannot show what small amounts do.
how: Some people carry genes that make them drink a bit less, or more. Researchers compared heart disease between these groups.
In studies of people of European descent, genes for drinking less went with slightly less heart disease, not more.
In a large study of Chinese men, genes for drinking more made no clear difference to heart attacks, though a small effect either way cannot be ruled out.

Three researchers argue that gene studies can be misled, for example by family background or by heavy drinking days. They did not measure how much, and they note some Asian gene studies pointing the other way.
cl_alc_heart_genes.rate: Gene studies compare people whose genes push them to drink more or less, but those genes may affect smoking too, and European and Chinese studies point different ways. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_alc_heart_heavy_days.short: Heavy drinking days went with more heart disease than drinking the same amount evenly.
cl_alc_heart_heavy_days.but: This comes from one team's review of seven studies, and it does not say what counted as heavy.
how: One team pooled seven studies of people who drank under 30 grams of alcohol a day on average.
Compared with people who had never drunk, those without heavy days had about a third lower heart risk. Those with heavy days had no lower risk.
The team's earlier review pointed the same way.
Genes that lower drinking also lower heavy drinking, so critics say gene studies cannot tell the two apart.
cl_alc_heart_heavy_days.rate: One team pooled seven studies of adults without checking how well each was done. Drinking was asked about once, and 'heavy' probably meant different things in different studies.

cl_alc_stroke.short: In gene studies, more drinking went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.
cl_alc_stroke.but: For small amounts it is less clear: older studies found slightly fewer strokes, but the Chinese gene study did not.
how: In a study of more than 160,000 Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes. The risk rose steadily with the amount.
For each extra 100 grams of alcohol a week (about 14 grams a day), bleeding strokes were almost a fifth more common, and strokes from blocked vessels about a tenth more common.
Women in China, who mostly don't drink, showed no link with the same genes. Most gene studies of people of European descent found the same direction.
Older studies comparing people who drink with people who don't found more strokes at high amounts, but no difference overall.
cl_alc_stroke.rate: Large gene studies in China and Europe agree, and the link held when smoking was allowed for. But gene studies are not trials, and the genes could still act in other ways.

cl_alc_blood_pressure.short: People whose genes made them drink more had higher blood pressure.
cl_alc_blood_pressure.but: The studies do not say how many more people out of 100 get high blood pressure.
how: In a Chinese study, men's top blood-pressure number was about 4 points higher for each extra 40 grams of alcohol a day that their genes predicted.
Asking the men how much they drank gave about the same rise.
In European studies, people with a gene that makes them drink a little less had slightly lower blood pressure and less high blood pressure, most clearly among heavier drinkers.
That gene also went with lower blood pressure in people who said they didn't drink, so it may act in other ways too.
cl_alc_blood_pressure.rate: Four studies in China and in people of European descent compared people whose genes make them drink more or less. All agree, but those genes might also affect blood pressure in other ways.

cl_alc_vessels_other.short: In gene studies, more drinking went with more narrowed leg arteries; other results were unclear.
cl_alc_vessels_other.but: These results come from two studies using the same UK volunteers, with few cases of some problems.
how: Two gene studies used data from UK Biobank, a large study of UK volunteers.
Genes for drinking more went with more narrowed arteries, mostly in the legs, even after allowing for genes linked to smoking.
In one study, links with an irregular heartbeat and a swollen main artery became unclear after allowing for those smoking genes. The other study found a link with an irregular heartbeat.
For heart failure the two studies disagreed. For blood clots in the veins, no clear link was found, but one could not be ruled out.
cl_alc_vessels_other.rate: Two studies comparing people by genes linked to drinking, both using the same UK volunteers. Some results faded once smoking was allowed for, and the studies disagree on heart failure.

cl_alc_cancer_sites.short: More drinking went with more mouth, throat, gullet, bowel, liver and breast cancer than not drinking.
cl_alc_cancer_sites.but: These studies watched groups of people, and about half did not take smoking or other differences into account.
how: A review pooled 572 studies of almost half a million people with cancer. It compared people who drank with people who did not drink.

At more than four drinks a day (a drink here is 12.5 g of alcohol), mouth and throat cancer and one type of gullet cancer were about 5 times as common. Breast cancer was about 1.6 times as common, and bowel cancer about 1.4 times. The bowel cancer link was clear in men but not in women.
Kidney and thyroid cancer and cancers of the lymph glands were less common in people who drank. For the lymph glands, the authors think some people cut down when they first feel ill.
The review gives no numbers out of 100, and it did not check the quality of the studies. An international cancer agency judges that alcohol causes these cancers; this review alone cannot show it.
cl_alc_cancer_sites.rate: 572 studies compared people's drinking and cancer; many asked people with cancer to recall past drinking, and smoking may explain part of the link. Still, the more people drank, the stronger the link.

cl_alc_cancer_light.short: Compared with not drinking, up to one drink a day went with slightly more of some cancers, fewer of others.
cl_alc_cancer_light.but: The differences are so small that errors in reporting drinking, or other differences between the groups, could explain them.
how: A review of 572 studies compared people who had up to 12.5 g of alcohol a day, about one drink, with people who did not drink.
Breast cancer was 1.04 times as common, and one type of gullet cancer 1.26 times. Mouth and throat cancer was 1.13 times as common, but not in studies that followed people over time.
Lung, kidney and thyroid cancer and cancers of the lymph glands were a little less common in people who had up to one drink a day.
People who drink more sometimes report less, and some people counted as not drinking had stopped. Small results like these can come from such errors. The review gives no numbers out of 100.
cl_alc_cancer_light.rate: A review of 572 studies, but the differences are as small as the likely errors: people reported their own drinking, some people counted as non-drinkers drank now and then, and the studies disagree.

cl_alc_cancer_burden.short: A model estimated that drinking caused about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
cl_alc_cancer_burden.but: It is a computer estimate, not a count. It applies risks from studies of groups of people to every country.

freq.what: new cancers worldwide in 2020 were estimated to be caused by alcohol
freq.note: Model estimate (Rumgay et al., 2021) against a world in which no one had ever drunk: 4.1 in 100 (3.1 to 5.3); men 6.1, women 2.0.

how: Researchers combined how much people drink in each country with cancer risks from earlier studies. They compared this with a world where no one had ever drunk.
They estimated 741,000 new cancers in 2020: about 6 in 100 new cancers in men and 2 in 100 in women. Gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer made up the most.
Most were linked to more than 20 g of alcohol a day, about two drinks. About 103,000 were linked to less than that.
The model counted only harms, for the cancers an international agency lists. An older model by an overlapping team estimated 487,000 cancer deaths from alcohol in 2004.
cl_alc_cancer_burden.rate: A computer model that takes, at face value, risk figures from studies of people who drink, and applies them, measured mostly in high-income countries, to every country.

cl_alc_cirrhosis_amount.short: The more people drank, the higher their cirrhosis risk, compared with people who did not drink.
cl_alc_cirrhosis_amount.but: How much the risk rose differed a lot between studies, and drinking was asked about only once.

freq.what: men in a Danish study were diagnosed with alcohol-related cirrhosis over about 15 years
freq.note: People aged 50 to 64 at the start, followed 1993 to 2011, all levels of drinking together (editors' calculation: 257 of 26,696 men, 85 of 29,221 women).

how: In a Danish study of 55,917 people aged 50 to 64, about 1 in 100 men and 3 in 1,000 women got alcohol-related cirrhosis over about 15 years.

A review of 9 studies, mostly counting deaths from cirrhosis, compared people who drank with people who did not. A drink here is 12 g of alcohol. At two drinks a day the risk was about 3 times as high, and at seven or more about 11 times (from 4 studies).
At seven or more drinks a day, studies of men found from about 2 times to 22 times the risk.
At up to about two drinks a day, results disagree: some found a rise, some none, and some studies of men even found less cirrhosis.
cl_alc_cirrhosis_amount.rate: Mostly studies that followed people for years, asking about drinking only once. They disagree on how big the rise in risk is, but it was very large with heavy drinking and grew step by step.

cl_alc_cirrhosis_women_men.short: At the same amount, studies found a bigger rise in cirrhosis risk for women than for men.
cl_alc_cirrhosis_women_men.but: No study tested the difference, and much of the evidence on women comes from one old American study.
how: Each figure compares people who drank with people of the same sex who did not drink, or drank little.

At about five drinks a day (48 to 60 g), studies of cirrhosis deaths found 14.7 times the risk for women and 7.0 times for men. In a newer review and a Danish study, the gap was within the margins of error.
In a Danish study, fewer women than men got alcohol-related cirrhosis (19 against 66 in 100,000 a year), but the women drank less.
No study gave the risk, out of 100, for women and men who drink the same amount.
cl_alc_cirrhosis_women_men.rate: Two reviews and a Danish study. In two of the three, the gap between women and men could be chance, and the key study of women, from 1959–60, took only age into account.

cl_alc_cirrhosis_daily.short: In one study, men who drank daily had more cirrhosis than men drinking 2 to 4 days a week.
cl_alc_cirrhosis_daily.but: People who drank daily also drank more, and the study could not fully separate how often from how much.
how: The study followed 55,917 people aged 50 to 64 for about 15 years. It asked once how often and how much they drank.
After taking into account how much they drank, smoking, schooling and waist size, men who drank every day had 3.7 times the risk of men who drank on 2 to 4 days a week.
Women showed no clear pattern. A review reported that, in a large British study of women, daily drinking was linked to 1.6 times the risk.
The study could not look at drinking a lot on a few days (binge drinking).
cl_alc_cirrhosis_daily.rate: One Danish study followed thousands of adults for about 15 years after asking once how they drank. People who drank daily also drank more, and for women the studies disagree.

cl_alc_deaths_global.short: Global models estimated alcohol caused about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, compared with no one drinking.
cl_alc_deaths_global.but: These are computer estimates built on studies of groups of people, not counted deaths.

freq.what: deaths of men worldwide in 2016 were estimated to be caused by alcohol
freq.note: Model estimate (Global Burden of Disease 2016), age-standardised: men 6.8 in 100, women 2.2 in 100.

how: The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016: about 7 in 100 deaths of men and 2 in 100 of women.
At ages 15 to 49, alcohol was the top risk factor in that study: about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women.
An older model using WHO data estimated about 2.5 million deaths caused in 2004, mostly from injuries, heart disease, cancer and cirrhosis, minus about 0.2 million it counted as prevented.
A later round of the global study, quoted second-hand, put it at about 1.8 million in 2020. The numbers move with the method, so they do not show a trend.
cl_alc_deaths_global.rate: Two computer models treat links seen in studies of groups of people as causes, and estimate drinking partly from sales figures and expert guesses. A newer run gave fewer deaths.

cl_alc_aud_prevalence.short: In a US survey, 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year.
cl_alc_aud_prevalence.but: Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.

freq.what: US adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year (2012–2013 survey)
freq.note: By the same older definition, this survey found 13 in 100. World estimate for 2016, passed on by a review: about 5 in 100 people aged 15 or older.

how: Alcohol use disorder is found with a list of 11 signs of problem drinking: 2 or more in a year count. In 2012 and 2013, a US survey asked 36,309 adults set questions to find it.
About 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year, and 29 in 100 at some time in their lives. About half of the past-year cases were mild. It was most common at ages 18 to 29: about 27 in 100.
The survey's authors think it became more common after 2001. We think their two surveys were run too differently to show that.
The survey missed people who were homeless or in prison, and most people in treatment. For the world, a review passes on an estimate of about 5 in 100 people aged 15 or older.
cl_alc_aud_prevalence.rate: Two national US surveys disagree. The one behind this figure left out people who were homeless or in prison, and many people asked did not take part.

cl_alc_aud_treatment_gap.short: In a US survey, 20 in 100 people who ever had it sought help.
cl_alc_aud_treatment_gap.but: People said this themselves, and the survey left out most people who were in treatment.

freq.what: US adults who had ever had alcohol use disorder had ever looked for treatment or help
freq.note: Self-reported, 2012–2013; counts groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous.

how: In 2012 and 2013, a US survey asked people with alcohol use disorder whether they had ever looked for treatment or help.
About 20 in 100 who had ever had it said yes, and about 8 in 100 of those who had it in the past year.
Groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous were the most common kind of help. People with severe disorder looked for help more often: about 35 in 100, against 4 in 100 with mild disorder.
A review passes on about 22 in 100 for Europe and the world, but these count people who got treatment, not people who looked for it.
cl_alc_aud_treatment_gap.rate: One large US survey from 2012–2013, where people looked back over their whole lives and reported help they had sought. It missed most people who were in treatment.

cl_alc_withdrawal_delirium.short: Sudden confusion in alcohol withdrawal; a few in 100 people in hospital get it.
cl_alc_withdrawal_delirium.but: Most figures are passed on by one review or come from old trials, mostly one from 1969.

freq.what: people in withdrawal given dummy pills in old trials developed delirium
freq.note: Four trials, 1961 to 1980, most people in one of them. A review passes on 3 to 5 in 100 for people in hospital for withdrawal.

how: The DTs are confusion that comes on fast and comes and goes, together with signs of withdrawal such as shaking or a fast pulse.
A review says the DTs usually start about 3 days after withdrawal begins and last 2 or 3 days. It says 3 to 5 in 100 people in hospital for withdrawal get them.
In old trials, about 6 in 100 people in withdrawal who got dummy pills developed delirium. Most of these people were in one trial from 1969.
The review says about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. It names recent seizures, earlier DTs, older age and other illnesses as signs they are more likely.
cl_alc_withdrawal_delirium.rate: Figures passed on by one review that does not show its sources, and four old trials where only 11 people had it. No study counted it in people stopping outside hospital.

cl_alc_withdrawal_medicines.short: In old trials, benzodiazepines cut seizures: about 1 in 100, against 8 on dummy pills.
cl_alc_withdrawal_medicines.but: The trials were from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.

freq.what: had a seizure during withdrawal with a benzodiazepine
freq.note: Three trials, 1969 to 1983; the review's illustration is 13 against 80 per 1,000.

how: Benzodiazepines are calming medicines. Old trials gave them or dummy pills to people going through alcohol withdrawal.
About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills. Delirium was also less common: about 2 in 100 against 6.
Other medicines were not clearly better or worse. One kind of antipsychotic given on its own was followed by more seizures and delirium than benzodiazepines.
Few trials looked at people who already had the DTs.
cl_alc_withdrawal_medicines.rate: Old trials, all pointing the same way. Only 15 people had seizures in the main review, and most trials don't say whether staff knew in advance who would get the medicine.

cl_alc_naltrexone.short: On naltrexone, 46 in 100 went back to heavy drinking, against 54 on dummy pills.
cl_alc_naltrexone.but: Most people in the trials were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.

freq.what: on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking during treatment
freq.note: Totals across 19 trials, most of them 12 weeks long (editors' arithmetic).

how: Naltrexone is a tablet. Dozens of trials gave it or dummy pills, mostly for 3 months, usually with counselling as well.
About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills. It helped less, if at all, with stopping completely.
People on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100. Feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common.
When compared directly, naltrexone and acamprosate did about the same, but most people in that comparison were in one trial.
cl_alc_naltrexone.rate: Many trials, with thousands of people, where chance decided who got naltrexone or dummy pills. Most point the same way, but few were run without flaws, and people reported their own drinking.

cl_alc_acamprosate.short: In trials, 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83 on dummy pills.
cl_alc_acamprosate.but: The most carefully run trials found no clear difference.

freq.what: on acamprosate drank again during treatment
freq.note: Totals across 16 trials (editors' arithmetic); no clear difference in the trials at low risk of bias.

how: Acamprosate is a tablet. Most trials were in Europe, in people who had already stopped drinking.
About 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again during treatment, against 83 in 100 on dummy pills. It did not cut heavy drinking.
The most carefully run trials, including the two largest of them, both in the US, found no clear difference. Most trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly its maker.
Diarrhoea was more common: about 11 more people in every 100. In one review, more people stopped taking it because of side effects.
cl_alc_acamprosate.rate: Reviews of up to 24 trials. They disagree: mostly European trials found a benefit, the largest US trials did not, and the most carefully run trials showed no clear effect.

cl_alc_aud_other_medicines.short: Topiramate was linked to fewer drinking days; disulfiram showed no clear benefit in blinded trials.
cl_alc_aud_other_medicines.but: Most of these medicines were tested in only a few trials.
how: A large review pooled trials that compared each medicine with dummy pills, mostly alongside counselling.
Topiramate: about 7 fewer drinking days in every 100, and about 2 fewer drinks on drinking days. Tingling, changes in taste and trouble thinking were more common.

Baclofen and gabapentin were linked to small benefits, but the evidence is weak. A long-acting naltrexone injection did not clearly change going back to drinking, but was linked to fewer heavy-drinking days.
Disulfiram showed no clear benefit in blinded trials. None of them tested taking it with someone watching, which may make it look less helpful.
cl_alc_aud_other_medicines.rate: Trials compared each medicine with a dummy pill, but most results rest on only 2 to 9 trials, some come close to no effect, and people reported their own drinking.

cl_alc_combine_talking_therapy.short: In one large trial, adding talking therapy to naltrexone did not help more.
cl_alc_combine_talking_therapy.but: It was one US trial, not built to test combinations.
how: 1,383 adults who had just stopped drinking got naltrexone, acamprosate, both or dummy pills, with or without up to 20 sessions of therapy. Everyone taking pills also had 9 short check-ins with a health worker.
Naltrexone with therapy did no better than either one alone. On days without alcohol, only naltrexone without therapy was clearly better than dummy pills.
With dummy pills, adding therapy was linked to more days without alcohol in one comparison.
People who had therapy without pills or check-ins had fewer days without alcohol. In the year after, no difference between the groups was clear.
cl_alc_combine_talking_therapy.rate: One US trial of 1,383 adults. People knew whether they had the therapy and reported their own drinking, and even that many were too few to judge what therapy adds to medicine.

cl_alc_pregnancy_drinking.short: About 10 in 100 pregnant women worldwide drank some alcohol. By region, from under 1 to 25.
cl_alc_pregnancy_drinking.but: Most countries had too few studies, so a model filled them in. Women may not report all drinking.

freq.what: pregnant women worldwide drank some alcohol in pregnancy
freq.note: One review's estimate, labelled 2012, mostly from a model. By world region it ran from under 1 in 100 to 25 in 100.

how: Researchers pooled 328 studies from 50 countries, published from 1984 to 2014. In them, pregnant women or new mothers said if they drank.
Only 29 countries had enough studies to pool. For the other 158, a model worked out a number from the country's income, how much its women drink, and its region.
In each WHO world region, out of 100 pregnant women: African 10. Americas 11. Eastern Mediterranean under 1. European 25. South-East Asia 2. Western Pacific 9.
Groups who may drink more, such as teenagers or women with an alcohol use disorder, were left out. How much and when women drank was not studied.
cl_alc_pregnancy_drinking.rate: One review gathered surveys asking women about drinking in pregnancy, and some may not report all of it. For 158 of 187 countries, the figures are a model's estimates, not measurements.

cl_alc_fasd_fas_prevalence.short: About 8 in 1,000 children are thought to have FASD. About 1.5 in 1,000 people have FAS.
cl_alc_fasd_fas_prevalence.but: Few countries had counted it. Most numbers were worked out from how many women said they drank.

freq.what: children and youth worldwide estimated to have FASD
freq.note: About 1.5 in 1,000 people were estimated to have FAS, one of the diagnoses within FASD. Most countries' figures were worked out from drinking surveys, not counted.

how: FASD is the name for the effects of alcohol on a child before birth. It covers several diagnoses, and FAS is one of them.
Researchers found 24 studies in 8 countries that looked for FASD in children. Results ranged from under 1 to about 208 in 1,000, by place and method.

For most countries there was no count. The team took the estimated share of women who drank in pregnancy and divided it by one fixed number. In the regions with the lowest figures, no study had counted it.
That number is an average from a few countries. It is not the chance for any one pregnancy. Ways to diagnose FASD also differ.
cl_alc_fasd_fas_prevalence.rate: Two reviews from one team. Most figures were estimated, not counted, and the studies that did count disagree a lot and were often done where many cases were expected.

cl_alc_fas_first_description.short: In 1973, doctors described 8 children of mothers who drank heavily. All grew poorly and developed slowly.
cl_alc_fas_first_description.but: Some children were picked because they had these signs. They were not compared with other children.
how: A team in Seattle, USA, examined 8 children: 5 girls and 3 boys from three ethnic groups, aged 3 months to almost 5 years when tested.
All 8 were small before and after birth and did not catch up. All had short eye openings and were behind in development. Seven had small heads.
Many also had a small upper jaw (7 children), unusual palm creases (6), joint problems (5) or heart problems (5). The paper did not yet use the name fetal alcohol syndrome.
Milder cases were left out, and how much the mothers drank was not recorded. Four of six mothers with a record lost weight in pregnancy, and the study could not separate nutrition from alcohol.
cl_alc_fas_first_description.rate: A single 1973 report on 8 children, with no comparison group. Some were picked because they already had the signs, and the doctors knew about the mothers' drinking.

cl_ket_bioavailability_oral_im.short: Nearly all of an injected dose reaches the blood. Swallowed, only about a sixth does.
cl_ket_bioavailability_oral_im.but: Both figures come from four people each, in one study from 1982.
how: Healthy volunteers were given ketamine three ways on different days, with blood tests each time.
Each person's own dose into a vein was the yardstick for the other two ways.
Into a muscle, about 93 parts in 100 reached the blood; swallowed, about 17 in 100.
A later study of three men found about the same, but they swallowed a tablet, not a drink.
cl_ket_bioavailability_oral_im.rate: Two tiny lab studies: one from 1982, reporting just 4 of its 6 people without saying why, and one of 3 men. Neither gave a margin of error.

cl_ket_bioavailability_other_routes.short: In three men, the nose spray reached the blood best, then tongue and suppository.
cl_ket_bioavailability_other_routes.but: Only three men took part, and two of the methods were not carried out as described.
how: Three healthy men tried five forms of ketamine, a week or more apart, with blood tests.
Against a dose into a vein: nose spray about 45 in 100, tongue tablet and suppository about 30 in 100.
The men swallowed the tablets that were meant to stay under the tongue.
The suppository results differed so much between the three men that the average says little.
cl_ket_bioavailability_other_routes.rate: One study of just three men, so one unusual man can sway every figure. Two of the five tests were not done as labelled, and the paper gives no individual results.

cl_ket_halflife_norketamine.short: It drops fast at first, then falls by half every two to three hours.
cl_ket_halflife_norketamine.but: The two studies had only six and three people, and timed mainly doses into a vein.
how: Blood samples after a dose into a vein show a quick fall, then a slower one.
One study found a half-life of about three hours, the other about two hours.
The body turns most ketamine into norketamine; after a swallowed dose there is far more norketamine than ketamine.
Only one rough figure is given for a swallowed dose, and none for a nose spray.
cl_ket_halflife_norketamine.rate: Two small lab studies in healthy volunteers, with 6 and 3 people. The blood tests were not shown to be accurate, and some values are missing or misprinted.

cl_ket_brain_imaging_acute.short: In scans, brain activity went up, not down, most of all at the front.
cl_ket_brain_imaging_acute.but: The scans show one session only, and cannot show which brain change causes which feeling.
how: Ten healthy people were scanned with and without ketamine, each person compared with themselves.
Whole-brain energy use rose about a quarter, and it rose in every single person.
A 2024 summary of 33 imaging studies found the clearest agreement at one spot near the front.
One mirror-image form of ketamine, called R, moved the other way and lowered energy use.
cl_ket_brain_imaging_acute.rate: Two scan studies of 10 healthy volunteers each from one Zurich lab, and a review that checked no study's quality. One had no dummy comparison; in the other, everyone recognised the drug.

cl_ket_enantiomers.short: In one small study the S form caused psychosis-like effects; the R form did not.
cl_ket_enantiomers.but: Only ten people took part, and everyone could tell when they had been given a drug.
how: Ten healthy people had the S form, the R form and a dummy, a month apart.
On the S form, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self.
On the R form, the same people described relaxation, and their brain scans moved the other way.
The ordinary mix of the two forms was never given to these same ten people.
cl_ket_enantiomers.rate: One lab study: each of 10 volunteers had both forms and a dummy. All 10 scored higher on the S form, but everyone could tell when they'd had a drug.

cl_ket_night_of_use_tests.short: That night, memory scores were far below other partygoers'. Three days later the gap was mostly gone.
cl_ket_night_of_use_tests.but: Two small studies by one team, and nobody tested what people had taken.
how: People were tested within half an hour of taking ketamine. They remembered less than half as much of a short story as people at the party who had not taken it.
They felt strongly cut off from their body and surroundings, numb, and as if time had changed.
Three days later, at home, their attention scores matched the other group's, and most of these feelings had gone. In one of the two studies, feeling detached was still higher.
Some memory scores were still lower. People may have remembered little of the first test, so had less practice. Or the groups were different to begin with.
cl_ket_night_of_use_tests.rate: Two small studies tested people at parties, grouped by what they chose to take that night. The gaps that night were large, but the studies disagree on what remained three days later.

cl_ket_frequent_use_cognition.short: On some memory tests, people who used ketamine most days did worse than others.
cl_ket_frequent_use_cognition.but: They also had less schooling. Nobody was tested before they started.
how: A London team tested people who used ketamine more than four times a week. The tests were a day or a few days after they last used it.
They made more mistakes when asked to remember which boxes they had already looked in. They also knew fewer of the patterns they had seen. This was compared with people who used other drugs or none.
They did as well at remembering a story and finding words. People who used ketamine a few times a month did as well too, though a smaller study found lower scores three days after a night out.
A year later, their scores were closer to the others', though most still used ketamine.
cl_ket_frequent_use_cognition.rate: Studies from one London team, comparing groups of 30 people or fewer. Testers knew who was who, and the studies disagree on which tests showed a difference.

cl_ket_cognition_after_stopping.short: Nobody knows yet. People who had stopped did as well as people who don't use it.
cl_ket_cognition_after_stopping.but: The people who had stopped had mostly used less, and nobody was tested before starting.
how: In one London team's study, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month did as well on memory tests as people who don't use ketamine. They still did a year later.
But most of them had used less than the people who used most days, so this does not show that stopping fixed anything.
In 18 people who had cut down, one word test caught up after 3 to 4 years. Story memory and speed stayed lower, as at their first test.
People who were still using also scored better on average a year later, perhaps partly from practice.
cl_ket_cognition_after_stopping.rate: Small studies from one London group, mostly comparing people who stopped with other people. Only 18 were tested before and after cutting down, and testers knew who was who. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_ket_mood_dissociation_beliefs.short: People who used ketamine most days more often reported unusual beliefs, feeling detached or feeling low.
cl_ket_mood_dissociation_beliefs.but: Mostly mild. Nobody was asked before they started, so the cause is not known.
how: A London team asked three groups: people who used ketamine more than four times a week, people who used other drugs, and people who used none.
The frequent group reported more unusual beliefs. In daily life, they also more often felt cut off from themselves or the world around them.
Their low-mood scores were a little higher, at most mild to moderate on average. A year later the scores had gone up.
More of them had family members with mental illness. That may matter too.
cl_ket_mood_dissociation_beliefs.rate: All from one London research team, with groups of 10 to 30 volunteers who rated themselves. The groups also differed in family history of mental illness, and the testers knew who was who.

cl_ket_acute_memory_attention.short: People remembered far fewer words than on their salt-water day. An hour after it stopped, scores matched.
cl_ket_acute_memory_attention.but: Small studies, 14 to 18 people each, and no study checked that the raters stayed unaware.
how: The same people were tested twice: once with ketamine in a vein, once with salt water.
With ketamine they recalled and recognised fewer words, and were a little slower to notice a repeated word.
Two of the three studies tested again after the drip stopped. About an hour later, scores matched the salt-water day.
Counts like 13 of 15 compare each person with their own score before the drug, not with their salt-water day.
cl_ket_acute_memory_attention.rate: Three small lab studies of healthy volunteers, 14 to 18 each, who could probably tell ketamine from salt water. Still, all three labs found a drop in memory.

cl_ket_schizophrenia_challenge.short: In nine patients, symptoms rose for twenty minutes, then returned to their usual level.
cl_ket_schizophrenia_challenge.but: Nine people, one study, and staff chose the order of the days instead of leaving it to chance.
how: Nine inpatients with schizophrenia, all taking an antipsychotic medicine, had four days: a dummy injection (placebo) and three amounts of ketamine. Two of them never got the largest amount, because staff held it back.
Twenty minutes after the two larger amounts, their symptom scores were higher than after the dummy injection.
What they described often repeated their own illness: suspicion, delusions, hallucinations and muddled thinking. Their overall scores were back to their usual level an hour and a half later.
Four of the nine said symptoms came back hours later, which nobody had expected or measured.
cl_ket_schizophrenia_challenge.rate: One study of 9 people with schizophrenia in hospital. Ketamine's effects are hard to miss, yet nobody checked whether people could tell, and only a few of many results were reported.

cl_ket_acute_psychosis_dissociation.q: What does ketamine do to perception, thinking and the sense of self while it is working?
cl_ket_acute_psychosis_dissociation.short: Compared with a salt-water day, people felt cut off from themselves and their thinking got muddled.
cl_ket_acute_psychosis_dissociation.but: Raters could probably tell who had ketamine, and the studies disagree a lot about how big the effects are.
how: Healthy volunteers were given ketamine into a vein and, to compare, salt water, with the same ratings both times. One study had no salt-water day: it compared people with themselves before the drug.

On the ketamine day, scores for psychosis-like experiences, for feeling cut off, and for odd perceptions were much higher. Pooling 36 such studies in 725 volunteers gives the same answer, from the strongest moment of each study.
People became suspicious and their thinking became muddled. What was scored as hallucinations was mostly real sights and sounds that seemed changed, not seeing things that were not there.

Two studies rated people again after the drip stopped, and scores were back to their usual level within about a quarter of an hour to half an hour. The 36 pooled studies measured nothing after the session, so they say nothing about how long it lasts.
cl_ket_acute_psychosis_dissociation.rate: All 36 lab studies, with 725 healthy volunteers, found these effects. The doubt is about how strong they are: the review took each study's highest score, and the studies differ a lot.

cl_ket_mechanism_nmda_metabolites.q: How does ketamine work in the brain?
cl_ket_mechanism_nmda_metabolites.short: It blocks a docking point for the brain's main go-signal, called the NMDA receptor.
cl_ket_mechanism_nmda_metabolites.but: Nearly all these numbers come from animals and from cells in dishes, and reach us through reviews.
how: Ketamine sits inside the channel of the NMDA receptor and plugs it.
The body turns ketamine into norketamine, which blocks the same receptor more weakly, and then into substances that hardly block it at all.
Ketamine also touches other targets in the brain. Most need far more ketamine than a person's blood holds, but the review says a few are reached at the levels people do get.
The review says nobody knows how much ketamine reaches the human brain, so a lot of this is animal work. Six of its eleven authors are named on a patent application for the breakdown products.
cl_ket_mechanism_nmda_metabolites.rate: Lab tests mostly on animal tissue and cells in dishes, not people, known to us only through reviews. Six of the main review's eleven authors are named on a patent application for compounds it discusses.

cl_can_cognition_frequent_use.q: Do people who use cannabis often do worse on memory and thinking tests?
cl_can_cognition_frequent_use.short: On average they score a little lower than people who use little or none.
cl_can_cognition_frequent_use.but: People were tested only after they had started, so the studies can't show that cannabis caused it.
how: A review pooled 69 studies of young people, about 21 years old on average, who used cannabis often.
They scored a little lower on learning, memory, attention and planning tests. Language, shape and movement tests showed no clear gap.
The gap was smaller in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days before the test, and bigger in people getting help for their cannabis use. Small studies found bigger gaps.
In a British twin study, the gap at age 18 was no longer clear when each twin was compared with their own twin.
cl_can_cognition_frequent_use.rate: Mostly studies that tested people once, without scores from before they started and without allowing for schooling or other drugs. Results vary widely, and studies that found nothing may never have been published.

cl_can_cognition_after_stopping.q: Do memory and thinking differences last after people stop using cannabis?
cl_can_cognition_after_stopping.short: Not clear. Where studies asked people to stop for over 3 days, the gap was small.
cl_can_cognition_after_stopping.but: This compared different studies, not the same people before and after they stopped.
how: A review of 69 studies found a smaller gap in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days. The gap might be zero, but one almost as big as the overall gap is not ruled out.
Studies of people who had stopped for about 3 to 8 weeks disagree. Some found lower scores on some tests; others found none.
Few studies followed people for longer. In one, people who had stopped heavy use for a year or more did not score differently on any test from people who had not used.
Two reviews read this evidence in opposite ways. Researchers disagree.
cl_can_cognition_after_stopping.rate: The main result compares different studies, not the same people before and after stopping, and only 14 of 69 checked that people had really stopped. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_can_teen_iq.q: Does using cannabis as a teenager lower IQ later in life?
cl_can_teen_iq.short: Not shown either way. In one study, people dependent for years lost about 6 IQ points.
cl_can_teen_iq.but: Other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of lighter use found no clear extra loss.
how: In New Zealand, 874 people took IQ tests as children and again at 38.
The 38 people who were dependent on cannabis at 3 or more of 5 check-ups lost about 6 points from their childhood scores. People who never used gained a little.
Another researcher showed that differences in family background could produce a similar pattern. The first team found that family background did not change their result.
In US and British twin studies, mostly of lighter teenage use, the twin who used did not lose clearly more than the twin who did not. These studies could miss a small loss.

freq.what: people in the New Zealand study were dependent on cannabis at 3 or more of 5 check-ups from 18 to 38
freq.note: 38 of 874 people. This is the group whose IQ fell by about 6 points.

cl_can_teen_iq.rate: The IQ drop rests on 38 people in one New Zealand study; twin studies found no clear drop, but they were small and measured lighter use. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_can_teen_depression_anxiety.q: Is teenage cannabis use linked to depression or anxiety later?
cl_can_teen_depression_anxiety.short: Teens who used cannabis the most were a bit more often depressed later than teens who didn't.
cl_can_teen_depression_anxiety.but: These studies can't show that cannabis caused it; other differences between the teens may explain it.
how: Seven long-term studies followed teens who did and did not use cannabis until they were young adults.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. The studies did not say how many in 100 became depressed.
The studies took into account how depressed or anxious the teens were at the start, but not always tobacco or other drugs.
Anxiety did not clearly differ, but only three studies measured it.
cl_can_teen_depression_anxiety.rate: 7 studies followed teens into adulthood, but other differences, such as tobacco or a hard childhood, may not have been allowed for. The anxiety result rests on just 3 studies, too few to be sure.

cl_can_teen_suicidality.q: Is teenage cannabis use linked to suicidal thoughts or attempts?
cl_can_teen_suicidality.short: Teens who used cannabis the most reported suicidal thoughts or attempts more often than teens who didn't.
cl_can_teen_suicidality.but: Only three studies each, mostly measured in the teen years; they cannot show cause.
how: A review combined three long-term studies on suicidal thoughts and three on suicide attempts.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and about 3.5 times the odds of attempts, compared with teens who did not use cannabis.
In two of the three studies for each, this was measured while the young people were still teenagers.
In other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were taken into account.
cl_can_teen_suicidality.rate: Studies that followed teens, three per question, pooled by a weak review. Other such studies found weaker or no links after allowing for other differences, so findings disagree.

cl_can_pregnancy_birth.q: Is using cannabis in pregnancy linked to a smaller baby, early birth or intensive care?
cl_can_pregnancy_birth.short: Babies were a bit lighter, and more of them went to intensive care after birth.
cl_can_pregnancy_birth.but: Many mothers also smoked or drank. Most studies could not tell this apart from cannabis.
how: Researchers combined 19 studies, mostly from before 2000. They compared babies of mothers who did and did not use cannabis while pregnant.
Babies of mothers who used cannabis weighed about 109 grams less. More of them went to newborn intensive care.
It is not clear whether they were born early more often. Birth defects and deaths around birth were not clearly more common.
Most studies did not keep tobacco and alcohol apart from cannabis. So they cannot show that cannabis caused the differences.
cl_can_pregnancy_birth.rate: A review of 19 studies of pregnant women, mostly from before 2000. Tobacco and alcohol use were not separated from cannabis, and most single studies found no link.

cl_can_heart_vascular.q: Is cannabis linked to heart attacks and strokes?
cl_can_heart_vascular.short: Some studies link it to heart attacks and strokes; a 25-year study found no link.
cl_can_heart_vascular.but: These figures come from reviews. The studies could not fully tell cannabis and tobacco apart.
how: In one study, a heart attack was more likely to start in the hour after using cannabis. Only a few people had used it in that hour.
Two surveys found more strokes, mostly in people who used cannabis every week or more.
A study that followed young adults for over 25 years found no link with heart disease or stroke.
The American Heart Association said the evidence is not yet clear.
cl_can_heart_vascular.rate: We know these studies only through reviews: mostly hospital records and surveys that could not fully tell cannabis and tobacco apart, and one key figure rests on 9 people. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_can_med_chronic_pain.q: Do cannabis medicines help long-lasting pain?
cl_can_med_chronic_pain.short: Slightly: about half a point less pain out of 10 than with a dummy medicine.
cl_can_med_chronic_pain.but: The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined trials. People with long-lasting pain got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
Pain scores were about half a point lower out of 10 with the medicine.
37 in 100 people on the medicine and 31 in 100 on the dummy had their pain cut by at least 30%; this difference may be due to chance.
Most of the combined trials tested a mouth spray with THC and CBD, and none lasted more than 15 weeks.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people in the trials, how many had their pain cut by at least 30%?
pairs: people given a cannabis medicine
people given a dummy medicine (placebo)
freq.note: Simple totals from 8 short trials, 7 of them of one THC and CBD mouth spray. The difference may be due to chance.

cl_can_med_chronic_pain.rate: Eight trials with 1,370 people. Effects like dizziness could have shown people they got the drug, and whether more people get a clear drop in pain is still unclear.

cl_can_med_ms_spasticity.q: Do cannabis medicines ease muscle stiffness in multiple sclerosis (MS)?
cl_can_med_ms_spasticity.short: People felt a little less stiff than with a dummy, but doctors' tests showed no clear change.
cl_can_med_ms_spasticity.but: The trials were short, most often tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined trials. People with MS got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
On the medicine, people rated their stiffness a little lower. The gap was about three quarters of a point.
Doctors' stiffness ratings did not clearly change. Neither did daily activities or walking speed.
Most trials tested a mouth spray with THC and CBD, for 15 weeks or less.
cl_can_med_ms_spasticity.rate: Short trials in people with multiple sclerosis; many had weaknesses, and people may have guessed from its effects whether they got the real medicine. The three trials where patients rated stiffness vary a lot.

cl_can_med_chemo_nausea.q: Do cannabis medicines help with sickness from chemotherapy?
cl_can_med_chemo_nausea.short: In three small trials, more people had their sickness fully controlled than with a dummy.
cl_can_med_chemo_nausea.but: Only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined three trials. People having chemotherapy got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
About 47 in 100 people on the medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on the dummy.
Most other trials compared cannabis medicines with other sickness medicines. The review says these leaned towards cannabis too. But it did not combine them.
23 of the 28 trials had serious weaknesses in how they were run or reported.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people having chemotherapy in three trials, how many had their sickness fully controlled?
pairs: people given a cannabis medicine
people given a dummy medicine (placebo)
freq.note: The review's figures from three small trials (102 people), with dronabinol or a THC and CBD spray. Most trials had weaknesses.

cl_can_med_chemo_nausea.rate: Three small trials with 102 people in all, which agree with each other. But feeling high may have told people whether they got the drug, and most trials had other weaknesses.

cl_can_med_other_conditions.q: Do cannabis medicines help sleep, anxiety, appetite or other conditions?
cl_can_med_other_conditions.short: Too few small trials to tell; sleep scores were slightly better than with a dummy.
cl_can_med_other_conditions.but: Each condition had only a few small trials. Many had serious weaknesses.
how: In trials for pain or MS, sleep scores were a little better with the medicine than with a dummy (placebo). This evidence is very weak.
Anxiety, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome had only one or two small trials each. Appetite in HIV had four.
No trial treated depression. In trials for other illnesses, depression scores mostly did not differ.
Epilepsy was not part of this review. Trials of a CBD medicine for epilepsy were not read for this answer.
cl_can_med_other_conditions.rate: Each condition had one to four small trials, of 6 to 88 people, and many had serious flaws. The sleep scores came mostly from trials for pain or multiple sclerosis.

cl_can_med_side_effects.q: What side effects do cannabis medicines cause?
cl_can_med_side_effects.short: More side effects than with a dummy, such as dizziness, feeling high, confusion and dry mouth.
cl_can_med_side_effects.but: Short trials at the highest dose tested; long-term harms were not studied.
how: Researchers put together trials of cannabis medicines. They were compared with a dummy (placebo) or another medicine, at the highest dose each trial gave.
About 81 in 100 people on cannabis medicines had at least one side effect. So did 62 in 100 on the comparison.
The odds of quitting a trial because of side effects were about three times higher, and of a serious side effect 1.4 times. Deaths did not differ.
The review gave counts out of 100 only for having any side effect, not for each one.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people in 29 short trials, how many had at least one side effect?
pairs: people given a cannabis medicine
people given a dummy medicine or another medicine
freq.note: Simple totals across trials of different lengths and illnesses, at the highest dose each trial gave.

cl_can_med_side_effects.rate: A review of 79 trials, whose results agree. But 55 had weak spots, often many people dropping out without this being allowed for.

cl_can_dependence_how_many.q: How many people who use cannabis become dependent on it?
cl_can_dependence_how_many.short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.
cl_can_dependence_how_many.but: The surveys are from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition than today's.
how: A US survey in 1990 to 1992 asked about 8,000 people aged 15 to 54 about drug use and dependence.
Of those who had ever used cannabis, even once, about 9 in 100 had been dependent at some point: fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.
A second US survey, in 2001 to 2005, estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime; half of those who became dependent did so within about 5 years of first use.
Newer US figures are higher, about 3 in 10, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

freq.what: of people who had ever used cannabis had been dependent at some point
freq.note: US survey of people aged 15 to 54, 1990 to 1992, with an older, narrower definition of dependence; the tobacco figure was worked out from two surveys.

cl_can_dependence_how_many.rate: Two large US surveys, a decade apart, give almost the same figure. But they asked people in their homes between 1990 and 2005, so other countries and today's cannabis may differ.

cl_can_dependence_frequency_onset.q: Are frequent use and starting young linked to cannabis dependence?
cl_can_dependence_frequency_onset.short: People who use more often are more often dependent; for starting young, studies disagree.
cl_can_dependence_frequency_onset.but: Most numbers come second-hand from reviews, and none can show what causes what.
how: Reviews give figures from about 1 in 5 to 1 in 2 for people who use daily; one often-quoted figure (25 to 50 in 100) cannot be traced to any study.
Reviews say about 1 in 6 people who start as teenagers become dependent, against about 1 in 10 of everyone who has used.
In a large US survey, starting before 14 went with more dependence until other mental health and drug problems were counted, then with less; that does not mean starting early protects.
Dependence partly means using more than you meant to, so using often and being dependent are hard to pull apart.
cl_can_dependence_frequency_onset.rate: Studies where people recalled their own use, mostly known second-hand. Figures vary widely, and the link with starting young reverses once other problems are taken into account. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_can_withdrawal.q: How common is withdrawal when people who use cannabis regularly stop, and what is it like?
cl_can_withdrawal.short: About 17 in 100 in general surveys; more than half in clinic and hospital groups.
cl_can_withdrawal.but: Studies counted it in different ways, and none checked how often people get these feelings anyway.
how: A 2020 review pooled 50 groups of people who used cannabis regularly or had a use disorder.
Withdrawal means at least 3 of 7 problems within about a week of stopping heavy use: irritability, nervousness, poor sleep, less appetite, restlessness, low mood or body symptoms such as headache.
Reviews say it usually starts 1 to 2 days after stopping, is worst in the first week and fades within 1 to 2 weeks; one statement says it can last about a month.
Counted person by person, about 28 in 100 in the review had withdrawal; its headline of 47 in 100 mostly reflects small clinic groups.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who used cannabis regularly, how many had withdrawal?
pairs: in general-population surveys
in outpatient groups (clinics and research studies)
in inpatient or residential groups
freq.note: Pooled from 50 groups that defined regular use and withdrawal in different ways (2020 review).

cl_can_withdrawal.rate: A review of 50 groups of people who used cannabis regularly. Results vary hugely: two analyses of the same national survey found 8.0% and 34.4%, and many people answered from memory.

cl_can_chs_features_course.q: What is cannabis hyperemesis syndrome (repeated severe vomiting), and does stopping end it?
cl_can_chs_features_course.short: Bouts of severe vomiting with regular cannabis use; in reported cases, stopping ended them.
cl_can_chs_features_course.but: Published cases only: nobody knows how common it is, and fewer than half were followed up.
how: A 2017 review pooled 211 published cases; all had bouts of vomiting with severe nausea, and most had belly pain.
About 3 in 4 used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before it started.
Most found that hot baths or showers eased it for a while, but many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.
Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better; the 21 who kept using did not.

freq.what: of reported cases who stopped using got completely better
freq.note: 62 of 64 published cases in which stopping was recorded; most published cases had no follow-up written down.

cl_can_chs_features_course.rate: Reports of 211 patients that doctors chose to publish, mostly hospital cases, which may not be typical. Only 85 were followed up, and nobody checked whether people really stopped using cannabis.

cl_can_thc_pk_route.q: How does THC move through the body after smoking and after eating, and how long does it stay in blood and urine?
cl_can_thc_pk_route.short: Smoked, THC peaks in the blood within minutes; eaten, it rises slowly over hours.
cl_can_thc_pk_route.but: Old, small lab studies of weak cannabis, described in one review.
how: After smoking, THC in the blood peaked within minutes and fell to low levels within 2 hours.
After eating, it peaked 1 to 6 hours later, at lower levels, and the effects started later and lasted longer.
THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly; in people who use often, it can be found for days to weeks.

After one cigarette the last positive urine test came about 1 to 4 days later on average, and cannabis was found for 67 and 93 days in two people who used heavily; a positive test does not show when or how much.
cl_can_thc_pk_route.rate: Lab studies with as few as 6 people, known only through one review, with much of the data from its author's own lab. People differed a lot, and the cannabis was weaker than today's.

cl_can_psychosis_frequency.q: Can cannabis cause psychosis, and does using it daily matter?
cl_can_psychosis_frequency.short: People who use cannabis, most of all daily, get psychosis more often than people who don't.
cl_can_psychosis_frequency.but: This is a link: these studies cannot show that cannabis was the cause.
how: Seven big studies followed young people for years. Those who had ever used cannabis had about 1.4 times the odds of psychosis later, mostly symptoms rather than a diagnosed illness, compared with people who never had.

For each study's heaviest-use group (from more than 50 times to daily use or dependence), the odds were about twice as high. In two studies of people with a first psychosis, daily use went with about 3 times the odds, and using now and then was not linked.
