In a big Swedish study of men, about 6 in 1,000 who had never used cannabis, and about 38 in 1,000 who had used it more than 50 times, later went to hospital with schizophrenia. These counts do not allow for other differences between the men.
Taking other differences between people into account, such as other drug use and other mental health problems, shrank the link by about half.

freq.what: men in a large Swedish study were diagnosed with schizophrenia by about age 45, whether or not they used cannabis
freq.note: 362 of 50,087 men conscripted in 1969 (editors' calculation from a review's table), all levels of cannabis use together.

cl_can_psychosis_frequency.rate: Studies that followed thousands of people in several countries mostly agree. But people who use cannabis differ in other ways too, and allowing for some of those shrank the link by about 45%.

cl_can_psychosis_potency.q: Is strong cannabis more closely linked to psychosis than weaker cannabis?
cl_can_psychosis_potency.short: Daily use of strong types had the strongest link with psychosis, but the gap from weaker types could be chance.
cl_can_psychosis_potency.but: Strength was guessed from the type people named, and both studies come from one team.
how: Two studies by one team, one in south London and one in 11 places in Europe and Brazil, compared people who had a first psychosis with people from the same areas who had not.

In 11 places in Europe and Brazil, daily use of strong types (10% THC or more on average) went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis, compared with never using. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times; the gap between the two could be chance.

In the 11 places, using any type only now and then was not linked to psychosis. In London, using strong types less than once a week went with nearly 2 times the odds, but some numbers in that study do not add up. In both studies, weaker types were not linked once all patterns of use were counted together.
Nobody tested the cannabis: people named the type they had used after they became ill, and its strength was taken from police, European and national figures.
cl_can_psychosis_potency.rate: Two studies by one team, comparing people with a first psychosis with people without. The type of cannabis was recalled after illness began, and family history and genes were not taken into account.

cl_can_psychosis_causation.q: Does cannabis cause psychosis, or could something else explain the link?
cl_can_psychosis_causation.short: Not known. Part of the link seems to come from other differences between people.
cl_can_psychosis_causation.but: The gene studies only looked at ever trying cannabis, not at daily or strong use.
how: In seven big studies, taking other differences between people into account shrank the link by about half, on average.
In a Swedish study of relatives, the link got smaller the more closely related two people were. It was still there in identical twins, but nobody checked whether that could be chance.
Gene studies found that genes linked to schizophrenia go with trying cannabis. Evidence that genes linked to trying cannabis go with schizophrenia was weaker.
The researchers who did these studies, and experts reading them, disagree about whether cannabis itself raises the risk.
cl_can_psychosis_causation.rate: Studies following people, gene studies and sibling and twin comparisons. People who use cannabis differ in other ways too, and early illness may itself lead to cannabis use. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_can_schizophrenia_trends.q: Has schizophrenia become more common as more people used cannabis?
cl_can_schizophrenia_trends.short: Studies disagree: some places saw more psychosis over time, others no rise as use grew.
cl_can_schizophrenia_trends.but: We know these studies only through reviews, and changes in diagnosis can blur trends.
how: In Australia, a study found no clear rise in psychosis after cannabis use went up in the 1980s and 1990s.
In south-east London and in Zurich, psychosis became more common in people born more recently.
A review says that in the UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s, while first hospital stays for schizophrenia did not rise.
Even if cannabis played a part, the rise would be small and hard to see in health records.
cl_can_schizophrenia_trends.rate: Mostly counts of people treated for psychosis across whole countries or cities over time. These cannot link any person's cannabis use to their illness, and the places studied point different ways.

cl_xc_mindset_before.short: It may. Feeling calm, open and ready beforehand went with easier trips, and feeling anxious went with more anxiety during the trip.
cl_xc_mindset_before.but: These are links: no study we read changed how people felt beforehand to test it.
how: About 650 people planning their own trip answered surveys; about 200 answered enough to be counted. Those who felt calm, open and ready the day before said the trip was less hard.
In lab studies of LSD, feeling anxious before the dose went with more anxiety. A better mood beforehand went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones.
Bigger links come from people looking back on how they'd felt, asked at the same time as how the trip went, so they don't show what came first.
Clinical trials prepare people with meetings and advice. But a review of 25 trials found none that compared different ways of preparing.
cl_xc_mindset_before.rate: Only links, from one online study and nine lab studies in Basel. The online one shrank from 654 people to about 198 and didn't allow for which drug people took.

cl_xc_setting_support.short: Maybe a little. In surveys, people who felt safe and supported reported slightly fewer hard moments.
cl_xc_setting_support.but: People rated this looking back, and the one study that asked beforehand found only a weak link.
how: In a study that asked the day before, feeling good about the place and people went with slightly easier trips. But the link was weak and could be chance.
Almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca answered a survey. Those who felt safer and better supported at the ceremony reported a little less fear.
In a US survey, people who blamed a lack of support for their hardest trip said it was harder than people who did not.

No study we read put people in different places, or with different people, to compare them. A review of 25 trials found none either; some used plain hospital rooms, others disguised them as living rooms.
cl_xc_setting_support.rate: Four studies, mostly surveys of people who chose to answer and rated everything afterwards. Results differ by what was asked: blaming the people around showed no link with how hard trips were.

cl_aya_ceremony_setting.q: Does the kind of ayahuasca ceremony matter for how it goes?
cl_aya_ceremony_setting.short: Maybe a little. People who felt safer and better supported at their last ceremony recalled a bit less fear. They also reported fewer problems later.
cl_aya_ceremony_setting.but: One survey: people rated the ceremony and how it went at the same time, looking back.
how: Almost 7,000 people who had drunk ayahuasca answered one online survey about their last ceremony.
Each step up on a 1-to-4 rating of feeling safe and supported went with about 0.3 points less fear, out of 10, and slightly fewer problems in the weeks after.
More traditional practices, and drinking in Amazon countries other than Brazil, went with more fear. Church hymns or sermons went with less.
Fasting showed no link the study could detect with fear or later problems. All the differences were small, and nothing was measured before people drank.
cl_aya_ceremony_setting.rate: One large survey, recruited through the groups whose ceremonies were rated. People rated the ceremony and how it went at the same sitting, looking back, so each answer could colour the other.

cl_xc_difficult_how_common.q: How common are bad trips, and can problems last?
cl_xc_difficult_how_common.short: Fairly common: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip. 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life.
cl_xc_difficult_how_common.but: That's one online survey, and people were looking back over their whole lives.
how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.
Most were glad they had used psychedelics: 79 in 100 agreed, at least a little.
In the days or weeks after their hardest trip, 7 in 100 said they'd thought of hurting themselves or others, or tried to.

57 in 100 said a problem like worry or poor sleep lasted at least a few days, and put it down to psychedelics. But people who hadn't used them weren't asked, so it's unknown how many would have had these anyway.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who had ever used a psychedelic, in one US online survey:
pairs: said they had had at least one difficult experience
said one had severely affected their ability to get through daily life
sought medical or psychological help afterwards
freq.note: 613 US adults asked once, in 2021, looking back over their whole life (251, 28 and 16 people). No one who had not used psychedelics was asked.

cl_xc_difficult_how_common.rate: One online survey of 613 US adults from a sign-up panel, matched only on sex, age and ethnicity. Two of its questions gave counts that don't agree, and no one who hadn't used psychedelics was asked.

cl_xc_music.short: Nobody knows for sure: no study we read compared music with silence. 18 of 19 patients said music helped at times; 10 said it sometimes made things harder.
cl_xc_music.but: The one test that compared two playlists had just 10 people, so it could easily miss a difference.
how: 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression took psilocybin in a clinic with music. Almost all said it helped at times; about half said it sometimes made things harder.

Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression a week later. But both were measured at the same time, so feeling better may have made them describe the music more warmly.

In a trial of 10 people trying to quit smoking, each had one session with classical music and one with gongs and singing bowls, in random order. How mystical or hard the sessions felt did not clearly differ.
In a US survey, people who linked their hardest trip to music they disliked didn't rate that trip as harder than others did.
cl_xc_music.rate: One small trial of 10 people compared two playlists, not music with silence, and everyone knew which music played. The rest is what people said afterwards.

cl_ket_music.short: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how a session feels or how well ketamine works. One trial found the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music.
cl_ket_music.but: Just 32 patients; the report gave no results on how the sessions felt.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression were starting a course of six ketamine drips. Chance decided who heard music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip. The bottom number didn't clearly differ.
Before that, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine. In most, ketamine came with other drugs during medical procedures. None compared music with no music in treating depression.
The review's case reports and interviews had no comparison. Some said music eased the detached feeling or blocked distractions; others heard it warped, or felt it kept them tied to the outside world.
cl_ket_music.rate: One trial of 32 patients, reporting only blood pressure. The earlier studies are small, mostly during medical procedures, and known only through a review.

cl_mdma_response_predictors.q: Do some people feel MDMA more strongly than others?
cl_mdma_response_predictors.short: Yes. The biggest link was the amount per kilo of body weight. Given the same amount, lighter people got more per kilo, which went with stronger effects.
cl_mdma_response_predictors.but: That's one lab, with healthy volunteers in a hospital, most of them trying MDMA for the first time.
how: 194 healthy adults aged 18 to 45 took MDMA in hospital, one set amount each time. On another day they took a dummy pill.
The amount per kilo of body weight went most with how strong it felt. Women and men didn't clearly differ once weight was counted, though an earlier report suggested women may feel more bad effects.

People who tend to worry, or who felt anxious and low just before, said they felt more anxious than calmer people did. People more open to new things felt closer to others. None of these links was strong.
Each session had one fixed amount, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.
cl_mdma_response_predictors.rate: Ten pooled studies from one lab, with 194 healthy volunteers. It compares different people, so it shows links, not causes, and traits that go together weren't pulled apart.

cl_lsd_response_predictors.q: Do some people feel LSD more strongly than others?
cl_lsd_response_predictors.short: In lab studies, the dose went most with how strong LSD felt. Mood and personality did too.
cl_lsd_response_predictors.but: The paper says which way each link goes, not how big it is.
how: 213 healthy adults took LSD in a hospital room and, in most studies, a dummy pill on another day.
People who felt well just before had stronger effects than others. People who felt anxious had more anxiety during the session.
Open people had more spiritual feelings. People who had used drugs like LSD more often felt less overall than people who had used them less.
People whose genes make a liver enzyme slower had more LSD in the blood. Each session had one fixed dose, so taking more was not tested.
cl_lsd_response_predictors.rate: One analysis of nine studies by a single Basel lab, with 213 healthy volunteers. People who differ in mood or personality may differ in other ways too, and no sizes are given.

cl_benzo_harm_reduction_services.q: Which harm reduction services exist for benzos, and do they work?
cl_benzo_harm_reduction_services.short: Drug checking, prescribed benzos and stricter rules exist. No study has shown whether they lower harm.
cl_benzo_harm_reduction_services.but: The review did not judge how good the studies were, and most had no comparison group.
how: A 2025 review found 35 reports on harm reduction for benzos.

About half of the drug-checking reports tested how well testing machines find drugs. A portable machine found the designer benzo etizolam in 36 of 100 samples that had it; an infrared machine found it in 9.
At one service in Canada, people brought 139 samples they thought were Xanax. An infrared machine found alprazolam, the drug in Xanax, in 33 of them.
Studies of benzos on prescription and of stricter rules could not show what caused what. Their results were mixed.

freq.what: samples that people thought were Xanax had alprazolam in them, by infrared testing
freq.note: 33 of 139 samples at one Canadian drug-checking service, as reported in a 2025 review.

cl_benzo_harm_reduction_services.rate: A single review of 35 sources that did not check their quality; most were surveys or descriptions, and none compared groups in a way that could show less harm.

cl_opi_using_alone.q: How common is using drugs alone, and why do people do it?
cl_opi_using_alone.short: Very common: 76 in 100 people at harm reduction sites said they'd used alone at least once in the past week. The most-picked reason: it's easier and more comfortable at home.
cl_opi_using_alone.but: It's one survey in one part of Canada, of people who already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, answered a survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone more often had no steady home: 38 in 100, against 24 in 100 of those who didn't.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.

freq.what: had used drugs alone at least once in the past week
freq.note: 314 of 414 people at 27 harm reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, in 2018.

cl_opi_using_alone.rate: One survey of 414 people who happened to visit harm reduction sites in British Columbia in 2018. Nobody told them what counted as alone, and reasons were picked from a short list.

cl_can_cbd_with_thc.q: Does CBD taken with THC change THC's effects?
cl_can_cbd_with_thc.short: Studies disagree on CBD and THC; no reliable pattern has been shown across different conditions.
cl_can_cbd_with_thc.but: The studies used different amounts and timings. Most were small, and earlier trials were read through a review.
how: A review gathered 16 lab studies of healthy volunteers, from 1974 to 2019. In most, adding CBD made no clear difference to feeling high, heart rate or THC in the blood.
A few small studies, where THC was swallowed or injected, found less anxiety or fewer paranoid feelings with CBD. The review found no pattern by amount or way of taking it.
In a later trial, 18 adults ate brownies with THC alone or the same THC plus a large amount of CBD. With CBD, blood THC was higher and they felt sicker and more impaired.
Other test medicines, including a sedative, were given in that trial. They may have added to the effects.
cl_can_cbd_with_thc.rate: Small lab studies in healthy volunteers, mostly seen only through one weak review. They disagree, and the lab products rarely match what people use.

cl_gen_telescoping.q: Do drug and alcohol problems develop faster in women than in men?
cl_gen_telescoping.short: Not shown for women in general. It was seen mostly in people in treatment.
cl_gen_telescoping.but: All these studies rest on memory. People said years later how old they were at each step.
how: The idea came mostly from people in treatment or in Alcoholics Anonymous. Years later, they had to say when each step came.

In two US treatment studies, some of women's steps looked 1 to 5 years shorter. In one, women started getting drunk regularly about 4 years later than men but reached their worst drinking at the same age.
In big US surveys of adults, fewer women than men became dependent on alcohol. Those who did got there about as fast as men: about 6 years after their first drink.
Among people with a cannabis problem in a US survey, women got there about 5 months sooner after first use than men. A review said 2.5 years, which is wrong.
cl_gen_telescoping.rate: Surveys and treatment studies, where everyone recalled each step years later. People who reach treatment are not typical, and the general surveys only partly agree. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_gen_women_treatment_entry.q: Are women less likely than men to get alcohol or drug treatment?
cl_gen_women_treatment_entry.short: For alcohol, somewhat less likely, mostly years after problems start. For drugs, about the same.
cl_gen_women_treatment_entry.but: The surveys are from the US, and people remembered dates years later.
how: In US surveys from 1991 to 2002, men with alcohol dependence got treatment more often or sooner than women in some age groups.
In a 1992 survey, as a review describes it, 23 in 100 men and 15 in 100 women with alcohol problems had ever been treated. The gap appeared only 8 or more years after the problems began.
For drug problems, and for treatment in the past year, reviews describe no difference. In 2015, about 10 in 100 women and 11 in 100 men who needed treatment got it.
Women more often went to mental health services. Reviews list barriers such as childcare and fear of losing custody, but several surveys found few differences in the barriers women and men named.

freq.what: women with alcohol problems had ever been treated
freq.note: One US survey, 1991 to 1992, as a review describes it; treatment includes Alcoholics Anonymous.

cl_gen_women_treatment_entry.rate: Two big US surveys on alcohol, where people recalled their ages years later and nobody defined what counted as treatment. Figures for drugs come second-hand from reviews.

cl_gen_women_treatment_outcomes.q: In drug or alcohol treatment, do women do as well as men?
cl_gen_women_treatment_outcomes.short: Most large studies found no difference between women and men once in treatment.
cl_gen_women_treatment_outcomes.but: This comes from two reviews by one research group; we have not read the studies themselves.
how: Two reviews by one research group looked at many studies of people who had already started treatment. They did not check how good the studies were.
In large studies, women and men mostly stayed in treatment about as long and had similar results. Finding no difference does not prove the results are the same.
Where differences appeared, the older review found women mostly did better. The newer one found more cases where women did worse, mainly in quitting smoking and with some medicines.
Women-only programmes gave mixed results. In the one trial that compared results, a women-only programme showed no difference from two mixed ones, and did less well than a costlier hospital one.
cl_gen_women_treatment_outcomes.rate: Two reviews by one team, mostly of US programmes, describe studies they did not check for quality. Most comparisons give no margin of error, so 'no difference found' does not prove there is none.

cl_gen_genes_family.q: Do genes and the home you grow up in shape drug problems?
cl_gen_genes_family.short: Both are linked: what comes from birth parents, and the home a child grows up in.
cl_gen_genes_family.but: One Swedish study. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.
how: In Sweden, 18,115 adopted children born 1950 to 1993 were followed in health, prescription and court records until 2009.
Some birth parents had a drug problem on record. Their children, raised by adoptive parents, had one about twice as often: about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did.
Adoptive brothers and sisters are not related by birth. Still, 6 in 100 of them had a drug problem when the adopted child had one, against 3 in 100 when the child did not.

The study did not work out a share due to genes. Where studies give one, it is about differences between people in one place and time. It does not say how much of your own risk comes from genes, and it can change when living conditions change.

freq.what: adopted children whose birth parent had a drug problem record had one themselves
freq.note: Children born 1950 to 1993 and adopted in Sweden; records up to 2009.

cl_gen_genes_family.rate: One Swedish study of 18,115 adopted people, using national records. 'Drug problems' included some convictions, not only diagnoses, and families known to police may simply be recorded more.

cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.q: Do words about drug use change how others see a person?
cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.short: Yes, some do. People judged a person more harshly when their troubles were said to come from drug use, not a health concern.
cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.but: These are views given after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are really treated.
how: 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. People with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or close family with one, couldn't take part.
When Alex's trouble was put down to drug use, not a health concern, readers wanted much more distance and saw Alex as more dangerous. In a pretend money game, they took slightly more from Alex.
Calling it a brain disease instead of a problem made readers think more that genes or illness caused it. Its other effects were small and unclear.

An older study tested labels on about 500 people at mental health conferences. Those whose story called a man a substance abuser, not someone with a substance use disorder, agreed slightly more with blaming and punishing him. It's a shaky result.
cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.rate: A fair test: chance decided which story each of 1,613 online volunteers read. But readers gave their views after one made-up story, and many were young.

cl_alc_early_drinking_later_problems.short: Not known. Some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.
cl_alc_early_drinking_later_problems.but: Only a few small studies followed young people over time; the big survey relied on memory.
how: In a big US survey in 1992, about 4 to 5 in 10 adults who started drinking at 14 or younger had been dependent on alcohol at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. They had to remember their first drink.
A review found only four groups of young people whose first drink was recorded as teenagers and who were followed into adulthood.
Drinking early went with more drinking problems in some of them. In others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems, were taken into account.

In US twins, the twin who drank without permission by about 15 drank more as an adult than the other twin, even in identical twins. But in identical twins it was not clearly linked to signs of an alcohol disorder.
cl_alc_early_drinking_later_problems.rate: A survey relying on memory and a few small studies following young people. People who start drinking early differ in other ways too, and the findings conflict. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_coc_alcohol_cannabis_couse.q: How often do people who use cocaine also drink or use cannabis?
cl_coc_alcohol_cannabis_couse.short: On average, about 3 in 4 also used alcohol, and 4 to 6 in 10 cannabis.
cl_coc_alcohol_cannabis_couse.but: These averages mix very different studies, from about 1 in 10 to nearly all.
how: A review put together 16 counts of people who used cocaine, mostly from the US.
On average, about 3 in 4 had used alcohol on the same occasion or in the same period, and 4 to 6 in 10 had used cannabis.
None of 40 recent brain-scan studies of cocaine left out people who drink or use cannabis (two left out recent cannabis use), so their results may mix up different drugs.
Animal studies almost never gave a second drug, so they did not copy how people use cocaine.

freq.what: people who used cocaine had also used alcohol on the same occasion
freq.note: Averages of 16 very different studies, 1985 to 2017, mostly US; single studies ranged from about 1 in 10 to nearly all, depending on the drug, the group and the question. The alcohol average could not be checked against the review's own table.

cl_coc_alcohol_cannabis_couse.rate: A review of 16 very different groups, from household surveys to emergency departments, whose figures vary enormously. The review did not check how good its sources were.

cl_caf_panic.q: Can caffeine bring on panic attacks in people with panic disorder?
cl_caf_panic.short: About half had a panic attack after one big dose; none after a dummy.
cl_caf_panic.but: Most studies used one large amount. The review cannot show what ordinary smaller servings do.
how: A 2022 review included 10 small lab studies of adults with panic disorder during a break from psychiatric medicines.
After caffeine, 121 of 237 had a panic attack. None was reported after a dummy drink or capsule, though not everyone completed both conditions.
In studies with both groups, about 54 in 100 people with panic disorder had an attack after caffeine, against 2 in 100 without it.
Anxiety also rose more after caffeine than a dummy in all five studies that tested that comparison. The pooled anxiety result was a different comparison: change after caffeine in the two groups.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people given one large dose of caffeine in a lab, how many had a panic attack?
pairs: people with panic disorder
people without panic disorder
freq.note: Six studies with both groups: 69 of 128 people with panic disorder against 2 of 115 without it. None was reported after placebo. The caffeine-equivalent amount of one citrate-labelled study is unclear.

cl_caf_panic.rate: 10 lab studies of people with panic disorder, on a break from their medicines, not in daily life. Two always gave caffeine last, and we know the studies only through one review.

cl_alc_meals_bac.q: Does eating before drinking change blood alcohol?
cl_alc_meals_bac.short: In 9 men, a meal just before drinking roughly halved peak blood alcohol.
cl_alc_meals_bac.but: One small lab study of young men. It measured blood alcohol, without testing impairment.
how: Nine healthy young men were given the same small amount of alcohol on five days: after three kinds of breakfast, after a night without food, or through a drip.
After a breakfast, the highest blood alcohol was about half the level after no food: 13 to 18 against 31 mg per 100 ml.
The kind of breakfast made no clear difference, but the study was too small to tell.
After food, blood alcohol varied more from person to person. Larger amounts, women and other meals were not studied.
cl_alc_meals_bac.rate: One careful lab trial: 9 young men each drank alcohol with and without breakfast. Too few to be sure of the size, and women were not tested.

cl_inh_sudden_death.short: Sudden deaths after sniffing solvents and sprays were reported in one old survey.
cl_inh_sudden_death.but: It counted deaths, without measuring risk among everyone who used these products.
how: A 1969 US survey described 110 deaths among young people aged 11 to 23, mostly involving sprays or a cleaning solvent. The report did not list poppers.
In several witnessed deaths, the person suddenly ran or panicked before collapsing. Where autopsies were described, they found no other cause.
The author proposed an effect on the heart's rhythm. No heart trace was recorded.
Families or friends hid the sniffing in 8 deaths, so some other deaths may have been missed.
cl_inh_sudden_death.rate: One US survey of 110 deaths in the 1960s, with no stated rules for which deaths counted, no comparison group, and no record of how many bodies were tested.

cl_gen_deaths_missed.short: Some deaths are missing; others are counted without showing which drug was involved.
cl_gen_deaths_missed.but: The gaps differ by place and rules. Most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths.
how: In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 out of 100 overdoses had only an unspecified-drug code.
Models guessed which drugs those counted deaths involved. They did not find deaths missing from the total.
In Stockholm, lists with similar totals disagreed about which people to include. They used different rules.
An England and Wales estimate suggests counts held about two thirds of deaths involving each opioid. It did not match each death across lists.
cl_gen_deaths_missed.rate: Studies comparing official death counts with other records or computer estimates, in the US and Europe. None had a sure answer to check against, and the estimates rest on unchecked assumptions.

cl_opi_deaths_heroin_missed.q: Do official counts miss heroin deaths?
cl_opi_deaths_heroin_missed.short: In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than records did.
cl_opi_deaths_heroin_missed.but: Each review used its own rules for what counts as a heroin death.
how: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine. Some death records said morphine or mixed drugs instead of heroin.
In Maryland (2012 to 2015), certificates named heroin in about 52 in 100 of the deaths a fuller review linked to heroin.

In Victoria, Australia (2012 to 2013), about 34 in 100 deaths a review linked to heroin lacked the heroin code in national figures. A few deaths coded as heroin were judged to involve it only by chance.
In England and Wales, an estimate came out about half as large again as the official count. It mixed heroin with morphine and did not match each death.
cl_opi_deaths_heroin_missed.rate: Re-checks of death files in Maryland and in Victoria, Australia, plus an estimate for England and Wales. Nobody has shown the fuller rules are right, and who did the re-checks isn't described.

cl_gen_deaths_autopsy_testing.q: Do autopsies and drug tests change which deaths count as drug deaths?
cl_gen_deaths_autopsy_testing.short: Sometimes: at one centre, about 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths had another cause.
cl_gen_deaths_autopsy_testing.but: Only two US places have been studied, so other places may differ.
how: At a North Carolina autopsy centre (2016 to 2021), 2,719 deaths were thought to be drug deaths. After a full autopsy and drug tests, about 10 in 100 had another cause, like a blood clot in the lungs. In some, the tests found no drug at all.
It went the other way too. Of 237 deaths nobody thought were from drugs, drug tests showed that about 49 in 100 were.

In Alabama, three doctors were told everything about 60 chosen deaths except what the autopsy found inside the body. Their cause of death matched the autopsy doctor's in 67 to 80 of every 100. They did not always agree with each other either.
In 2018, about 11 in 100 US death investigation offices said they had no access to drug tests. Small offices had them less often than big ones.

freq.what: of deaths suspected to be drug deaths had another cause after a full autopsy and drug tests
freq.note: One autopsy centre in North Carolina, 2016 to 2021 (265 of 2,719). An upper limit, and only for the suspected deaths, because it includes deaths where tests found no drug.

cl_gen_deaths_autopsy_testing.rate: Two US centres compared causes of death with and without a full autopsy. The yardstick was the autopsy doctor's own judgment, and one study picked its 60 deaths without saying how.

cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.short: Yes, somewhat. Readers judged the person who died more harshly when the story said heroin, not ecstasy, or an older person with years of use.
cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.
cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.rate: One online experiment in which chance decided which version of a made-up news story 1,248 UK adults read. The plan was not published first, and the stigma questions were new.

cl_cath_deaths_news_mephedrone.short: Not always: several deaths blamed on it in the news had other causes.
cl_cath_deaths_news_mephedrone.but: One study, and the later test results are second-hand reports, not official records.
how: From late 2009 to around April 2011, online news in the UK linked 18 named deaths to mephedrone.
Later reports said mephedrone was not found in 4, was found but did not cause the death in 4, and played a part in 7, mostly together with other drugs or illnesses.
The two deaths most linked to mephedrone online were later found to be from alcohol and methadone.
Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths were in the news. The author thinks the news raised interest in the drug, but search data cannot show that the news made people use it.
cl_cath_deaths_news_mephedrone.rate: One researcher checked 18 deaths named in UK online news during one news scare, using later press reports. Too few deaths to be sure, and nobody double-checked his work.

cl_gen_deaths_level_changes.short: Yes. Levels can rise or fall after death and differ between blood vessels, so a drug can look more or less involved in a death than it was.
cl_gen_deaths_level_changes.but: Nobody knows how often, or by how much, levels change in an ordinary death.
how: In four suspected overdose deaths picked as examples, a drug's level could be 3.5 to 6.6 times higher in one blood vessel than another in the same body. A hospital medicine varied only 1.6 times.
In one person, all imipramine samples after death were about 2 to 8 times the earlier hospital level.
A collection of 5,375 cases from published reports and Finnish lab records found that the gap between samples from different body parts varied more than tenfold between drugs.
In bodies tested more than once, levels of about a dozen drugs rose, including fentanyl and methadone; others, like THC, fell. First samples came about 17 hours after death on average.
cl_gen_deaths_level_changes.rate: Different kinds of study agree that levels change. But the evidence is four deaths picked as examples, 5,375 cases gathered mostly from published reports without a quality check, and reviews mostly about medicines.

cl_can_deaths_attributed.short: These studies do not settle that question.
cl_can_deaths_attributed.but: The linked deaths are selected reports with no comparison group.
how: A review collected 13 deaths linked to recent use. Eight had significant heart disease or other illness; five lacked a blood test showing recent use.
Larger studies, relayed by the review, point both ways. Some found no increase in deaths.
A Finnish table prints 0% as poisonings mainly attributed to THC, rounded to whole percent. That does not prove an exact zero count.
The reviewers encourage counting cannabis as a contributor in appropriate cases, but give no estimate of missed deaths.
cl_can_deaths_attributed.rate: Reports of 13 deaths, each published because someone suspected a link, with no comparison group; five lacked a blood test. Studies of heart attacks point different ways. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_cath_deaths_mephedrone_confirmed.short: In 25 of 128 alleged deaths, tests after death found no mephedrone.
cl_cath_deaths_mephedrone_confirmed.but: A positive test does not prove cause. A negative test may miss earlier use.
how: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to mephedrone; 13 results were still pending.
Of 62 deaths studied, mephedrone was the only substance found in 8. Other drugs were common.
One person died weeks later in hospital and had none found after death. Their earlier test evidence is not given.
The authors say tests and incomplete reporting may also miss deaths. They cannot give a death rate.

freq.what: of the 128 alleged deaths had no mephedrone found after death
freq.note: Editors’ rounded calculation: 25/128≈20 in 100; 13 results pending. Negative does not prove no earlier exposure.

cl_cath_deaths_mephedrone_confirmed.rate: One UK count of 128 deaths, included only because someone suspected mephedrone. How the tests were done is not described, and the numbers are small.

cl_opi_deaths_heroin_alone.short: Not necessarily. Older studies often found other drugs too: alcohol in 29 to 75 in 100 of these deaths. But finding a drug doesn't show it caused the death.
cl_opi_deaths_heroin_alone.but: These old records cannot tell how many deaths heroin alone caused.
how: In older studies from the USA, Australia and Europe, morphine was the only drug found in 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose. Alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100.
Many deaths took hours, and other people were often there: more than half the time, in four studies. These come second-hand, from a review.

In England and Wales in 2000, researchers classed 23 in 100 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners as something other than a direct overdose, like an infection, an injury, or drug effects plus an illness.
Heroin use can also be missed, because its marker can fall after death. Levels also depend on where and when samples are taken.
cl_opi_deaths_heroin_alone.rate: Old death records, mostly from 1967–1996, retold by a review that did not check its studies, plus one register from England and Wales in 2000. Neither describes today's drug supply.

cl_mdma_deaths_fatal_level.short: These studies do not establish a fatal cutoff; the measured levels overlap.
cl_mdma_deaths_fatal_level.but: The groups are small, and some London table decimals are unclear in the scan.
how: In Sheffield, England (1992–2008), levels in deaths attributed to MDMA overlapped levels in injury deaths. The middle value was about 7 times the injury-group value, but was not a cutoff.
The London table values overlap if unclear decimal points have been read correctly. Its survivors included severely ill people, not healthy people after ordinary use.
A Finnish table’s 0% concerns poisoning with MDMA as the main finding, not every possible contribution. It records what certifiers decided.
Sampling time and specimen matter. The London tables do not say when every sample was taken. No study here gives a healthy ordinary-use comparison.
cl_mdma_deaths_fatal_level.rate: Autopsy and poisons-service records from England and Finland. It's unclear who decided each cause of death or what they knew, and no study measured people who use MDMA without becoming ill.

cl_gen_deaths_excited_delirium.short: The label alone does not establish what caused a death.
cl_gen_deaths_excited_delirium.but: The cases were selected for reports. They cannot give the risk per encounter.
how: The reviews describe extreme agitation, but no validated definition or specific autopsy sign. The label is also used with living people.
In 168 published cases, force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths. That included sedation and electrical weapons as well as physical restraint.
Only 3 cases explicitly had no force; 28 had missing information. A later review also cites deaths attributed to the label without overt restraint.
Researchers disagree about restraint, drugs and the agitated state. These reports cannot tell how much each caused.
cl_gen_deaths_excited_delirium.rate: Two reviews of case reports picked for publication, which cannot show how often anything happens. They read the cases in opposite ways; only 3 of 168 clearly say no force was used.

cl_gen_early_drug_use.q: Does starting drugs young go with drug problems later?
cl_gen_early_drug_use.short: People who started young more often had drug or drinking problems later on.
cl_gen_early_drug_use.but: Studies can't show that starting young is the cause. Much of the link runs in families.
how: A 1992 US survey asked adults who had used drugs at least 12 times. About 1 in 3 who started at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs. For those who started at 21 or older, it was about 1 in 7.

In New Zealand, children were asked about drinking and drugs at 13 and 15, not years later. At 32, 29 in 100 of those who used several times by 15, mostly alcohol, were dependent on alcohol or drugs. For teens with similar childhoods who had not, it was 15 in 100.
In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often had drug problems by the study's rules. It was about 48 in 100, against 33 in 100 for the other twin.
A bigger twin study found the link was not strong, and much of it ran in families. Its authors think waiting longer to start would cut the risk only a little.

freq.what: adults who started using drugs at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs at some time
freq.note: US adults in 1992 who had used drugs at least 12 times; ages remembered at one interview.

cl_gen_early_drug_use.rate: Four separate groups of people, including twins and a New Zealand group followed from birth, point the same way. But most were adults asked to remember, years later, when they started.

cl_gen_gateway.q: Does using cannabis lead to other drugs (the 'gateway' idea)?
cl_gen_gateway.short: Not known. Cannabis usually comes first, but that does not prove it leads on.
cl_gen_gateway.but: Shared risks and access to other drugs could still explain the cannabis link.
how: In New Zealand, at least 86 in 100 young people who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis a year or more before.
Australian twins grew up together. The one starting cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants: 48 in 100 against 26 in 100.
A computer model where cannabis did nothing still made the same pattern. Some people were likelier to use any drug, and were offered cannabis first.
Experts disagreed about the New Zealand cannabis link. One said hidden factors no longer explain it away; another said factors changing with age still could.
cl_gen_gateway.rate: Surveys and interviews where people were asked, 1971 to 2005; the link varies hugely by country, and a computer model where cannabis has no effect gives the same pattern. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_gen_polydrug.q: How common is using several drugs, and why does it matter?
cl_gen_polydrug.short: Common among people who use illegal drugs. It makes one drug's effects hard to study.
cl_gen_polydrug.but: The numbers come second-hand from reviews. They vary a lot between groups and studies.
how: In ecstasy studies, 90 to 100 in 100 people also used cannabis. So a study of ecstasy may be measuring several drugs at once.
At underground raves, up to 75 in 100 people used several drugs, five on average at the last rave.
In most of 23 studies of teens, the biggest group used little or nothing. But every study found a group that used several. Most often it was alcohol, tobacco and cannabis: 6 to 29 in 100 teens.
Studies that sort adults into groups by the drugs they use found 2 to 8 groups. Bigger studies, and ones that asked about more drugs, found more. So what they find depends partly on how they look.
cl_gen_polydrug.rate: Mostly US and Australian studies of very different groups, known only through reviews, most of which did not check the quality of the studies they describe.

cl_coc_heat.q: Are cocaine deaths more common in hot weather, and why?
cl_coc_heat.short: In 1990s New York, hot days had about a third more cocaine overdose deaths.
cl_coc_heat.but: The study compared days, not people, and did not allow for season.
how: In New York City in 1993 to 1995, there were 2.34 cocaine overdose deaths a day on hot days and 1.76 on other days.

Deaths in the opiate group, where cocaine was absent or present only in amounts judged clinically insignificant, did not clearly rise. The study could not show that the rise happened only with cocaine.

In a lab, 7 healthy people who had never used cocaine were warmed in a heated suit after one small dose. They began to sweat later, warmed up more and felt less hot than after a numbing drug used for comparison.
The lab study used one small dose in people at rest, so it may not match real use in hot weather.
cl_coc_heat.rate: Deaths counted day by day in New York, 1993 to 1995, without allowing for season, plus one lab test of just 7 people who had never used cocaine.

cl_gen_deaths_how_counted.q: How is a death counted as a drug death?
cl_gen_deaths_how_counted.short: Different lists use different rules, so they do not always count the same deaths.
cl_gen_deaths_how_counted.but: The matching studies cover three places. The newest linked data are from 2012.
how: Some lists count drug poisoning as the main cause. Others count drugs found in tests, with age limits.
One death can be counted under several drugs. Finding a drug does not by itself show that it caused the death.
About 49 out of 100 people were on both lists in Norway. Fewer than half were on both in Sweden.
In New Mexico, about 89 out of 100 were on both lists. This study included other poisons too.
cl_gen_deaths_how_counted.rate: Three studies in Norway, Sweden and New Mexico matched death records person by person, and all found the lists differ. Studies that describe records, rather than test something, get two bars at most.

cl_gen_deaths_who_investigates.q: Does it matter whether a coroner or a medical examiner investigates?
cl_gen_deaths_who_investigates.short: Not clear. Coroner areas recorded deaths less precisely, but switching showed no clear change.
cl_gen_deaths_who_investigates.but: No study checked which records were right, and the study of switching used data up to 1998.
how: In the US, medical examiners are usually doctors appointed to the job. Coroners are often elected, and in some states need no medical training.

In nine US states (2019 to 2021), deaths in coroner areas were more often recorded without saying whether the death was an accident or a suicide than deaths in medical examiner areas of the same state.
Other US studies found that death certificates named no drug more often where coroners work.
But seven states that switched to medical examiners showed no clear change in how precisely poisoning deaths were recorded, although that study could not rule out a real improvement.
cl_gen_deaths_who_investigates.rate: One-time comparisons of US counties, which can't separate who investigates from local resources, and other studies point the opposite way or find nothing. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_gen_deaths_level_cause.q: Can a blood level show that a drug caused death?
cl_gen_deaths_level_cause.short: Not on its own. Levels overlap between deaths with different causes.
cl_gen_deaths_level_cause.but: The rules and tests used to decide the cause also affect the comparison.
how: In an English autopsy study, MDMA levels in drug deaths overlapped with levels in injury deaths.
An older review reports a similar overlap for morphine. It also cites comparisons with people who survived an overdose.
Finnish data compare blood after death with treatment ranges, not the same people before and after death.
At one US centre, full autopsy changed suspected drug-death classifications in both directions. This study tested drug presence, not levels.
cl_gen_deaths_level_cause.rate: Autopsy records, the biggest from 57,903 deaths in Finland, mostly involving medicines. Doctors deciding the cause often already knew the test results, and no study tested living people who use drugs for comparison.

cl_gen_stigma_health_care.q: Do health workers see and treat people who use drugs differently?
cl_gen_stigma_health_care.short: Many health workers said they felt negative. Whether care was worse is not clear.
cl_gen_stigma_health_care.but: Mostly surveys of what workers said, from 2000 to 2011, in a few countries.
how: A review gathered 28 studies, mostly from Australia, the UK and the US. In them, health workers described their views of patients with drug or alcohol problems.

Many workers felt negative about these patients, or less positive than about people with other illnesses. This was more common outside drug and alcohol services. Some studies found neutral or positive views.
Only a few studies asked whether this changes care, and they disagreed. In one, people who felt staff treated them unfairly were less likely to finish treatment.
In another, doctors' views were not linked to what patients said about their care. The one study that watched real visits, from the 1980s, found better care for these patients.
cl_gen_stigma_health_care.rate: One review of 28 papers, mostly surveys of what health workers said, answered by those who chose to. We know them only through the review, whose summaries contain errors.

cl_gen_release_deaths.q: Is the risk of dying highest just after leaving prison?
cl_gen_release_deaths.short: Yes. In the first week out, the risk of dying was about 1.5 to 2 times that of later weeks. Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause.
cl_gen_release_deaths.but: It's death records only: they don't name the drugs, and nobody measured tolerance, so the study can't say why.
how: Researchers used death records for about 1.5 million people who left prison or jail in eight countries, between 1980 and 2018.
16 of the 18 groups had records for each day. In them, the risk of dying in days 2 to 7 after release was about 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks.
Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause, in that first week and overall. Yet 91 in 100 of those deaths came after week 4, since people were followed for much longer than that.
The study had no information on drug use, treatment or tolerance. So it cannot say why the first week is riskier.
cl_gen_release_deaths.rate: Death records of 1,471,526 people released from prison or jail in eight countries, all analysed the same way. But it is one study, and how causes were recorded wasn't checked.

cl_gen_remission.q: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?
cl_gen_remission.short: Many do. For alcohol, many people who recovered were never treated. In a US survey, 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer counted as dependent about 3 years later.
cl_gen_remission.but: How many depends on who is counted, and in the studies we read, recovery without treatment was measured only for alcohol.
how: Of US soldiers back from Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics there, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.

In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later. Some may still have had one or two, and treatment in between wasn't reported.

Across 21 studies, mostly of people found through treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, depending on how deaths and dropouts are counted. For many, the authors say, the problem is long-lasting.

For alcohol, figures for recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100, mostly because studies count different groups. Many who recovered were never treated. Far fewer of everyone with a problem recover untreated in a year.

freq.what: adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent about 3 years later
freq.note: US national survey, 2001–2002 and 2004–2005; some still had one or two signs; the editors’ count from the study’s numbers, not weighted, so not a national estimate.

cl_gen_remission.rate: Interviews with soldiers back from Vietnam and a US national survey, plus reviews. Figures on recovery without treatment come second-hand from a review that did not check how good its 27 studies were.

cl_gen_rat_park.q: What did the 'Rat Park' studies show about environment and morphine?
cl_gen_rat_park.short: Less than is often said. Rats living together drank less morphine water, but only in some tests.
cl_gen_rat_park.but: All of this was in rats, so it says nothing direct about people.
how: In 1979, by the last test, rats kept alone drank 5 to over 16 times as much sweet morphine water as rats living together.
In 1978, when morphine water was almost all they had to drink, the rats living together drank more of it.
In all three studies, the two groups drank morphine water from different machines, measured differently. That could explain part of the gap.
Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result.
cl_gen_rat_park.rate: Three small experiments in rats from one lab, with groups as small as 2 rats and different drinking machines for the two groups; a later repeat failed. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_coc_alternative_rewards.q: Will people who use cocaine choose another reward instead?
cl_coc_alternative_rewards.short: Sometimes. Six people picked $5 over real cocaine doses about 1 time in 3 or 4.
cl_coc_alternative_rewards.but: Only six people, in a lab, and cocaine was never offered without another choice.
how: Six people who smoked cocaine almost daily lived in a research hospital. Many times, they chose between a dose of smoked cocaine and a $5 voucher they could use only when they left.
With real doses, they took the voucher about 1 time in 3 or 4. At the smallest dose it was about half the time; at the largest, 1 or 2 times in 10.
They took a cash voucher a little more often than a voucher for goods, but the cash sessions always came first, so the order may explain it.
The study measured choices in a lab, not drug use in daily life, and no session offered cocaine with no other choice.
cl_coc_alternative_rewards.rate: One lab study of only six people, choosing between cocaine and vouchers they could spend only on leaving. Lab choices may not match what happens in daily life.

cl_alc_expectancy.q: Does believing you've had alcohol change how you act?
cl_alc_expectancy.short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.
cl_alc_expectancy.but: Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, with low blood alcohol.
how: 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Half had a history of drinking problems.
Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass. Real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank.
Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking, but not with changes in mood or memory. Sexual arousal rose on average, but that varied a lot between studies.
The alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. Blood alcohol in the drinking study stayed low, so heavier drinking may differ.
cl_alc_expectancy.rate: Lab experiments from the 1970s and 1980s. In most, the person running them knew who got what, and a 15-minute taste test is far from real life.

cl_coc_pk_route.q: How fast does cocaine act, and for how long?
cl_coc_pk_route.short: Smoked or injected, the high peaks in about a minute and fades within 30 minutes.
cl_coc_pk_route.but: Small lab studies of men who used cocaine often. Snorting was not measured.
how: Nine men who both smoked and injected cocaine stayed on a research ward. They got set doses, each given over 15 seconds.
The high, a faster heartbeat and higher blood pressure peaked after about a minute. The high was low by 15 to 30 minutes.
Cocaine stayed in the blood after the high had gone. In 4 other men, the level halved only about every 40 to 80 minutes in the later hours.
An older review says snorted cocaine peaks later, with the high at 10 to 20 minutes, and lasts longer. No study here tested what happens when people then take more.
cl_coc_pk_route.rate: Two small lab studies of 9 and 4 men who used cocaine often. The order of tests was not left to chance, and lab conditions differ from everyday use.

cl_coc_crack_powder.q: Is crack more addictive or more harmful than powder?
cl_coc_crack_powder.short: Possibly, though it's the same drug. People new to crack reported each sign of dependence more often: about 18 to 32 in 100, against 5 to 12 for powder.
cl_coc_crack_powder.but: Each person was asked once, so the surveys cannot show that crack itself is the reason.
how: Powder can't be smoked; crack is. A 1996 review links most differences to how each is taken, how fast and how much cocaine that delivers, and how much people use, not the form itself.
In US surveys from 1995 to 1998, about 18 to 32 in 100 people who had just started crack reported each sign of dependence. For people who had just started powder, it was 5 to 12 in 100.
After allowing for how many days people had used, and for age, drinking, smoking and injecting, the gap was smaller but did not go away.
A review of 302 studies found comparisons of crack with other cocaine mixed. Its authors say crack is not a likely direct cause of the infections and violence linked to it.
cl_coc_crack_powder.rate: US household surveys from 1995–1998 that asked people once, with no way to know how people differed before they started. A review of 302 articles says the wider research disagrees.

cl_coc_dependence_onset.q: How fast can you get hooked on cocaine?
cl_coc_dependence_onset.short: Within a year of starting, about 5 in 100 who used only powder were dependent; 22 in 100 who went on to crack.
cl_coc_dependence_onset.but: People answered once, about themselves. The survey cannot show that crack itself made the difference.
how: US surveys from 2002 to 2016 asked people who had first used cocaine less than a year before.
About 5 in 100 of those who had used only powder met the criteria for cocaine dependence. So did about 22 in 100 of those who had gone on to crack.
In both groups the most common problem was wanting or trying to cut down or stop: about 45 in 100 and 58 in 100.
People who go on to crack may differ to begin with, and some may already have had problems with powder. The survey did not ask which form caused a problem.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who had started cocaine in the past year, how many met the criteria for dependence?
pairs: people who had used only powder
people who had also gone on to crack
freq.note: US household surveys, 2002 to 2016. People were asked once, less than a year after they first used cocaine.

cl_coc_dependence_onset.rate: Yearly US surveys from 2002–2016. Only 275 people went on to crack, too few to be sure, and the two groups may have differed before they ever started.

cl_coc_levamisole.q: What is levamisole in cocaine, and what harm can it do?
cl_coc_levamisole.short: An animal worm medicine often found in cocaine, linked to blood and skin harm.
cl_coc_levamisole.but: This comes from case reports, so how often it causes harm is unknown.
how: Around 2010 it was in about 7 in 10 cocaine samples tested by US drug police, and in 8 or 9 in 10 urine samples that tested positive for cocaine in two US cities.
In some people the white blood cells that fight infection fell very low. Counts came back 5 to 10 days after the exposure stopped, or sooner with a hospital medicine.
Others had painful purple skin patches, sometimes with dying skin, often on the ears, cheeks or nose. Most healed within weeks of stopping cocaine, but some needed skin grafts or amputation.
Cases were linked to levamisole mainly because the person used cocaine. Since most cocaine held it, finding it shows a person was exposed, not that it caused the harm.
cl_coc_levamisole.rate: Reports of single patients and small groups, known only through two reviews. It is unclear how many were tested for levamisole, and most figures come from the US around 2008–2011.

cl_coc_psychosis.q: How common is cocaine psychosis among people treated for cocaine use?
cl_coc_psychosis.short: 68 in 100 people treated for cocaine reported psychotic symptoms; 16 in 100 had a diagnosed disorder.
cl_coc_psychosis.but: These were people in treatment, and many also used alcohol or other drugs.
how: One review pooled 17 studies of 5,286 people, mostly in treatment for cocaine in the US and Spain.
Asked about symptoms such as paranoia, 68 in 100 said they had had them with cocaine. Strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100.
The review could not separate cocaine from the alcohol and other drugs people used, so it cannot show cocaine alone caused it.
Other studies the review cites say the symptoms usually pass after stopping, but can get worse with more use and last for weeks.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people in treatment for cocaine:
freq.what: said cocaine had at some time given them psychotic symptoms, such as paranoia
freq.note: From 13 studies pooled in one review. With strict diagnostic interviews, 16 in 100 had a psychotic disorder.

cl_coc_psychosis.rate: A review of 17 studies of 5286 people in treatment, mostly asked to remember past symptoms. Figures vary hugely between questionnaires and regions, and other drug use could not be separated out.

cl_coc_stimulant_medicines.q: Do stimulant medicines help people stop using cocaine?
cl_coc_stimulant_medicines.short: In nine trials up to 2006, they did no better than a dummy pill.
cl_coc_stimulant_medicines.but: The trials were small, and newer reviews of these medicines have not been read yet.
how: Nine trials gave 640 people with cocaine dependence a stimulant medicine or a dummy pill. Everyone also had talking therapy.
There was no clear difference in staying in treatment or in urine tests positive for cocaine, but the trials were too small to rule out a modest benefit.
About 4 in 100 stopped the medicine because of unwanted effects, against about 1 in 100 on the dummy pill. The commonest were trouble sleeping, anxiety and feeling jittery.
One extra analysis found fewer positive tests with dexamphetamine, but it leans on filled-in results and on one group in which 42 of 46 people dropped out.
cl_coc_stimulant_medicines.rate: Nine trials of 640 people against dummy pills, but about 48% dropped out, and there were too few people to rule out a worthwhile benefit.

cl_ket_motivations.q: Why do people take ketamine, and what do they want from it?
cl_ket_motivations.short: Most said: for its effects, like melting into their surroundings, and for fun.
cl_ket_motivations.but: These 202 people were not picked at random, so their reasons may not be everyone's.
how: In Sydney in 1998 and 1999, 62 in 100 people said they first took ketamine for its effect, and 25 in 100 because friends did. In London, 81 in 100 said they were offered some and enjoyed it, and 17 in 100 that they wanted to forget their troubles.

The best parts named in Sydney were changed senses (78 in 100) and feeling outside the body (52 in 100). The worst was fear of the 'K-hole', a state of feeling deeply cut off (45 in 100). In London, 72 in 100 liked feeling they melted into their surroundings, and half disliked memory problems.

In London, the places most named were a friend's house (84 in 100) and home (71 in 100), more than clubs (52 in 100). In long interviews with 12 people in England, fun came first: some wanted a mild, chatty feeling, others a strong one.

Some people feel little from an amount. Reasons given here were tolerance and a weaker product: 22 in 100 in Sydney needed more for the same effect. In England, people said an unwanted K-hole came mostly from taking more than they meant to. Some sought one out.
cl_ket_motivations.rate: Three groups of volunteers found through friends and club scenes in Sydney, London and north-west England, mostly asked with untested questionnaires. People elsewhere, or today, may give other reasons.

cl_coc_mortality.q: How much more likely are people with problem cocaine use to die?
cl_coc_mortality.short: Each year, 5 to 62 in 1,000 died: 4 to 8 times others their age.
cl_coc_mortality.but: All groups injected, smoked crack daily, were in treatment or arrested; none only snorted.
how: Seven groups in six countries were studied between 1985 and 2005. Each year, between about 5 and 62 in 1,000 died.
Four groups were compared with people of the same age and sex: 4 to 8 times as many died.
Among people who injected, AIDS and overdose were the main causes. In a crack treatment group in Brazil, it was gunshot wounds and AIDS.
Many also used heroin or had HIV, and only age and sex were taken into account. So this does not show what cocaine itself does.

freq.title: Out of every 1,000 people in each group, how many died each year?
pairs: people who injected cocaine, Vancouver
people who injected cocaine, Baltimore
people arrested for cocaine, France
people treated for cocaine dependence, Italy
freq.note: Four of the seven groups, studied between 1988 and 2005. Where groups were compared with others of the same age and sex, 4 to 8 times as many died.

cl_coc_mortality.rate: Seven groups followed over time, known only through one review that does not say how deaths were found. Most people were disadvantaged, many had HIV, and all were studied between 1985 and 2005.

cl_coc_chest_pain_mi.q: How often is chest pain after cocaine a heart attack?
cl_coc_chest_pain_mi.short: US studies looked at people in hospital with chest pain after cocaine. About 1 to 6 in 100 were having a heart attack.
cl_coc_chest_pain_mi.but: These were 1990s studies, and their blood tests could miss small heart attacks.
how: One US hospital kept everyone with chest pain after cocaine in for a day of blood tests. 6 in 100 were having a heart attack.
In 136 heart attacks after cocaine, no one died in hospital. About half the problems, like an uneven heartbeat, were there on arrival.
A year after a hospital visit, 3 in 100 had died, none of a heart attack; 1 in 100 had a heart attack and lived.
The few later heart attacks were all in people who said they still used cocaine: 2 in one study, 4 in another.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who went to hospital with chest pain or similar symptoms after cocaine, how many were having a heart attack?
pairs: a 10-hospital trial that took many kinds of symptoms (1993)
one hospital that kept everyone in for a day of tests (1996 to 1998)
people kept in hospital, in a six-hospital study (1991 to 1992)
freq.note: 2 of 293, 15 of 250, and 8.6 in 100 of those admitted. US hospitals, older blood tests; mostly young men.

cl_coc_chest_pain_mi.rate: Several US hospital studies from 1987 to 1999, whose figures disagree. They found and tested patients in different ways, and mainly those kept in hospital got full blood tests.

cl_coc_cognition.q: Does cocaine affect memory and thinking?
cl_coc_cognition.short: On average, people with cocaine problems score somewhat lower on memory and attention tests.
cl_coc_cognition.but: No one was tested before they started, so we can't tell if cocaine caused the gap.
how: Five reviews pulled together small studies that compared people with cocaine problems with people who don't use cocaine.
Most gaps were small to medium, and studies disagree about the size. The newest review got the numbers of two small studies wrong, which made its gap look bigger.
Many also drank or used other drugs, some were tested within three days of last use, and most studies did not check scores against the normal range.
In 5 studies of people who had stopped for more than about 5 months, scores were close to the comparison groups. But these were other people, not the same people tested again.
cl_coc_cognition.rate: Small studies that tested people once, against comparison groups that often had more schooling. Results vary widely, and reviews of the same studies disagree about what the gaps mean.

cl_coc_beta_blockers.q: Does cocaine narrow heart arteries, and do beta-blockers make it worse?
cl_coc_beta_blockers.short: Yes, in a lab cocaine narrowed heart arteries a little. After a beta-blocker, blood flow fell further in all 10 patients, but its effect on heart attacks is unknown.
cl_coc_beta_blockers.but: No trial has ever tested beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine.
how: That lab test used 10 heart patients who had never used cocaine. The beta-blocker, propranolol, went straight into a heart artery.
In 2008, US heart doctors advised against beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine. That rests mainly on small lab tests, animal tests and expert opinion.
In hospital records of about 2,000 people, heart attacks and deaths were not clearly different with beta-blockers. But doctors chose who got them.
Two reviews counted one cocaine study's blood tests as heart attacks or damage. That study of 58 people reported no heart complications or deaths.
cl_coc_beta_blockers.rate: No fair test has counted heart attacks, only hospital records: doctors chose who got a beta-blocker, so the groups differed, and the numbers are small. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_ket_bladder.q: Is using ketamine linked to bladder problems?
cl_ket_bladder.short: Ketamine is linked to bladder problems seen in over 4,000 patients. In one survey, about 1 in 4 people who used it blamed it for urine problems.
cl_ket_bladder.but: No study compared how often people who use ketamine and people who don't get these problems. So none can show ketamine caused them.
how: In over 4,000 patients seen by doctors, mostly in Asia, about 77 in 100 needed to pee often and 60 in 100 had bladder pain.
In about 3 in 10 of these patients, urine had backed up and swollen a kidney. About 8 in 100 had weaker kidney function.
The survey was online, mostly in the UK: 1,285 people who had used ketamine in the past year. Those who used more reported more symptoms.
Of 251 people who described how symptoms changed, 128 said they eased after stopping. No study compared people who stopped with those who kept using.
cl_ket_bladder.rate: Reports on over 4,000 patients who already had urine problems, plus one online survey where people blamed their own symptoms on ketamine. None looked at people who don't use it, or ruled out other causes.

cl_ket_deaths_uk.q: How many UK deaths were linked to ketamine, and what were they?
cl_ket_deaths_uk.short: In England, ketamine was found or named in 283 deaths from 1999 to 2019, about 30 a year lately. Most had other drugs found too.
cl_ket_deaths_uk.but: Finding ketamine after a death does not show it caused the death.
how: A national register counted deaths in England where coroners' records named ketamine or tests found it. The rest of the UK wasn't included.
On average, 4 to 5 drugs were found. Records linked only ketamine to 32 deaths; it was the only drug found in 14 of those.
An earlier count by the same team found 23 UK deaths with ketamine from 1993 to 2006. It was the only drug found in 4.
About 3 in 4 deaths were recorded as accidental poisoning. 16 were suicides; others included drownings, falls and road crashes.
cl_ket_deaths_uk.rate: Counts of deaths where ketamine was found or named in records that coroners send in by choice. Not every death is tested for ketamine, and no matching count of people who use it exists.

cl_ket_vs_ect.q: Is ketamine as good as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) for hard-to-treat depression?
cl_ket_vs_ect.short: Two big trials disagree: a US trial found ketamine drips at least as good as ECT. But in Swedish hospital patients, 63 in 100 got well on ECT, against 46.
cl_ket_vs_ect.but: Everyone knew whether they got ketamine or ECT, and the trials took different people, so nobody knows why they disagree.

freq.what: on ECT got well (few depression symptoms left), in a Swedish trial of hospital patients
freq.note: One open-label trial: 57 of 91 on ECT and 44 of 95 on ketamine. A US trial of mostly outpatients found ketamine at least as good.

how: In a US trial of 403 adults, mostly outpatients without psychosis, 55 in 100 on ketamine drips said their depression halved, against 41 on ECT.
In a Swedish trial of 186 hospital patients, some with psychosis, 63 in 100 got well after ECT, against 46 after ketamine.
A review combining hospital trials also found ECT eased depression more than ketamine, but about half its data came from that Swedish trial.
In Sweden, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips.
cl_ket_vs_ect.rate: Two big trials of ketamine and ECT point opposite ways, one in hospital patients and one mostly in people living at home, and in both everyone knew their treatment. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_ket_treatment_side_effects.q: What side effects do people have from ketamine treatment for depression?
cl_ket_treatment_side_effects.short: With ketamine for depression, studies most often found headache and dizziness. Next came feeling unreal and higher blood pressure. Most soon passed.
cl_ket_treatment_side_effects.but: Only 12 of 60 studies checked again 2 weeks or more after the last dose, and just 5 checked the bladder.
how: A review of 60 studies up to 2016 listed side effects but could not say how often each happens. Most people had a single dose.
Raised blood pressure and heart rate came during or just after the drip and mostly settled within 90 minutes.
In a 7-person trial, all felt 'high' on ketamine and none on salt water. On average it was gone within 2 hours after the drip.
In a large trial, 25 in 100 on ketamine had a moderate or severe side effect within 3 weeks, against 32 in 100 on ECT.
cl_ket_treatment_side_effects.rate: A review of 60 studies that mostly noted side effects only when patients mentioned them, and counted studies, not people. The one large trial listed only moderate or severe ones.

cl_can_legal_teens.q: Did teen cannabis use rise after US states legalised it?
cl_can_legal_teens.short: Not in one big US study. After states made recreational cannabis legal, teens in school were a bit less likely to say they had used it in the past month.
cl_can_legal_teens.but: Just 7 states had surveys from both before and after the change, and only for its first few years.
how: Surveys gathered 1.4 million answers from US high school students, 1993 to 2017. Each state was compared before and after its law, against other states.
After recreational laws, the odds of past-month cannabis use were 8% lower. That is not 8 fewer teens in 100, but at most about 2.
Laws for medical cannabis, in 27 states and Washington, DC, were not linked to teen use either way, once other things were counted.
The authors suggest shops that check age make cannabis harder for teens to get. Their source: a 2012 news article. The study didn't test it.
cl_can_legal_teens.rate: Surveys in US schools, not a fair test. Only 7 states had legal cannabis with surveys before and after, no one checked if they were already changing, and other studies were mixed.

cl_can_cbd_epilepsy.q: Does a CBD medicine reduce seizures in a severe childhood epilepsy?
cl_can_cbd_epilepsy.short: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in Dravet syndrome. Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 on a dummy liquid.
cl_can_cbd_epilepsy.but: The maker ran both trials, and in its own backup checks the result did not always hold up.
how: First trial, 120 children: seizures at least halved in 43 in 100 on CBD and 27 on the dummy liquid. That gap could be chance.
Second trial, 198 children: 44 and 49 in 100 in two CBD groups saw seizures at least halve. On the dummy liquid, 26 did.
The second report said backup checks agreed. Yet with missing diary days filled in, one CBD group no longer clearly beat the dummy liquid.
On CBD, 23 to 36 in 100 children were sleepy, against 10 to 14 on the dummy liquid. Shop CBD was not tested.
cl_can_cbd_epilepsy.rate: Two trials where chance decided who got CBD, 319 children in all. But families could have guessed from side effects, and in both trials the result did not hold up in every planned check.

cl_psi_emergency.q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after magic mushrooms?
cl_psi_emergency.short: About 2 in 1,000 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After LSD: 10 in 1,000.
cl_psi_emergency.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, and people who could not answer were not counted.

freq.what: people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment afterwards
freq.note: Global Drug Survey 2017, online volunteers: 19 of 9,233 for magic mushrooms and 102 of 10,293 for LSD, all self-reported.

how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year answered this question; 19 said yes.
Of the 19, 13 reported anxiety or panic and 13 paranoia; 8 said they were admitted to hospital.
17 of the 18 who answered felt back to normal within a day, and all within a week.
Those who sought treatment were younger: typically 19, against 23 for the others who answered.
cl_psi_emergency.rate: One online survey of volunteers in 2016–17, who reported on themselves. Nobody checked hospital records or what they took, people who could not answer are missing, and only 19 described what happened.

cl_lsd_emergency.q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after LSD?
