cl_lsd_emergency.short: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year, and answered, said they'd sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.
cl_lsd_emergency.but: Volunteers took an online survey about themselves. Nobody checked their answers, or if the drug was really LSD.

freq.what: people who had used LSD in the past year said they sought emergency treatment afterwards
freq.note: Global Drug Survey 2017, online volunteers: 102 of 10,293 for LSD and 19 of 9,233 for magic mushrooms, all self-reported.

how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year answered this question; 102 said yes.
Most of the 102 ticked panic, anxiety or confusion. 21 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm. About half said they were admitted to hospital.
Of about 98 who said how long it lasted, 58 felt back to normal within a day, 40 took longer, and 11 still had problems after 4 weeks.
People with a past mental health diagnosis reported seeking emergency treatment more often: 1.8 in 100, against 0.7 in 100.
cl_lsd_emergency.rate: One online survey of volunteers in 2016–17, who reported on themselves. Nobody checked hospital records or whether the drug was really LSD, and people who could not answer are missing.

cl_aya_dmt_entities.q: What do people say they meet on DMT?
cl_aya_dmt_entities.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
cl_aya_dmt_entities.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who said they met a being on DMT, in one survey:
pairs: said it gave them a message
felt fear at some point
called it an 'elf'
freq.note: 2,561 adults recruited online in 2018, each describing their most memorable meeting after smoking or vaping DMT; only people who reported a meeting took part.

how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before the meeting, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.
cl_aya_dmt_entities.rate: Two online surveys from one team, only of people who'd had such a meeting, looking back years later. They show what people believe, not how often this happens or whether the beings are real.

cl_ket_depression_infusion.q: Can a ketamine drip lift depression within hours, and for how long?
cl_ket_depression_infusion.short: It can, within hours. A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. For most, it faded within weeks.
cl_ket_depression_infusion.but: People can often tell they got ketamine, which may make the lift look bigger.

freq.what: were much better a day after one ketamine drip
freq.note: One trial at two US research centres, 2010 to 2012: 30 of 47 given ketamine and 7 of 25 given midazolam.

how: In a 2006 trial, 12 of 17 people were much better a day after a ketamine drip. After a salt-water drip, none of 14 were.
In a 2013 trial, 72 people got ketamine or a sedative, picked to make it harder to guess which. Other medicines had failed them.
Pooled trials show the gap is biggest about a day after ketamine. In the 2013 trial, it was not clear by a week.
Two of the 2013 trial's authors were named on patent applications for ketamine in depression. One gave up any share of the money.
cl_ket_depression_infusion.rate: Many trials agree, but people could often tell they got ketamine. Trials that found nothing may also be missing.

cl_can_potency_trends.q: Is cannabis stronger than it used to be?
cl_can_potency_trends.short: Yes, on average. In cannabis from 7 countries, 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash.
cl_can_potency_trends.but: Most samples were cannabis seized by police, not picked at random, so they may not match what people buy.
how: Researchers combined 12 studies from 7 countries that measured THC in cannabis. Most tested police seizures; two Dutch studies bought samples at random in shops.
A point is a share of the weight: 5% to 6% THC is one point. These numbers describe the cannabis, not what people took in.
Not everywhere: US weed rose in every period studied, but weed in the UK (1975–1989) and New Zealand (1979–1996) showed no clear rise.
CBD, another substance in cannabis, did not change. The authors put the weed rise down to stronger kinds selling more, but sales were not measured.
cl_can_potency_trends.rate: One review of 12 studies, mostly testing cannabis seized by police rather than picked at random. The countries disagreed, some rising a lot and others not at all, so the average could be off.

cl_can_motivation.q: Does cannabis make people lazy or unmotivated?
cl_can_motivation.short: In a London study, people using cannabis about 4 days a week felt no less motivated than people who had used it fewer than 10 times, and were as willing to work for sweets.
cl_can_motivation.but: A one-time snapshot of people using about 4 days a week: it can't show what cannabis does over years or with heavy daily use.
how: In London, 147 teens and adults using cannabis 1 to 7 days a week were compared with 127 who had used it under 10 times.
About half also did two tasks: pressing buttons to earn sweets, and rating how much they wanted and liked a song, chocolate and a coin.
Scores differed more by age than by cannabis use: teens reported less motivation and less pleasure than adults, whether or not they used cannabis.
It tested people at least 12 hours after their last cannabis, with questionnaires and lab tasks, not school or work; small differences could be missed.
cl_can_motivation.rate: One study that looked at people only once. People who use cannabis may differ in other ways, school and work were not measured, and the tasks had about 35 people per group.

cl_can_secondhand_test.q: Can other people's cannabis smoke make you fail a urine drug test?
cl_can_secondhand_test.short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in a smoky sealed room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.
cl_can_secondhand_test.but: One small lab test in a sealed room, mostly in thick smoke; everyday smoke wasn't tested.
how: In a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres, 6 people smoked cannabis freely for an hour. 6 people who didn't smoke sat between them. This was done 3 times, each time with 6 new people sitting in: 18 in all.
Only 1 of 250 urine samples went over the US government's workplace limit. It did so on just 1 of 5 labs' tests.
Some private tests use a lower limit. There, 12 of the 18 tested positive at least once on at least one of 4 tests. A lab check would have confirmed it for 3 to 7, depending on the test.
A positive is a urine result: a THC breakdown product above a set level. It is not a measure of being high.
cl_can_secondhand_test.rate: One lab experiment: 18 people, 6 in each of three settings, sat beside people smoking in a sealed room, in thick smoke in two of them. Everyday exposure was not tested.

cl_opi_poppy_seeds.q: Can eating poppy seeds make you fail a sports drug test?
cl_opi_poppy_seeds.short: Yes, it can. In one study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake had morphine in their urine above the sports limit of the time.
cl_opi_poppy_seeds.but: The cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested, which had about 18 to 250 times more morphine than the rest.
how: Researchers in Germany tested 8 poppy seed products from shops and a bakery. All held some morphine; one held far more than the rest.
9 volunteers ate cake made with that one. Every person's urine went over the sports limit in at least 2 samples.
One of the 9 was still above the limit about 2 days later; the other 8 had their last positive within a day.
Only the sports limit was checked; workplace tests were not studied. A positive is a urine result, not a measure of any effect.
cl_opi_poppy_seeds.rate: One small study: 9 volunteers, one very morphine-rich batch of seeds, no comparison cake and no urine sample before eating. Workplace tests were not checked.

cl_can_cbd_labels.q: Do CBD products contain what their labels say?
cl_can_cbd_labels.short: Mostly not. Of 84 CBD products bought online in the US in 2016, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label. About 1 in 5 also held THC.
cl_can_cbd_labels.but: One test of products bought online in 2016; products sold in shops, or today, may differ.

freq.what: CBD products bought online held within a tenth of the CBD on their label
freq.note: One lab test of 84 products bought online in the US in 2016: 26 within 10% of the label, 36 above, 22 below.

how: CBD is a substance from the cannabis plant. Researchers bought every CBD oil, tincture and vape liquid with a CBD label they found online.
A lab that did not know the labels tested them. 36 held more CBD than the label said, and 22 held less.
Vape liquids were most often wrong: 21 of 24 were off by more than a tenth, mostly holding more CBD than labelled.
No one took the products, and no urine was tested. So this can't say if they cause a high or a positive drug test.
cl_can_cbd_labels.rate: A single lab check of 84 CBD products bought online in the US in 2016. Products sold in shops, elsewhere or today may differ.

cl_gen_portugal.q: What happened after Portugal decriminalised all drugs?
cl_gen_portugal.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
cl_gen_portugal.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.

freq.what: adults (aged 15 to 64) in Portugal said in 2007 that they had ever used an illegal drug
freq.note: National surveys: 7.8 in 100 in 2001 (7.6 in the paper's table) and 12.0 in 2007. Use in the past year: 3.4 and 3.7 in 100.

how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.
cl_gen_portugal.rate: National figures before and after the law, loosely set beside Spain and Italy; treatment grew at the same time, and some counts changed method. The figures point both ways; both sides are below.

cl_coc_banknotes.q: Do most US dollar bills carry traces of cocaine?
cl_coc_banknotes.short: In one US study, about 9 in 10 one-dollar bills had traces of cocaine. The typical bill held a little over a millionth of a gram.
cl_coc_banknotes.but: One small study of 50 US one-dollar bills collected by 2000. Cocaine on money today, or elsewhere, may differ.

freq.what: US one-dollar bills in one study carried traces of cocaine
freq.note: 46 of 50 bills from everyday purchases in Baltimore, Chicago, Denver, Honolulu and San Juan, collected by 2000.

how: The bills came from everyday purchases, 10 each in Baltimore, Chicago, Denver, Honolulu and San Juan. Only 4, all from Chicago, had no cocaine.
One bill from Honolulu held about 7 in 10 of all the cocaine found. So the average was far above what most bills held.
A few bills also carried heroin (7 of 50), methamphetamine (3) or PCP (2).
No people were tested here. The author doubts handling these bills could make you fail a urine test, citing one person in an older study.
cl_coc_banknotes.rate: One lab test of 50 one-dollar bills from five cities in the US and Puerto Rico, collected by 2000. No unused bills were tested for comparison, and money today may differ.

cl_gen_harm_ranking.q: Can drugs be ranked by how much harm they do?
cl_gen_harm_ranking.short: Experts have tried: a UK panel ranked alcohol most harmful overall, mostly for harm to other people. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst.
cl_gen_harm_ranking.but: The scores are one panel's views, not measures, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.
how: In 2010, experts scored 20 drugs on 16 harms in one day. A 2007 expert ranking put legal alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy.
Alcohol scored 72 of 100, 46 of them for harm to others. Critics say one score mixes harm per person with how many people use.
Tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere. The authors agreed it probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined.
In an online survey, 1,501 people rated drug harms much like experts did. Of the 603 allowed to rate heroin, 467 had never used it.
cl_gen_harm_ranking.rate: Opinions, not measurements: two UK expert rankings and an online survey of volunteers; the newer ranking checked only two of its 16 harm types against real data. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_gen_dare.q: Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs?
cl_gen_dare.short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as kids who didn't.
cl_gen_dare.but: Only the original classes were tested: DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.
how: A 2004 review combined 11 studies, published 1991 to 2002, of 11,505 students in grades 5 to 12, comparing those who had DARE with those who didn't.
Students who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as others. The studies checked from right after the classes to 10 years later.
In 8 of the 11 studies, the result couldn't be told apart from no difference. Two small ones found less use with DARE; the biggest, of 2,878 students, found slightly more.
Four results, including the only 10-year one, weren't worked out but filled in as zero.
cl_gen_dare.rate: One short review that didn't check how well its 11 studies were done, and filled in four results as zero. That's no hint of a hidden benefit: the flaws expected in such studies would, if anything, make DARE look better.

cl_gen_antidrug_ads.q: Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis?
cl_gen_antidrug_ads.short: No sign they did. Despite nearly $1 billion from Congress, teens' reported cannabis use stayed flat in a national survey, and those who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.
cl_gen_antidrug_ads.but: Nearly every teen saw the ads, so there was no group without them to compare cannabis use with.
how: A national survey interviewed 8,117 US kids aged 9 to 18 at home, and many again up to three times, between 1999 and 2004.
94 in 100 remembered seeing anti-drug ads at least monthly. About 24 in 100 teens said they'd ever used cannabis, in 2000 and again in 2004.
Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start cannabis by the next interview. Fewer said they definitely wouldn't.
In one of three periods, more ads even went with more first use of cannabis. The authors call this tentative, not definitive.
cl_gen_antidrug_ads.rate: One national survey followed US teens from 1999 to 2004. Almost every teen saw the ads, so no group without them could be compared, and teens reported their own ad viewing and cannabis use.

cl_caf_hydration.short: Not in a 3-day test. Men who drink coffee daily peed 2.41 litres a day on coffee days and 2.43 on water days.
cl_caf_hydration.but: One 3-day test in 50 men who already drank coffee daily, too small to rule out a small effect.
how: In Birmingham, UK, 50 healthy men who drink coffee daily had coffee for 3 days. Another time, they had the same amount of water instead.
Their food and other drinks were the same both times, so only the coffee changed.
Urine strength, blood tests and body weight did not differ. The one difference: a little more salt in the urine on coffee.
A coffee research institute paid for it, and body water results were shown for only 25 of the 50 men.
cl_caf_hydration.rate: One 3-day trial in 50 men who already drank coffee daily. Too small to rule out a small effect, and body water was reported for only half of them.

cl_amph_smart_drugs.q: Do 'smart drugs' like Adderall make healthy people smarter?
cl_amph_smart_drugs.short: Barely. A single pill of Adderall (amphetamine) or methylphenidate gave healthy adults at most a small lift on some lab tests. In one trial, people felt helped; scores didn't rise.
cl_amph_smart_drugs.but: These studies tested a single pill in a lab, in healthy volunteers. Daily use, studying and exams were not tested.
how: In a US trial, 46 healthy young adults took Adderall or a dummy pill on different test days. None of 13 tests improved.
They still rated the Adderall pill as more helpful than the dummy pill, but feeling helped was not clearly linked to scoring better.
Across 48 studies of a single pill of amphetamine or methylphenidate, the average lift was small, clearest for holding back an automatic response.
A bigger boost to memory tested hours or days later came mostly from one lab's studies of men. Adjusted for missing studies, it nearly halved.
cl_amph_smart_drugs.rate: Dozens of small lab studies gave healthy volunteers one pill of the drug or a dummy. Studies that found nothing may never have been published, and no one checked how well each was run.

cl_benzo_dementia.short: Not known. In Quebec health records, long use of benzodiazepines was linked to Alzheimer's. A Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.
cl_benzo_dementia.but: Neither study could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions.
how: In Quebec records, 50 in 100 older people with Alzheimer's had filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years before, against 40 in 100 without it.
The link appeared only with longer use. The records often missed why the pills were taken, and held nothing on education, smoking or drinking.
A Seattle study tested 3,434 older people every 2 years. About 3 in 100 a year got dementia, with the heaviest use or none.
A small extra risk showed up with light or moderate use, not the heaviest. The authors say early dementia symptoms may explain it.
cl_benzo_dementia.rate: Only two studies of older people's prescription records, and their results clash. Neither can rule out that early signs of dementia led to the prescriptions. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_kra_use_survey.q: Why do people use kratom, and what do they say it does?
cl_kra_use_survey.short: Mostly for pain, anxiety or depression, people told two surveys, and most felt it helped. In one, about 4 in 10 had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids.
cl_kra_use_survey.but: Both surveys reached people mostly through a pro-kratom group, and those who quit after bad experiences were left out of one and may be too few in the other.
how: In 2016 and 2017, online surveys asked 8,049 and 2,798 US adults who used kratom. Most were White, working and middle-aged.
Pain was the top reason (68 and 91 in 100), then anxiety or depression. In 2017, kratom's 'good effects' scored 86 of 100, 'high' 12.
In 2017, 1,144 had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids; 849 credited it with 6 months or more off opioids. Nobody checked.
703 felt unwell after 12 to 48 hours without kratom (2016). On a checklist, 68 of 2,798 had moderate or severe kratom use disorder (2017).
cl_kra_use_survey.rate: Two online surveys of volunteers, found mostly through a group that backs kratom. People described their own use, and those who quit after bad experiences were missing or may be too few.

cl_kra_deaths.q: How often is kratom found in overdose deaths?
cl_kra_deaths.short: Kratom turned up in about 6 of every 1,000 overdose deaths in 27 US states in 2016–17. It was almost always found with other drugs.
cl_kra_deaths.but: Testing for kratom varied and was not recorded, so some deaths with kratom were probably missed.

freq.title: Out of every 1,000 overdose deaths in the records, how many had kratom found?
freq.what: had kratom found in tests after death
freq.note: 152 of 27,338 deaths in 27 US states, July 2016 to December 2017. Testing for kratom varied and was not recorded, so some were probably missed.

how: A CDC system gathered 27,338 overdose deaths from 27 US states, July 2016 to December 2017. Kratom was found in 152.
Kratom was named as a cause in 91 deaths. Other drugs turned up in 84 of them; fentanyl was named as a cause in 51.
Only 7 deaths had kratom as the only drug found. Even then, the report says other drugs cannot be ruled out.
The system counts mostly deaths where opioids played a part. With no count of people who use kratom, there is no death rate.
cl_kra_deaths.rate: One CDC count from death records in 27 US states. Labs tested for kratom in different ways and didn't record how, so some cases may have been missed.

cl_psi_depression.short: It may. In one trial, 42 in 100 given psilocybin kept their depression score at least halved from week 1 to week 6, against 11 in 100 given a vitamin pill.
cl_psi_depression.but: People could probably tell they had taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the gap look bigger.

freq.what: in the psilocybin group had their depression score at least halved at every check, week 1 to week 6
freq.note: One US trial of 104 adults: 20 of 48 against 5 of 44, counting only those checked at every visit.

how: In 10 countries, 233 adults whose depression had resisted 2 to 4 treatments got a full, medium or tiny psilocybin dose.
After 3 weeks, only the full psilocybin dose showed bigger falls in depression than the tiny dose. By 12 weeks the gap could be chance.
In the US, 104 adults got psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin that makes skin flush. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin, through 6 weeks.
In the bigger trial, serious suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on every dose, more often on higher ones. The US trial recorded none.
cl_psi_depression.rate: Two trials where chance decided who got psilocybin. But people could probably tell whether they had it, nobody checked, and in one, many more dropped out of the vitamin-pill group.

cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.q: Is psilocybin better than a standard antidepressant for depression?
cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.short: Not shown. In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression, at 6 weeks or 6 months.
cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.but: The trial was too small to show they work equally well, and people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin.
how: At one London centre, 59 adults with depression got two psilocybin sessions, or 6 weeks of escitalopram pills plus two tiny psilocybin doses.
After 6 weeks, self-rated depression fell 8 points with psilocybin and 6 with escitalopram, on a 27-point scale: a gap that could be chance.
At 6 weeks, 57 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms with psilocybin and 28 with escitalopram, an extra result the authors drew no conclusions from. Six months on: 37 against 34.
People had higher hopes for psilocybin. Allowing for those hopes, the team found no clear gap on any of six scales.
cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.rate: One small trial of 59 people: too few to tell whether psilocybin and escitalopram work equally well. People rated their own depression, expected more from psilocybin, and by 6 months most had other treatment.

cl_alc_brain_cells.short: In one study, men who drank alcohol heavily for years had about as many nerve cells in the brain's outer layer as other men: about 23 billion each.
cl_alc_brain_cells.but: Only the outer layer was counted, in 22 men, so it can't say what heavy drinking does to other areas.
how: In Denmark, scientists counted nerve cells in brains after death. 11 men had drunk alcohol heavily for years; 11 others had not.
Both groups had about 23 billion. The numbers rule out a loss bigger than about 1 in 10 in the men who drank heavily.
Only 11 of 55 brains were used. Men who had had the DTs, withdrawal fits or an alcohol-related brain illness were left out.
The brain's wiring (white matter) was not clearly smaller with heavy drinking; only its share of brain weight was lower.
cl_alc_brain_cells.rate: One study of 11 men's brains after death, compared with 11 others: too few to spot a small loss, and men with alcohol-related brain illness or fits were left out.

cl_alc_moderate_brain.q: Is moderate drinking linked to changes in the brain?
cl_alc_moderate_brain.short: In one UK study, people who drank more alcohol more often had a memory area rated 'shrunken' on a scan. So did 35 in 100 who barely drank.
cl_alc_moderate_brain.but: Each brain was scanned once, so the study shows a link, not shrinking, and not that alcohol caused it.

freq.what: people who averaged under 1 UK unit of alcohol a week had their right hippocampus, a memory area, rated 'shrunken' on their one scan
freq.compare_k: In the same study, by the study's groups:
compare: averaging 7 to under 14 units a week
averaging 14 to under 21 units a week
freq.note: 13 of 37, 87 of 165 and 63 of 97 people. The paper's 'three times the odds' is the 65 against 35. At 7 to under 14 units, the study was too small to tell.

how: 527 UK government workers, mostly men, reported how much alcohol they drank over 30 years, then had one brain scan around age 70.
'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. Even 35 in 100 people who barely drank alcohol got that rating.
The paper's 'three times the odds' came from the top of its 'moderate' range for men; lower down, the study was too small to tell.
Only one of three thinking tests (naming words that start with a letter) fell slightly faster with more drinking. No test at the scan differed.
cl_alc_moderate_brain.rate: One UK study with a single brain scan per person at the end. People who drank more also differed in other ways, like smoking, and only 37 barely drank.

cl_psi_mystical.q: Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?
cl_psi_mystical.short: It can: most people in one lab study scored as having a full mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
cl_psi_mystical.but: Everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.

freq.what: volunteers ranked their psilocybin session among the 5 most meaningful experiences of their lives, 2 months later
compare: after methylphenidate (a stimulant used for comparison)
freq.note: One study: 16 of 24 after psilocybin, 2 of 24 after methylphenidate (counted from a figure). All took part in religious or spiritual activities.

how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.

Mystical here means high questionnaire scores for things like unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 had a full mystical experience on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.

Two months on, 19 of the 24 who answered said it had raised their wellbeing, against 5 after the stimulant. People close to them saw a small change for the better; personality and mood tests showed no difference.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.
cl_psi_mystical.rate: The lasting part comes from one study of 24 religious or spiritual volunteers rating their own psilocybin sessions. Another trial found high scores during sessions, but almost everyone guessed which pill they got.

cl_caf_withdrawal_reversal.q: Does caffeine make you sharper, or just undo withdrawal?
cl_caf_withdrawal_reversal.short: In one lab study, caffeine made everyone faster. But those who often have it only got as alert as those who rarely do.
cl_caf_withdrawal_reversal.but: Only one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.
how: In Bristol, UK, 416 adults were asked to skip caffeine overnight. The next day, chance decided who got caffeine pills and who got dummy pills.
By the afternoon, people who often have caffeine but got dummy pills were the sleepiest and slowest. They made the most mistakes.
Caffeine brought them about level with people who rarely have it, no higher. In those people, caffeine raised jitters, not alertness.
Five people who often have caffeine quit the test day early. All five had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons.
cl_caf_withdrawal_reversal.rate: One study of 416 adults, written up twice. Chance decided who got caffeine, but people chose their own caffeine habits, so the groups may differ in other ways; the authors say other studies disagree.

cl_ket_near_death.q: Do people describe ketamine trips the way others describe near-death experiences?
cl_ket_near_death.short: More than for any other drug, going by the words alone: of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports read most like near-death accounts. Salvia and LSD came close behind.
cl_ket_near_death.but: Only words were compared. Nobody showed the trips and the near-death experiences feel alike.
how: Researchers took about 15,000 drug reports from the Erowid website. A computer compared their words with 625 near-death accounts.
Ketamine came first with the main settings, and with about 4 in 5 of all the settings tried. On average it led LSD only narrowly, and lower down, drugs swapped places.
The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event, on average, and some were linked to anaesthesia or drug use. Nobody checked what the online writers took, or how much.
Some think the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death. The authors say their study can't show that, though their summary says it supports the idea.
cl_ket_near_death.rate: One study comparing words in reports people chose to post online with near-death accounts written years later. Nobody checked the drugs, and ketamine's lead over LSD was small.

cl_psi_addiction.q: Can psilocybin help people drink less?
cl_psi_addiction.short: Maybe. In one trial, people given psilocybin with talk therapy drank heavily on about 10 in 100 days, against 24 with a comparison pill.
cl_psi_addiction.but: Almost everyone could tell if they got psilocybin, and people reported their own drinking.

freq.title: Out of every 100 days in the 8 months after the first dose, how many were heavy-drinking days?
pairs: days for people given psilocybin with talk therapy
days for people given a comparison pill with the same therapy
freq.note: One trial of 93 adults with alcohol use disorder at two US universities: 9.7 against 23.6 in 100 days, as people reported them. Heavy drinking had more than halved in both groups before any pill.

how: At 2 US universities, 93 adults dependent on alcohol were offered 12 talk-therapy sessions. Chance decided who also got psilocybin twice or a comparison pill.
Heavy drinking had already more than halved in both groups during 4 weeks of therapy. That was before any psilocybin or comparison pill.
After about 94 in 100 sessions, people guessed right whether they had psilocybin. So what they expected may explain part of the gap.
cl_psi_addiction.rate: One trial of 93 adults with drinking problems: almost everyone could tell whether they got psilocybin, and they reported their own drinking. It was too small to be sure how big the difference is.

cl_psi_smoking.q: Can psilocybin help people quit smoking?
cl_psi_smoking.short: Not known. In one small study, 12 of 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later.
cl_psi_smoking.but: There was no comparison group, so no one can tell what psilocybin added to all the counselling.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 15 adults who had smoked for 31 years on average got 15 weeks of counselling and psilocybin two or three times.
Six months on, breath and urine tests confirmed 12 of 15 given psilocybin weren't smoking. Four of those 12 had smoked again at some point.
The psilocybin paper cites 45 to 59 in 100 not smoking after intensive standard treatment. With so few people, 12 of 15 isn't clearly better.
cl_psi_smoking.rate: One small study: just 15 volunteers, all given psilocybin and lots of counselling, with no comparison group, so nobody can tell what psilocybin itself did.

cl_xc_psychedelics_mental_health.q: Is using LSD, mushrooms or mescaline linked to mental health problems?
cl_xc_psychedelics_mental_health.short: People who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline reported mental health problems 2 to 3 times as often. The gap vanished once other drug use and life stress were counted.
cl_xc_psychedelics_mental_health.but: People were asked once, so the survey can't show whether LSD, mushrooms or mescaline cause or prevent problems.

freq.what: who had ever used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline reported serious distress in their worst month of the past year
freq.note: US survey, 2001 to 2004 (15.5% against 7.5%). Once other drug use, risk-taking and stressful events were counted, the gap disappeared.

how: 130,152 US adults answered private computer questions at home in 2001 to 2004; 21,967 had ever used LSD, mushrooms, mescaline or peyote.
At first glance, all 20 mental health measures were 2 to 3 times as common in people who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline.
Those who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline used far more other drugs: 98 in 100 had used cannabis, against 33 in 100 of others.
Once that, risk-taking, stressful events and background were counted, no measure was higher for LSD, mushrooms or mescaline. A few were lower, maybe by chance.
cl_xc_psychedelics_mental_health.rate: One huge US survey, but people were asked only once, nobody's mental health was known from before they first used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline, and the answer depends on what else was counted.

cl_caf_coffee_health.q: Is drinking coffee linked to better or worse health?
cl_caf_coffee_health.short: Mostly better: in studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often. In pregnancy, and for women's bones, the links went the other way.
cl_caf_coffee_health.but: These studies only watched people, and gene studies found no sign that coffee itself lowers the risk of dying.
how: A big review gathered the research on coffee and health. Most of it came from studies that followed people for years.
People who drank coffee had lower rates of death, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and, most of all, liver disease.
In pregnancy, more coffee was linked to low birth weight and losing the pregnancy. Women who drank more had more fractures; men had fewer.
A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked; people who smoke tend to drink more coffee.
cl_caf_coffee_health.rate: Mostly studies that followed people for years, not fair tests. Other things about people who drink coffee, like smoking, could explain the links, and results varied a lot between studies.

cl_opi_naloxone_programs.q: Does giving out naloxone kits prevent opioid overdose deaths?
cl_opi_naloxone_programs.short: Naloxone kits are linked to fewer deaths from heroin and other opioids, but it's not proven. At least 96 in 100 people given naloxone by someone trained survived.
cl_opi_naloxone_programs.but: Surviving doesn't prove naloxone saved a life, since most overdoses aren't fatal, and only one study compared death rates.
how: In 19 Massachusetts towns, 2006 to 2009, 2,912 people who might see an opioid overdose got training and nasal naloxone. They reported 327 rescue attempts.
Where more than 1 in 1,000 people were trained, opioid death rates were about a fifth lower, and nearly half lower after allowing for other differences.
Every town had the programme by 2008, so the study mostly compared later years with earlier ones. It never printed how many people died.
Across 17 studies, trained people gave naloxone 2,336 times, mostly for heroin overdoses; 20 are known to have died. Since most overdoses aren't fatal, lives saved are unknown.
cl_opi_naloxone_programs.rate: No fair test exists: the one death-rate study mostly compared later years with earlier ones in 19 Massachusetts towns, and the other studies only counted who survived, which can't show lives saved.

cl_n2o_nerve_damage.q: Is nitrous oxide (laughing gas) linked to nerve damage?
cl_n2o_nerve_damage.short: Yes: doctors have described nerve damage after nitrous oxide (laughing gas). In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used it in the past year reported lasting numbness.
cl_n2o_nerve_damage.but: No doctor checked these answers and people chose to take part, so it can't show how common lasting numbness is after nitrous oxide.
how: A review pooled doctors' reports on 100 people with health problems after nitrous oxide (laughing gas): 57 had used it for fun, 25 in surgery.
80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Of 75 who had a spine scan, 51 showed a change in the spinal cord.
58 of 82 tested had low vitamin B12. But the search only found reports mentioning B12, so this is partly built in.
In an online survey, 200 of 4,633 people who used nitrous oxide in the past year reported numbness or tingling lasting days or weeks.
cl_n2o_nerve_damage.rate: Doctors' reports on 100 patients, written up because something went wrong, plus one online survey where people chose to join and no doctor checked their answers. Neither compares people with and without nitrous oxide.

cl_opi_supervised_injection.q: Do supervised injection sites reduce overdose deaths?
cl_opi_supervised_injection.short: Not proven: near Vancouver's site for injecting heroin, cocaine and other drugs, overdose deaths fell about a third after it opened. Elsewhere in the city, about a tenth.
cl_opi_supervised_injection.but: Just one site, before and after, and nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.
how: Coroners recorded 290 overdose deaths from illegal drugs in Vancouver, 2001 to 2005. About half involved opioids, and about 6 in 10 cocaine.
Within 500 metres: 56 deaths in the 2.7 years before it opened in 2003, 33 in the 2.3 after, about 6 fewer a year.
Critics blamed extra police from April 2003. The authors said that crackdown ended within weeks of the opening.
Critics also blamed the study's start in 2001, a year with more heroin around. The two papers they cited show overdoses falling since the late 1990s, but neither measured heroin's strength or price.
cl_opi_supervised_injection.rate: One before-and-after study of one site in Vancouver, which could not rule out other changes, like policing or a fall in overdoses already under way. With few deaths, the drop was barely bigger than chance.

cl_psi_microdosing.q: Does microdosing magic mushrooms do anything, or is it placebo?
cl_psi_microdosing.short: In two trials, people could feel a magic mushroom or LSD microdose on the day. But their mood and thinking were not clearly better than with a dummy capsule.
cl_psi_microdosing.but: Only a small one-week trial used just magic mushrooms; the bigger one was mostly LSD, and neither lasted months.

freq.what: weeks, people guessed right whether they had taken magic mushroom or dummy capsules
freq.note: 49 of 68 weeks, by the counts in the paper's figure (its text says 49 of 64). Guessing at random would be right about half the time. In the larger study, mostly of LSD, people guessed right on 72 of 100 capsule days, against about 62 for someone guessing from the known share of dummies.

how: In Argentina, 34 people took magic mushroom capsules one week and look-alike capsules of an ordinary mushroom another. Mood and creativity did not improve.
A bigger study: 240 people mixed their own microdoses, mostly LSD, with empty capsules. After 4 weeks, the dummy group was not clearly worse off.
People guessed right about 7 times in 10. Ratings followed what they believed they took, though feeling an effect may have shaped the belief.
Everyone in both studies took capsules, so neither can show it is all placebo. People might have got better anyway.
cl_psi_microdosing.rate: Two trials where chance decided who got real or dummy capsules agree. But people often guessed which they had while rating how they felt, and both were too small to rule out small benefits.

cl_ket_esketamine.q: Does esketamine nasal spray work for hard-to-treat depression?
cl_ket_esketamine.short: In two big trials, esketamine spray (a form of ketamine) did a little better than a dummy spray. Only one trial passed its main test.
cl_ket_esketamine.but: About 1 in 4 felt detached or unreal on esketamine, so many may have known which spray they got, and nobody asked.
how: In two trials, adults whose depression had not lifted on two antidepressants got esketamine or a dummy spray. All started a new antidepressant.
After 4 weeks, depression scores fell about 3 to 4 points more out of 60 with esketamine. A fast start was not shown.
Among people whose depression had lifted, 45 in 100 switched to a dummy spray relapsed, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine.
The company behind it paid for every trial. Two critics argue relapses may partly be effects of stopping; the trial could not tell.
cl_ket_esketamine.rate: In trials, chance decided who got esketamine or a dummy spray, but esketamine's noticeable effects may have told people which they got, and the differences were small and uncertain. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_fent_touch.q: Can touching fentanyl make you overdose?
cl_fent_touch.short: Poison experts call it very unlikely for police and paramedics, and no overdose from touching fentanyl has been confirmed. In 214 news stories about exposed responders, none had proof.
cl_fent_touch.but: Nobody has measured real touches, and finding no proven case is not proof it never happens.
how: Poison experts did sums from fentanyl skin patches, made to deliver it. Powder on skin, they argue, is taken up more slowly and can be washed off.
Researchers checked 214 news stories about police or paramedics exposed to opioids. Only one incident mentioned any test, probably one that misses fentanyl.
A federal safety agency looked into three cases where seven officers felt ill. It found no signs of a serious overdose. No officer had a test that finds fentanyl.
Splashes into the eyes or mouth are treated as a real risk. No sums were done for carfentanil, far stronger than morphine in animals.
cl_fent_touch.rate: Expert sums from skin patches, 214 news stories and three incidents a safety agency looked into; nobody measured real touches. Finding no proven case can't show how often, if ever, it happens.

cl_fent_police_beliefs.q: Do police believe touching fentanyl can cause overdose? Does training change that?
cl_fent_police_beliefs.short: In three US surveys, about 4 in 5 police and other first responders thought touching fentanyl could cause an overdose or death. Right after trainings, far fewer did.
cl_fent_police_beliefs.but: No survey picked people at random. Answers came right after training, with no untrained group or later check.

freq.what: Indiana police officers agreed, before training, that responders are at great risk of overdose from touching or breathing in fentanyl
compare: right after training, among the 69 who answered again
freq.note: 103 of 129 officers before; 27 of 69 after. Only 69 answered both times, and nobody untrained was compared.

how: In Missouri, only about 1 in 5 of 140 police, paramedics and firefighters rejected the idea before training; about 5 in 6 did right after.
Officers in five US police forces said they heard it from colleagues, a federal drug agency video and bulletins; none could confirm a colleague's overdose.
506 of 551 US news articles were coded misinformation, even plain reports of ill officers. They got about 450,000 Facebook shares; clear corrections, under 30,000.

In a 2019 New York online survey, 149 of 187 police, fire and ambulance workers agreed a brief touch could be deadly. For fentanyl safety information, most named courses and training; about 1 in 7, the news.
cl_fent_police_beliefs.rate: Three surveys in three US states, none picking people at random, two of them at trainings by partly the same researchers, plus interviews. Answers after training came at once, with no untrained group.

cl_lsd_chromosomes.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.
cl_lsd_chromosomes.but: Small studies that only looked at blood cells under a microscope; the best had no group without LSD.
how: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells from two people in a lab dish, plus one patient with no 'before' test.
Two 1967 studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD, with no 'before' test. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks.
The best study tested 32 patients before and after pure LSD. Damaged cells went from about 4 in 100 to 6, maybe by chance.
All these studies looked at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs. A 1971 review linked raised breaks mainly to street LSD and many other drugs.
cl_lsd_chromosomes.rate: Small, old studies of blood cells under a microscope. The best had no group without LSD, the studies disagree, and those that found more damage could not tell LSD apart from other drugs.

cl_xc_psychedelic_beliefs.q: Do trips show you the truth, or just change your beliefs?
cl_xc_psychedelic_beliefs.short: These studies can't say if it's the truth. But beliefs do shift a bit, towards ideas like other worlds and a conscious universe. The shift was still there 6 months later.
cl_xc_psychedelic_beliefs.but: There was no comparison group, and only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey. Most already leaned that way.
how: People answered questions a week before a psychedelic retreat or ceremony, then 4 weeks and 6 months after. In the 122 who answered all three, belief in things like other worlds rose a little.
First-timers shifted more. In one exploratory analysis, the shift went with feeling in tune with the group, not clearly with how mystical or visual the trip felt.
In a trial in depression, beliefs shifted after psilocybin. They shifted a little after a standard antidepressant too, and the gap was too small to be sure of.

A survey asked 1,606 people whose beliefs had changed to look back, about 8 years on average. 26 in 100 recalled thinking plants could be conscious before, and 61 in 100 after. Superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.
cl_xc_psychedelic_beliefs.rate: Mostly one study with no comparison group, where most people stopped answering, plus a small trial and a survey of people chosen because their beliefs had changed. None can say whether the beliefs are true.

cl_psi_personality.short: Not proven. After psilocybin, people rated themselves about 3 to 5 points more 'open' 1 to 3 months later, on a scale where the average adult scores 50.
cl_psi_personality.but: These were people rating themselves, before and after. The one test against another drug found no difference. Neither study checked how people acted.
how: 52 healthy volunteers, new to psychedelics and mostly religious or spiritual, rated themselves 2.8 points more open 1 to 2 months after their psilocybin session. Their other four traits didn't clearly change.

The rise came from the 30 who had a full mystical experience, and about a third of all the volunteers scored lower afterwards. Over a year later, that group was still about 4 points up, a result right on the edge of chance.
Most of them came from one trial. There, 15 people who got psilocybin first and 15 who got a stimulant first scored no differently on personality 2 months later.

In 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression, openness rose 4.9 points by 3 months, and they rated themselves less anxious and more sociable. The researchers say mood may explain those last two changes.
cl_psi_personality.rate: Two small before-and-after studies of selected volunteers and patients rating themselves. The one test against another drug found no difference. Both sides are below.

cl_xc_visual_patterns.q: Why do psychedelic visuals look like tunnels, spirals and honeycombs?
cl_xc_visual_patterns.short: Maybe the visual brain's own wiring. A maths model shows how tunnels, spirals, cobwebs and honeycombs could arise there. It wasn't tested in people on a drug.
cl_xc_visual_patterns.but: It's only maths: the drug is just a setting for how excitable the brain is. The match was judged by eye against a few drawings.
how: People see simple shapes after LSD or cannabis. They also come with flickering light or when falling asleep. Long ago, these were sorted into four types: lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals.
The wiring from eye to brain turns a tunnel or a spiral into plain stripes. These run across the brain's first area for sight.
In the model, when that area gets too excitable, stripes and lattices of activity form by themselves, shaped by how its cells connect. Mapped back to what you'd see, they look like all four types.
The wiring data came mostly from cats and monkeys. The best matches needed wider connections than that anatomy shows, and some complex visions don't fit the model.
cl_xc_visual_patterns.rate: One maths model, built on brain wiring measured mostly in animals and checked by eye against a few drawings. It wasn't tested against brain activity in people on a drug.

cl_mdma_sex.q: What does MDMA do to sex drive, erections and orgasm?
cl_mdma_sex.short: Desire often goes up, erections can go either way, and orgasm often takes longer. In one survey, 8 of 20 men said erections got weaker on MDMA, and 8 stronger.
cl_mdma_sex.but: It's 35 people who chose to talk about it, remembering past experiences. Nobody tested their pills.
how: In Israel, 20 men and 15 women who had used MDMA before sex compared it, from memory, with their usual sex. All 35 said desire went up, and 32 said they were more satisfied.
Of the 20 men, 8 said erections got weaker and 8 stronger. Orgasm took longer for 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women, and 3 people couldn't reach it, yet still felt more satisfied.
In Northern Ireland, 98 people were interviewed. A little over half said MDMA was more about closeness than sex. Some men couldn't get an erection; others described strong desire.
Some described one-night stands and regret. Condoms were rare on ecstasy, but also rare without drugs, so the study can't show MDMA made sex riskier.
cl_mdma_sex.rate: Two small studies from the 1990s: a survey of 35 people who chose to take part and remembered the past, and interviews without counts. Nobody tested the pills or compared times with and without MDMA.

cl_mdma_vs_mda.q: How is MDA different from MDMA?
cl_mdma_vs_mda.short: It seemed to last longer, with more visuals and less anxiety: at 6 hours MDA was still clearly felt and MDMA wasn't. That's one small lab study.
cl_mdma_vs_mda.but: MDA and MDMA weren't tested on the same people. The MDMA results, from other people in earlier studies, stop at 6 hours.
how: 12 healthy adults who had used MDA, or MDMA and LSD-type drugs, took MDA and a dummy pill in hospital, not told which. Their results were set beside earlier MDMA results from other people.
MDA brought more visions with eyes closed and more 'spiritual' feelings than MDMA, and less anxiety and loss of control. Both made people feel close to others.
Heart rate rose about 20 beats a minute after MDA and 31 after MDMA, though the paper calls them similar. Top blood pressure rose about 30 points with both.
The paper calls MDA well tolerated but gives no side-effect data at all. Why MDMA is more popular wasn't studied.
cl_mdma_vs_mda.rate: One small lab study of 12 people, set beside MDMA results from different people whose results stop sooner. So the differences may come from the people or the timing, not the drugs.

cl_lsd_vs_psilocybin.q: LSD or mushrooms: what's actually different?
cl_lsd_vs_psilocybin.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 people in a lab rated the trips alike.
cl_lsd_vs_psilocybin.but: Finding no difference in 28 people doesn't prove there is none. And most could tell which drug they'd had.
how: 28 healthy adults each had five hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got a dummy, two amounts of LSD and two of psilocybin, in random order, not told which.
LSD lasted longer at both amounts. It also began a bit sooner, which the authors put down to it being a liquid, not a capsule.
The higher psilocybin amount raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more. LSD raised heart rate more. Both brought complaints like headaches; nobody had a serious problem.
By the study's own figures, people named the right drug in most sessions, which may have shaped their ratings. It used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms.
cl_lsd_vs_psilocybin.rate: One careful lab study of 28 people, who took both drugs in random order. But most could tell which drug they had, and 'alike' only means no clear difference was found.

cl_mix_mdma_alcohol.q: What happens when you mix MDMA with alcohol?
cl_mix_mdma_alcohol.short: Just as drunk, but less sleepy, and about as bad on a test at its worst. Blood MDMA also peaked 13% higher, in a lab study of 9 men.
cl_mix_mdma_alcohol.but: Only 9 men, in a lab. Heart measurements were taken but never reported.
how: 9 healthy men who had taken MDMA before each had four lab sessions, a week apart. They got MDMA, alcohol, both, or neither, with dummy pills and drinks so they didn't know which.
With both, the sleepy feeling from alcohol went away. Feeling drunk didn't: if anything, it was rated a bit higher, though not clearly.
On a timed symbol test, scores at their worst fell about as much as with alcohol alone, but for about 1 hour, not 2 to 3. Only with both was reaction time clearly slower than with the dummy.

Blood MDMA peaked 13% higher and blood alcohol 15% lower; the authors call these small changes. Nobody rated how well they thought they did, though they felt more energetic and efficient than with alcohol alone. Nobody drove.
cl_mix_mdma_alcohol.rate: One small lab study of 9 young men who knew MDMA well, with one amount of each drug. 'Just as drunk' means no clear difference was found, and the heart results were never reported.

cl_mix_mdma_lsd.q: What if I take LSD and MDMA at the same time?
cl_mix_mdma_lsd.short: Blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone, and bad feelings weren't clearly eased. In a lab study of 24 people, top blood pressure was 13 points higher.
cl_mix_mdma_lsd.but: Healthy people took one amount of each, in a calm hospital room. Nothing serious happened, but 24 people can't show rare dangers.
how: 24 healthy adults each had four hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got LSD, MDMA, both at once, or a dummy, in random order and without being told which.

With both, top blood pressure averaged 150, against 137 on LSD alone and 148 on MDMA alone; heart rate 100 beats a minute, against 92 and 95. Body temperature was not clearly higher than on LSD alone.
Bad-feeling, fear and complaint scores were not clearly lower than on LSD alone. Nobody had a serious problem. On nausea, the paper contradicts itself.
The two drugs changed each other's blood levels: more LSD stayed in the blood for longer, while MDMA peaked lower and later.
cl_mix_mdma_lsd.rate: One careful lab study of 24 healthy people, with one amount of each drug taken together. The blood pressure results are clear; the rest rests on people's own ratings, and rare dangers can't show up in so few.

cl_fent_fake_pills.q: Are fake pills with fentanyl getting more common?
cl_fent_fake_pills.short: Yes, in US records to 2021. Overdose deaths with signs of fake pills rose from 2 to about 5 in 100, and to about 15 in 100 in western states.
cl_fent_fake_pills.but: Nobody tested what share of street pills hold fentanyl. These are police and death records, and death records likely miss many fake pills.
how: US police records: of seizures that held fentanyl, pills were 14 in 100 in early 2018 and 29 in 100 in late 2021. The rest were powder. Fentanyl pills seized in three months rose from about 42,000 to about 2.1 million.

Death records from 29 states and Washington, DC: deaths with signs of fake pills went from 2 in 100 in mid-2019 to a high of about 5 in 100 in mid-2021, then stayed near there. In western states, about 5 became about 15 in 100.

In 2021, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30', and 17 in 100 fake alprazolam (Xanax) only. Fentanyl or similar drugs were among the recorded causes in 93 in 100.
Neither record shows what the pills held: police data have no pill contents, and death records don't say how many pills were tested. A drug-checking study in Vancouver tested too few pills to say.
cl_fent_fake_pills.rate: Big US record sets. But seizures depend on what police target and test, death records likely miss fake pills, more in some places than others, and nobody tested a fair sample of pills.

cl_opi_overdose_recognition.q: Would I know if someone was overdosing on opioids?
cl_opi_overdose_recognition.short: Not always. On a written test, people trained by overdose programmes spotted about 7 of 9 opioid overdoses. People without that training spotted about 5 of 9.
cl_opi_overdose_recognition.but: It was a paper test with 62 people that staff picked, not real overdoses. Nobody was tested before training, so training may not be the reason.
how: In 2005 and 2006, 62 people at six US overdose programmes read 16 short stories. Each was based on what someone who injects drugs had called an overdose. Medical experts had decided 9 were opioid overdoses needing naloxone, and 7 were not.
Trained people spotted about 7 of the 9 opioid overdoses, untrained people about 5. Trained people still didn't choose naloxone in about 2 of the 9; untrained people missed about 3.
Both groups got only about 4 or 5 of the other 7 stories right. Even the experts said there wasn't enough information in about a quarter of their answers.
The paper doesn't say which stories people got wrong. So it can't show which signs get missed, or whether people can tell a heavy nod from an overdose.
cl_opi_overdose_recognition.rate: One small study. Staff picked who took part, nobody was tested before training, and it used written stories, not real overdoses. It doesn't say which stories people got wrong.

cl_opi_conditioned_tolerance.q: Can using in a new place make an overdose more likely?
cl_opi_conditioned_tolerance.short: Maybe. In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place. In people, nobody has tested it well. One study asked 10 overdose survivors what was different.
cl_opi_conditioned_tolerance.but: That's 10 people's memories, about 5 years later, with nobody to compare them with. Only 3 of them recalled a new place or crowd.
how: The idea: the place, the people and the ritual that come with a drug start to trigger the body's push-back against it. That push-back is part of tolerance, so it may be weaker somewhere new.
In rat studies from the same researcher, tolerance was weaker in a new place, and a large dose of heroin was more often deadly there. Rats aren't people.
Of 10 overdose survivors, 7 recalled something unusual that day: 3 a new place or crowd, 2 a different way of injecting, 2 a different mix of drugs. The other 3 recalled nothing unusual.
Nobody counted how often people use somewhere new without an overdose. The review suggests a treatment based on the idea, but cites no test of it.
cl_opi_conditioned_tolerance.rate: One tiny study of 10 people's memories, with nobody to compare them with, plus rat experiments from the same researcher. Rat findings don't show what happens in people.

cl_opi_treatment_mortality.q: Is it dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine (Suboxone)?
cl_opi_treatment_mortality.short: The weeks after leaving were the riskiest. In 5 studies, deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against 6 in steady treatment.
cl_opi_treatment_mortality.but: These studies counted everyone who left, for any reason. People who leave differ in other ways, so the studies can't show that stopping itself caused the deaths.
how: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. Every group had more deaths out of treatment.
In the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller: about 6 or 7 deaths a year per 1,000 people in treatment, against 12 to 18 out of it.
Deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against about 14 later on. The first month on methadone looked riskier too, but that could be chance.
Deaths counted as overdoses didn't clearly rise after leaving, in the 3 groups that split them by time. Buprenorphine had just three groups, mostly one Australian study.
cl_opi_treatment_mortality.rate: Sixteen studies in several countries all found more deaths out of treatment than in it. But nobody chose at random who stayed, and people who leave may differ in other ways, so how much is due to stopping is unknown.

cl_opi_withdrawal_deaths.q: Can opioid withdrawal itself kill you?
cl_opi_withdrawal_deaths.short: It has happened, but nobody knows how often. One editorial lists 11 deaths, all in jail. It links them to vomiting and diarrhoea that dried people out and went untreated.
cl_opi_withdrawal_deaths.but: It's one editorial's list, built from news reports and a court case. With no count of how many people went through withdrawal, there's no rate.
how: The authors' idea: vomiting and diarrhoea that don't stop, left untreated, dry the body out. Blood sodium rises, and the heart can fail.
The cases: a woman in custody in the UK in 1998, and 10 people in US jails reported in the press from 2013 to 2016, aged 18 to 49.
The authors say each death came slowly, with time to treat it, and call the deaths neglect or a lack of medical care.
They say such deaths are rising but give no counts over time. Nothing here covers withdrawal outside custody.
cl_opi_withdrawal_deaths.rate: One editorial, using cases from news reports and a court case, all in custody. Nobody counted how many people went through withdrawal, so how often it kills is unknown.

methamphetamine.q: In small lab studies, what did a single dose of meth do to attention and memory?
methamphetamine.why: Attention, memory and reaction time did not get measurably worse, but the studies were small and binges were not tested.

methamphetamine.q: Has it been shown that meth, as people use it, damages dopamine nerve cells?
options: No, it has been ruled out
methamphetamine.why: Not shown either way: scans show less of one dopamine protein, but that can happen without nerve cells dying. Experts disagree.

methamphetamine.q: Which set of signs fits meth poisoning?
options: A racing heart, fast breathing and wide pupils
methamphetamine.why: Meth poisoning looks like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart, fast breathing, wide pupils and restlessness.

methamphetamine.q: In an old US survey, how many in 100 people who used stimulants like meth were ever dependent?
methamphetamine.why: About 11 in 100, but the survey counted people who had just started, who had little time to become dependent.

methamphetamine.q: In one small study of people stopping meth, which lasted longest?
methamphetamine.why: Most symptoms eased in one to two weeks, low mood lasted about three, and craving lasted to week five.

methamphetamine.q: In Taiwan, how many adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs like meth got psychosis diagnoses within 10 years?
methamphetamine.why: An estimated 4 in 100 in Taiwan, against under 1 in 100 with no drug record; this can't show which came first.

methamphetamine.q: In a typical study of meth psychosis, how many still had symptoms over a month after stopping meth?
methamphetamine.why: About 1 in 4 in the typical study, but single studies ranged from none to almost all, mostly in hospital patients.

methamphetamine.q: Compared with people who use other drugs, how often do people who use meth report low mood?
methamphetamine.why: No clear difference. They report somewhat more low mood than people who don't use meth, but other drug use may explain part.

methamphetamine.q: In one study, people dependent on meth reported violent crime in how many of 100 months of use?
methamphetamine.why: About 12, against 3 of 100 months without meth; people reported both for the same months, so which came first is unclear.

methamphetamine.q: In the largest trial of mirtazapine for meth, people said they used less. What did saliva tests show?
options: No difference from a dummy pill
Much less use than on a dummy pill
More use than on a dummy pill
methamphetamine.why: No difference, though people said they cut down by about 2 more days in 4 weeks; most kept using.

methamphetamine.q: In trials, how many people stopped meth on bupropion or modafinil, versus a dummy pill?
options: Twice as many on the medicines
methamphetamine.why: About 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, on medicine or a dummy pill; small trials can't rule out a modest benefit or harm.

methamphetamine.q: People with regular or problematic meth use died how many times as often as others their age?
methamphetamine.why: Nearly 7 times others of the same age and sex, about 1 in 90 a year; many also used opioids, so not all is meth.

methamphetamine.q: In US death reports, about how many in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids?
methamphetamine.why: Death reports from 2021 to mid-2024 found opioids in about 7 in 10 of these deaths.

methamphetamine.q: In one study of people dependent on meth, which crimes were most linked to months of use?
methamphetamine.why: Selling drugs and property crime, even after money and housing problems were counted; the study can't show which came first.

methamphetamine.q: The morning after the biggest lab dose of meth, how did people feel versus a dummy dose?
methamphetamine.why: Less alert and friendly, but not sadder or more worried, and no more eager for meth; one small study of eleven people.

methamphetamine.q: In the US, deaths involving meth were about 550 in 1999. About how many were there in 2023?
methamphetamine.why: About 35,000, though many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids.

methamphetamine.q: In an old US survey, which drug had the most people ever dependent per 100 who used it?
methamphetamine.why: Tobacco 32 in 100, cocaine 17, alcohol 15, stimulants like meth about 11; there is no figure for meth alone.

methamphetamine.q: Among Utah patients with meth or amphetamine but no other drug or alcohol diagnoses, how common was Parkinson's?
options: Diagnosed no more often than in others
methamphetamine.why: About 3 in 1,000 against 1 in 1,000 over about 7 years; some diagnoses are probably other movement conditions.

mdma.q: People resting in a cool lab took MDMA. How many in 100 had a temperature above 38 degrees?
mdma.why: 24 in 100 went above 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill. Heat and dancing were not tested.

mdma.q: Compared with others at all-night dances, how did people using ecstasy but little else score on memory tests?
mdma.why: Scores did not differ, in one study where breath, urine and hair tests checked little else was used. Medium-sized differences could not be ruled out.

mdma.q: In one UK study, how many in 100 babies exposed to ecstasy in pregnancy had a birth defect?
mdma.why: About 15 in 100, against 2 to 3 expected. But there was no comparison group, and almost half the enquiries were lost to follow-up.

mdma.q: In MDMA trials, how many in 10 finishing on a dummy pill plus therapy no longer had PTSD?
mdma.why: 3 to 5 in 10 on a dummy pill with the same therapy no longer had PTSD, against about 7 in 10 on MDMA.

mdma.q: Why was the famous 2002 study on ecstasy and monkeys' brains withdrawn?
options: The monkeys got a different drug by mistake
Other labs could not repeat the result
The monkeys turned out to be fine
mdma.why: The animals had been given a different drug, from a wrongly labelled bottle. Fewer newspapers reported the withdrawal than the original story.

mdma.q: Of the minor problems listed in MDMA trial records, how many made it into the published papers?
mdma.why: More than half of the minor problems, and 4 serious ones, never made it into the published papers.

mdma.q: In small MDMA trials, what was common in the week after a session?
mdma.why: Tiredness was common in the week after, while a tight jaw, thirst and sweating came during sessions.

mdma.q: A 2004 review of pill tests: in the mid-1990s, how many in 100 ecstasy pills held MDMA?
mdma.why: It was 90 to 98 earlier and nearly all by the early 2000s. Tests end around 2002, so pills today may differ.

mdma.q: Among people ill after taking MDMA who had a blood test, who more often had low blood salt?
mdma.why: 52 in 100 women against 22 in 100 men. These were people who became ill, not everyone who takes MDMA.

interactions.q: In 2017 US death records, about how many in 100 opioid overdose deaths also involved benzos (calming medicines)?
interactions.why: Death certificates listed benzos in 21 of 100 opioid overdose deaths in 2017, up from 9 in 1999.

interactions.q: US death records listed alcohol in about how many in 100 opioid overdose deaths?
interactions.why: Death certificates listed alcohol in about 15 of 100, but alcohol is often left off death records.

interactions.q: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, how many people with benzo prescriptions died of poisoning each year?
interactions.why: About 1 in 100 a year with a benzo prescription, 1 in 200 without. The study did not allow for alcohol or street drugs.

interactions.q: Which signs do doctors look for to spot serotonin syndrome, caused by drugs that raise serotonin?
interactions.why: Muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, sweating and restlessness; when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever.

interactions.q: In a small lab study, what happened to heart rate when alcohol was added to cocaine?
options: It was faster than with cocaine alone
It was slower than with cocaine alone
interactions.why: Heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute with both drugs, against 74 with cocaine alone, in 8 people.

interactions.q: What happens to the link between cannabis and car crashes when studies take drinking into account?
interactions.why: Studies that allowed for alcohol found 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash; studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8.

interactions.q: Of people kept in hospital after taking GHB with alcohol, how many in 100 went to critical care?
interactions.why: 55 in 100 went to critical care, against 22 in 100 of those without alcohol. Alcohol use was reported, not measured.

alcohol.q: In acamprosate trials, how many in 100 drank again during treatment, against 83 on dummy pills?
alcohol.why: About 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83 on dummy pills. The most carefully run trials found no clear difference.

alcohol.q: In one US survey, how many in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year?
alcohol.why: A survey of 36,309 US adults found this, though another US survey found a little over half as many.

alcohol.q: How many in 100 new cancers worldwide did a model estimate were caused by drinking?
alcohol.why: The model estimated 741,000 new cancers in 2020: about 6 in 100 in men and 2 in 100 in women.

alcohol.q: In one global study, for people aged 15 to 49, where did alcohol rank among risks for death?
options: It was not on the list
alcohol.why: At those ages it caused an estimated 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women.

alcohol.q: In a US survey, how many who first drank at 14 or younger had been dependent on alcohol?
alcohol.why: About 4 to 5 in 10, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. People relied on memory; cause is not known.

alcohol.q: In a lab test of 64 men, what made them drink more?
options: Having real vodka in their drink
Being told their drink had vodka
Neither: they all drank the same
alcohol.why: Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was in the glass. Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s.

alcohol.q: About how many children in 1,000 are thought to have FASD, the effects of alcohol before birth?
alcohol.why: About 8 in 1,000. Few countries had counted it; most numbers were worked out from how many women said they drank.

alcohol.q: Compared with people who never drank, did people who drink a little alcohol live longer?
alcohol.why: No clear difference against people who never drank. Few studies made that comparison, so a small gain or loss is still possible.

alcohol.q: In naltrexone trials, how many in 100 went back to heavy drinking, against 54 on dummy pills?
alcohol.why: About 46 in 100 on naltrexone, against 54 on dummy pills. Most were middle-aged men who had already stopped and had counselling.

alcohol.q: In gene studies, drinking more alcohol went with more strokes. Which kind rose most?
alcohol.why: Both kinds rose with drinking in men, bleeding strokes more steeply, in a gene study of over 160,000 Chinese adults.

alcohol.q: In hospital for alcohol withdrawal, how many in 100 people get the DTs, a sudden confusion?
alcohol.why: A review says 3 to 5 in 100 people in hospital for withdrawal get them. Most figures come from that review or old trials.

alcohol.q: In alcohol withdrawal, how many in 100 on benzodiazepines had a seizure, against 8 on dummy pills?
alcohol.why: About 1 in 100 on a benzodiazepine, against 8 on dummy pills. The trials ran from the 1960s to 1983, and few had seizures.

alcohol.q: About how many deaths a year did global models estimate alcohol caused worldwide?
alcohol.why: Global models estimated about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, against a world where no one drank. Computer estimates, not counted deaths.

alcohol.q: How many people who barely drank alcohol had a 'shrunken' memory area in a UK scan study?
alcohol.why: About 35 in 100 did. People who drank more got the rating more often, but one scan can't show alcohol caused it.

heroin.q: In trials for constipation caused by opioids, how many in 100 got better on a medicine?
heroin.why: About 52 in 100, against 33 on a dummy pill. Nearly all trials were in people taking opioids for pain.

heroin.q: Why can a death record say morphine when the person took heroin?
options: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine
Heroin and morphine are the same drug
heroin.why: Heroin quickly turns into morphine in the body, so some death records said morphine instead of heroin.

heroin.q: In a Canadian survey at harm reduction sites, about how many people had used drugs alone that week?
heroin.why: About 3 in 4 had; the top reason was comfort at home. It was one survey, of people who already went to these sites.

heroin.q: In trials, how many in 100 coming off heroin had bad withdrawal on clonidine or lofexidine?
heroin.why: About 19 in 100, against about 59 on a dummy pill. Only three small, old trials, and none with people coming off fentanyl.

heroin.q: In trials, which helped more people finish opioid withdrawal treatment?
heroin.why: About 72 in 100 finished on buprenorphine, against about 45 on clonidine or lofexidine. No trial reported people coming off fentanyl.

heroin.q: In one study, before Vancouver's site for injecting heroin and other drugs opened, how did reported overdoses change?
options: They fell by more than half
heroin.why: About 12 in 100 people who inject drugs reported an overdose in 2001, and 5 in 100 in 2002. The site opened in 2003.

heroin.q: After Vancouver's site for injecting heroin and other drugs opened, how much did overdose deaths nearby fall?
heroin.why: About a third within 500 metres, against about a tenth elsewhere, in one study where nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.

methylphenidate.q: In trials, how often was trouble falling asleep recorded on the ADHD medicine methylphenidate versus a dummy pill?
methylphenidate.why: Nearly three times as often, though who recorded sleep problems changed how big the difference looked.

methylphenidate.q: How much sooner did children on ADHD medicine fall asleep with melatonin than with a dummy pill?
methylphenidate.why: About 16 minutes, in one small study of 19 children paid for by the company that made the melatonin.

methylphenidate.q: In studies of healthy adults, what did a single pill of methylphenidate or amphetamine do to thinking?
options: Gave a small lift on some tests
Gave a big lift on most tests
Made scores worse on most tests
methylphenidate.why: A small average lift, clearest for holding back an automatic response; memory gains shrank after allowing for unpublished studies.

ghb-gbl.q: In one Dutch study, which people who used GHB had worse memory than others?
options: Those who passed out from it many times
Those who used it regularly without passing out
Memory was the same in every group
ghb-gbl.why: Those who had passed out from GHB many times remembered worse than people using it regularly without passing out. One study: it cannot show cause.

psilocybin.q: In a US survey, how many in 100 people who used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip?
psilocybin.why: 41 in 100 recalled one, looking back over their whole life in an online survey. Most were still glad they had used psychedelics.

psilocybin.q: In lab studies of LSD and psilocybin, what was a flashback usually like?
options: A few seconds of changed seeing
Hours of living through the whole trip again
A vision problem that never went away
psilocybin.why: Most came in the days after, usually lasting seconds, and nobody was found with a lasting vision problem.

psilocybin.q: In a 233-person psilocybin trial for hard-to-treat depression, what did the benefit look like by 12 weeks?
options: A gap that could be chance
psilocybin.why: By 12 weeks, the gap between full and tiny psilocybin doses could be chance. People could probably tell what they got.

psilocybin.q: Two months after a psilocybin session, how many volunteers ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences?
psilocybin.why: About 2 in 3 did, in one lab study. All took part in religious or spiritual activities.

psilocybin.q: In a psilocybin quit-smoking study, most weren't smoking 6 months later. How many took part?
psilocybin.why: Just 15 people, and 12 weren't smoking. All got psilocybin plus lots of counselling, with no comparison group.

psilocybin.q: Two months after a psilocybin session, how many volunteers ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences?
psilocybin.why: 67 in 100 did. All took part in religious or spiritual activities.

psilocybin.q: Before a trial of psilocybin against the antidepressant escitalopram, what did people expect?
