options: Nearly twice as much from psilocybin
psilocybin.why: Nearly twice as much from psilocybin. Allowing for those hopes left no clear difference between the groups on any of six scales.

psilocybin.q: In a 233-person psilocybin trial for hard-to-treat depression, what did the benefit look like by 12 weeks?
options: A gap that could be chance
psilocybin.why: By 12 weeks, the gap between full and tiny psilocybin doses could be chance. People could probably tell what they got.

psilocybin.q: In microdosing trials of magic mushrooms or LSD, how often did people guess right which capsule they had?
psilocybin.why: People guessed right about 7 times in 10. Their ratings followed what they believed they took, though feeling an effect may have shaped the belief.

methadone-buprenorphine.q: Just before the next dose, how did methadone blood levels compare in people with and without withdrawal?
options: Much lower in those with withdrawal
Much higher in those with withdrawal
methadone-buprenorphine.why: About the same. In those with withdrawal, the level tended to drop faster after its daily high; only 18 people were tested.

alkyl-nitrites-and-inhalants.q: In people with eye problems after poppers, what did scans mostly show?
options: A cloudy lens, like a cataract
Damage to light-sensing cells at the back
Scratches on the front of the eye
alkyl-nitrites-and-inhalants.why: Scans mostly showed damage to light-sensing cells at the centre of the retina. People reported blurry central vision, flashes or a blank spot.

benzodiazepines.q: The day after some benzodiazepine sleeping pills, how did lane weaving compare with alcohol at a driving limit?
options: About half as bad as the alcohol
benzodiazepines.why: With some pills, weaving was worse than with alcohol at a limit several countries use. Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers.

benzodiazepines.q: Why is it hard to tell whether benzodiazepines cause dementia?
options: Early dementia symptoms can lead to prescriptions
People forget whether they took them
Too few older people take them
benzodiazepines.why: Worry and poor sleep can come before dementia and lead to benzodiazepine prescriptions. Quebec's study used prescription records, not memory.

caffeine.q: In studies, how much less did people sleep on nights after caffeine than on nights without it?
caffeine.why: That was the average across 24 studies comparing nights with and without caffeine in the same healthy adults.

caffeine.q: Before surgery, people who drank lots of caffeine got dummy pills instead. How many had headaches by evening?
caffeine.why: 10 of the 20 on dummy pills had a headache by evening; none given caffeine pills did. Only 40 hospital patients took part.

caffeine.q: In lab studies, how many with panic disorder had a panic attack after one large amount of caffeine?
caffeine.why: 121 of 237 had a panic attack after caffeine; none was reported after a dummy. The review cannot show what ordinary smaller servings do.

caffeine.q: In people who rarely have caffeine, what did caffeine change in a lab study?
caffeine.why: They got faster and more jittery, not more alert. One study.

caffeine.q: In people who had never smoked, how was coffee linked to lung cancer?
caffeine.why: No clear link: it disappeared in people who never smoked. People who smoke tend to drink more coffee.

caffeine.q: In a caffeine study, who quit the test day early with headache and feeling sick?
options: People who often have caffeine, on dummy pills
People who rarely have caffeine, on caffeine
People who often have caffeine, on caffeine
caffeine.why: All five people who often have caffeine and quit early had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons. One study.

cocaine.q: What did people describe in the crash after a cocaine binge?
options: Days of extra energy, little need for sleep
Very low mood, then long, heavy sleep
Feeling normal again by the next day
cocaine.why: Very low mood, then long, heavy sleep and hunger. Some had passing thoughts of suicide, limited to the crash. From 30 people in treatment.

cocaine.q: Among people treated for cocaine use, how many said they had had symptoms such as paranoia with cocaine?
cocaine.why: A review of 17 studies; strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100.

cocaine.q: Within a year of starting, how many people who used only powder cocaine met the criteria for dependence?
cocaine.why: For people who went on to crack it was about 22 in 100; the survey cannot show that crack made the difference.

cocaine.q: Among people who injected cocaine, what were the main causes of death?
cocaine.why: In a crack treatment group in Brazil, it was gunshot wounds and AIDS.

cocaine.q: What is levamisole, often found in cocaine around 2010?
options: A numbing medicine used by dentists
A sugar used to bulk up the powder
cocaine.why: Case reports link it to blood and skin harm; how often it causes harm is unknown.

cocaine.q: In a lab, what happened to heart blood flow when 10 people got the beta-blocker propranolol after cocaine?
cocaine.why: It fell in all 10 heart patients. None had used cocaine before.

cocaine.q: Of people tracked a year after cocaine-linked chest pain, 3 in 100 died. How many from heart attacks?
cocaine.why: None of the deaths were from a heart attack; 1 in 100 had a heart attack and lived.

cocaine.q: Of all the cocaine on 50 US dollar bills, how much was on the bill with the most?
cocaine.why: About 7 in 10 sat on one Honolulu bill, so the average was far above what most bills held.

cocaine.q: In a lab, what happened to heart blood flow when 10 people got the beta-blocker propranolol after cocaine?
cocaine.why: It fell in all 10 heart patients. None had used cocaine before.

lsd.q: The day after LSD in one lab study, how did people do on thinking tests?
options: A few small ups and downs
lsd.why: A few tests went slightly better and one slightly worse, in 24 people after one small lab dose. Some may be luck.

lsd.q: Where did the 1967 LSD chromosome scare come from?
options: Cells from two people in a dish
Tests on thousands of people who used LSD
Babies born to mothers who took LSD
lsd.why: Cells from two people in a dish: LSD was added to their blood cells in a lab. Cells in a dish aren't people.

pcp.q: In three reported cases after drugs thought to contain PCP, how long did a severe breakdown last?
options: Two to four weeks, then it passed
For the rest of their lives
pcp.why: Two to four weeks, then it passed in all three. Only three cases from 1975, and nobody tested the drugs.

cannabis.q: In sleep-lab studies, how did sleep change in the first nights after stopping heavy cannabis use?
options: Longer sleep, quicker to start, less dream sleep
Shorter sleep, slower to start, more dream sleep
cannabis.why: They slept less, took longer to fall asleep and had more dream sleep. Three small studies, two from the 1970s.

cannabis.q: In trials, how much did cannabis medicines lower long-lasting pain on a 0-to-10 scale, versus a dummy?
cannabis.why: About half a point lower than with a dummy. The trials were short and mostly tested one mouth spray.

cannabis.q: In two older US surveys, how many people who had ever tried cannabis became dependent at some point?
cannabis.why: About 9 in 100: in the first survey, fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.

cannabis.q: In a Swedish study, how many men who used cannabis over 50 times went to hospital with schizophrenia?
cannabis.why: About 38 in 1,000 later did, against about 6 in 1,000 who never used. These counts do not allow for other differences between the men.

cannabis.q: In 11 places in Europe and Brazil, daily use of strong cannabis went with what odds of psychosis?
options: About the same as those who never used
About 50 times those who never used
About 5 times those who never used
cannabis.why: About 5 times; daily use of weaker types, about 2 times. The gap between strong and weaker types could be chance.

cannabis.q: In a New Zealand study, how many IQ points did people dependent on cannabis for years lose?
cannabis.why: About 6 points from their childhood scores, in 38 people. Another researcher showed family background differences could produce a similar pattern.

cannabis.q: In one study, how did people who had quit heavy cannabis use for a year or more score?
options: Much lower than people who had not used
Slightly lower than people who had not used
No differently from people who had not used
cannabis.why: They did not score differently on any test from people who had not used. Few studies have followed people this long.

cannabis.q: Babies of mothers who used cannabis while pregnant: how did they compare with other babies?
options: No difference in weight or care
A bit lighter; more went to intensive care
Heavier; fewer went to intensive care
cannabis.why: About 109 grams lighter, and more went to newborn intensive care. But many mothers also used tobacco or alcohol.

cannabis.q: In three small trials, how many people having chemotherapy had sickness fully controlled on a cannabis medicine?
cannabis.why: About 47 in 100, against 20 in 100 on a dummy medicine. Only 102 people took part.

cannabis.q: In trials, how many people on cannabis medicines had at least one side effect?
cannabis.why: About 81 in 100, against 62 in 100 on a dummy or another medicine. Long-term harms were not studied.

cannabis.q: In two trials of a CBD medicine for Dravet syndrome, how many children saw seizures at least halve?
cannabis.why: 43 to 49 in 100 on the CBD medicine, against 26 to 27 in 100 on a dummy liquid.

synthetic-cannabinoids.q: How did people who had used both rate synthetic cannabis against ordinary cannabis while high?
options: More bad feelings, much less enjoyment
synthetic-cannabinoids.why: They said it gave more bad feelings and fear of others, and much less enjoyment; most preferred ordinary cannabis. Nobody tested the products.

drug-checking.q: When people tested opioids with take-home fentanyl strips, how many in 100 results showed fentanyl?
drug-checking.why: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 tested by staff. People reported results, often from memory.

drug-checking.q: In lab tests of 106 police-seized samples containing fentanyl, how many showed it on a fentanyl strip?
drug-checking.why: Strips showed fentanyl in 104 of 106. Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand; home testing was not studied.

drug-checking.q: In lab tests, did fentanyl strips pick up drugs related to fentanyl, like carfentanil?
options: Most but not all; carfentanil needed large amounts
Yes, all of them, even in tiny amounts
drug-checking.why: At high amounts, 21 to 24 of 28 related drugs showed up; three never did, on any brand.

drug-checking.q: Xylazine test strips caught 37 of 38 samples with enough xylazine. With less, how many of 28?
drug-checking.why: Only 6 of 28 with less xylazine read positive. The samples were residues wiped from used equipment, not powders.

drug-checking.q: In one lab study, some MDMA samples also had caffeine or amphetamine. What did a colour test show?
options: The same colour as MDMA alone
drug-checking.why: Seven MDMA samples with another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine, gave the same colour. One small 2003 study, with a kit of that time.

drug-checking.q: At one festival, when tests showed drugs were not as sold, how many in 100 handed them over?
drug-checking.why: 30 of 45 people handed drugs over to be destroyed, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched. One festival, with chemists testing.

drug-checking.q: Two people new to an MDMA colour test kit tested 8 known drugs. How did they do?
drug-checking.why: One missed both MDMA samples; the other called four other drugs MDMA. Lab experts got MDMA right. One small 2003 study.

drug-checking.q: After US states made fentanyl test strips legal, how did drug deaths compare with the expected trend?
drug-checking.why: About 7 in 100 fewer than expected. The study looked at laws, not at people using strips; other changes could explain it.

drug-checking.q: In Baltimore, women given fentanyl test strips reported fewer overdoses later. What about those who used none?
drug-checking.why: They also reported fewer. Overall, 6 said they had an overdose in the month before the start, 1 before the last visit; no comparison group.

ketamine.q: In one small study, what did ketamine's S form do that its R form did not?
ketamine.why: On the S form, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self; on R, they described relaxation. Only ten people.

ketamine.q: Tested soon after taking ketamine at a party, how much of a short story did people remember?
options: Less than half as much as others
ketamine.why: Less than half as much as partygoers who had not taken it. Nobody tested what people had taken.

ketamine.q: In one study, people had quit ketamine for at least a month. How did their memory scores compare?
options: Far below people who don't use it
As good as people who don't use it
A bit below people who don't use it
ketamine.why: As good, still a year later. But most had used less to begin with, so stopping may not be why.

ketamine.q: In a large trial, how many in 100 on ketamine drips had a moderate or severe side effect?
ketamine.why: 25 in 100 had one within 3 weeks of ketamine drips, against 32 in 100 on ECT.

ketamine.q: In one survey, what did people say happened to bladder symptoms after they stopped ketamine?
options: Many got better, but not all
ketamine.why: 128 of 251 survey respondents said they got better after stopping. No study compared them with people who kept using.

ketamine.q: How did a study link ketamine trips to near-death experiences?
options: By comparing words in written reports
By scanning people's brains on ketamine
ketamine.why: A computer compared words in about 15,000 online drug reports and 625 near-death accounts. Nobody was given ketamine.

ketamine.q: In a Swedish trial, after which treatment did people have memory loss lasting over a day?
ketamine.why: After ECT: 19 of 90 had it, against none of 91 after ketamine drips.

ketamine.q: Adults whose depression lifted on esketamine spray were switched to a dummy spray. How many relapsed?
ketamine.why: 45 in 100, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine. The trial cannot tell relapse from effects of stopping.

general.q: At one US autopsy centre, deaths nobody thought were from drugs were tested. How many were drug deaths?
general.why: Drug tests showed about 49 in 100 were drug deaths. Only two US places have been studied, so other places may differ.

general.q: In a UK study, readers saw a made-up drug death story. Whom did they judge more harshly?
options: A man rather than a woman
A woman rather than a man
general.why: Readers judged a man more harshly, and someone who took heroin rather than ecstasy; differences were small to moderate.

general.q: A US survey asked adults who used drugs 12+ times. How many who started by 13 became dependent?
general.why: About 1 in 3, against about 1 in 7 who started at 21 or older. Studies can't show starting young is the cause.

general.q: In a Swedish study, how many adopted children whose birth parent had a recorded drug problem had one?
general.why: About 9 in 100, about twice the 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did. Birth parents pass on the pregnancy, not just genes.

general.q: In a study of about 1.5 million people leaving prison, when was the risk of dying highest?
options: More than a year after release
general.why: About 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks. With no information on drug use or tolerance, the study cannot say why.

general.q: In Vietnam, 20 in 100 US soldiers reported narcotic dependence. How many did in their first year home?
general.why: About 1 in 100 had been, in the year after coming home. How many had treatment was not counted.

general.q: In 168 published 'excited delirium' cases, how many of the 104 deaths had force such as restraint recorded?
general.why: Force included sedation, electrical weapons and restraint. Selected reports can't tell how much restraint, drugs or agitation caused.

general.q: Two lists of drug deaths in Norway were compared. About how many out of 100 were on both?
general.why: Only about 49 out of 100 were on both; in Sweden, fewer than half. Different lists use different rules.

general.q: In US death records from 1999 to 2015, how many overdoses had no specific drug named?
general.why: About 23 out of 100 had only an 'unspecified drug' code. The gaps differ by place and rules.

general.q: In Australian twins, one started cannabis before 17. Who more often used cocaine or other stimulants?
options: The twin who started cannabis early
general.why: 48 in 100 against 26 in 100. Growing up together can't explain it, but other differences between the twins could.

general.q: Two later experiments tried to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study. What happened?
options: They found the same big difference
They did not find the same result
They found an even bigger difference
general.why: The result was not repeated. In the original studies the two groups were also measured differently, and all were rats.

general.q: Portugal's crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year. Mainly why?
options: Possession stopped counting as a crime
general.why: Possession for your own use stopped counting as a crime in 2001, so those cases left the arrest count.

general.q: A 2004 review found DARE had no clear effect on alcohol, tobacco or drug use. Which version?
general.why: All 11 studies tested the original classes. DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.

general.q: Were US teens who remembered more anti-drug ads (1999–2004) less likely to start using cannabis?
general.why: No favourable link was found. In one of three periods, more ads went with more first use; the authors call this tentative.

general.q: In a UK expert ranking of harm to the person using, which drug was among the worst three?
general.why: Crack cocaine, heroin and meth scored worst for the person using. Alcohol topped the overall list mostly through harm to others.

general.q: A UK expert ranking scored each drug for deaths like overdose. What did tobacco get?
general.why: Zero: that score covered deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere; the authors agreed tobacco probably kills more than the other 19 combined.

synthetic-cathinones.q: By 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands were linked to mephedrone. In how many did tests find none?
synthetic-cathinones.why: Tests after death found no mephedrone in 25. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one does not prove cause.

nicotine.q: After stopping smoking, when were most feelings like grumpiness and restlessness strongest, in older studies?
nicotine.why: Most were gone within 2 to 4 weeks, but for some people they lasted longer or came back.

dmt-ayahuasca.q: In a survey of almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca, what went with less fear?
options: Drinking in Amazon countries outside Brazil
dmt-ayahuasca.why: Church hymns or sermons went with less fear, more traditional practices with more. Differences were small, and people rated everything looking back.

dmt-ayahuasca.q: After DMT 'being' meetings, fewer called themselves atheists. Did that happen after 'God' meetings without drugs too?
dmt-ayahuasca.why: Yes: the share fell without drugs too, as after DMT (28 to 10 in 100). People recalled 'before' years later.

kratom.q: In 27 US states in 2016–17, how many overdose deaths had kratom found in them?
kratom.why: 152 of 27,338 deaths. Testing for kratom varied and was not recorded, so some were probably missed.

mescaline.q: In a US survey, what erased the mental health gap for people who'd used LSD or mescaline?
options: Counting their other drug use and life stress
Leaving out people who used only once
mescaline.why: Once other drug use, risk-taking and stressful events were counted, none of 20 measures was higher. Asked once, the survey can't show cause.

nitrous-oxide.q: In 100 published cases of health problems after nitrous oxide (laughing gas), what was the commonest symptom?
nitrous-oxide.why: 80 of 100 had numbness or tingling and 58 trouble walking.

fentanyl-and-analogues.q: How many police or paramedics poisoned by touching fentanyl do poison experts know of?
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: None: no such overdose has been confirmed. Their view rests on sums from skin patches, not measurements.

fentanyl-and-analogues.q: Of 214 news stories about police or paramedics exposed to opioids like fentanyl, how many had lab proof?
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: None: only one incident mentioned any test, probably one that misses fentanyl. That can't prove such poisonings never happen, either.

fentanyl-and-analogues.q: Where did officers at five US police forces say they had heard about fentanyl overdoses from contact?
options: Colleagues, a federal drug agency video, bulletins
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: Colleagues, a federal drug agency video and bulletins. None could confirm a colleague's overdose. Only five forces took part.

fentanyl-and-analogues.q: A federal safety agency looked into three cases where officers felt ill near drugs. What did it find?
options: No signs of a serious overdose
Clear signs of a serious overdose
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: No signs of a serious overdose. But no officer had a test that finds fentanyl, so these cases can't confirm or rule out poisoning.

fentanyl-and-analogues.q: A New York survey asked police, fire and ambulance workers about fentanyl. About how many agreed a brief touch could be deadly?
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: About 4 in 5: 149 of 187. No survey picked people at random, so it may not speak for all responders.

methamphetamine.statement: A medicine on sale today has been clearly shown to ease meth withdrawal.
methamphetamine.why: None has; in nine small trials, only one drug clearly helped, and it is no longer sold. A benefit can't be ruled out.

methamphetamine.statement: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look so alike that no symptom has been shown to reliably tell them apart.
methamphetamine.why: Hallucinations and delusions were not clearly different in 12 small studies; flatness and withdrawal were somewhat milder in meth psychosis.

methamphetamine.statement: In one big trial, most people given naltrexone with bupropion had mostly meth-free urine tests.
methamphetamine.why: About 1 in 7 did by the end, against about 1 in 40 on dummy medicines: about 1 extra person for every 9 treated.

methamphetamine.statement: Meth comes in two mirror-image forms, and which form it is depends on how it was made.
methamphetamine.why: In one small study of 12 men, the two forms acted differently: the 'l' form raised blood pressure less.

methamphetamine.statement: Meth poisoning can make the body get very hot.
methamphetamine.why: Reviews of hospital studies list getting very hot among the signs of a body in overdrive.

methamphetamine.statement: In lab choice tests, people who use meth almost always chose the drug over small amounts of cash.
methamphetamine.why: They often chose cash, picking the drug about 4 times in 10 in one group, fewer than 2 in 10 in another. Only 13 men.

methamphetamine.statement: In one small study, most symptoms of stopping meth eased within one to two weeks.
methamphetamine.why: On a hospital research ward, most reported symptoms eased in that time, though low mood and craving lasted longer.

methamphetamine.statement: Brain studies agree that meth use shrinks the brain.
methamphetamine.why: Some studies found smaller brain areas soon after stopping, but others found some areas larger.

methamphetamine.statement: In one study, brothers and sisters without drug problems shared some brain differences with their sibling dependent on stimulants.
methamphetamine.why: This suggests some may run in families, though 94 in 100 of the dependent siblings were dependent on cocaine.

methamphetamine.statement: On average, people dependent on meth score far below the normal range on memory and thinking tests.
methamphetamine.why: They score somewhat lower on average, and group averages are mostly still in the normal range.

methamphetamine.statement: In studies of stopping meth, people who don't use meth also scored better from retaking the tests.
methamphetamine.why: People who stopped meth did not clearly improve more than them, in two small studies, so we don't know yet if thinking recovers.

methamphetamine.statement: Psychosis (losing touch with reality) linked to meth often comes back when people use again.
methamphetamine.why: It often returns with renewed use; most of the studies reviewed were of hospital patients with meth psychosis.

methamphetamine.statement: In one small study, people slept about two hours less after the biggest meth dose than after a dummy dose.
methamphetamine.why: A wrist monitor in 6 people showed this, and they also woke more than with any other dose.

methamphetamine.statement: In a small study, the biggest meth dose left heart rate and blood pressure higher the next morning than a dummy dose.
methamphetamine.why: Next morning their heart beat faster and blood pressure was higher; but this was one small study of eleven people.

methamphetamine.statement: In one trial, people in meth treatment felt much less sad and worried whether they did exercise or health classes.
methamphetamine.why: Both groups improved a lot and the exercise group only a little more; people knew their group, so hope may explain part.

methamphetamine.statement: In one study, people who used meth already had lower school grades from before they started.
methamphetamine.why: Their adult scores were also lower than those grades predicted. Nobody took these tests before they started using.

methamphetamine.statement: Meth seems to make nerve cells' chemical pumps run in reverse, pushing brain chemicals out.
methamphetamine.why: It makes nerve cells let out dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. How is not fully known; this comes from a review.

methamphetamine.statement: In studies mostly from compulsory drug rehab centres in China, meth craving fell during and after exercise.
methamphetamine.why: Craving fell compared with control groups, but these studies are known only through one weak review that gives no numbers.

methamphetamine.statement: When meth's good feelings fade over days of use, the bad effects fade too.
methamphetamine.why: In a small lab study, the good feelings were gone within three days, while dizziness, sickness and a pounding heart grew and appetite stayed down. Only six to nine people took part, on small doses.

methamphetamine.statement: One dose of meth leaves people sadder and craving it the next morning.
methamphetamine.why: In one small lab study, the biggest dose left people less alert and friendly the next morning than a dummy dose, but not sadder or more worried, and they didn't want meth more. Only eleven people took part, in a hospital unit.

methamphetamine.statement: Brain scans prove that meth kills dopamine nerve cells.
methamphetamine.why: Scans show less of one dopamine protein in people who used heavily, but it can drop without nerve cells dying, and other markers aren't always lower. Experts disagree, and nobody has shown it either way.

methamphetamine.statement: In one study, violent crime was the crime most tied to months of meth use.
methamphetamine.why: Among 469 people dependent on meth in Australia, the link was strongest for selling drugs and property crime, even after money and housing problems were counted. People reported use and crime for the same months, so it can't show which came first.

methamphetamine.statement: Meth cravings go away as quickly as the other withdrawal symptoms.
methamphetamine.why: In one small hospital-ward study, most symptoms eased within one to two weeks and low mood lasted about three, but craving lasted to week five, though weaker. The people in it weren't seeking treatment.

methamphetamine.statement: Psychosis linked to meth always clears up within a month of stopping.
methamphetamine.why: In a typical study, about 1 in 4 people with meth psychosis still had symptoms over a month after stopping. Studies ranged from none to almost all, and most were of hospital patients.

methamphetamine.statement: Almost everyone who tries stimulants like meth gets hooked.
methamphetamine.why: It depends how you count: an old US survey found about 11 in 100 had ever been dependent, and a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years. Neither had a number for meth alone.

methamphetamine.statement: Parkinson's disease is common in people diagnosed with meth or amphetamine problems.
methamphetamine.why: In Utah health records of people with such diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis, it was diagnosed about 3 times as often, but that's about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years, against 1 in 1,000. Some diagnoses were probably other movement conditions.

methamphetamine.statement: In most recent US overdose deaths involving meth, meth was the only drug.
methamphetamine.why: Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024 found fentanyl or other opioids in about 7 in 10 of these deaths. That's a different kind of record from the yearly death counts.

methamphetamine.statement: A US survey found tobacco hooked a bigger share of people who'd used it than cocaine or meth-like stimulants.
methamphetamine.why: Tobacco 32 in 100, cocaine 17, stimulants other than cocaine about 11, in an early-1990s survey that included people who'd only just started. A broader Australian count, done differently, estimated about 50 in 100 for stimulants within 14 years of starting.

methamphetamine.statement: In the largest trial, drug tests confirmed the antidepressant mirtazapine cut meth use.
methamphetamine.why: People on mirtazapine said they used meth about 2 fewer days in 4 weeks than people on a dummy pill, but saliva drug tests showed no difference, and most kept using. Two small San Francisco trials did find fewer meth-positive urine tests.

methamphetamine.statement: Bupropion and modafinil have been shown to help people stop using meth.
methamphetamine.why: Across five trials, about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, whether on medicine or a dummy pill. The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.

methamphetamine.statement: Most people who use meth end up diagnosed with psychosis.
methamphetamine.why: In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs got a psychosis diagnosis within 10 years, against under 1 in 100 with no drug record. No study has settled which comes first.

methamphetamine.statement: In lab studies, meth made attention and memory clearly worse at the time.
methamphetamine.why: In small lab studies, attention, memory and reaction time didn't get measurably worse. But small or moderate harm can't be ruled out, and binges weren't tested.

methamphetamine.statement: People who use meth report much more low mood than people who use other drugs.
methamphetamine.why: Against people who use other drugs, there was no clear difference. Against people who don't use meth, low mood was somewhat more common, and things like a hard life may explain part of that.

methamphetamine.statement: People with regular or problematic meth or amphetamine use died nearly 7 times as often as others their age.
methamphetamine.why: That's about 1 in 90 a year, in studies of people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Many also used opioids, so not all of it is the drug.

methamphetamine.statement: In one study, people dependent on meth reported more violent crime in months they used it.
methamphetamine.why: It was about 12 in 100 months with meth use, against 3 in 100 without, comparing each person with themselves. But use and crime were reported for the same months, so which came first is unclear.

methamphetamine.statement: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart and fast breathing.
methamphetamine.why: The body can also overheat, chest pain can happen, and some people lose touch with reality. That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.

mdma.statement: MDMA has been tried in couples therapy for PTSD, and both partners felt happier together afterwards.
mdma.why: Two small studies, 14 couples in all. Neither had a group without MDMA, and this couples therapy helps PTSD even without it.

mdma.statement: In a small MDMA study for depression, 4 to 6 of 12 people had worse thoughts of suicide at some point.
mdma.why: 4 to 6 of 12 had worse thoughts of suicide at some point, though depression fell a lot overall. No group went without MDMA.

mdma.statement: In a club study, people who took ecstasy felt sadder and less sociable two days later than other clubbers.
mdma.why: A week later they felt like the others again, but the study did not check what was in the pills.

mdma.statement: In lab studies, 15 in 100 people later called their MDMA experience disappointing or bad.
mdma.why: Looking back, 15 in 100 called it disappointing or bad and 67 in 100 positive. They were healthy volunteers with researchers present.

mdma.statement: In one small study, heart valve changes were more common in people who had taken MDMA for six months or more.
mdma.why: 8 of 29 met a definition of drug-related valve disease, against none of 29 students reporting no drug use. Nobody was scanned before taking MDMA.

mdma.statement: MDMA therapy has even been tried, in a small trial, for ringing in the ears (tinnitus).
mdma.why: Reviews found single small trials for tinnitus and two kinds of anxiety. Outside PTSD, nobody can yet say whether MDMA therapy helps.

mdma.statement: In studies linking ecstasy to lower memory scores, almost everyone also used other drugs, most often cannabis.
mdma.why: People who use ecstasy score lower on some tests, on average, but these studies cannot show ecstasy caused it; the gap may have come first.

mdma.statement: Research shows most people feel a mid-week low a few days after taking ecstasy.
mdma.why: Two small studies disagree; the one that measured people a week before found no difference from people who use ecstasy but skipped it.

mdma.statement: Ecstasy has been proven to cause lasting brain damage in people.
mdma.why: Experts disagree. Scans find less of a serotonin marker, but almost nobody was scanned before starting, so a difference may have come first.

mdma.statement: In two small studies, people felt much sadder the day after ecstasy than others did.
mdma.why: People felt very tired and had slept less, but their next-day mood was about the same as others'.

mdma.statement: After MDMA in a sleep lab, dreaming (REM) sleep almost disappeared that night, then came back the next night.
mdma.why: A short night without MDMA did not remove dreaming sleep this way, in this study of 7 people.

mdma.statement: In the MDMA trial for PTSD that asked, most people could tell MDMA from the dummy pill.
mdma.why: 94 in 100 on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right; neither trial reports measuring what people expected.

mdma.statement: In 2024 the US regulator approved MDMA therapy for PTSD.
mdma.why: It said no. Its expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show the treatment works.

mdma.statement: When a 2002 study on ecstasy and monkeys' brains was withdrawn, more big US newspapers reported the withdrawal than the study.
mdma.why: Of 50 big US newspapers, 26 wrote about the study and 20 about the withdrawal.

mdma.statement: In one study, a few ecstasy pills did not change a serotonin marker in young people scanned before and after.
mdma.why: Scanned before and about 17 months later, the marker had not changed. But most had taken only one or two pills in all.

mdma.statement: MDMA therapy for PTSD has been shown to work better than usual talking therapy.
mdma.why: Neither trial tested that: both compared MDMA plus therapy with a dummy pill plus the same therapy.

mdma.statement: A US judge said the strictest ban on MDMA was not needed, but the drug agency imposed it anyway.
mdma.why: Before the 1985 ban, a few dozen US therapists used MDMA in therapy. This comes second-hand from one history review.

mdma.statement: In the one study that followed people dependent on ecstasy, 93 in 100 were no longer dependent about three years later.
mdma.why: But that group was small, about 12 to 14 people by our count, and studies disagree on how many become dependent.

mdma.statement: In 2024, a journal withdrew three MDMA therapy studies, saying the authors had not told it of serious rule-breaking at one site.
mdma.why: Most authors who answered disagreed with the withdrawals, and the journal did not say how much data came from that site.

mdma.statement: In lab studies, people who felt anxious and low just before MDMA felt more anxious than calm people did.
mdma.why: So did people who tend to worry. These were healthy young volunteers in a hospital, most trying MDMA for the first time.

mdma.statement: A journal withdrew three earlier MDMA therapy studies over rule-breaking at one trial site.
mdma.why: The rule-breaking was at one site. In 2024 the US regulator also said no; whether MDMA itself helps PTSD is not settled.

mdma.statement: People who had taken more ecstasy showed less of a serotonin marker, in most studies.
mdma.why: Four studies found this link and two smaller ones didn't. But amounts came from memory, and people who take more ecstasy also take more of other drugs.

mdma.statement: If an antidepressant mutes MDMA's effects, that means less MDMA is in your blood.
mdma.why: In small trials, two antidepressants lowered how strongly people rated MDMA's effects, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher. That's second-hand, from single trials of 16 healthy people each.

mdma.statement: In safety reports about ecstasy, cases that also named an antidepressant more often ended in death.
mdma.why: In US reports, those cases had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome, and reports naming muscle relaxants or anesthetics had higher odds still. These are voluntary reports, so they can't show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.

mdma.statement: In MDMA trials for PTSD, many people given a dummy pill plus therapy also no longer had PTSD.
mdma.why: 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill no longer had PTSD about 4 months later, against 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA. In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.

mdma.statement: Once people stop using ecstasy, their test scores bounce back, research shows.
mdma.why: Nobody knows yet: in a few small studies, people who had stopped for at least 6 months scored about the same as people still using, and both scored lower than people who had never used. But these compared different people, not the same people over time.

mdma.statement: Ecstasy has been shown to damage dopamine nerve cells in people.
mdma.why: The study that claimed this harm was withdrawn because its animals got a different drug, and five human scan studies showed no clear dopamine change. But very little has been measured in people, so this doesn't show it's safe.

mdma.statement: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well.
mdma.why: In questionnaires retold in one review, most said the first time was the strongest. But nobody checked what the tablets held, different people were compared rather than followed, and no lab study has tested it.

mdma.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
mdma.why: At least 10 of 17 cases reported to a UK poisons service had, and the 2 who died had brain swelling. These reports count only people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens or whether drinking more changes the risk.

mdma.statement: The 2002 study claiming ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains had actually given the animals a different drug.
mdma.why: The drug came from a wrongly labelled bottle, and the study was withdrawn a year later. The withdrawal notice doesn't say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

mdma.statement: People who use ecstasy score worse on memory tests even if they use hardly any other drug.
mdma.why: In one study where breath, urine and hair tests checked that people used little else, memory scores didn't differ from others in the same all-night dance scene. Medium-sized differences couldn't be ruled out, and heavier use went with worse scores on one planning test.

mdma.statement: People with no working version of the enzyme that clears MDMA get far higher levels of it.
mdma.why: Their peak level was only about 15 percent higher, and only in the first 3 hours: MDMA seems to switch that enzyme off itself, so these body differences matter less. Just 7 such people were studied.

mdma.statement: In one study, more babies exposed to ecstasy in pregnancy had birth defects than expected.
mdma.why: 12 of 78 babies born alive, about 15 in 100, had a birth defect, against the 2 to 3 in 100 the authors expected. But there was no comparison group, almost half the enquiries were lost to follow-up, and many pregnancies also involved other drugs.

mdma.statement: MDMA only raises body temperature when people dance in hot, crowded places.
mdma.why: Even resting in a room at about 23 degrees, 24 in 100 lab volunteers went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill. Heat, dancing and crowds weren't tested.

mdma.statement: The serotonin changes seen on scans of people who used ecstasy are known to be permanent.
mdma.why: Nobody knows: three studies found more of the scan marker in people who had stopped longer ago, two found no link with time, and no one has been scanned while using and again years later.

mdma.statement: In small MDMA trials, tiredness was common in the week after a session.
mdma.why: Five small trials gave MDMA to 58 people with conditions like anxiety or depression; a tight jaw, thirst and sweating were common during sessions, and none of the side effects were serious. The trials were too small to show rare or later harms.

mdma.statement: If a friend took the same MDMA and didn't overheat, you won't either.
mdma.why: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others: in one case of severe overheating, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat. That's second-hand, from one review of small studies and cases.

mdma.statement: All antidepressants carry about the same serotonin risk when mixed with ecstasy.
mdma.why: One 2007 review ranked MAOI antidepressants highest and SSRI-type antidepressants lower. That's the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work; no study counted how often each mix causes harm.

mdma.statement: MDMA therapy papers left out side effects that their own trial records listed.
mdma.why: More than half of the less serious problems in the trial records never made it into the papers, and neither did 4 of 13 serious ones, all 4 in people on MDMA. Most studies also noted only problems people raised themselves.

mdma.statement: Among people who got ill after MDMA, low blood salt was more common in women than men.
mdma.why: In one poison-centre study, 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men. It counted only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.

mdma.statement: Brain scans prove that ecstasy destroys serotonin nerve cells.
mdma.why: Four teams found less of a serotonin marker in the outer brain of people who use ecstasy, but less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone. Nobody was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.

mdma.statement: Only a few psychiatric medicines have been tested together with MDMA in studies.
mdma.why: Each was tested once, in 14 to 16 healthy people, and results differed: with MDMA, the antipsychotic haloperidol lowered well-being and raised anxiety. For several others, a 2022 review found no controlled study at all.

mdma.statement: An SSRI antidepressant that dulls MDMA's effects also lowers MDMA levels in your blood.
mdma.why: In 12 men, the SSRI paroxetine lessened MDMA's rises in blood pressure, heart rate and pupil size, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 1 in 6 higher. Only healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most.

mdma.statement: When MDMA is found in the blood of someone who died, it usually caused the death.
mdma.why: In 106 Australian coroners' cases with MDMA in the blood, 6 in 10 died of injuries, such as a crash. A blood test after death can't show who took what, when or why.

interactions.statement: People prescribed both opioids and benzos (calming medicines) had more overdoses than people on opioids alone.
interactions.why: Among US veterans, overdose deaths were about 3 in 1,000 a year with both, against under 1 without.

interactions.statement: In Ontario studies, gabapentin or pregabalin taken with opioid painkillers was linked to more opioid overdose deaths.
interactions.why: 12 in 100 people who died had a recent gabapentin prescription, against 7 in 100 similar living people. Reasons for prescribing were not given.

interactions.statement: Mild signs of serotonin syndrome (too much serotonin activity) can look like ordinary drug effects.
interactions.why: The condition ranges from mild to severe, and doctors look for signs like muscle jerks and very brisk reflexes.

interactions.statement: When people use cocaine with alcohol, the body makes a new substance, cocaethylene, that forms only when both are there.
interactions.why: Cocaethylene formed in two small hospital studies, never without alcohol. Neither measured heart attacks or rhythm problems.

interactions.statement: In a driving simulator, cannabis and alcohol together made lane weaving worse than either one alone.
interactions.why: A model of 18 adults' driving gave a 3.4 cm rise with both, against 1.3 and 2.1 alone.

interactions.statement: A positive cannabis test shows that a driver was impaired.
interactions.why: It shows cannabis was in the body, not that the driver was impaired.

interactions.statement: Among people on prescribed opioids who died of overdose, half to three in four also had benzo prescriptions.
interactions.why: Half among US veterans and three in four in Ontario. A share of deaths does not measure risk.

interactions.statement: Among emergency patients who'd taken GHB or GBL, those who'd also had alcohol more often went to critical care.
interactions.why: Of those kept in hospital, 55 in 100 with alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts weren't known.

interactions.statement: Alcohol is listed in about 1 in 7 US opioid overdose deaths.
interactions.why: Death certificates have listed alcohol in about 15 of 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share steady since 2008, and more often for men than women. Alcohol is often left off death records, and counts like these can't say how much it adds to risk.

interactions.statement: Benzos were listed in about 1 in 5 US opioid overdose deaths in 2017.
interactions.why: That's 21 in 100 death certificates, up from 9 in 1999, with benzos listed more often alongside prescription opioids or methadone than heroin or fentanyl. Records miss some drugs, and a share of deaths doesn't measure risk.

interactions.statement: The link between cannabis and car crashes stays just as strong when studies allow for drinking.
interactions.why: It shrinks: studies that allowed for alcohol found about 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash, against 1.7 to 1.8 in studies that didn't. These compare crashed drivers with others, so they can't show one driver's chance of crashing.

interactions.statement: People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
interactions.why: In two studies of people on methadone, tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete. Reviews add that tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, so the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.

interactions.statement: Mild serotonin syndrome is easy to tell apart from ordinary drug effects.
interactions.why: Mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects; doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, sweating and restlessness, and, when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever. A checklist of these signs was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses.

interactions.statement: Cocaine with alcohol makes the heart beat faster than cocaine alone.
interactions.why: In 8 people on a hospital ward, heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute with both, against 74 with cocaine alone. These small studies didn't measure heart attacks or rhythm problems.

interactions.statement: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, people also prescribed benzos died of poisoning more often.
interactions.why: Poisoning deaths were about 1 in 100 people a year with a benzo prescription, against 1 in 200 without, even though those on benzos stayed in treatment longer. The study didn't allow for mental health, alcohol or street drug use.

interactions.statement: Reviews rank MDMA with moclobemide or similar antidepressants as the riskiest mix they list.
interactions.why: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide in their blood, and pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs. Four deaths can't give a rate, and all four also had other drugs.

alcohol.statement: The most carefully run acamprosate trials found it clearly helped people stop drinking.
alcohol.why: The most carefully run trials found no clear difference; overall, 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83.

alcohol.statement: In trials where people did not know which pill they got, disulfiram, a medicine for drinking problems, showed no clear benefit.
alcohol.why: Disulfiram showed no clear benefit in these trials, but none tested taking it with someone watching, which may make it look less helpful.

alcohol.statement: In one US survey, alcohol use disorder was most common in people over 65.
alcohol.why: It was most common at ages 18 to 29, at about 27 in 100.

alcohol.statement: In a US survey, most people who had ever had alcohol use disorder had looked for help.
alcohol.why: Only about 20 in 100 who had ever had it said they looked for treatment or help.

alcohol.statement: In a big review, more drinking went with more breast cancer, as well as mouth, throat and liver cancer.
alcohol.why: Breast cancer was about 1.6 times as common at more than four drinks a day, against not drinking.

alcohol.statement: In a large trial, naltrexone plus talking therapy worked much better than either one alone.
alcohol.why: Naltrexone with therapy did no better than either one alone in this one US trial.

alcohol.statement: Starting to drink alcohol young has been shown to cause alcohol problems later in life.
alcohol.why: Not known: some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both, such as behaviour problems. Few studies followed young people.

alcohol.statement: Thinking you've drunk alcohol, when you haven't, is enough to change your mood and memory.
alcohol.why: Across 36 experiments, the belief went with more drinking but not mood or memory changes; the alcohol itself affected those.

alcohol.statement: The morning after heavy drinking, people remembered less and reacted more slowly than on alcohol-free days.
alcohol.why: Memory and reaction tests were worse than on alcohol-free days. Studies were small, and a short night's sleep may explain part.

alcohol.statement: If a breath test finds no alcohol left the morning after drinking, your driving is back to normal.
alcohol.why: In a lab driving machine, young drivers with no alcohol left in their breath still drove worse than after alcohol-free nights. Sleep went unchecked.

alcohol.statement: In studies, people felt more anxious and low when hungover from alcohol than when sober.
alcohol.why: Most of 22 studies, with over 6,000 people, found worse mood when hungover. Poor sleep or regret may explain part.

alcohol.statement: Drinking a little alcohol has been shown to protect the heart.
alcohol.why: People who drank a little had less heart disease, but non-drinkers included people who stopped, perhaps through illness. Alcohol may not be why.

alcohol.statement: In studies of people of European descent, genes for drinking a bit less alcohol went with slightly less heart disease, not more.
alcohol.why: These gene studies did not find that drinking a little protects the heart. They have possible biases of their own.

alcohol.statement: In many alcohol studies, the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill.
alcohol.why: People who had stopped died more often; against people who never drank, those drinking a little showed no clear difference.

alcohol.statement: In one world model, the risk of every cancer it looked at rose with drinking.
alcohol.why: The model's lowest-risk point balanced gains for some illnesses against losses; cancer risks still rose with drinking.

alcohol.statement: Naltrexone helped less, if at all, with stopping drinking completely.
alcohol.why: Trials found its benefit in heavy drinking: about 46 in 100 went back to it, against 54 on dummy pills.

alcohol.statement: In one estimate, about 25 in 100 pregnant women in the European region drank some alcohol.
alcohol.why: Regional figures ran from under 1 to 25 in 100, mostly from a model, and the European region was highest.

alcohol.statement: On average, an alcoholic drink before bed helps people fall asleep faster.
alcohol.why: On average, falling asleep took about the same time with or without alcohol, across 27 small sleep-lab studies.

alcohol.statement: In three of five studies, people felt they fell asleep faster after alcohol.
alcohol.why: That was how people felt; measured on average, falling asleep took about the same time with or without alcohol.

alcohol.statement: Alcohol before bed cuts dream sleep: it starts later and is shorter than on nights without alcohol.
alcohol.why: In small sleep-lab studies, dream sleep started later and was shorter after drinking. Results were not the same in every study.

alcohol.statement: A review says the DTs usually start about 3 days after alcohol withdrawal begins.
alcohol.why: The review describes the DTs as fast-coming confusion with withdrawal signs, usually lasting 2 or 3 days.

alcohol.statement: In several studies, people who said they slept badly soon after stopping heavy drinking were more likely to drink again.
alcohol.why: Long heavy drinking can leave sleep poor for months. This comes second-hand from a review that did not check study quality.

alcohol.statement: In one study, men who drank alcohol heavily for years had fewer nerve cells in the brain's outer layer than other men.
alcohol.why: Both groups had about 23 billion. But only the outer layer was counted, in 22 men; other areas were not.

alcohol.statement: A UK study scanned people's brains over 30 years and saw them shrink as people drank more alcohol.
alcohol.why: Each brain was scanned once, at the end. It found a link: people drinking more were more often rated as having a shrunken memory area.

alcohol.statement: Worldwide, alcohol is estimated to cause millions of deaths a year.
alcohol.why: Global models put it at about 2.3 to 2.8 million a year, against a world where no one drank, and at ages 15 to 49 it was the top risk factor in one study. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths.

alcohol.statement: Studies show people who drink a little live longer than people who never drank.
alcohol.why: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths in people who drink a little, but compared with people who had never drunk, there was no clear difference. Few studies made that comparison, so a small gain or a small loss is still possible.

alcohol.statement: In gene studies, drinking more went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.
alcohol.why: In a big study of Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes, and bleeding strokes rose most. Women, who mostly don't drink, showed no link with the same genes.

alcohol.statement: In a global study, alcohol was the top risk factor for death among people aged 15 to 49.
alcohol.why: The Global Burden of Disease study put about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women at those ages down to alcohol. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths.

alcohol.statement: Most people on acamprosate in trials still drank again during treatment.
alcohol.why: About 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83 in 100 on dummy pills, and the most carefully run trials found no clear difference. Most trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly its maker.

alcohol.statement: In one US survey, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year.
alcohol.why: Two or more of 11 signs of problem drinking in a year count, and about half the cases were mild. Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.

alcohol.statement: In a UK scan study, 35 in 100 people who barely drank had a memory area rated 'shrunken'.
alcohol.why: 'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. People who drank more got the rating more often, but the study can't show alcohol caused it.

alcohol.statement: Most people treated in hospital for alcohol withdrawal get the DTs (sudden confusion).
alcohol.why: A review says 3 to 5 in 100 of them do, and that about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. Most of these figures are passed on by that review or come from old trials.

alcohol.statement: People who had their first drink at 14 or younger more often had alcohol dependence than late starters.
alcohol.why: In a big US survey, about 4 to 5 in 10 who started at 14 or younger had been dependent at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. But people had to remember their first drink, and some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.

alcohol.statement: In lab tests, men told their drink had vodka drank more, whatever was really in it.
alcohol.why: They drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, while real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

alcohol.statement: Drinking alcohol was estimated to cause about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
alcohol.why: A model put it at 741,000 new cancers, about 6 in 100 in men and 2 in 100 in women, led by gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer. It's a computer estimate built on risks from studies of groups, not a count.

alcohol.statement: Fewer people went back to heavy drinking on naltrexone than on dummy pills.
alcohol.why: About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills; feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common. Most were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.

alcohol.statement: In old trials, benzodiazepines made seizures during alcohol withdrawal much rarer.
alcohol.why: About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills, and delirium was less common too. The trials ran from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.

cocaine.statement: In one study, sleep after stopping cocaine got better both on sleep-lab machines and in how people felt.
cocaine.why: Machines showed people slept less and took longer to fall asleep, while their own ratings got better.

cocaine.statement: People who sought help for heavy cocaine use said the crash after a binge usually ended within a few days.
cocaine.why: It usually ended within a few days. This is what 30 people in treatment told doctors, with no comparison group.

cocaine.statement: An older study of people stopping cocaine at home described craving coming back after a few calm days.
cocaine.why: In the closed unit, craving eased over weeks, but that place had no cocaine and nothing to remind the men.

cocaine.statement: In 1990s New York, cocaine overdose deaths were more common on hot days.
cocaine.why: 2.34 deaths a day on hot days against 1.76 on other days, but the study compared days, not people.

cocaine.statement: Crack and powder cocaine are two different drugs.
cocaine.why: They are the same drug: crack is the form that can be smoked, and powder can't be smoked.

cocaine.statement: In a lab, people given cocaine felt less hot in a heated suit, even though their bodies warmed up more.
cocaine.why: They began to sweat later and warmed up more than after a comparison drug, yet felt less hot. Only 7 people, at rest.

cocaine.statement: People who use cocaine almost daily will always choose cocaine over any other reward.
cocaine.why: In a lab, six people who smoked cocaine almost daily picked a $5 voucher over real cocaine about 1 time in 3 or 4.

cocaine.statement: In four groups who used cocaine, 4 to 8 times as many died as others of the same age and sex.
cocaine.why: Yes, 4 to 8 times. But all groups injected, smoked crack daily, were in treatment or arrested; many also used heroin.

cocaine.statement: In 5 studies, people who had stopped cocaine for more than about 5 months still scored clearly lower on memory tests.
cocaine.why: Their scores were close to the comparison groups. But these were other people, not the same people tested again.

cocaine.statement: Research shows crack cocaine itself directly causes the infections and violence linked to it.
cocaine.why: The authors of a review of 302 studies say crack is not a likely direct cause of these.

cocaine.statement: None of 40 recent brain-scan studies of cocaine left out people who drink or use cannabis.
cocaine.why: Two studies left out only people who had used cannabis recently. So these scans may mix up the effects of different drugs.

cocaine.statement: Studies cited in a review say symptoms such as paranoia with cocaine usually pass after stopping.
cocaine.why: Usually yes, but they can get worse with more use and last for weeks; most people studied were in treatment.

cocaine.statement: Around 2010, most cocaine tested by US drug police contained an animal worm medicine.
cocaine.why: About 7 in 10 samples held levamisole. Case reports link it to blood and skin harm; how often it harms is unknown.

cocaine.statement: The warning against beta-blockers after cocaine is based on big trials.
cocaine.why: It rests mainly on small lab studies, animal tests and expert opinion. No trial has tested beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine.

cocaine.statement: In US hospitals, most people with chest pain after cocaine were having a heart attack.
cocaine.why: About 1 to 6 in 100 were, in 1990s studies whose blood tests could miss small heart attacks.

cocaine.statement: In one US study, most one-dollar bills had traces of cocaine.
cocaine.why: About 9 in 10 did, typically a little over a millionth of a gram. But it was 50 bills collected by 2000.

cocaine.statement: Levamisole, an animal worm medicine often found in cocaine around 2010, has been linked to blood and skin harm.
cocaine.why: Case reports describe infection-fighting white blood cells falling very low, and painful purple skin patches, sometimes with dying skin. But since most cocaine held it, finding it shows exposure, not that it caused the harm, and how often harm happens is unknown.

cocaine.statement: After cocaine, a beta-blocker improves blood flow to the heart.
cocaine.why: In a lab test of 10 heart patients given cocaine, blood flow in the heart fell further in all 10 after the beta-blocker propranolol. None had used cocaine before, and what this means for heart attacks is unknown.

cocaine.statement: Most people in treatment for cocaine say they've had paranoia or similar symptoms with it.
cocaine.why: In a review of 17 studies, 68 in 100 said so, while strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100. Many also used alcohol or other drugs, so the review can't show cocaine alone caused it.

cocaine.statement: Most people who start using cocaine are hooked within a year.
cocaine.why: In US surveys, about 5 in 100 people who had used only powder were dependent within a year of starting, and about 22 in 100 of those who went on to crack. People answered once, so the surveys can't show crack itself made the difference.

heroin.statement: In one study, fentanyl withdrawal got worse over the first days before easing, unlike heroin-type withdrawal.
heroin.why: The other group's withdrawal eased from the start, but the two groups were studied ten years apart.

heroin.statement: In Maryland, death certificates named heroin in almost every death a fuller review linked to heroin.
heroin.why: They named it in only about 52 in 100. Each review used its own rules for what counts as a heroin death.

heroin.statement: Some people who took very large amounts of loperamide (Imodium) got serious heart-rhythm problems.
heroin.why: Some needed a breathing tube or a pacemaker. Poisons doctors tend to see sicker cases, so the study cannot show how often this happens.

heroin.statement: Slowly cutting down methadone took away all the aches, bad sleep and worry of withdrawal.
heroin.why: Neither way seemed to remove all of these symptoms, whether methadone or clonidine-type medicines.

heroin.statement: Buprenorphine helped far more people finish withdrawal treatment than slowly cutting down methadone.
heroin.why: They worked about the same: about 55 in 100 finished on buprenorphine and about 53 in 100 on methadone, in six small trials.

heroin.statement: Long-term opioid use is linked with pauses in breathing during sleep.
heroin.why: Many people on methadone also sleep badly. This comes second-hand from a review that did not check study quality.

heroin.statement: Heroin overdose deaths are almost always instant.
heroin.why: Many deaths took hours, and other people were often present, in older studies relayed by a review.

heroin.statement: In British Columbia in 2016 and 2017, about 7 in 10 people who died of a drug overdose were using alone.
heroin.why: Coroners' reports, cited by a survey, found this. On its own, it cannot show whether using alone changes overdose risk.

heroin.statement: When 96 in 100 people given naloxone for an opioid overdose survive, naloxone saved 96 lives in 100.
heroin.why: False. Most opioid overdoses don't end in death, so survival can't count lives saved.

heroin.statement: A study proved that Vancouver's site for injecting heroin and other drugs cut overdose deaths nearby.
heroin.why: Not proven: deaths nearby fell more than elsewhere, but nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.

heroin.statement: Overdoses were already falling years before Vancouver's injection site opened.
heroin.why: In the two papers critics cited, overdoses fell from the late 1990s on, and the site opened in 2003.

heroin.statement: More people finish opioid withdrawal treatment on buprenorphine than on clonidine or lofexidine.
heroin.why: In 14 trials, about 72 in 100 finished on buprenorphine, against about 45 on the other medicines, and withdrawal was milder on average. No trial reported people coming off fentanyl.

heroin.statement: Eating poppy seeds can make you fail a sports drug test.
heroin.why: In a German study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake went over the sports limit of the time for morphine in their urine. But the cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested, and workplace tests weren't studied.

heroin.statement: Few people who go to harm reduction sites use drugs alone.
heroin.why: In a survey at 27 sites in British Columbia, about 3 in 4 had used alone at least once in the past week, most often because it was easier and more comfortable at home. It's one survey, of people already going to these sites.

heroin.statement: Clonidine and lofexidine barely help with heroin withdrawal.
heroin.why: In three trials, about 19 in 100 on them had bad withdrawal, against about 59 in 100 on a dummy pill, and more finished treatment. But the trials were small and old, and none included people coming off fentanyl.

heroin.statement: A death record can say morphine even when the person took heroin.
heroin.why: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine, and some death records named morphine or mixed drugs instead. In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than the records did.

methylphenidate.statement: Studies prove children's sleep gets better the longer they take ADHD stimulants like methylphenidate.
methylphenidate.why: Not proven: in studies of longer use, the effect on the share of time in bed spent asleep only looked smaller.

methylphenidate.statement: Pills like Adderall give healthy people a big boost on thinking tests.
methylphenidate.why: Across 48 studies of a single pill of amphetamine or methylphenidate, the average lift was small, clearest for holding back an automatic response. Daily use, studying and exams weren't tested.

methylphenidate.statement: Children on the ADHD medicine methylphenidate had trouble falling asleep far more often than on a dummy pill.
methylphenidate.why: Across 35 trials, it was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine, though who recorded it changed how big the gap looked. A drug company paid for the review.

ghb-gbl.statement: In a lab driving test soon after GHB, every person who finished crashed more than after a dummy drink.
ghb-gbl.why: In this lab driving-machine study of 16 adults, four threw up and could not finish; all the rest crashed more.

ghb-gbl.statement: Passing out from GHB again and again has been linked to worse memory.
ghb-gbl.why: In one Dutch study, people who had passed out many times remembered worse than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs. It can't show GHB caused it, and nobody checked whether memory improves.

psilocybin.statement: In studies that looked for problems after psychedelics like psilocybin or LSD, severe anxiety was the most common.
psilocybin.why: Headaches were the most common; one person had a severe worsening of anxiety. Most studies were in labs or ceremonies with support.

psilocybin.statement: In lab studies, about 1 in 11 volunteers reported a short flashback after LSD or psilocybin.
psilocybin.why: Of 142 healthy lab volunteers, 13 said they had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.

psilocybin.statement: In one psilocybin clinic study, about half of 19 patients said the music sometimes made things harder.
psilocybin.why: Almost all also said it helped at times. They were patients with hard-to-treat depression, in one small study.

psilocybin.statement: In surveys, feeling safe and supported on a psychedelic trip went with far fewer difficult moments.
psilocybin.why: It went with fewer difficult moments, but only by small amounts, rated looking back. No study we read put people in different places on purpose.

psilocybin.statement: In surveys, people who felt calm, open and ready the day before a psychedelic trip said it was less hard.
psilocybin.why: Surveys of about 200 people planning their own trip found this link; no study we read changed how people felt beforehand to test it.

psilocybin.statement: In a US trial, one psilocybin session with therapists lowered depression scores more than a vitamin pill did.
psilocybin.why: Over 6 weeks, in 104 adults. But people could probably tell they had psilocybin, and nobody checked.

psilocybin.statement: In a trial of 59 people, psilocybin clearly beat the antidepressant escitalopram on the main depression score.
psilocybin.why: No clear difference after 6 weeks (8 against 6 points), and the trial was too small to show psilocybin and escitalopram work equally well.

psilocybin.statement: In a lab psilocybin study, fewer than 1 in 20 volunteers felt strong fear.
psilocybin.why: 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point.

psilocybin.statement: In a psilocybin trial for drinking problems, heavy drinking more than halved before anyone was given psilocybin.
psilocybin.why: It more than halved in both groups during 4 weeks of talk therapy. Later, psilocybin was linked to fewer heavy-drinking days than a comparison pill.

psilocybin.statement: In a US survey, people who used LSD or mushrooms still had more mental health problems once other differences were counted.
psilocybin.why: Before counting, problems were about 2 to 3 times as common; after counting other drugs, risk-taking and stressful events, none of 20 was higher.

psilocybin.statement: In a Johns Hopkins psilocybin study, fewer than 5 in 100 volunteers felt strong fear.
psilocybin.why: No: 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.

psilocybin.statement: Six months after a trial, the psilocybin group was clearly less depressed than the group on the antidepressant escitalopram.
psilocybin.why: No clear difference: six months on, 37 in 100 on psilocybin and 34 on escitalopram were nearly free of symptoms, in one small trial.

psilocybin.statement: In a US trial, people got one psilocybin session or a vitamin pill. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin.
psilocybin.why: Over 6 weeks, in 104 adults. But people could probably tell they had psilocybin, and nobody checked.

psilocybin.statement: In a trial with dummy capsules, microdosing magic mushrooms made people more creative.
psilocybin.why: Creativity tests showed no real gain in the week people took magic mushroom capsules, though they did feel something on the day.

psilocybin.statement: In trials with dummy capsules, microdosing magic mushrooms or LSD made people's mood better than the dummies did.
psilocybin.why: Mood was not clearly better than with dummies, though people could feel a microdose on the day. Only one small trial used just magic mushrooms.

psilocybin.statement: Most volunteers in one lab study ranked a single psilocybin session among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
psilocybin.why: Two months later, 67 in 100 did. But everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.

psilocybin.statement: In a big trial for hard-to-treat depression, psilocybin's benefit was still clear after 12 weeks.
psilocybin.why: By 12 weeks, the gap between the full dose and a tiny dose could be chance, though the full dose did better at 3 weeks. Everyone in that trial of 233 adults got some psilocybin, so it compared doses.

psilocybin.statement: Lots of people who take magic mushrooms end up seeking emergency treatment.
psilocybin.why: In one big online survey, about 2 in 1,000 people who'd used them in the past year said they had, and nearly all of those felt back to normal within a day. But nobody checked their answers, and anyone who couldn't answer wasn't counted.

psilocybin.statement: Bad trips are fairly common among people who've used psychedelics.
psilocybin.why: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip, and 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life. That's one online survey of US adults looking back over their whole lives.

psilocybin.statement: Psilocybin has been shown to help people quit smoking.
psilocybin.why: In one small study, 12 of just 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later. With no comparison group, no one can tell what psilocybin added.

psilocybin.statement: People who microdose can't tell a real microdose from a dummy capsule.
psilocybin.why: In trials, people guessed right about 7 times in 10, and their ratings followed what they believed they'd taken. Feeling an effect may have shaped that belief.

psilocybin.statement: A psychedelic flashback means reliving the whole trip for hours.
psilocybin.why: In Swiss lab studies of LSD and psilocybin, a flashback was usually a few seconds of changed seeing, mostly in the days after, and most people didn't mind it. These were healthy, screened volunteers, with no drug-free group to compare.

alkyl-nitrites-and-inhalants.statement: Eye problems after poppers have only been reported after years of heavy use.
alkyl-nitrites-and-inhalants.why: Reports from at least 12 countries include some people affected after using poppers once, though such reports cannot prove poppers were the cause.

alkyl-nitrites-and-inhalants.statement: Scans of people with vision problems after poppers mostly showed damaged light-sensing cells at the back of the eye.
alkyl-nitrites-and-inhalants.why: People described blurry or dim vision in the middle; of those scanned again, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing. These are reports of about 113 people, so they can't prove poppers caused it or show how often it happens.

benzodiazepines.statement: A benzodiazepine sleeping pill at bedtime can't affect your driving the next day.
benzodiazepines.why: Some made people drive worse the next day than dummy pills did. Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers.

benzodiazepines.statement: With one benzodiazepine sleeping pill, flurazepam, next-day driving got slightly worse over a week of nightly use, not better.
benzodiazepines.why: Most pills' morning effect seemed to shrink over several nights, but not flurazepam's. Studies were small; none followed people beyond about two weeks.

benzodiazepines.statement: In studies, older people taking sleeping pills had more falls than those not taking them.
benzodiazepines.why: These studies watched what happened, so they cannot prove the pills caused the falls.

benzodiazepines.statement: Studies have shown that benzodiazepines cause dementia.
benzodiazepines.why: Not shown. Quebec records linked long use to Alzheimer's; a Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.

benzodiazepines.statement: Taking benzodiazepines for a long time has been shown to cause dementia.
benzodiazepines.why: Not shown: neither of two studies could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions. Quebec records linked long use to Alzheimer's, but a Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.

benzodiazepines.statement: The day after some benzo sleeping pills, people drove worse than with alcohol at a common drink-driving limit.
benzodiazepines.why: In tests in a real car or a driving machine, weaving inside the lane was worse with some pills than with alcohol at the limit used in several countries. Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers, not people who take these pills for months.

caffeine.statement: In one small trial, caffeine pills around surgery meant fewer headaches afterwards for people who usually had lots of caffeine.
caffeine.why: Fewer got headaches after surgery on caffeine pills than on dummy pills. Too small a trial to show the pills are safe for everyone.

caffeine.statement: Caffeine added time awake in the night, yet in five studies people did not report more time awake.
caffeine.why: Across 24 studies, caffeine made falling asleep slower and time awake longer; in five, people did not report more time awake.

caffeine.statement: In a 3-day test, men who drink coffee daily peed much more on coffee days than on water days.
