caffeine.why: They peed about the same: 2.41 litres a day on coffee days, 2.43 on water days. One test, 50 men used to coffee.

caffeine.statement: In a lab study, caffeine made people who have it often more alert than people who rarely have it.
caffeine.why: Caffeine only brought them up to the alertness of people who rarely have it. One study; people chose their own habits.

caffeine.statement: In studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often.
caffeine.why: True, but only a link: studies of genes found no sign that coffee itself lowers the risk of dying.

caffeine.statement: In one study, caffeine made people who often have it more alert than people who rarely do.
caffeine.why: Caffeine only brought them up to the alertness of people who rarely have it. One study; people chose their own habits.

caffeine.statement: Caffeine makes people who rarely have it more alert.
caffeine.why: In one lab study, caffeine made them faster but raised their jitters, not their alertness. It's one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits.

caffeine.statement: Caffeine can set off panic attacks in people with panic disorder.
caffeine.why: In 10 small lab studies, 121 of 237 people with panic disorder had a panic attack after caffeine, and none were reported after a dummy. What ordinary, smaller servings do isn't known.

caffeine.statement: Caffeine doesn't really change how much you sleep that night.
caffeine.why: Across 24 studies comparing nights with and without caffeine in the same people, they slept about 45 minutes less after caffeine, and their sleep was lighter. These were healthy adults with low to moderate usual intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.

caffeine.statement: Drinking coffee raises your risk of lung cancer.
caffeine.why: A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked: people who smoke tend to drink more coffee. These studies only watched people.

caffeine.statement: Headaches from skipping caffeine come from expecting them, not from the missing caffeine.
caffeine.why: Off their usual caffeine before a small operation, 10 of 20 people on dummy pills had a headache by evening and none of 20 on caffeine pills did, and neither they nor the doctor checking knew who got which. Only 40 patients took part, though, and surgery can also cause headaches.

lsd.statement: In lab studies, people who felt anxious just before taking LSD had more anxiety during the session.
lsd.why: This held in 213 healthy adults in a hospital room; the paper gives the link's direction, not its size.

lsd.statement: Studies of people given pure LSD found clearly more broken chromosomes.
lsd.why: In studies from 1967 to 1970, microscope tests found no clear rise. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.

lsd.statement: The early studies that linked LSD to broken chromosomes ruled out other drugs.
lsd.why: They did not. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks as people who had taken LSD.

lsd.statement: The LSD chromosome scare began with LSD added to blood cells in a lab dish.
lsd.why: The cells came from just two people, plus a patient with no 'before' test; studies up to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. But those were small and looked only at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs.

lsd.statement: In one big survey, people sought emergency treatment more often after LSD than after magic mushrooms.
lsd.why: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year said they had, mostly for panic, anxiety or confusion, against 2 in 1,000 after magic mushrooms. Nobody checked the answers, or whether the drug was really LSD.

lsd.statement: In a lab study, people's thinking was clearly worse the day after LSD.
lsd.why: In 24 people, a few memory and word tests went a little better the next morning and one rule-switching puzzle a little worse, which may just be chance. The report gave no mood or sleep data.

pcp.statement: In one reported case, a man in a long breakdown after drugs thought to contain PCP calmed in a dim, quiet room.
pcp.why: He calmed when put in a dim, quiet room; medicines for psychosis did not visibly help two of the men. Only three cases.

pcp.statement: A bad reaction to PCP always wears off within about a day.
pcp.why: In three cases reported in 1975, a severe breakdown after drugs thought to contain PCP lasted two to four weeks, then passed. Only three cases, and nobody tested the drugs they'd taken.

cannabis.statement: Soon after THC, the main active part of cannabis, people did just as well on lab driving tests as after a dummy.
cannabis.why: In 80 pooled lab studies, people weaved more in their lane and reacted more slowly than after a dummy.

cannabis.statement: Sleep-lab studies found cannabis taken by mouth helps people fall asleep faster.
cannabis.why: Time to fall asleep did not change compared with a dummy pill. Most tested CBD or mild THC medicines; smoking was not tested.

cannabis.statement: Regular cannabis use can come with bouts of severe vomiting that ended when people stopped, in most reported cases.
cannabis.why: Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better. Nobody knows how common it is.

cannabis.statement: CBD reliably weakens the high from THC, the main active part of cannabis.
cannabis.why: In most of 16 lab studies, adding CBD made no clear difference to feeling high. Most were small.

cannabis.statement: You can't become dependent on cannabis, even if you use it every day.
cannabis.why: Reviews give figures from about 1 in 5 to 1 in 2 for people who use daily, though none can show what causes what.

cannabis.statement: Gene studies found that genes linked to schizophrenia go with trying cannabis.
cannabis.why: Evidence the other way round was weaker, and these studies looked only at ever trying cannabis, not daily use.

cannabis.statement: In twin studies of mostly light teen use, the twin who used cannabis lost clearly more IQ than the other.
cannabis.why: No clear extra loss, though these studies could miss a small one. One study found about 6 points lost after years of dependence.

cannabis.statement: In published cases of repeated vomiting with regular cannabis use, most people found hot baths or showers eased it for a while.
cannabis.why: Most of the 211 people in published cases found this. But many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.

cannabis.statement: Trials show cannabis medicines help with anxiety and depression.
cannabis.why: Not shown: in the review we read, anxiety had only one or two small trials, and no trial treated depression.

cannabis.statement: A review says UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s, while first hospital stays for schizophrenia did not rise.
cannabis.why: In south-east London and Zurich, psychosis became more common in people born more recently; changes in diagnosis can blur trends.

cannabis.statement: There is no such thing as cannabis withdrawal.
cannabis.why: In general surveys, about 17 in 100 people who used regularly had it, such as irritability, poor sleep and low mood.

cannabis.statement: No death has ever been linked to recent cannabis use.
cannabis.why: A review collected 13 deaths linked to recent use, but 8 had significant heart disease or other illness, so cause is not settled.

cannabis.statement: In two studies linking strong cannabis to psychosis, researchers tested the cannabis people had used.
cannabis.why: Nobody tested it: people named the type they had used after becoming ill, and strength came from police, European and national figures.

cannabis.statement: Trials show that CBD oil from a shop cuts seizures in children with a severe epilepsy.
cannabis.why: Not shown: the trials tested a drug company's CBD medicine. CBD products from shops were not tested.

cannabis.statement: Most men who used cannabis heavily never went to hospital with schizophrenia, in a big Swedish study.
cannabis.why: About 38 in 1,000 men who'd used it more than 50 times later did, against about 6 in 1,000 who had never used it. These counts don't allow for other differences between the men.

cannabis.statement: Teen cannabis use has been shown to lower IQ later in life.
cannabis.why: Not shown either way: in one New Zealand study, people dependent on cannabis for years lost about 6 IQ points, but other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of mostly lighter teenage use found no clear extra loss, though they could miss a small one.

cannabis.statement: In one study, people off heavy cannabis use for a year or more scored like people who hadn't used.
cannabis.why: They scored no differently on any test, and a big review found smaller gaps in studies that asked people to stop for over 3 days. But few studies have followed people that long, and researchers disagree.

cannabis.statement: Stopping regular cannabis use can mess with your sleep and bring strange dreams.
cannabis.why: Between about a third and three quarters of people with withdrawal symptoms had sleep problems, often with strange dreams for days or weeks, and in the lab they took longer to fall asleep. That's second-hand, from a review that didn't check how good the studies were.

cannabis.statement: Teen cannabis use went up after US states made recreational cannabis legal.
cannabis.why: Not in one big study of 1.4 million US high school answers: after recreational laws, teens were a bit less likely to say they'd used it in the past month. But only 7 states had surveys from before and after, and only for the first few years.

cannabis.statement: Cannabis medicines have hardly any side effects.
cannabis.why: In trials, about 81 in 100 people on cannabis medicines had at least one, such as dizziness or dry mouth, against 62 in 100 on a dummy or another medicine, and more quit because of them. The trials were short, and long-term harms weren't studied.

cannabis.statement: Weed really is stronger than it used to be, on average.
cannabis.why: Across 7 countries from 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash. But most samples were seized by police, so they may not match what people buy.

cannabis.statement: On average, people who often use cannabis score a little lower on memory tests.
cannabis.why: A big review found small gaps in learning, memory, attention and planning, but none clear for language, shape or movement. People were tested only after they'd started, so it can't show cannabis caused the gap.

cannabis.statement: In small trials, cannabis medicines controlled sickness from chemotherapy better than a dummy did.
cannabis.why: About 47 in 100 on a cannabis medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on a dummy. But only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials in the review had serious weaknesses.

cannabis.statement: In one study, daily use of strong cannabis went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis.
cannabis.why: That's compared with never using, in 11 places in Europe and Brazil. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times, and the gap between strong and weaker could be chance.

cannabis.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than teens who don't.
cannabis.why: Combining three studies on thoughts and three on attempts, a review found about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and 3.5 times the odds of attempts in teens who used the most. That can't show cause: in other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were counted.

cannabis.statement: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in children with Dravet syndrome, a form of epilepsy.
cannabis.why: Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children on it, against 26 to 27 in 100 on a dummy liquid. But the maker ran both trials, in its own backup checks the result didn't always hold up, and shop CBD wasn't tested.

cannabis.statement: In sleep labs, people who stopped heavy cannabis use got more dream sleep in the first nights.
cannabis.why: They also slept less and took longer to fall asleep. That's from three small studies, two of them from the 1970s, and the data cover only the first week after stopping, so how long it lasts isn't known.

cannabis.statement: Other people's cannabis smoke can never make you fail a urine drug test.
cannabis.why: After an hour in a sealed, smoky room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over the US government's workplace limit, and 12 tested positive at least once at a lower limit some private tests use. That was one small lab test, mostly in thick smoke, not everyday smoke.

cannabis.statement: In older US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who ever tried cannabis became dependent.
cannabis.why: In the first survey, that was fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol. The surveys ran from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition; newer US figures that count milder cases are higher.

cannabis.statement: Cannabis medicines work much better than a dummy medicine for long-lasting pain.
cannabis.why: In combined trials, pain was only about half a point lower out of 10 than with a dummy medicine. The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.

cannabis.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis are a bit more likely to be depressed as young adults.
cannabis.why: Across seven long-term studies, teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. That's a link, not proof: other differences between the teens may explain it.

cannabis.statement: Babies whose mothers used cannabis in pregnancy went to newborn intensive care more often.
cannabis.why: Across 19 studies, mostly from before 2000, these babies were also about 109 grams lighter. But many mothers also smoked or drank, and most studies couldn't tell that apart from cannabis.

cannabis.statement: CBD products usually contain what their labels say.
cannabis.why: In a 2016 US test of 84 CBD products sold online, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label, and about 1 in 5 also held THC. Shop products, or today's, may differ.

synthetic-cannabinoids.statement: People who had used both said synthetic cannabis gave a slightly worse hangover than ordinary cannabis.
synthetic-cannabinoids.why: About a thousand people who had used both said synthetic cannabis made it harder to get on with things afterwards.

synthetic-cannabinoids.statement: People who've used both say synthetic cannabis is as enjoyable as ordinary cannabis.
synthetic-cannabinoids.why: In a 2011 online survey of about a thousand people who'd used both, they reported much less enjoyment, more bad feelings and more fear of others, and most preferred ordinary cannabis. Nobody tested the products.

drug-checking.statement: Large amounts of meth or MDMA can make a fentanyl strip show fentanyl when there is none.
drug-checking.why: In the lab, meth or MDMA turned strips positive only at thousands of times the smallest fentanyl amount detected.

drug-checking.statement: All fentanyl test strips work about the same, whatever the brand or batch.
drug-checking.why: In lab tests, one brand's 2021 batches needed ten times more fentanyl to show it than its 2017 batches.

drug-checking.statement: Nitazene test strips pick up every kind of nitazene.
drug-checking.why: In a lab they showed 24 of 33 nitazenes, missing 6 of the 7 desnitazenes. Only pure or nearly pure drugs were tested.

drug-checking.statement: Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, can also make xylazine test strips read positive.
drug-checking.why: In a lab, lidocaine also made xylazine strips read positive. Only one batch of strips was tested.

drug-checking.statement: A negative benzodiazepine test strip means a drug has no newer benzodiazepines in it.
drug-checking.why: At one drug-checking service, strips missed 9 of 24 samples with newer benzodiazepines, and showed only 8 of 16 with etizolam alone.

drug-checking.statement: At one drug-checking service, nobody who brought a sample with a newer benzodiazepine expected it to be there.
drug-checking.why: At one service, 24 of 159 lab-checked samples had a newer benzodiazepine, and most also had fentanyl.

drug-checking.statement: At a Vancouver supervised injection site offering a fentanyl check every visit, about 1 visit in 100 included one.
drug-checking.why: Strip use varied a lot between places, from 1 in 100 to 77 in 100, by people's reports or service records.

drug-checking.statement: Studies have compared people given fentanyl test strips with people not given them, to see what strips change.
drug-checking.why: No study has. What we know comes from what people said they did; nobody watched what they actually did.

drug-checking.statement: Most people throw their drugs away when a fentanyl test strip shows fentanyl.
drug-checking.why: Few do. At a supervised injection site, people said they would throw it away after only 11 in 100 checks showing fentanyl.

drug-checking.statement: In the one year-long study of fentanyl test strips, recent strip use rose between the start and the end.
drug-checking.why: Recent strip use fell by the end. More had ever tried a strip, among those who answered all three surveys. Many people left the study.

drug-checking.statement: At one English festival, drug-related hospital cases fell from 19 to 1 the year on-site testing began.
drug-checking.why: Drug cases went from 19 in 2015 to 1 in 2016, but other hospital admissions rose from 40 to 49, and no festival was compared.

drug-checking.statement: At first glance, people who used fentanyl test strips in the largest US study looked twice as likely to overdose.
drug-checking.why: They more often injected and used fentanyl. Once other differences were allowed for, overdose rates were not clearly different.

drug-checking.statement: Fentanyl test strips do not show other drugs, such as xylazine.
drug-checking.why: This is one of the strips' known limits, along with some people misreading them.

drug-checking.statement: In lab tests, one brand of fentanyl test strip read positive with large amounts of vitamin C alone.
drug-checking.why: The same brand never showed carfentanil. Brands and batches differed, and each difference comes from one or two lab studies.

drug-checking.statement: People who use fentanyl test strips have been shown to have fewer overdoses.
drug-checking.why: No one knows yet: one US study of 732 people found no clear difference over four weeks; it could not rule out fewer or more.

drug-checking.statement: With opioids, take-home fentanyl strips showed fentanyl about as often as staff tests on site.
drug-checking.why: In British Columbia, 90 in 100 take-home results on opioids showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site; with meth and cocaine, home strips showed it far more often, though the authors think most extra positives were false. The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.

drug-checking.statement: When testing at one festival showed a drug wasn't as sold, most people handed drugs over to be destroyed.
drug-checking.why: At an English festival, 30 of 45 people whose drug wasn't as sold handed drugs over, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched. That was one festival with chemists doing the testing, and people may have kept other drugs.

drug-checking.statement: Making fentanyl test strips legal has been shown to cut drug deaths.
drug-checking.why: After the laws, deaths ran about 7 in 100 below the expected trend, but the study didn't check whether more people used strips, and the drop came in each law's very first month. Other changes at the same time could explain it.

drug-checking.statement: Fentanyl test strips can miss some drugs related to fentanyl, like carfentanil.
drug-checking.why: In lab tests of 28 related drugs on four brands, three never showed up on any brand, and carfentanil showed only at high amounts. These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by lab staff.

drug-checking.statement: In lab tests, fentanyl test strips often missed fentanyl that was really there.
drug-checking.why: Strips showed fentanyl in 104 of 106 police-seized samples that had it. But trained lab staff did the tests, mostly with one brand, and testing at home wasn't studied.

drug-checking.statement: Colour test kits for MDMA are easy to read, even for first-timers.
drug-checking.why: In one small 2003 lab study, two people new to the kit made many mistakes: one missed both MDMA samples, and the other called four other drugs MDMA. Lab experts got MDMA right.

drug-checking.statement: A negative xylazine test strip means there's no xylazine.
drug-checking.why: With less xylazine than strips are made to find, only 6 of 28 samples read positive, against 37 of 38 with at least that much. That was one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment.

drug-checking.statement: If a colour test shows MDMA, the pill has nothing else in it.
drug-checking.why: In one small 2003 lab study, seven MDMA samples that also held another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine, gave the same colour as MDMA alone. A review adds that drugs close to MDMA, like MDA, give a similar colour.

ketamine.statement: Brain scans show that ketamine turns overall brain activity down.
ketamine.why: In scans, brain activity went up, not down, most of all at the front.

ketamine.statement: In a London study, people who used ketamine most days more often felt cut off from themselves in daily life.
ketamine.why: They also reported more unusual beliefs, mostly mild. Nobody was asked before they started, so the cause is not known.

ketamine.statement: In a Sydney study, most said they first took ketamine because friends did.
ketamine.why: 62 in 100 said they first took it for its effect; 25 in 100 because friends did.

ketamine.statement: In a London study, more people had taken ketamine at home than in clubs.
ketamine.why: 71 in 100 had taken it at home and 84 in 100 at a friend's house; 52 in 100 in clubs.

ketamine.statement: In ketamine lab studies, hallucinations mostly meant seeing things that were not there.
ketamine.why: In lab studies of healthy volunteers, what was scored as hallucinations was mostly real sights and sounds that seemed changed.

ketamine.statement: Given ketamine in one study, people with schizophrenia often described experiences that repeated their own illness.
ketamine.why: These included suspicion, delusions and hallucinations. Nine patients in hospital, one study, and staff chose the order of the days.

ketamine.statement: Six of the eleven authors of a big review of how ketamine works are named on a patent application for its breakdown products.
ketamine.why: The idea that those breakdown products help in depression comes mostly from mouse studies by the review's own authors.

ketamine.statement: A review of how ketamine works says nobody knows how much of it reaches the human brain.
ketamine.why: So a lot of what we know about how it works comes from animals and from cells in dishes.

ketamine.statement: In a big US trial, ketamine drips eased depression at least as much as ECT.
ketamine.why: 55 in 100 on ketamine and 41 in 100 on ECT said their depression halved. But in Swedish hospital patients, more got well on ECT.

ketamine.statement: Most of 60 studies of ketamine for depression checked the bladder.
ketamine.why: Only 5 of the 60 checked the bladder, and only 12 looked for side effects 2 weeks or more after the last dose.

ketamine.statement: In one survey of people who used ketamine, about 1 in 4 blamed it for urine problems.
ketamine.why: About 1 in 4 did, in an online survey. But nobody who didn't use ketamine was asked, so the survey can't show ketamine caused it.

ketamine.statement: In UK deaths linked to ketamine, other drugs were always found too.
ketamine.why: From 1993 to 2006, ketamine was the only drug found in 4 of 23 deaths. Finding it does not show it caused them.

ketamine.statement: Of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports used words most like accounts of near-death experiences.
ketamine.why: Narrowly ahead of Salvia and LSD. Only the words were compared, not the experiences themselves.

ketamine.statement: Two big trials comparing ketamine drips with ECT for depression came to the same answer.
ketamine.why: No: a US trial found ketamine at least as good; in Swedish hospital patients, 63 in 100 got well on ECT, against 46.

ketamine.statement: Esketamine nasal spray passed its main test in both of its big 4-week trials.
ketamine.why: Only one of the two passed. In both, depression scores fell about 3 to 4 points more out of 60 with esketamine.

ketamine.statement: People whose depression lifted on esketamine relapsed more often when switched to a dummy spray.
ketamine.why: Of those switched to a dummy spray, 45 in 100 relapsed, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine. The company behind it paid for the trials, and critics argue some relapses may be effects of stopping, which the trial couldn't tell apart.

ketamine.statement: People who've quit ketamine do worse on memory tests than people who don't use it.
ketamine.why: In one London team's study, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month did as well as people who don't use ketamine, and still did a year later. But most had used less than people who used most days, so this doesn't show stopping fixed anything.

ketamine.statement: In a big trial, ketamine treatment for depression caused more moderate or severe side effects than ECT.
ketamine.why: Within 3 weeks, 25 in 100 on ketamine had a moderate or severe side effect, against 32 in 100 on ECT. Across studies, headache and dizziness were most common, and most side effects soon passed.

ketamine.statement: One ketamine drip can lift depression within hours.
ketamine.why: A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. But for most the lift faded within weeks, and people can often tell they got ketamine, which may make it look bigger.

ketamine.statement: Ketamine drips for depression cause memory loss as often as ECT does.
ketamine.why: In a Swedish trial, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips. Everyone knew which treatment they got.

ketamine.statement: Music has been shown to make ketamine treatment for depression work better.
ketamine.why: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how well ketamine works. In a trial of 32 patients, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music, and the report gave no results on how sessions felt.

ketamine.statement: Ketamine trip reports read more like near-death accounts than those for any other drug.
ketamine.why: In one study, a computer compared the words in about 15,000 online reports on 165 drugs with 625 near-death accounts, and ketamine's came out closest, with salvia and LSD close behind. Only words were compared, though: nobody showed the experiences themselves feel alike.

ketamine.statement: Bladder problems linked to ketamine never ease, even after people stop using it.
ketamine.why: In one survey, 128 of 251 people who described how their symptoms changed said they eased after stopping. No study has compared people who stopped with people who kept using, though.

ketamine.statement: Ketamine's two mirror-image forms, S and R, have the same effects.
ketamine.why: In one study of ten healthy people, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self on the S form, while on the R form they described relaxation. Everyone could tell when they'd been given a drug, though.

general.statement: About 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths at one US autopsy centre had another cause, like a blood clot in the lungs.
general.why: Full autopsies and drug tests showed it; in some, no drug was found at all. Only two US places have been studied.

general.statement: Once a person has died, the level of a drug in their blood no longer changes.
general.why: Levels can rise or fall and differ between blood vessels, though these studies can't predict the change in one death.

general.statement: In some US states, coroners, who are often elected, need no medical training.
general.why: Medical examiners are usually appointed doctors. Where coroners work, death certificates more often named no drug, but switching to examiners showed no clear change.

general.statement: Studies show that starting to drink or use drugs young is what causes drug or drinking problems later.
general.why: Studies show a link but can't show starting young is the cause; much of the link runs in families.

general.statement: In a Swedish study, adoptive brothers and sisters, not related by birth, more often had drug problems when the adopted child did.
general.why: 6 in 100 did, against 3 in 100 when the child did not. The home a child grows up in is linked too.

general.statement: In studies of ecstasy, almost everyone also used cannabis.
general.why: 90 to 100 in 100 did, so a study of ecstasy may be measuring several drugs at once.

general.statement: In one large study, most alcohol or drug poisoning deaths after leaving prison came in the first 4 weeks.
general.why: 91 in 100 came more than 4 weeks after release, though poisoning was also the most common recorded cause in the first week.

general.statement: In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer counted as dependent three years later.
general.why: Some still had a few signs, and numbers depend on who is counted. Many who recovered from alcohol problems were never treated.

general.statement: The one study that watched real health care visits found worse care for patients with drug or alcohol problems.
general.why: It found better care for these patients, but it is one study from the 1980s; whether care is worse is not clear.

general.statement: In big US surveys, women who became dependent on alcohol got there faster than men did.
general.why: They got there about as fast as men. The idea that women get there faster came mostly from people in treatment.

general.statement: In the US, women with drug problems were much less likely than men to get treatment.
general.why: Reviews describe no difference: in 2015, about 10 in 100 women and 11 in 100 men who needed treatment got it.

general.statement: In one experiment, describing a person's trouble as 'drug use', not a 'health concern', made readers see them as more dangerous.
general.why: Readers also wanted more distance from the person. They rated made-up stories; no one checked how people are really treated.

general.statement: Most large studies found that women do worse than men once in treatment.
If a drug is found in someone's body after death, that shows the drug caused the death.
general.why: Finding a drug does not by itself show that it caused the death, and one death can be counted under several drugs.

general.statement: In an English autopsy study, MDMA levels in drug deaths overlapped with MDMA levels in deaths from injuries.
general.why: So a blood level cannot, on its own, show that a drug caused a death. An older review reports a similar overlap for morphine.

general.statement: A computer model gave cannabis no effect at all. Yet people in it still mostly used cannabis first.
general.why: Some people were likelier to use any drug and were offered cannabis first. So cannabis coming first does not prove it leads on.

general.statement: In the 1978 Rat Park study, rats living together refused morphine water.
general.why: They drank it, and when it was almost all they had, they drank more than rats kept alone. All of this was in rats.

general.statement: After Portugal stopped treating having any drug for your own use as a crime in 2001, drug use fell.
general.why: It rose slightly, from about 8 to 12 in 100 adults ever trying one. Treatment grew too, so the law's effect is unclear.

general.statement: Kids who had the original DARE classes went on to use less alcohol, tobacco and drugs than other kids.
general.why: Across 11 studies, they used them about as much as other kids. Only DARE before its 2001 rebuild was tested.

general.statement: The US government's anti-drug ads of 1999 to 2004 cut cannabis use among teens.
general.why: Teen cannabis use stayed flat (about 24 in 100 had ever used it), and teens who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.

general.statement: UK experts judged legal alcohol and tobacco less harmful than LSD and ecstasy.
general.why: The reverse: experts ranked alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy in 2007, and alcohol top overall in 2010. These are expert opinions, not measurements.

general.statement: In a UK expert ranking, alcohol came top mostly because of the harm it does to other people.
general.why: 46 of its 72 points were for harm to others. But the scores are one panel's views, and alcohol's score partly reflects how many people drink.

general.statement: In a UK expert ranking, alcohol scored worse than heroin or crack for the person using it.
general.why: False. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worse; alcohol came top overall mostly through harm to other people.

general.statement: Official records name the drug involved in nearly every overdose death.
general.why: In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 in 100 overdose deaths had only an 'unspecified drug' code. The gaps differ by place and rules, and most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths.

general.statement: Most US soldiers who were hooked on narcotics in Vietnam stayed hooked after coming home.
general.why: About 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics in Vietnam, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.

general.statement: At one US autopsy centre, deaths nobody thought were from drugs almost never turned out to be drug deaths.
general.why: Drug tests showed about 49 in 100 of the 237 deaths nobody thought were from drugs actually were, and about 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths had another cause. Only two US places have been studied, so others may differ.

general.statement: In one twin study, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants.
general.why: It was 48 in 100 against 26 in 100, in Australian twins who grew up together. That's a link, not proof cannabis led on: shared risks and access to other drugs could still explain it.

general.statement: Teens who remembered more of the US government's anti-drug ads were, if anything, more likely to try cannabis.
general.why: In a national survey, they were no less likely to start, fewer said they definitely wouldn't, and in one of three periods more ads went with more first use. The authors call that tentative, not definitive.

general.statement: Children adopted away from a birth parent with a drug problem still have drug problems more often.
general.why: In a Swedish study, about 9 in 100 of them had one on record, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.

general.statement: In most published 'excited delirium' deaths, force such as restraint was recorded.
general.why: Force, including sedation and electrical weapons as well as restraint, was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths among published cases. These were selected reports, so they can't tell how much restraint, drugs or the agitated state caused a death.

general.statement: Rat Park has been repeated, with the same result.
general.why: Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result. In the original studies, the two groups also drank from different machines, measured differently, and all of it was in rats.

general.statement: In a UK study, readers judged a man who died from drugs more harshly than a woman.
general.why: With story details picked at random, readers were also harsher when the story said heroin rather than ecstasy, or an older person with years of use. The differences were small to moderate, and readers answered straight after one made-up story.

general.statement: In a UK expert ranking of 20 drugs, tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose.
general.why: Lung cancer was counted elsewhere, and the authors agreed tobacco probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined. The scores are one panel's views, not measures.

general.statement: There's one agreed way to count a death as a drug death.
general.why: Lists use different rules, some counting drug poisoning as the main cause and others drugs found in tests. In Norway, only about 49 in 100 deaths were on both of two lists, and in Sweden fewer than half.

general.statement: The risk of dying is highest in the first week after leaving prison.
general.why: In death records of about 1.5 million people, days 2 to 7 after release carried about 1.5 to 2 times the risk of later weeks, and drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause. Tolerance was never measured, so the records can't say why.

general.statement: People who started using drugs at 13 or younger more often became dependent than later starters.
general.why: In a US survey of adults who'd used drugs at least 12 times, about 1 in 3 who started by 13 had been dependent, against about 1 in 7 who started at 21 or older. A big twin study found much of the link runs in families, so starting young isn't shown to be the cause.

synthetic-cathinones.statement: The two UK deaths most linked to mephedrone in online news were later found to be from alcohol and methadone.
synthetic-cathinones.why: One study, and the later test results are second-hand reports, not official records.

synthetic-cathinones.statement: Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths linked to it were in the news, one study found.
synthetic-cathinones.why: The author thinks the news raised interest, but search data cannot show the news made people use it.

synthetic-cathinones.statement: When deaths were blamed on mephedrone, tests always found the drug in the body.
synthetic-cathinones.why: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to it, and tests after death found none in 25. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one doesn't prove cause.

nicotine.statement: In older studies, headaches and sweating went up after people stopped smoking.
nicotine.why: Tiredness, headaches and sweating did not rise; feeling grumpy, anxious or restless did. This comes from one expert's summary of older studies.

nicotine.statement: The grumpiness and restlessness of quitting smoking usually last for months.
nicotine.why: Most of these feelings were strongest in the first week and gone within 2 to 4 weeks, though for some people they lasted longer or came back. That comes from one expert's summary of older studies.

dmt-ayahuasca.statement: In a survey of almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca, fasting went with less fear or fewer later problems.
dmt-ayahuasca.why: Fasting showed no link the study could detect. Nothing was measured before people drank, and all differences were small.

dmt-ayahuasca.statement: Only people on DMT describe meeting a kind being that gives them a message.
dmt-ayahuasca.why: Of 809 people who said they met 'God' without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind; 78 in 100 reported a message.

dmt-ayahuasca.statement: The more traditional the ayahuasca ceremony, the less fear people feel.
dmt-ayahuasca.why: In one big survey, more traditional practices went with a little more fear, and church hymns or sermons with less. The differences were small, and people rated everything looking back.

dmt-ayahuasca.statement: Fewer people call themselves atheists after a DMT 'being' encounter, and after drug-free 'God' encounters too.
dmt-ayahuasca.why: Among people who'd had such meetings, 28 in 100 recalled being atheists before a DMT encounter and 10 in 100 said they were now, and the share fell without drugs too. But they were recalling old beliefs years later.

amphetamine.statement: In one trial, healthy adults' test scores rose after taking Adderall.
amphetamine.why: They rose on none of 13 tests, though people rated the Adderall pill as more helpful than a dummy pill.

kratom.statement: In a 2017 kratom survey, about 4 in 10 people said they had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids.
kratom.why: 1,144 of 2,798 said so, and 849 reported 6 months or more off opioids. Nobody checked, and most were found through a pro-kratom group.

kratom.statement: In death records from 27 US states, most deaths where kratom was named as a cause had no other drug found.
kratom.why: Only 7 of 91 had kratom alone; other drugs turned up in the rest, and fentanyl was named as a cause in 51.

kratom.statement: Kratom shows up in a large share of US overdose deaths.
kratom.why: In 27 US states in 2016–17, kratom was found in 152 of 27,338 overdose deaths, about 6 in 1,000. Testing for kratom varied and wasn't recorded, so some deaths with it were probably missed.

nitrous-oxide.statement: In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used nitrous oxide (laughing gas) in the past year reported lasting numbness.
nitrous-oxide.why: 200 of 4,633 said so. But no doctor checked these answers and people chose to take part, so it can't show how common this is.

nitrous-oxide.statement: In doctors' reports of health problems after laughing gas, most people had numbness or tingling.
nitrous-oxide.why: Of 100 people in published reports, 80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Not all used it for fun: 25 had been given it in surgery.

fentanyl-and-analogues.statement: When two officers felt ill after powder hit their faces, the lab found fentanyl in the seized drugs.
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: It found no fentanyl or other opioid, though a field test said fentanyl.

fentanyl-and-analogues.statement: Before training, most Indiana officers surveyed thought touching fentanyl could make them overdose.
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: About 4 in 5 did. Right after training, far fewer did, but only 69 of 204 answered both times; nobody untrained was compared.

fentanyl-and-analogues.statement: Poison experts say fentanyl splashed into the eyes or mouth is no real risk.
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: They treat splashes into the eyes or mouth as a real risk, unlike a brief touch on the skin, which they call very unlikely to poison.

fentanyl-and-analogues.statement: Poison experts said a quick, accidental touch of fentanyl can easily make a police officer overdose.
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: They called it very unlikely, and no such overdose has been confirmed. But nobody has measured real touches, so it can't be ruled out.

fentanyl-and-analogues.statement: Most first responders in a New York survey said the news was their source on fentanyl.
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: Most named courses and training; about 1 in 7 named the news.

fentanyl-and-analogues.statement: Before a training, most first responders surveyed in Missouri thought touching fentanyl could make them overdose.
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: Only about 1 in 5 rejected the idea before; about 5 in 6 did right after. But nobody untrained was compared, and there was no later check.

fentanyl-and-analogues.statement: Police officers have had confirmed overdoses from just touching fentanyl.
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: None has been confirmed: a federal safety agency looked into cases where officers felt ill and found no signs of a serious overdose, though no officer had a test that finds fentanyl. Finding no proven case isn't proof it never happens.
